rewritten_html:
The Flynn Effect

Now that we understand how IQ scores are classified — and how meaningful a few points can be when someone's score falls near a diagnostic boundary — consider this unsettling reality: the very same person can obtain meaningfully different IQ scores depending on which edition of a test they take. Not because their intelligence changed, but because the yardstick shifted. This phenomenon has profound consequences in clinical practice, and understanding it is essential for any psychologist who interprets cognitive test results.

In the 1980s, political scientist James Flynn noticed something remarkable when he examined IQ test data spanning decades across dozens of countries. Generation after generation, people were scoring higher on intelligence tests — not by trivial amounts, but at a rate of roughly 3 points per decade. This steady, population-wide increase in IQ scores became known as the Flynn Effect (Flynn, 1984, 1987). The gains were not explained by changes in test content or administration procedures; they appeared to reflect genuine improvements in the kinds of abstract reasoning and problem-solving that IQ tests measure, likely driven by improvements in nutrition, education, environmental complexity, and familiarity with test-like thinking demands.

Why does this matter for practicing clinicians? Because intelligence tests must be periodically re-normed to keep the mean at 100. When a new edition of the WAIS or WISC is normed, the normative sample — drawn from the current population — performs better than the previous edition's sample did. As a result, the same level of raw performance that once earned a score of, say, 105 on an older edition may now earn only a 102 on the newer one. The bar, in effect, has been raised. This creates several key implications that every clinician and EPPP candidate should understand:

  • When a new edition of a test is normed, the normative sample performs better than the previous edition's sample, resulting in slightly lower scores on the new edition
  • Using an outdated test version can inflate IQ scores by approximately 3 points per decade since the norms were established
  • The Flynn Effect is larger for fluid intelligence measures (~5 points/decade) than for crystallized measures (~2 points/decade)
  • This has significant forensic implications, particularly in Atkins v. Virginia (2002) intellectual disability death penalty cases, where the version of the test used can affect whether an individual falls above or below the IQ 70 cutoff

The differential impact on fluid versus crystallized intelligence is particularly worth noting. Fluid intelligence — the capacity for novel reasoning and pattern recognition — has shown the steepest gains over time, climbing roughly 5 points per decade. Crystallized intelligence, which reflects accumulated knowledge and vocabulary, has risen more modestly at about 2 points per decade. This discrepancy means that the Flynn Effect is not uniform across subtests, and clinicians interpreting historical scores must consider which abilities were being measured and how much inflation to expect.

The forensic stakes of the Flynn Effect cannot be overstated. Following the U.S. Supreme Court's decision in Atkins v. Virginia (2002), individuals with intellectual disability cannot be sentenced to death. Because this determination often hinges on whether someone's IQ falls at or below 70, even a 3-point difference between test editions can literally be the difference between life and death. A psychologist who administers an outdated test — or who fails to account for the Flynn Effect when interpreting older scores — may produce results that misrepresent the examinee's true standing relative to current population norms.

EPPP Application: If a person was tested with the WAIS-III (normed in 1997) and obtained an FSIQ of 73, retesting with the WAIS-IV (normed in 2008) might yield an FSIQ of approximately 70 due to the Flynn Effect. This difference can have legal consequences in intellectual disability determinations.

Think of it this way: imagine you measured your height against a doorframe in 1997 and marked it at a certain point. If someone later replaced that doorframe with a taller one, your mark would appear lower — not because you shrank, but because the reference point changed. The Flynn Effect operates similarly. Clinicians must always check whether the test edition they are using — or interpreting results from — has current, appropriate norms, and they should be prepared to discuss the Flynn Effect whenever historical IQ scores are being used in high-stakes decisions.

section_html:
Commonly Tested EPPP Summary

Score conversions: z = (X-M)/SD. T = 10z + 50. IQ = 15z + 100. Scaled = 3z + 10. Know how to convert between all types.
Normal curve: 34-14-2 rule for percentage of scores in each SD band. 1 SD below mean ~ 16th percentile. 2 SDs below ~ 2nd percentile.
SEM: SEM = SD * sqrt(1 - reliability). Used to build confidence intervals. 95% CI = Score +/- 1.96 SEM.
RCI: (Score2 - Score1) / (SEM * sqrt(2)). If |RCI| > 1.96, change is reliable at p < .05.
Regression to the mean: Extreme scores become less extreme on retest. Estimated true score = M + r(X - M). More regression when reliability is lower.
Percentile ranks: Ordinal, not interval. Cannot be averaged. Compressed near the mean, spread at extremes.

References: Anastasi & Urbina (1997). Psychological Testing. Jacobson & Truax (1991). Reliable Change Index. Nunnally & Bernstein (1994). Psychometric Theory. Cohen & Swerdlik (2018). Psychological Testing and Assessment.
prev_last_paragraph: Sten scores (standard ten) have M = 5.5 and SD = 2, with a range of 1-10. Used by the 16PF and some other personality measures. Scores of 4-7 are average; 1-3 are low; 8-10 are high.
rewritten_html:
Commonly Tested EPPP Summary

Now that we have explored the full landscape of score types — from z-scores and T-scores to stanines, sten scores, and percentile ranks — it is time to consolidate the most critical formulas and principles into a single quick-reference summary. Think of this section as the material you would want on a single index card the night before your exam: the conversions, the rules of thumb, and the conceptual traps that appear repeatedly on the EPPP. Each box below distills a high-yield topic, but remember that genuine understanding — not rote memorization — is what allows you to handle novel question stems with confidence.

A useful mental exercise is to imagine a concrete case and walk it through every formula below. For instance, picture a client who earns a raw score of 78 on a measure with a mean of 60 and a standard deviation of 10. That single data point can be converted to a z-score, then to a T-score, then to an IQ-equivalent, and then located on the normal curve to determine its percentile rank. If you can trace that journey fluently, you have mastered the core quantitative reasoning the EPPP expects.

Score conversions: z = (X-M)/SD. T = 10z + 50. IQ = 15z + 100. Scaled = 3z + 10. Know how to convert between all types. The z-score is always the gateway: once you have it, every other standard score is simply a linear transformation. For example, a z of +1.0 becomes a T of 60, an IQ-deviation score of 115, and a scaled score of 13. Practicing this chain of conversions with different starting values is one of the most efficient ways to prepare for computational items on the exam.
Normal curve: 34-14-2 rule for percentage of scores in each SD band. 1 SD below mean ~ 16th percentile. 2 SDs below ~ 2nd percentile. Remember that approximately 68% of scores fall within ±1 SD of the mean, roughly 96% within ±2 SDs, and about 99.7% within ±3 SDs. This mental map lets you instantly translate any standard score into an approximate percentile rank — a skill tested in many EPPP items. For instance, a Wechsler IQ of 85 (one SD below the mean) corresponds to approximately the 16th percentile, while an IQ of 130 (two SDs above) corresponds to approximately the 98th percentile.
SEM: SEM = SD * sqrt(1 - reliability). Used to build confidence intervals. 95% CI = Score +/- 1.96 SEM. The standard error of measurement reminds us that every observed score contains measurement error. A test with SD = 15 and reliability of .91 has an SEM of 4.5; a 95% confidence interval around an observed score of 100 would therefore span from approximately 91 to 109. Notice that higher reliability shrinks the SEM and narrows the confidence band, giving you more precision in clinical decision-making.
RCI: (Score2 - Score1) / (SEM * sqrt(2)). If |RCI| > 1.96, change is reliable at p < .05. The Reliable Change Index is essential whenever you need to determine whether a client's score truly changed between two testing occasions — or whether the difference could be attributed to measurement error alone. For example, if a client's depression inventory score drops from 30 to 22 and the SEM is 3, the RCI = (22 − 30) / (3 × 1.414) = −8 / 4.24 = −1.89, which does not exceed the 1.96 threshold and therefore does not reach statistical significance at the .05 level.
Regression to the mean: Extreme scores become less extreme on retest. Estimated true score = M + r(X - M). More regression when reliability is lower. This principle is a frequent source of EPPP items because it is counterintuitive: a client who scores exceptionally high (or low) on an initial administration is statistically likely to score closer to the mean on retesting, even without any real change. With a reliability of .80 and an observed score of 130 (M = 100), the estimated true score would be 100 + .80(130 − 100) = 124 — a six-point regression toward the mean. The lower the reliability, the greater this pull.
Percentile ranks: Ordinal, not interval. Cannot be averaged. Compressed near the mean, spread at extremes. Because percentile ranks reflect the proportion of scores falling below a given point on a normal distribution, the distance between the 50th and 60th percentiles represents a much smaller difference in raw performance than the distance between the 90th and 99th percentiles. This non-linearity is why percentile ranks should never be subjected to arithmetic operations like averaging — a mistake that appears in several common EPPP distractors.

Taken together, these six high-yield topics form the quantitative backbone of score interpretation on the EPPP. Mastery means more than knowing the formulas — it means understanding when each concept applies clinically, recognizing the assumptions behind each calculation (especially normality of the score distribution), and being alert to common misinterpretations that the exam is designed to test. Revisiting these principles through practice problems that combine multiple concepts — for example, computing a confidence interval and then determining whether a retest score falls outside it — is the most effective path to exam readiness.

References: Anastasi & Urbina (1997). Psychological Testing. Jacobson & Truax (1991). Reliable Change Index. Nunnally & Bernstein (1994). Psychometric Theory. Cohen & Swerdlik (2018). Psychological Testing and Assessment.

Commonly Tested EPPP Summary

WAIS-IV: Ages 16-90. Four indices (VCI, PRI, WMI, PSI) + FSIQ. Subtest M = 10, SD = 3. Index/FSIQ M = 100, SD = 15. GAI = VCI + PRI (excludes working memory and speed).
WISC-V: Ages 6-16. Five indices (VCI, VSI, FRI, WMI, PSI). Separates Visual Spatial from Fluid Reasoning. Includes Picture Span for visual working memory.
SB5: Ages 2-85+. Five factors, each measured verbally and nonverbally. Uses routing procedure. Wider score range (40-160). Introduced the original IQ concept (ratio IQ, now replaced by deviation IQ).
Flynn Effect: ~3 IQ points per decade increase. Using outdated norms inflates scores. Forensically significant (Atkins v. Virginia). Larger for Gf than Gc.
Classic aging pattern: Gf and Gs decline with age; Gc remains stable or increases. On WAIS-IV: VCI preserved, PSI declines most.

References: Wechsler (2008). WAIS-IV Manual. Wechsler (2014). WISC-V Manual. Roid (2003). SB5 Manual. Flynn (1987). Massive IQ gains. McGrew (2009). CHC theory and the human cognitive abilities project.
prev_last_paragraph: The age-related decline in fluid intelligence is not simply a unitary phenomenon — research has identified processing speed and working memory as key mediating mechanisms. Salthouse's processing speed theory proposes that the slowing of basic cognitive operations with age creates a cascade effect: when mental processing takes longer, relevant information may decay before it can be utilized, and less information can be simultaneously activated. Similarly, age-related reductions in working memory capacity limit the ability to hold multiple elements in mind while reasoning through novel problems. Structural equation modeling studies have shown that when processing speed and working memory are statistically controlled, much of the age-related variance in Gf is accounted for. On the WAIS-IV, this is reflected in the observation that PSI and WMI scores show earlier and steeper declines than VCI, and that these declines closely track the trajectory of fluid reasoning losses across the lifespan.
rewritten_html:
Commonly Tested EPPP Summary

Now that we have explored the theoretical foundations, structural architecture, and clinical applications of the major intelligence tests, it is time to consolidate the high-yield facts that appear most frequently on the EPPP. Think of this section as your rapid-review anchor — the essential details about each instrument, distilled into the format most likely to match exam questions. Before diving into these summary boxes, remember that each fact listed here connects to deeper conceptual understanding covered in earlier sections. When you encounter a question about score metrics, age ranges, or index compositions, these reference points will serve as your mental scaffolding for quick, confident retrieval.

WAIS-IV: Ages 16-90. Four indices (VCI, PRI, WMI, PSI) + FSIQ. Subtest M = 10, SD = 3. Index/FSIQ M = 100, SD = 15. GAI = VCI + PRI (excludes working memory and speed).

The WAIS-IV is the most widely used adult intelligence measure, and its scoring architecture is one of the most commonly tested topics on the EPPP. A critical clinical detail: the General Ability Index (GAI) was developed specifically for situations in which working memory or processing speed deficits might unfairly depress a client's Full Scale IQ — for example, when evaluating an older adult with slowed processing who retains strong verbal and perceptual reasoning skills. Knowing when and why to report the GAI alongside the FSIQ is a hallmark of competent interpretive practice and a favorite exam scenario.

WISC-V: Ages 6-16. Five indices (VCI, VSI, FRI, WMI, PSI). Separates Visual Spatial from Fluid Reasoning. Includes Picture Span for visual working memory.

The WISC-V represents a significant structural evolution from its predecessor. By separating visual-spatial processing from fluid reasoning into distinct indices, the WISC-V aligns more closely with CHC theory and provides clinicians with more precise diagnostic information. For instance, a child struggling with mathematics may show intact visual-spatial skills (VSI) but weakened fluid reasoning (FRI), pointing toward a specific reasoning deficit rather than a broad nonverbal weakness. The addition of Picture Span to the Working Memory Index also acknowledges that working memory is not exclusively verbal — a distinction with real implications for identifying learning disabilities in children who perform differently across modalities.

SB5: Ages 2-85+. Five factors, each measured verbally and nonverbally. Uses routing procedure. Wider score range (40-160). Introduced the original IQ concept (ratio IQ, now replaced by deviation IQ).

The Stanford-Binet 5 holds a unique historical position as the instrument that gave us the very concept of the intelligence quotient. Its routing procedure — in which initial subtests determine the starting difficulty level for subsequent subtests — makes administration more efficient and less frustrating for examinees at the extremes of ability. The extended score range (40–160) compared to Wechsler instruments makes the SB5 particularly valuable when assessing individuals with intellectual disability or intellectual giftedness, where precise differentiation at the tails of the distribution is clinically and educationally essential.

Flynn Effect: ~3 IQ points per decade increase. Using outdated norms inflates scores. Forensically significant (Atkins v. Virginia). Larger for Gf than Gc.

The Flynn Effect is deceptively simple as a concept — population IQ scores rise roughly 3 points per decade — but its clinical and forensic implications are profound. Consider a capital case in which a defendant scored 72 on a Wechsler test normed 15 years earlier. Correcting for the Flynn Effect might place the true score closer to 67 or 68, potentially meeting the intellectual disability threshold that would render execution unconstitutional under Atkins v. Virginia. The EPPP frequently tests whether examinees understand that outdated norms inflate scores and that this inflation disproportionately affects fluid intelligence measures, since Gf gains are larger than Gc gains across generational cohorts.

Classic aging pattern: Gf and Gs decline with age; Gc remains stable or increases. On WAIS-IV: VCI preserved, PSI declines most.

The classic aging pattern is one of the most reliably tested findings in cognitive aging research and a perennial EPPP favorite. As discussed in the preceding section on age-related cognitive decline, this pattern reflects the divergence between crystallized abilities — vocabulary, general knowledge, and overlearned skills that accumulate across the lifespan — and fluid abilities that depend on processing speed and novel reasoning. On the WAIS-IV, this manifests as relatively preserved Verbal Comprehension Index scores with the steepest declines on the Processing Speed Index. Clinically, recognizing this pattern helps differentiate normal aging from neurodegenerative conditions: when crystallized abilities also decline significantly, pathological processes rather than normal senescence should be suspected.

References: Wechsler (2008). WAIS-IV Manual. Wechsler (2014). WISC-V Manual. Roid (2003). SB5 Manual. Flynn (1987). Massive IQ gains. McGrew (2009). CHC theory and the human cognitive abilities project.

Commonly Tested EPPP Topics

Construction method: Empirical criterion keying -- items selected based on ability to discriminate groups, not face validity or theory.
Validity scale summary: L = naive faking good. F = faking bad / random / severe pathology. K = sophisticated defensiveness. VRIN = random responding. TRIN = yea/nay-saying. Fp = distinguishes true pathology from overreporting.
Conversion V: 1-3/3-1 code type with Scale 2 depressed. Somatic complaints, denial of psychological distress, la belle indifference.
MMPI-2-RF key innovation: Removal of demoralization variance from clinical scales, creating purer RC scales with improved discriminant validity.
K-correction: Applied to MMPI-2 Scales 1, 4, 7, 8, 9. Eliminated in MMPI-2-RF and MMPI-3.

References: Butcher et al. (2001). MMPI-2 Manual. Ben-Porath & Tellegen (2008). MMPI-2-RF Manual. Ben-Porath & Tellegen (2020). MMPI-3 Manual. Graham (2012). MMPI-2: Assessing Personality and Psychopathology.
rewritten_html:
Commonly Tested EPPP Topics

Now that we have explored the major interpretation strategies used with the MMPI family of instruments, it is time to consolidate the high-yield facts that appear most frequently on the EPPP. Think of this section as a rapid-review guide — the concepts you want at your fingertips when you sit for the exam. Each topic below represents a point of emphasis that licensing boards have historically targeted, so understanding not just the "what" but the "why" behind each fact will give you a decisive edge.

The MMPI stands apart from most personality measures because of the way it was built. Rather than writing items that seemed logically related to a disorder (face validity) or deriving items from a theoretical model, the original test developers took a radically pragmatic approach: they kept only those items that actually differentiated clinical groups from non-clinical groups in real data. This bottom-up strategy is called empirical criterion keying, and it remains one of the most commonly tested facts about the MMPI on the EPPP. Understanding this construction method explains why some MMPI items seem unrelated to the scale they score on — their inclusion was never about apparent logic but about empirical power to discriminate.

Construction method: Empirical criterion keying -- items selected based on ability to discriminate groups, not face validity or theory.

A test is only as trustworthy as the respondent's engagement with it, which is why the MMPI validity scales are essential knowledge for every clinician — and every exam candidate. Imagine a personal-injury claimant who endorses an implausible number of bizarre symptoms, or a parent in a custody evaluation who presents an impossibly rosy self-portrait. The validity scales help you detect these response styles before you ever look at clinical elevations. Each scale captures a slightly different form of distortion: the L (Lie) scale picks up on unsophisticated, "too-good-to-be-true" self-presentation, while the K scale detects more polished defensiveness in test-savvy respondents. On the other end, the F scale flags profiles marked by overreporting — whether from genuine severe pathology, deliberate faking bad, or random responding — and Fp (F-Psychopathology) helps tease apart true psychopathology from exaggeration. Meanwhile, VRIN (Variable Response Inconsistency) catches random responding by pairing items that should be answered consistently, and TRIN (True Response Inconsistency) identifies fixed acquiescent ("yea-saying") or non-acquiescent ("nay-saying") patterns.

Validity scale summary: L = naive faking good. F = faking bad / random / severe pathology. K = sophisticated defensiveness. VRIN = random responding. TRIN = yea/nay-saying. Fp = distinguishes true pathology from overreporting.

One of the most classic and frequently tested code types is the Conversion V pattern. Picture a patient who presents with debilitating back pain, numbness in both hands, and chronic fatigue — yet when asked about emotional distress, she shrugs and says, "I'm fine psychologically. It's just my body." Her MMPI-2 profile shows elevations on Scale 1 (Hypochondriasis) and Scale 3 (Hysteria) with a notable dip on Scale 2 (Depression), creating a distinctive V-shaped pattern. This configuration is the hallmark of conversion or somatoform presentations: the individual channels psychological conflict into physical symptoms while maintaining a striking lack of concern — what early clinicians termed la belle indifférence. Recognizing the 1-3/3-1 code type and its clinical correlates is high-yield EPPP material.

Conversion V: 1-3/3-1 code type with Scale 2 depressed. Somatic complaints, denial of psychological distress, la belle indifference.

A persistent problem with the original MMPI-2 clinical scales was that they were heavily saturated with a general distress factor — demoralization — which made it difficult to distinguish one form of psychopathology from another. If nearly every clinical scale rose together because the client was broadly demoralized, the profile lost much of its diagnostic specificity. The MMPI-2-RF addressed this directly by statistically extracting demoralization variance and constructing the Restructured Clinical (RC) scales, each reflecting a more focused, substantive core of the construct it was meant to measure. This innovation dramatically improved discriminant validity, making the RC scales better at telling different conditions apart — exactly what clinicians need in differential diagnosis.

MMPI-2-RF key innovation: Removal of demoralization variance from clinical scales, creating purer RC scales with improved discriminant validity.

Finally, be sure you know which scales receive K-correction and where this correction has been eliminated. On the MMPI-2, a proportion of the K scale raw score is added to five clinical scales — Scales 1 (Hs), 4 (Pd), 7 (Pt), 8 (Sc), and 9 (Ma) — to adjust for defensiveness. A helpful mnemonic: think of the numbers 1, 4, 7, 8, 9 as "the K-corrected club." The rationale was that defensive respondents would suppress endorsement on these scales, so adding K points would restore a more accurate estimate of pathology. However, research questioned whether K-correction consistently improved prediction, and both the MMPI-2-RF and the MMPI-3 eliminated it entirely, relying instead on restructured scales and updated validity indicators to handle response style. Knowing that K-correction applies only to the MMPI-2 — and to which specific scales — is a detail the EPPP expects you to have mastered.

K-correction: Applied to MMPI-2 Scales 1, 4, 7, 8, 9. Eliminated in MMPI-2-RF and MMPI-3.

References: Butcher et al. (2001). MMPI-2 Manual. Ben-Porath & Tellegen (2008). MMPI-2-RF Manual. Ben-Porath & Tellegen (2020). MMPI-3 Manual. Graham (2012). MMPI-2: Assessing Personality and Psychopathology.

section_html:
Commonly Tested EPPP Summary

Fagan Test of Infant Intelligence (FTII)

The Fagan Test of Infant Intelligence is a measure designed for infants aged 3 to 12 months that assesses visual recognition memory by measuring preferential attention to novel versus previously seen stimuli. Developed by Joseph Fagan, the test is based on the observation that cognitively intact infants naturally look longer at unfamiliar images after being habituated to familiar ones.

During administration, infants are first shown a photograph of a face for a standardized exposure period, allowing them to encode and habituate to the stimulus. They are then presented with a paired display containing both the familiar face and a novel face. The key metric is novelty preference — the proportion of total looking time directed toward the new stimulus. Higher novelty preference scores indicate more efficient information processing and encoding, reflecting the infant's ability to form mental representations and discriminate between stored and new information.

Longitudinal research has demonstrated that selective attention to novelty during infancy is a meaningful predictor of later cognitive performance. Studies have confirmed that infants who show stronger preferences for novel stimuli tend to score higher on standardized IQ measures during childhood, adolescence, and into young adulthood. This finding is significant because traditional sensorimotor-based infant assessments (e.g., Bayley Scales) show poor predictive validity for later intelligence, whereas the FTII's information-processing approach captures a cognitive capacity — encoding efficiency — that has continuity with later intellectual functioning.

Clinical Note

The Fagan Test is particularly useful as a screening tool for cognitive risk because it does not depend on motor responses, making it appropriate for infants with physical disabilities. Reduced novelty preference may serve as an early indicator of intellectual disability or developmental delay, prompting referral for further evaluation and early intervention services.

NEO-PI-R: Big Five (OCEAN): Neuroticism, Extraversion, Openness, Agreeableness, Conscientiousness. 240 items, 30 facets. Normal-range personality, not pathology.
16PF: Cattell's factor-analytic test. 16 primary factors, 5 global factors. Uses sten scores (1-10). Primarily used in I/O and career settings.
MCMI-IV: Clinical populations only. Uses Base Rate scores (75 = present, 85 = prominent). Personality disorder + clinical syndrome scales. Tied to Millon's theory.
Rorschach: 10 inkblots. CS (Exner) and R-PAS scoring systems. Key variables: EB, Lambda, X-%, S-CON. R-PAS uses standardized response process and evidence-based variable selection.
TAT: Murray's need-press theory. 20 ambiguous scenes. No standard scoring system. McClelland's nAch and Westen's SCORS are best validated.
Projective drawings (DAP, HTP): Poor reliability and validity. Hypothesis-generating only. Should not be used for diagnosis in isolation.

References: Costa & McCrae (1992). NEO-PI-R Manual. Millon et al. (2015). MCMI-IV Manual. Exner (2003). The Rorschach: A Comprehensive System. Meyer et al. (2011). R-PAS Manual. Murray (1943). TAT Manual. Mihura et al. (2013). Meta-analysis of Rorschach validity.
prev_last_paragraph: Projective drawing techniques ask the examinee to draw specific subjects. Interpretation is based on features of the drawing (size, placement, detail, pressure, omissions). These techniques are among the most controversial in clinical assessment.
rewritten_html:
Commonly Tested EPPP Summary

Having explored projective drawing techniques and the controversies surrounding their interpretation, we now shift to a broader perspective — pulling together the key personality measures and assessment tools most frequently tested on the EPPP. This section serves as both a consolidation of what you've learned throughout this chapter and a quick-reference guide that highlights the essential facts, distinctions, and clinical nuances you'll need at exam time. We begin with a measure that may seem out of place in a personality chapter but appears regularly on the EPPP: an infant cognitive assessment with surprising predictive power.

Fagan Test of Infant Intelligence (FTII)

The Fagan Test of Infant Intelligence is a measure designed for infants aged 3 to 12 months that assesses visual recognition memory by measuring preferential attention to novel versus previously seen stimuli. Developed by Joseph Fagan, the test is based on the observation that cognitively intact infants naturally look longer at unfamiliar images after being habituated to familiar ones.

Imagine a six-month-old sitting on a caregiver's lap, gazing at a photograph of a face. After a brief exposure period — long enough for the infant to encode the image — the examiner presents two photographs side by side: the familiar face and a brand-new one. Where does the baby look? That simple behavioral choice turns out to be remarkably revealing. During administration, infants are first shown a photograph of a face for a standardized exposure period, allowing them to encode and habituate to the stimulus. They are then presented with a paired display containing both the familiar face and a novel face. The key metric is novelty preference — the proportion of total looking time directed toward the new stimulus. Higher novelty preference scores indicate more efficient information processing and encoding, reflecting the infant's ability to form mental representations and discriminate between stored and new information.

Why does this matter for clinical practice and the EPPP? Because longitudinal research has demonstrated that selective attention to novelty during infancy is a meaningful predictor of later cognitive performance. Studies have confirmed that infants who show stronger preferences for novel stimuli tend to score higher on standardized IQ measures during childhood, adolescence, and into young adulthood. This finding is significant because traditional sensorimotor-based infant assessments (e.g., the Bayley Scales) show notoriously poor predictive validity for later intelligence — a frustrating limitation that clinicians have grappled with for decades. The FTII's information-processing approach captures something different: encoding efficiency, a cognitive capacity that has genuine continuity with later intellectual functioning. For the EPPP, remember this key distinction: sensorimotor infant tests predict later IQ poorly, but the FTII's novelty preference paradigm predicts it meaningfully better.

Clinical Note

The Fagan Test is particularly useful as a screening tool for cognitive risk because it does not depend on motor responses, making it appropriate for infants with physical disabilities. Reduced novelty preference may serve as an early indicator of intellectual disability or developmental delay, prompting referral for further evaluation and early intervention services. This motor-free quality also makes it valuable for assessing infants with cerebral palsy or other conditions that would compromise performance on tasks requiring reaching, grasping, or manipulation.

Now let's turn to the personality measures themselves. The following summaries distill the most EPPP-relevant facts about each instrument. As you review them, pay special attention to what differentiates each measure: the population it was designed for, its scoring approach, its theoretical foundation, and its primary clinical use. These distinctions are precisely what the exam tests.

NEO-PI-R: Big Five (OCEAN): Neuroticism, Extraversion, Openness, Agreeableness, Conscientiousness. 240 items, 30 facets. Normal-range personality, not pathology.

The NEO-PI-R is the gold standard for assessing normal-range personality dimensions. Remember that it was developed by Costa and McCrae to measure the Big Five — not to diagnose psychopathology. Each of the five broad domains breaks down into six specific facets (yielding 30 facets total across 240 items), allowing for a nuanced personality profile. A critical EPPP distinction: if the question describes a non-clinical population and asks about normal personality traits, the NEO-PI-R is your answer. If the question involves clinical or pathological personality, look elsewhere.

16PF: Cattell's factor-analytic test. 16 primary factors, 5 global factors. Uses sten scores (1-10). Primarily used in I/O and career settings.

Raymond Cattell built the 16PF from the ground up using factor analysis, distilling thousands of personality descriptors into 16 primary source traits. Results are reported as sten scores — a standardized ten-point scale ranging from 1 to 10, with a mean of 5.5. On the EPPP, you should associate the 16PF with industrial/organizational and career counseling contexts rather than clinical diagnosis. If a question mentions sten scores or career-related personality assessment, think Cattell's 16PF.

MCMI-IV: Clinical populations only. Uses Base Rate scores (75 = present, 85 = prominent). Personality disorder + clinical syndrome scales. Tied to Millon's theory.

The MCMI-IV is Theodore Millon's instrument, and two facts about it appear on the EPPP with striking regularity. First, it is designed exclusively for clinical populations — administering it to non-clinical individuals is inappropriate and will yield misleading results. Second, it uses Base Rate (BR) scores rather than T-scores, calibrated to reflect the actual prevalence of disorders in clinical settings. A BR score of 75 suggests a trait or syndrome is present, while 85 indicates it is prominent. The entire instrument is anchored to Millon's evolutionary theory of personality, making it unique among personality inventories in its tight theoretical integration.

Rorschach: 10 inkblots. CS (Exner) and R-PAS scoring systems. Key variables: EB, Lambda, X-%, S-CON. R-PAS uses standardized response process and evidence-based variable selection.

The Rorschach Inkblot Test consists of 10 symmetrical inkblots and has been scored using two major systems: Exner's Comprehensive System (CS) and the newer Rorschach Performance Assessment System (R-PAS). For the EPPP, know these key variables: the Experience Balance (EB) compares human movement to weighted color responses, Lambda reflects psychological complexity versus simplification, X-% indexes distorted perception, and S-CON is a suicide constellation. R-PAS was developed to address criticisms of the Comprehensive System by using standardized administration (including an optimal response range), selecting variables based on empirical evidence, and providing international reference data.

TAT: Murray's need-press theory. 20 ambiguous scenes. No standard scoring system. McClelland's nAch and Westen's SCORS are best validated.

Henry Murray's Thematic Apperception Test asks examinees to tell stories about ambiguous scene cards, revealing underlying needs (internal motivations) and press (environmental forces). A frequent EPPP point: unlike the Rorschach, the TAT has no universally accepted standard scoring system. However, two research-validated approaches stand out — McClelland's system for scoring need for Achievement (nAch), and Westen's Social Cognition and Object Relations Scale (SCORS), which assesses the quality of mental representations of self and others.

Projective drawings (DAP, HTP): Poor reliability and validity. Hypothesis-generating only. Should not be used for diagnosis in isolation.

As discussed in the preceding section, projective drawing techniques such as the Draw-A-Person (DAP) and House-Tree-Person (HTP) remain among the most commonly used yet most poorly supported assessment tools in clinical practice. The research consensus is clear: these techniques demonstrate poor reliability and limited validity. They may serve a useful role as rapport builders or as hypothesis-generating tools early in an assessment, but they should never be used as the sole basis for diagnostic conclusions. On the EPPP, if a question asks about the psychometric standing of projective drawings, "poor reliability and validity" is almost always the correct answer.

References: Costa & McCrae (1992). NEO-PI-R Manual. Millon et al. (2015). MCMI-IV Manual. Exner (2003). The Rorschach: A Comprehensive System. Meyer et al. (2011). R-PAS Manual. Murray (1943). TAT Manual. Mihura et al. (2013). Meta-analysis of Rorschach validity.

section_html:
Generalized Anxiety Disorder (GAD)

Generalized Anxiety Disorder is characterized by persistent and excessive worry about a variety of domains, including work, health, family, finances, and everyday matters. The worry is difficult to control and is associated with at least three somatic or cognitive symptoms.

DSM-5 Diagnostic Criteria

  1. Criterion A: Excessive anxiety and worry occurring more days than not for at least 6 months, about a number of events or activities.
  2. Criterion B: The individual finds it difficult to control the worry.
  3. Criterion C: The anxiety and worry are associated with three or more of the following (only one required in children): restlessness or feeling keyed up, being easily fatigued, difficulty concentrating or mind going blank, irritability, muscle tension, sleep disturbance.
  4. Criterion D: The disturbance causes clinically significant distress or impairment.
  5. Criterion E: Not attributable to substances or another medical condition.
  6. Criterion F: Not better explained by another mental disorder.

Clinical Pearl

GAD has the highest comorbidity rate of any anxiety disorder. Approximately 90% of individuals with GAD have at least one comorbid disorder, most commonly MDD. The intolerance of uncertainty model (Dugas et al., 1998) posits that individuals with GAD have difficulty tolerating ambiguous situations, which fuels the worry cycle.

Epidemiology

Lifetime prevalence of GAD is approximately 5.7% in adults. Women are twice as likely as men to be diagnosed. GAD has a gradual onset, with a median age of onset of 30 years, which is later than most other anxiety disorders. It tends to follow a chronic, waxing-and-waning course.
prev_last_paragraph: Anxiety disorders differ from normal developmental anxiety by being excessive, persistent (typically lasting 6 months or more), and causing clinically significant distress or impairment. The DSM-5 reorganized the anxiety chapter by removing OCD and PTSD into their own chapters, though they share features with anxiety disorders.
rewritten_html:
Generalized Anxiety Disorder (GAD)

Imagine a client who sits in your office and tells you she worries about everything — her job performance, her children's safety, whether she paid a bill on time, whether a mole on her arm looks different than it did last week. She knows the worry is excessive. She tries to stop, but the thoughts just keep cycling. She hasn't slept well in months, her neck and shoulders are locked in a permanent knot of tension, and she snaps at her partner over trivial things. She can't point to a single triggering event or a specific feared object — the worry simply saturates every domain of her life. This pervasive, free-floating pattern of apprehension is the hallmark of Generalized Anxiety Disorder, a condition characterized by persistent and excessive worry across a variety of domains including work, health, family, finances, and everyday matters. Unlike the focused dread we see in phobias or the episodic surges of panic disorder, GAD spreads its anxious net wide — and the person finds it extraordinarily difficult to rein the worry in.

As we discussed in the overview, anxiety disorders share the core feature of excessive, persistent fear and anxiety that causes significant distress or impairment. GAD exemplifies that definition in its purest form: the worry itself becomes the central problem, and it drags along at least three somatic or cognitive symptoms that compound the individual's suffering. Understanding GAD well prepares you not only for exam questions but also for clinical practice, because this disorder shows up frequently — and rarely travels alone.

DSM-5 Diagnostic Criteria

The DSM-5 lays out a structured set of criteria that capture both the cognitive and physiological dimensions of GAD. Pay close attention to the temporal requirement and the specific symptom threshold, as these details commonly appear on licensing examinations.

  1. Criterion A: Excessive anxiety and worry occurring more days than not for at least 6 months, about a number of events or activities.
  2. Criterion B: The individual finds it difficult to control the worry.
  3. Criterion C: The anxiety and worry are associated with three or more of the following (only one required in children): restlessness or feeling keyed up, being easily fatigued, difficulty concentrating or mind going blank, irritability, muscle tension, sleep disturbance.
  4. Criterion D: The disturbance causes clinically significant distress or impairment.
  5. Criterion E: Not attributable to substances or another medical condition.
  6. Criterion F: Not better explained by another mental disorder.

A few clinical details deserve emphasis here. First, notice that Criterion A demands worry across multiple events or activities — a person who worries exclusively about contamination or social evaluation likely meets criteria for a different diagnosis. Second, the "three or more" somatic/cognitive symptom threshold in Criterion C drops to just one symptom for children, reflecting the developmental reality that younger individuals may not yet articulate or manifest the full adult symptom profile. Third, muscle tension stands out among the Criterion C symptoms as particularly characteristic of GAD; many clients present initially to primary care physicians with chronic neck pain, headaches, or jaw clenching before anyone identifies the underlying anxiety disorder.

Clinical Pearl

GAD has the highest comorbidity rate of any anxiety disorder. Approximately 90% of individuals with GAD have at least one comorbid disorder, most commonly MDD. The intolerance of uncertainty model (Dugas et al., 1998) posits that individuals with GAD have difficulty tolerating ambiguous situations, which fuels the worry cycle.

That staggering 90% comorbidity figure deserves a moment of reflection. In clinical practice, "pure" GAD — without depression, another anxiety disorder, or a substance use problem alongside it — is the exception rather than the rule. This means that when you identify GAD, your next step should always involve a thorough assessment for co-occurring conditions, especially major depressive disorder. The intolerance of uncertainty model offers a particularly useful clinical lens: picture a client who cannot leave any question unanswered, who Googles every minor health symptom at 2 a.m., and who demands reassurance from loved ones about outcomes no one can predict. That intolerance of "not knowing" drives a relentless search for certainty that, paradoxically, generates more worry rather than less. Therapeutic approaches informed by this model — such as those developed by Dugas and colleagues — help clients gradually increase their tolerance for ambiguity, often through behavioral experiments that expose them to deliberately uncertain situations.

Epidemiology

GAD affects approximately 5.7% of adults over their lifetime, making it one of the more common anxiety disorders encountered in both outpatient mental health and primary care settings. Women receive the diagnosis roughly twice as often as men, a gender disparity consistent with most anxiety disorders. Unlike many anxiety conditions that emerge in childhood or adolescence, GAD tends to develop gradually, with a median age of onset around 30 years — later than most other anxiety disorders. Clinicians should keep this timeline in mind: a 35-year-old presenting with a years-long pattern of diffuse worry fits the typical GAD profile, whereas the same presentation in a 12-year-old warrants careful differential diagnosis.

Once established, GAD typically follows a chronic, waxing-and-waning course. Clients often describe periods where the worry becomes more manageable — perhaps during a vacation or a stretch of relative stability — only to intensify again when new stressors emerge. This fluctuating trajectory can mislead both clients and clinicians into believing the problem has resolved, when in reality the underlying vulnerability persists. Recognizing this pattern helps set appropriate treatment expectations: the goal is not just symptom relief during a "good phase" but durable skills and, when indicated, sustained pharmacological support that prevents the next escalation.

section_html:
Obsessive-Compulsive Disorder (OCD)

OCD is characterized by the presence of obsessions, compulsions, or both. Although OCD was reclassified into its own chapter in DSM-5 (Obsessive-Compulsive and Related Disorders), it remains a commonly tested topic tested alongside anxiety disorders on the EPPP.

Obsessions vs. Compulsions

Obsessions are recurrent, persistent, intrusive, and unwanted thoughts, urges, or images that cause marked anxiety or distress. The individual attempts to ignore, suppress, or neutralize them. Compulsions are repetitive behaviors or mental acts that the individual feels driven to perform in response to an obsession or according to rigid rules. They are aimed at preventing or reducing anxiety or a dreaded event but are not realistically connected to what they are designed to neutralize.

Common OCD Symptom Dimensions

DimensionObsessionsCompulsions
ContaminationFear of germs, dirt, illnessExcessive washing, cleaning
SymmetryNeed for exactness, orderArranging, ordering, counting
Forbidden thoughtsAggressive, sexual, or religious intrusionsMental rituals, checking
HarmFear of causing harm to self/othersChecking locks, stoves, appliances
HoardingDistress at discarding itemsExcessive saving, acquiring

DSM-5 Specifiers

The DSM-5 includes an insight specifier for OCD: good or fair insight, poor insight, or absent insight/delusional beliefs. Approximately 4% of individuals with OCD have absent insight, meaning they are completely convinced their OCD beliefs are true.

The tic-related specifier applies when the individual has a current or past history of a tic disorder. Tic-related OCD has an earlier onset, more frequent male predominance, and higher rates of symmetry/ordering compulsions.

EPPP Example

Distinguishing OCD from OCPD: In OCD, obsessions are ego-dystonic (experienced as unwanted and distressing). In OCPD, the preoccupation with orderliness and perfectionism is ego-syntonic (consistent with the person's self-image). Individuals with OCPD rarely seek treatment for these traits because they see them as desirable.
prev_last_paragraph: Approximately one-third to one-half of individuals with panic disorder also develop agoraphobia. Notably, agoraphobia can occur without a history of panic disorder.
