rewritten_html:
Obsessive-Compulsive Disorder (OCD)

Having explored how panic disorder and agoraphobia can trap individuals in cycles of fear and avoidance, we now turn to a condition that creates its own distinctive prison — one built not from feared places, but from feared thoughts. Imagine a new mother who cannot stop picturing herself harming her infant, even though she loves the child deeply. Or a medical student who washes his hands until they crack and bleed, yet still feels contaminated. These individuals are not dangerous, nor are they "dirty." They are caught in the relentless grip of OCD, a disorder characterized by the presence of obsessions, compulsions, or both — intrusive mental events paired with desperate attempts to neutralize them.

Although OCD was reclassified into its own chapter in DSM-5 (Obsessive-Compulsive and Related Disorders), reflecting growing recognition of its unique neurobiology and treatment profile, it remains a commonly tested topic alongside anxiety disorders on the EPPP. Understanding the distinction between obsessions and compulsions — and how they lock together into self-reinforcing cycles — is foundational to both clinical practice and exam preparation.

Obsessions vs. Compulsions

Obsessions are recurrent, persistent, intrusive, and unwanted thoughts, urges, or images that cause marked anxiety or distress. The individual attempts to ignore, suppress, or neutralize them — but the harder one tries to push an obsession away, the more forcefully it returns, much like trying not to think of a white bear. Compulsions are repetitive behaviors or mental acts that the individual feels driven to perform in response to an obsession or according to rigid rules. They aim to prevent or reduce anxiety or avert a dreaded event, but they are not realistically connected to what they are designed to neutralize. A person may tap a doorframe exactly seven times to "prevent" a loved one from dying — fully aware the action makes no logical sense, yet unable to resist performing it.

What makes OCD so clinically distinctive — and so agonizing for those who suffer from it — is the ego-dystonic nature of the obsessions. These thoughts feel alien, horrifying, and fundamentally at odds with who the person believes themselves to be. The compassionate parent tormented by violent images toward a child, the devoutly religious person plagued by blasphemous thoughts — these individuals do not want these mental intrusions. The compulsions then emerge as desperate coping strategies, momentarily reducing anxiety but ultimately reinforcing the obsessional cycle. Each time a compulsion "works" (the anxiety briefly drops), the brain learns that the ritual was necessary, strengthening the urge to repeat it next time.

Common OCD Symptom Dimensions

OCD does not present as a single, uniform condition. Researchers have identified several symptom dimensions that cluster together, each pairing characteristic obsessions with corresponding compulsions. Recognizing these dimensions helps clinicians assess the full scope of a patient's symptoms and guides treatment planning. A client who presents with contamination fears and washing rituals, for instance, may respond to different exposure hierarchies than one consumed by intrusive thoughts of harming others.

DimensionObsessionsCompulsions
ContaminationFear of germs, dirt, illnessExcessive washing, cleaning
SymmetryNeed for exactness, orderArranging, ordering, counting
Forbidden thoughtsAggressive, sexual, or religious intrusionsMental rituals, checking
HarmFear of causing harm to self/othersChecking locks, stoves, appliances
HoardingDistress at discarding itemsExcessive saving, acquiring

Note that some compulsions are purely mental — silently counting, praying, or repeating phrases — and can be invisible to outside observers. A client may appear to be staring into space when, in reality, they are performing an elaborate mental ritual to neutralize a terrifying intrusive thought. Clinicians who only ask about behavioral rituals may miss an entire category of compulsive activity, so thorough assessment should always probe for covert mental acts.

DSM-5 Specifiers

The DSM-5 includes two important specifiers for OCD that carry significant clinical and prognostic implications. The first addresses how much awareness the person has that their OCD beliefs may not be true — a dimension that directly affects treatment engagement and outcome.

The insight specifier categorizes individuals along a continuum: good or fair insight (recognizing that OCD beliefs are definitely or probably not true), poor insight (thinking OCD beliefs are probably true), or absent insight/delusional beliefs (completely convinced the beliefs are true). Approximately 4% of individuals with OCD fall into the absent insight category. Consider a man who is utterly certain that failing to check the stove exactly twelve times will cause his house to burn down — he does not merely worry it might happen; he knows it will. This conviction can make treatment especially challenging because the person sees no reason to resist the compulsion. Poor or absent insight also raises important differential diagnostic questions, as clinicians must distinguish OCD with delusional beliefs from a primary psychotic disorder.

The tic-related specifier applies when the individual has a current or past history of a tic disorder, such as Tourette's disorder. This specifier flags a clinically meaningful subtype: tic-related OCD typically presents with an earlier age of onset, shows a more frequent male predominance, and features higher rates of symmetry and ordering compulsions. Research suggests that tic-related OCD may involve somewhat different neural circuitry — particularly striatal pathways — and may show a somewhat different treatment response, with some evidence that augmentation with antipsychotic medications can benefit this subgroup when SSRIs alone prove insufficient.

EPPP Example

Distinguishing OCD from OCPD: In OCD, obsessions are ego-dystonic (experienced as unwanted and distressing). The person fights against the intrusive thoughts and recognizes them as irrational — a mother horrified by violent images of her child does not want those thoughts and finds them deeply disturbing. In OCPD, the preoccupation with orderliness and perfectionism is ego-syntonic (consistent with the person's self-image). A supervisor with OCPD who insists every report follow an exacting format sees this rigidity as a virtue, not a symptom. Individuals with OCPD rarely seek treatment for these traits because they see them as desirable. This ego-dystonic versus ego-syntonic distinction is one of the most frequently tested differentials on the EPPP.

As we move into the next section on etiological models, keep in mind that OCD's unique position — straddling the boundary between anxiety disorders and its own diagnostic category — reflects the complex interplay of cognitive, behavioral, and neurobiological factors that drive this condition. Understanding what causes anxiety and OCD will help you appreciate why certain treatments, particularly exposure and response prevention, target the very mechanisms that keep these disorders alive.

section_html:
Body Dysmorphic Disorder (BDD)

Body Dysmorphic Disorder is classified under Obsessive-Compulsive and Related Disorders in the DSM-5. It is characterized by a preoccupation with one or more perceived defects or flaws in physical appearance that are not observable or appear only slight to others. Despite the minimal or nonexistent nature of the appearance concerns, individuals with BDD experience significant distress and functional impairment.

DSM-5 Diagnostic Criteria

  1. Criterion A: Preoccupation with one or more perceived defects or flaws in physical appearance that are not observable or appear only slight to others.
  2. Criterion B: At some point during the course of the disorder, the individual has performed repetitive behaviors (e.g., mirror checking, excessive grooming, skin picking, reassurance seeking) or mental acts (e.g., comparing his or her appearance with that of others) in response to the appearance concerns.
  3. Criterion C: The preoccupation causes clinically significant distress or impairment in social, occupational, or other important areas of functioning.
  4. Criterion D: The appearance preoccupation is not better explained by concerns with body fat or weight in an individual whose symptoms meet diagnostic criteria for an eating disorder.

DSM-5 Specifiers

  • With muscle dysmorphia: The individual is preoccupied with the idea that his or her body build is too small or insufficiently muscular. This specifier applies even if the individual is also preoccupied with other body areas.
  • Insight specifier: With good or fair insight, with poor insight, or with absent insight/delusional beliefs.

Repetitive Behaviors in BDD

The repetitive behaviors in BDD are compulsive in nature and functionally analogous to OCD compulsions. Common behaviors include: mirror checking (or mirror avoidance), excessive grooming, skin picking to remove perceived flaws, camouflaging (with makeup, clothing, hats, posture), reassurance seeking about appearance, comparing appearance with others, and excessive exercise (particularly in muscle dysmorphia). These behaviors are time-consuming and difficult to resist or control.

Epidemiology and Clinical Features

BDD has a point prevalence of approximately 2% in the general population, with higher rates (7-8%) in dermatology and cosmetic surgery settings. Onset is typically during adolescence (mean age 16-17), and the course is usually chronic without treatment. The most common areas of concern involve the skin (e.g., acne, scars, wrinkles), hair (e.g., thinning, excessive body hair), and nose, though any body part can be the focus.

Clinical Pearl

BDD carries a significantly elevated suicide risk, with approximately 80% of individuals reporting lifetime suicidal ideation and 24-28% reporting suicide attempts. Comorbidity is high: approximately 75% of individuals with BDD have comorbid major depressive disorder, and 30-40% have comorbid OCD. Cosmetic procedures rarely improve BDD symptoms and may worsen them. Individuals with absent insight may present with delusional intensity and were historically diagnosed with "delusional disorder, somatic type," but DSM-5 allows the BDD diagnosis regardless of insight level.

Treatment

CBT with exposure and response prevention (ERP) is the first-line psychotherapy for BDD. Exposure involves confronting avoided situations (e.g., going out without camouflage, reducing mirror checking), while response prevention targets the repetitive behaviors. SSRIs are the first-line pharmacological treatment, often at higher doses similar to those used for OCD. Serotonergic medications are significantly more effective than non-serotonergic medications for BDD.
prev_last_paragraph: Separation anxiety disorder must be distinguished from agoraphobia (fear of being unable to escape, not specifically about separation from attachment figures), generalized anxiety disorder (worry about multiple topics, not limited to separation), and social anxiety disorder (avoidance of social scrutiny, not separation). In children, school refusal may stem from separation anxiety, social anxiety, or specific phobia of the school environment, and careful assessment is needed to determine the primary driving fear.
rewritten_html:
Body Dysmorphic Disorder (BDD)

Imagine a college student who spends three hours each morning examining her skin in the mirror, convinced that faint acne scars make her appear "grotesque" — even though her friends genuinely cannot see what she is describing. She arrives late to class, avoids social gatherings, and has consulted four dermatologists, none of whom found anything clinically notable. Her distress is real, her impairment is severe, and yet the perceived flaw that drives her suffering is essentially invisible to everyone around her. This painful disconnect between subjective experience and objective reality lies at the heart of Body Dysmorphic Disorder, a condition classified under Obsessive-Compulsive and Related Disorders in the DSM-5.

Having explored separation anxiety disorder — where distress centers on losing proximity to attachment figures — we now shift to a very different kind of preoccupation. In Body Dysmorphic Disorder (BDD), the individual fixates on one or more perceived defects or flaws in physical appearance that others either do not notice at all or consider only slight. Despite the minimal or nonexistent nature of these appearance concerns, the person experiences profound distress and significant functional impairment, often spending hours each day trapped in repetitive checking, grooming, or comparing rituals. BDD's placement alongside OCD in the DSM-5 reflects the striking parallels between the two disorders: intrusive, distressing preoccupations drive compulsive behaviors that temporarily reduce anxiety but ultimately perpetuate the cycle.

DSM-5 Diagnostic Criteria

The DSM-5 organizes the diagnosis of BDD around four core criteria. Clinicians should pay careful attention to each one, because the boundaries between BDD and related conditions — particularly eating disorders and delusional disorder — hinge on these distinctions.

  1. Criterion A: Preoccupation with one or more perceived defects or flaws in physical appearance that are not observable or appear only slight to others.
  2. Criterion B: At some point during the course of the disorder, the individual has performed repetitive behaviors (e.g., mirror checking, excessive grooming, skin picking, reassurance seeking) or mental acts (e.g., comparing his or her appearance with that of others) in response to the appearance concerns.
  3. Criterion C: The preoccupation causes clinically significant distress or impairment in social, occupational, or other important areas of functioning.
  4. Criterion D: The appearance preoccupation is not better explained by concerns with body fat or weight in an individual whose symptoms meet diagnostic criteria for an eating disorder.

Notice how Criterion B explicitly requires behavioral or mental responses to the appearance concern — not merely worry. This requirement highlights the obsessive-compulsive structure of BDD: the preoccupation functions like an obsession, and the checking, grooming, or comparing functions like a compulsion. Also note that Criterion D draws a critical diagnostic boundary: when a patient's appearance concerns focus specifically on body fat or weight and the clinical picture meets criteria for an eating disorder such as anorexia nervosa, the eating disorder diagnosis takes precedence rather than BDD.

DSM-5 Specifiers

The DSM-5 provides two important specifiers that help clinicians characterize the clinical presentation more precisely. These specifiers carry meaningful treatment and prognostic implications.

  • With muscle dysmorphia: The individual is preoccupied with the idea that his or her body build is too small or insufficiently muscular. This specifier applies even if the individual is also preoccupied with other body areas.
  • Insight specifier: With good or fair insight, with poor insight, or with absent insight/delusional beliefs.

The muscle dysmorphia specifier deserves particular attention on the EPPP. Picture a man who weighs 210 pounds of lean muscle yet perceives himself as "scrawny," wearing multiple layers of clothing to hide his frame and spending four or more hours daily at the gym. He may use anabolic steroids despite medical risks, driven by the unshakable conviction that he looks pathetically small. This presentation occurs almost exclusively in males and can easily go unrecognized because the culture often reinforces intensive exercise and muscular ideals. The insight specifier matters clinically because individuals with absent insight hold their appearance beliefs with delusional conviction — they are absolutely certain they look as terrible as they believe. Historically, clinicians diagnosed these individuals with delusional disorder, somatic type, but the DSM-5 now captures them under the BDD diagnosis with the "absent insight/delusional beliefs" specifier, recognizing that the underlying condition remains the same regardless of insight level.

Repetitive Behaviors in BDD

The repetitive behaviors in BDD are compulsive in nature and functionally analogous to OCD compulsions. Common behaviors include: mirror checking (or mirror avoidance — some individuals swing between compulsive checking and complete avoidance of reflective surfaces), excessive grooming, skin picking to remove perceived flaws (sometimes resulting in visible skin damage that paradoxically creates the very imperfections the person fears), camouflaging (with makeup, clothing, hats, posture), reassurance seeking about appearance from friends, family, or medical professionals, comparing appearance with others (in person or increasingly through social media), and excessive exercise (particularly in muscle dysmorphia). These behaviors consume significant time — often several hours per day — and prove extremely difficult to resist or control, much like the compulsions observed in OCD.

Epidemiology and Clinical Features

BDD affects approximately 2% of the general population, making it more common than many clinicians realize. Prevalence rates climb dramatically in settings where people actively seek appearance-related solutions — reaching 7-8% in dermatology clinics and cosmetic surgery practices. The disorder typically emerges during adolescence, with a mean age of onset around 16-17 years, a developmental period when identity formation and social comparison intensify. Without treatment, BDD usually follows a chronic and unremitting course, with symptoms waxing and waning but rarely resolving spontaneously.

The most commonly targeted areas of concern involve the skin (acne, scars, wrinkles, complexion), hair (thinning hair, excessive body hair, hairline), and nose (size, shape, symmetry), though individuals may fixate on virtually any body part — ears, teeth, jawline, hands, or genitalia. Many individuals with BDD focus on multiple areas simultaneously, and the specific focus may shift over time. A key clinical feature that distinguishes BDD from normal appearance dissatisfaction is the sheer amount of time consumed by the preoccupation — often three to eight hours per day — and the degree to which it disrupts daily functioning, relationships, and quality of life.

Clinical Pearl

BDD carries a significantly elevated suicide risk, with approximately 80% of individuals reporting lifetime suicidal ideation and 24-28% reporting suicide attempts — rates that rival or exceed those seen in major depressive disorder and bipolar disorder. Comorbidity compounds the clinical picture: approximately 75% of individuals with BDD meet criteria for comorbid major depressive disorder, and 30-40% also carry a diagnosis of OCD. Clinicians should always screen for suicidal ideation when BDD is suspected. Another critical point for both clinical practice and the EPPP: cosmetic procedures rarely improve BDD symptoms and may actually worsen them, often shifting the preoccupation to a new perceived flaw or intensifying dissatisfaction with the surgical result. Individuals with absent insight may present with delusional intensity and were historically diagnosed with "delusional disorder, somatic type," but DSM-5 allows the BDD diagnosis regardless of insight level — an important diagnostic update to remember.

Treatment

Effective treatment for BDD draws directly from the same principles that guide OCD intervention, reflecting their shared placement in the obsessive-compulsive spectrum. CBT with exposure and response prevention (ERP) stands as the first-line psychotherapy. In practice, exposure tasks involve systematically confronting the situations the individual avoids — going out in public without camouflage makeup, sitting under bright lighting, allowing others to see the "flawed" area — while response prevention targets the repetitive behaviors by having the person resist mirror checking, grooming rituals, and reassurance seeking. A therapist might ask a patient who spends 45 minutes applying concealer each morning to progressively reduce application time, then ultimately leave the house without it, tolerating the anxiety until it naturally diminishes.

On the pharmacological side, SSRIs serve as the first-line medication treatment for BDD, and clinicians typically prescribe them at doses higher than those used for depression — similar to the elevated doses effective for OCD. This dosing pattern reflects the serotonergic underpinnings shared across obsessive-compulsive spectrum disorders. Research consistently demonstrates that serotonergic medications produce significantly better outcomes than non-serotonergic alternatives for BDD, a finding that parallels the pharmacological response pattern seen in OCD. Combining CBT/ERP with SSRI treatment often yields the strongest results, particularly for individuals with severe symptoms or poor insight.

section_html:
Hoarding Disorder

Hoarding Disorder was introduced as a standalone diagnosis in the DSM-5, classified under Obsessive-Compulsive and Related Disorders. Previously, hoarding was considered a symptom or subtype of OCD. Research has demonstrated that hoarding is a distinct condition with unique neurobiological, cognitive, and behavioral features that warrant independent diagnostic status.

DSM-5 Diagnostic Criteria

  1. Criterion A: Persistent difficulty discarding or parting with possessions, regardless of their actual value.
  2. Criterion B: This difficulty is due to a perceived need to save the items and to distress associated with discarding them.
  3. Criterion C: The difficulty discarding possessions results in the accumulation of possessions that congest and clutter active living areas and substantially compromises their intended use. If living areas are uncluttered, it is only because of the interventions of third parties (e.g., family members, cleaners, authorities).
  4. Criterion D: The hoarding causes clinically significant distress or impairment in social, occupational, or other important areas of functioning (including maintaining a safe environment for oneself or others).
  5. Criterion E: The hoarding is not attributable to another medical condition (e.g., brain injury, cerebrovascular disease, Prader-Willi syndrome).
  6. Criterion F: The hoarding is not better explained by the symptoms of another mental disorder.

DSM-5 Specifiers

  • With excessive acquisition: If difficulty discarding possessions is accompanied by excessive acquiring of items that are not needed or for which there is no available space.
  • Insight specifier: With good or fair insight, with poor insight, or with absent insight/delusional beliefs.

Key Distinction: Hoarding Disorder vs. OCD Hoarding

Hoarding in the context of hoarding disorder is ego-syntonic -- individuals value their possessions and experience distress at the thought of discarding them. Hoarding in the context of OCD is ego-dystonic -- the accumulation is driven by obsessions (e.g., fear of contamination preventing disposal, need for symmetry/completeness) and is experienced as unwanted. This distinction is critical for differential diagnosis and treatment planning.

Epidemiology and Course

Hoarding disorder has a prevalence of approximately 2-6% in the general population, making it substantially more common than OCD. Symptoms typically emerge in adolescence (ages 11-15), become clinically significant in the mid-20s to 30s, and worsen progressively with age. The disorder is equally prevalent in males and females, though clinical samples are predominantly female. Hoarding disorder is associated with significant health and safety risks, including fire hazards, falls, unsanitary living conditions, and social isolation.

Clinical Pearl

Hoarding disorder is notoriously difficult to treat. Standard OCD treatments (ERP alone) have limited efficacy for hoarding. The most effective approach is CBT with motivational interviewing, which addresses the ambivalence about change, cognitive distortions about possessions (emotional attachment, perceived utility, aesthetic value), and skills deficits in organizing, decision-making, and categorizing. Home-based sessions are more effective than office-only treatment. Neuroimaging studies show distinct patterns from OCD, with abnormal activity in the anterior cingulate cortex and insula during decision-making about possessions.
prev_last_paragraph: CBT with exposure and response prevention (ERP) is the first-line psychotherapy for BDD. Exposure involves confronting avoided situations (e.g., going out without camouflage, reducing mirror checking), while response prevention targets the repetitive behaviors. SSRIs are the first-line pharmacological treatment, often at higher doses similar to those used for OCD. Serotonergic medications are significantly more effective than non-serotonergic medications for BDD.
rewritten_html:
Hoarding Disorder

Having explored how Body Dysmorphic Disorder revolves around perceived flaws in appearance — with its ego-dystonic preoccupations and ritualistic checking — we now turn to a condition that centers on a very different kind of distress: the anguish of letting go. Imagine a retired schoolteacher whose three-bedroom home has become virtually uninhabitable. Stacks of newspapers, broken appliances, clothing still bearing price tags, and bags of unread mail fill every room from floor to ceiling. Only a narrow pathway connects the front door to the kitchen and bedroom. She knows, on some level, that the accumulation has become unmanageable — and yet each item feels essential, irreplaceable, imbued with potential usefulness or emotional significance. When her adult children attempt to clear a pathway through the living room, she becomes tearful and panicked, pleading with them to stop. This is the clinical reality of Hoarding Disorder.

Hoarding Disorder earned its place as a standalone diagnosis in the DSM-5, classified under Obsessive-Compulsive and Related Disorders. For years, clinicians and researchers treated hoarding as merely a symptom or subtype of OCD, but a growing body of evidence revealed something more complex. Studies have demonstrated that hoarding involves distinct neurobiological signatures, unique cognitive patterns — particularly around decision-making and emotional attachment to objects — and behavioral features that clearly set it apart from OCD. These differences proved substantial enough to justify independent diagnostic status, a change that has meaningfully improved both clinical recognition and treatment planning.

DSM-5 Diagnostic Criteria

  1. Criterion A: Persistent difficulty discarding or parting with possessions, regardless of their actual value.
  2. Criterion B: This difficulty is due to a perceived need to save the items and to distress associated with discarding them.
  3. Criterion C: The difficulty discarding possessions results in the accumulation of possessions that congest and clutter active living areas and substantially compromises their intended use. If living areas are uncluttered, it is only because of the interventions of third parties (e.g., family members, cleaners, authorities).
  4. Criterion D: The hoarding causes clinically significant distress or impairment in social, occupational, or other important areas of functioning (including maintaining a safe environment for oneself or others).
  5. Criterion E: The hoarding is not attributable to another medical condition (e.g., brain injury, cerebrovascular disease, Prader-Willi syndrome).
  6. Criterion F: The hoarding is not better explained by the symptoms of another mental disorder.

Notice how Criterion C introduces a critical functional threshold: the clutter must congest active living areas enough to substantially compromise their intended use. A collector who fills a dedicated storage unit with vintage records does not meet this criterion. But when a person can no longer cook in the kitchen, sleep in the bed, or sit on the couch because possessions have overtaken those spaces, the line into disorder has clearly been crossed. Also note the important caveat — if living areas appear uncluttered only because third parties (family members, landlords, or city authorities) have intervened, the criterion is still met.

DSM-5 Specifiers

  • With excessive acquisition: If difficulty discarding possessions is accompanied by excessive acquiring of items that are not needed or for which there is no available space.
  • Insight specifier: With good or fair insight, with poor insight, or with absent insight/delusional beliefs.

The "excessive acquisition" specifier deserves clinical attention because it captures a subgroup that actively brings new items into an already overwhelmed space — purchasing, collecting free items, or even stealing objects they do not need. The insight specifier, meanwhile, carries direct treatment implications. Many individuals with hoarding disorder present with poor or absent insight, genuinely believing that their accumulation is reasonable and that others simply fail to appreciate the value of their possessions. This stands in stark contrast to most individuals with OCD, who typically recognize their obsessions as irrational. A person who insists, with delusional conviction, that their collection of 4,000 empty yogurt containers will be "needed someday" presents a very different clinical challenge than someone who tearfully acknowledges, "I know this is out of control, but I just can't let anything go."

Key Distinction: Hoarding Disorder vs. OCD Hoarding

This distinction can make or break a differential diagnosis on the EPPP. Hoarding in the context of hoarding disorder is ego-syntonic — individuals genuinely value their possessions, see the saving as meaningful, and experience distress primarily at the thought of discarding them, not at the act of accumulating. In contrast, hoarding in the context of OCD is ego-dystonic — the accumulation feels unwanted and distressing, driven by intrusive obsessions such as fear of contamination preventing disposal, or a need for symmetry and completeness that compels the person to keep acquiring. A person with OCD-related hoarding might say, "I can't throw away this newspaper because touching it might contaminate my hands, and I'd rather just leave it there." A person with hoarding disorder might say, "I can't throw away this newspaper because it contains important information I might need someday." This distinction is critical for both differential diagnosis and treatment planning.

Epidemiology and Course

Hoarding disorder affects approximately 2-6% of the general population — a figure that surprises many clinicians, since it makes hoarding substantially more common than OCD. The disorder follows a characteristic developmental trajectory: symptoms typically emerge during adolescence (ages 11-15), often as mild attachment to objects or reluctance to discard, then become clinically significant by the mid-20s to 30s, and worsen progressively with each passing decade. By the time most individuals present for treatment, they are middle-aged or older, and the accumulation has reached crisis proportions. The disorder affects males and females at roughly equal rates in the community, though clinical samples skew predominantly female, likely reflecting differences in help-seeking behavior.

The real-world consequences of hoarding disorder extend far beyond psychological distress. Clinicians should recognize the significant health and safety risks that accompany severe hoarding: fire hazards from blocked exits and piled combustible materials, falls caused by navigating through cluttered pathways, unsanitary living conditions that attract pests and breed infection, and profound social isolation as individuals become too embarrassed to invite anyone into their homes. In extreme cases, municipal authorities intervene with forced cleanouts — interventions that, without concurrent psychological treatment, typically lead to rapid re-accumulation and intense emotional distress.

Clinical Pearl

Hoarding disorder remains one of the most treatment-resistant conditions in the OCD-related spectrum — a fact that every clinician should internalize. Standard OCD treatments, including ERP alone, show limited efficacy for hoarding because the core problem is not an anxiety-driven compulsion but rather a deep emotional attachment to objects, faulty beliefs about their value, and genuine skills deficits. The most effective approach combines CBT with motivational interviewing, which directly targets the profound ambivalence about change that characterizes most individuals with this disorder. Treatment addresses three key domains: cognitive distortions about possessions (emotional attachment, perceived utility, aesthetic value), behavioral avoidance of discarding, and practical skills deficits in organizing, decision-making, and categorizing. Clinicians who conduct home-based sessions achieve significantly better outcomes than those who rely exclusively on office-based treatment, because the real therapeutic work happens at the site of the accumulation — sorting through actual possessions, practicing discarding in vivo, and building organizational systems in real time. Neuroimaging research further underscores the distinctness of hoarding from OCD: individuals with hoarding disorder show abnormal activity in the anterior cingulate cortex and insula specifically during decision-making tasks about their own possessions, a pattern not seen in typical OCD presentations.

section_html:
Excoriation (Skin-Picking) Disorder

Excoriation disorder, also known as skin-picking disorder or dermatillomania, is classified under Obsessive-Compulsive and Related Disorders in the DSM-5. It was newly added as a formal diagnosis in DSM-5 and, like trichotillomania, is categorized as a body-focused repetitive behavior disorder.

DSM-5 Diagnostic Criteria

  1. Criterion A: Recurrent skin picking resulting in skin lesions.
  2. Criterion B: Repeated attempts to decrease or stop skin picking.
  3. Criterion C: The skin picking causes clinically significant distress or impairment in social, occupational, or other important areas of functioning.
  4. Criterion D: The skin picking is not attributable to the physiological effects of a substance (e.g., cocaine) or another medical condition (e.g., scabies).
  5. Criterion E: The skin picking is not better explained by symptoms of another mental disorder (e.g., delusions or tactile hallucinations in psychotic disorder, attempts to improve perceived defect in BDD, stereotypies in stereotypic movement disorder, intention to harm oneself in nonsuicidal self-injury).

Behavioral Pattern

Like trichotillomania, excoriation disorder involves both focused picking (deliberate, in response to negative emotions or urges) and automatic picking (outside of awareness, during sedentary activities). The picking may target healthy skin, minor skin irregularities (e.g., pimples, calluses, scabs), or lesions from previous picking. Common sites include the face, arms, and hands. Individuals may use fingernails, tweezers, pins, or other implements. A similar tension/relief cycle may be present, though it is not required for diagnosis.

Epidemiology and Clinical Features

Excoriation disorder has a prevalence of approximately 1.4% in the general population and is predominantly diagnosed in females (approximately 75% of cases). Onset can occur at any age but frequently begins in adolescence, often coinciding with or following the onset of acne or other dermatological conditions. The course is typically chronic, with waxing and waning symptom severity. Significant medical complications can include tissue damage, scarring, and infection.

Clinical Pearl

Treatment for excoriation disorder closely parallels that for trichotillomania. Habit reversal training (HRT) combined with CBT is the first-line psychotherapy. The treatment approach includes awareness training to identify triggers and high-risk situations, competing response training to substitute incompatible behaviors, and stimulus control strategies (e.g., covering mirrors, wearing gloves, keeping hands occupied). SSRIs are sometimes used but evidence is mixed. N-acetylcysteine has also shown preliminary efficacy as a glutamate-modulating agent.

Differential Diagnosis

Excoriation disorder must be distinguished from: nonsuicidal self-injury (which involves intentional self-harm for emotional regulation, not repetitive picking driven by urge/habit), BDD (where skin picking is motivated by attempts to fix perceived appearance flaws), psychotic disorders (where picking may be driven by delusions of parasitosis or tactile hallucinations), and substance-induced picking (particularly stimulant-induced formication). When skin picking occurs exclusively in the context of one of these other conditions, excoriation disorder should not be diagnosed.
prev_last_paragraph: Trichotillomania is frequently comorbid with excoriation (skin-picking) disorder, OCD, major depressive disorder, and other anxiety disorders. Co-occurrence with excoriation disorder is particularly common, reflecting the shared classification as body-focused repetitive behavior disorders.
rewritten_html:
Excoriation (Skin-Picking) Disorder

Having just explored trichotillomania and its classification as a body-focused repetitive behavior disorder, we now turn to its close relative — a condition so frequently co-occurring with hair pulling that their shared features illuminate something fundamental about how the brain gets locked into repetitive, self-damaging loops. Consider a college student who spends an hour each evening in front of the bathroom mirror, methodically scanning her face for tiny imperfections — a barely visible bump, a clogged pore, the edge of a healing scab. She picks, squeezes, and digs with her fingernails until she has created raw, bleeding wounds far worse than anything she started with. She knows she should stop. She has promised herself, repeatedly, that tonight will be different. But the urge builds like a pressure she cannot contain, and before she fully realizes it, she is picking again. She wears heavy foundation to classes, avoids social gatherings, and has missed job interviews because her face looks too damaged. This is not vanity or a bad habit — this is excoriation disorder.

Also known as skin-picking disorder or dermatillomania, excoriation disorder earned its place as a formal diagnosis for the first time in the DSM-5, where it sits alongside trichotillomania under the Obsessive-Compulsive and Related Disorders chapter. Like trichotillomania, the DSM-5 categorizes it as a body-focused repetitive behavior disorder — recognizing that while these conditions share the compulsive quality of OCD, they involve repetitive behaviors directed at the body rather than ritualistic responses to obsessional thoughts. Understanding this disorder matters clinically because it is far more common than most practitioners realize, causes genuine physical harm, and responds to targeted interventions when correctly identified.

DSM-5 Diagnostic Criteria

The DSM-5 criteria for excoriation disorder mirror the structure you have already learned for trichotillomania, reinforcing their shared conceptual framework. The criteria establish a clear pattern: a repetitive behavior the person cannot stop, despite wanting to, that causes real harm and cannot be better attributed to another condition. Pay particular attention to Criterion E, which requires clinicians to carefully rule out several look-alike presentations before assigning this diagnosis.

  1. Criterion A: Recurrent skin picking resulting in skin lesions.
  2. Criterion B: Repeated attempts to decrease or stop skin picking.
  3. Criterion C: The skin picking causes clinically significant distress or impairment in social, occupational, or other important areas of functioning.
  4. Criterion D: The skin picking is not attributable to the physiological effects of a substance (e.g., cocaine) or another medical condition (e.g., scabies).
  5. Criterion E: The skin picking is not better explained by symptoms of another mental disorder (e.g., delusions or tactile hallucinations in psychotic disorder, attempts to improve perceived defect in BDD, stereotypies in stereotypic movement disorder, intention to harm oneself in nonsuicidal self-injury).

Notice that Criterion B — repeated attempts to stop — distinguishes excoriation disorder from casual or occasional skin picking, which many people do without distress. The individual with excoriation disorder experiences a distressing loss of control, recognizing the behavior as problematic yet finding themselves unable to resist it. This ego-dystonic quality parallels what we see in trichotillomania and, more broadly, across the OCD spectrum.

Behavioral Pattern

Like trichotillomania, excoriation disorder involves both focused picking (deliberate, in response to negative emotions or urges) and automatic picking (outside of awareness, during sedentary activities). Think of focused picking as the person who sits down at the mirror after a stressful day at work, driven by mounting tension and an urge to "fix" something on their skin — they experience a surge of relief or satisfaction with each extraction. Automatic picking, by contrast, looks like the student who absently runs her fingers along her arms while reading a textbook, picking at bumps and scabs without even noticing until she sees blood. Many individuals alternate between both styles, sometimes within the same episode. The picking may target healthy skin, minor skin irregularities (e.g., pimples, calluses, scabs), or lesions from previous picking — creating a self-perpetuating cycle where yesterday's wounds become today's targets. Common sites include the face, arms, and hands, though individuals may pick from virtually any accessible body area. Individuals may use fingernails, tweezers, pins, or other implements. A similar tension/relief cycle may be present, though it is not required for diagnosis.

Epidemiology and Clinical Features

Excoriation disorder affects approximately 1.4% of the general population — making it notably common among the OCD-spectrum disorders and far more prevalent than many clinicians expect. The condition disproportionately affects females, who represent approximately 75% of diagnosed cases, a gender ratio that mirrors what we see in trichotillomania. Onset can occur at any age but frequently begins in adolescence, often coinciding with or following the onset of acne or other dermatological conditions — a pattern that makes intuitive sense, as normal skin changes provide initial "targets" that trigger and reinforce the picking behavior in vulnerable individuals.

The course of excoriation disorder typically follows a chronic trajectory, with symptom severity that waxes and wanes over months and years, often intensifying during periods of heightened stress, boredom, or emotional distress. Clinicians should remain alert to the significant medical complications this disorder can produce: repeated picking causes tissue damage, permanent scarring, and creates entry points for serious infection. Some individuals develop disfiguring wounds that require medical attention. The psychosocial consequences can be equally devastating — individuals may avoid intimate relationships, withdraw from social activities, or restrict their career choices to avoid exposing damaged skin. The shame and secrecy surrounding the behavior often delay help-seeking by years or even decades.

Clinical Pearl

Treatment for excoriation disorder closely parallels that for trichotillomania, and for the EPPP, remembering the shared treatment approach across body-focused repetitive behavior disorders will serve you well. Habit reversal training (HRT) combined with CBT represents the first-line psychotherapy approach. The treatment package includes three core components: awareness training teaches clients to identify triggers, high-risk situations, and the earliest sensory cues that precede picking; competing response training helps them substitute physically incompatible behaviors (such as clenching fists, handling textured objects, or pressing palms flat on a surface) when urges arise; and stimulus control strategies modify the environment to reduce opportunities for picking — for example, covering or removing magnifying mirrors, wearing gloves during high-risk activities, or keeping hands occupied with fidget tools during sedentary tasks. SSRIs are sometimes used but evidence for their efficacy in excoriation disorder remains mixed — notably weaker than the evidence supporting their use in OCD proper. N-acetylcysteine has also shown preliminary efficacy as a glutamate-modulating agent, offering a novel pharmacological avenue that researchers continue to explore.

Differential Diagnosis

The differential diagnosis of excoriation disorder requires careful clinical reasoning because several other conditions can produce repetitive skin picking — but with fundamentally different motivations and mechanisms. Clinicians must distinguish excoriation disorder from nonsuicidal self-injury, in which an individual deliberately harms their skin to regulate intense emotions such as anger, emptiness, or dissociation. The key distinction lies in motivation and behavioral quality: nonsuicidal self-injury involves intentional self-harm rather than a repetitive urge-driven habit, and the individual typically selects cutting, burning, or hitting rather than the picking-and-extracting pattern seen in excoriation disorder. Similarly, when skin picking occurs in the context of BDD, the behavior is driven by a desire to fix perceived appearance flaws — the person picks because they believe something about their skin looks abnormal, not because of a compulsive urge. In psychotic disorders, picking may stem from delusions of parasitosis (the fixed belief that bugs are crawling under the skin) or tactile hallucinations — a qualitatively different experience from the urge-based picking of excoriation disorder. Finally, substance-induced picking — particularly the formication (sensation of insects crawling on the skin) produced by stimulants like cocaine and methamphetamine — must always be considered. When skin picking occurs exclusively in the context of one of these other conditions, clinicians should not assign a separate diagnosis of excoriation disorder. This principle underscores a broader diagnostic rule across the DSM-5: the specific diagnosis that best captures the primary driving mechanism takes diagnostic precedence.

section_html:
Oppositional Defiant Disorder (ODD)

Oppositional Defiant Disorder is a pattern of angry/irritable mood, argumentative/defiant behavior, or vindictiveness lasting at least 6 months, evidenced by at least four symptoms from three categories:

Although ODD and conduct disorder share features of defiance and conflict with authority, a critical diagnostic distinction involves the nature and severity of aggressive behavior. ODD is primarily defined by emotional dysregulation and oppositional attitudes — losing one's temper, arguing, and refusing to comply — but it does not include the pattern of serious physical aggression toward people or animals that is characteristic of conduct disorder. When a child presents with repeated acts of aggression, such as initiating physical fights, bullying, using weapons, or engaging in physical cruelty, the clinician should strongly consider the possibility that conduct disorder is present, either as a primary diagnosis or as a comorbid condition alongside ODD. In clinical practice, persistent aggression that escalates beyond verbal outbursts and minor provocations marks a qualitative shift from oppositional behavior into conduct-disordered territory. Because the two diagnoses frequently co-occur, careful assessment of the full behavioral picture — including whether acts of aggression are recurrent and involve violation of others' physical safety — is essential for accurate differential diagnosis and appropriate treatment planning.

Symptom Categories

Oppositional Defiant Disorder is organized around three distinct symptom clusters that reflect escalating levels of behavioral and emotional disturbance. Understanding these categories is essential for accurate diagnosis and for distinguishing ODD from normative developmental opposition.

Angry/Irritable Mood

  • Often loses temper
  • Is often touchy or easily annoyed
  • Is often angry and resentful

Argumentative/Defiant Behavior

  • Often argues with authority figures or adults
  • Often actively defies or refuses to comply with requests or rules
  • Often deliberately annoys others
  • Often blames others for his or her mistakes or misbehavior

Vindictiveness

  • Has been spiteful or vindictive at least twice within the past 6 months

Clinical Pearl

DSM-5 added severity specifiers for ODD: mild (symptoms confined to one setting), moderate (some symptoms in at least two settings), and severe (symptoms in three or more settings). Research suggests the angry/irritable mood dimension of ODD is a stronger predictor of later internalizing disorders (depression, anxiety), while the behavioral dimensions predict later conduct disorder and ASPD (Stringaris & Goodman, 2009).

ODD prevalence is approximately 3.3%, with a male predominance in childhood that equalizes by adolescence. It typically emerges in the preschool years and is usually evident before age 8. ODD often precedes the development of conduct disorder, but the majority of children with ODD do not progress to conduct disorder.

prev_last_paragraph: Disruptive and conduct disorders are classified as externalizing disorders, meaning the core symptoms are directed outward toward the environment (aggression, defiance, rule violation). This contrasts with internalizing disorders (e.g., depression, anxiety), where distress is directed inward. However, significant comorbidity between externalizing and internalizing disorders is common.
rewritten_html:
Oppositional Defiant Disorder (ODD)

Picture a seven-year-old who, when told it's time to turn off the video game for dinner, doesn't simply grumble — he erupts. He shouts that the rule is "stupid," slams the controller on the floor, and screams that his parents "never let him do anything." After the storm passes, he refuses to sit at the table and deliberately kicks his sister's chair until she cries. His parents feel like they're walking on eggshells, and his teacher reports the same hair-trigger defiance at school. An occasional tantrum is part of normal childhood, but when this level of emotional volatility and opposition becomes the rule rather than the exception — persisting for months and disrupting relationships across settings — clinicians begin to consider Oppositional Defiant Disorder.

Formally, ODD is defined as a pattern of angry/irritable mood, argumentative/defiant behavior, or vindictiveness lasting at least 6 months, evidenced by at least four symptoms drawn from three distinct categories. What sets ODD apart from the everyday pushback that most children display is the frequency, intensity, and persistence of these behaviors — and the degree to which they impair the child's functioning at home, in school, and with peers. As we discussed in the previous section, ODD falls squarely within the externalizing spectrum: distress is expressed outward, through conflict with others. Yet, as we will see, one of ODD's symptom dimensions — angry/irritable mood — actually serves as a bridge to the internalizing disorders, making this diagnosis a fascinating crossroads in developmental psychopathology.

Although ODD and conduct disorder share features of defiance and conflict with authority, a critical diagnostic distinction involves the nature and severity of aggressive behavior. ODD is primarily defined by emotional dysregulation and oppositional attitudes — losing one's temper, arguing, and refusing to comply — but it does not include the pattern of serious physical aggression toward people or animals that is characteristic of conduct disorder. When a child presents with repeated acts of aggression, such as initiating physical fights, bullying, using weapons, or engaging in physical cruelty, the clinician should strongly consider the possibility that conduct disorder is present, either as a primary diagnosis or as a comorbid condition alongside ODD. In clinical practice, persistent aggression that escalates beyond verbal outbursts and minor provocations marks a qualitative shift from oppositional behavior into conduct-disordered territory. Think of the difference this way: the child with ODD screams "You can't make me!" and slams a door; the child with conduct disorder punches a classmate in the face or threatens a peer with a sharp object. Both are externalizing, but they differ in kind, not just degree. Because the two diagnoses frequently co-occur, careful assessment of the full behavioral picture — including whether acts of aggression are recurrent and involve violation of others' physical safety — is essential for accurate differential diagnosis and appropriate treatment planning.

Symptom Categories

Oppositional Defiant Disorder is organized around three distinct symptom clusters that reflect different facets of the disorder — one primarily emotional, one primarily behavioral, and one reflecting a retaliatory interpersonal pattern. Understanding these categories is essential not only for accurate diagnosis but also for distinguishing ODD from the normative developmental opposition that nearly every parent witnesses during the toddler and early adolescent years. Importantly, research has shown that these three dimensions carry different prognostic implications, a point that has significant consequences for treatment planning and long-term risk assessment.

Angry/Irritable Mood

This first cluster captures the emotional core of ODD — the child who seems perpetually on the verge of an outburst. These are the children whose parents describe as "always in a bad mood" or who "go from zero to sixty in seconds." The symptoms in this cluster include:

  • Often loses temper
  • Is often touchy or easily annoyed
  • Is often angry and resentful

Clinically, this dimension is particularly important because it represents the affective dysregulation that links ODD to later emotional disorders. A child who is chronically irritable and resentful is not just difficult to manage — that child is often suffering internally as well, experiencing a persistent state of frustration and distress that can evolve into depression or anxiety over time.

Argumentative/Defiant Behavior

The second cluster captures the behavioral hallmark of ODD — active resistance to authority and a pattern of deliberately provocative conduct. These are the children who seem to draw energy from power struggles and who can turn a simple request like "Please put your shoes on" into a thirty-minute standoff. The symptoms include:

  • Often argues with authority figures or adults
  • Often actively defies or refuses to comply with requests or rules
  • Often deliberately annoys others
  • Often blames others for his or her mistakes or misbehavior

Notice the externalization of responsibility in the last symptom — blaming others for one's own mistakes. This pattern can be particularly frustrating for parents and teachers, who may feel that the child never takes accountability. It also has clinical relevance: children who consistently externalize blame may be more resistant to therapeutic interventions that require self-reflection and ownership of behavior.

Vindictiveness

The third and final cluster is the most narrowly defined, consisting of a single criterion, but it carries outsized diagnostic weight because it signals a retaliatory, spiteful quality that goes beyond mere defiance:

  • Has been spiteful or vindictive at least twice within the past 6 months

Vindictiveness involves intentionally causing distress or seeking revenge — for example, a child who deliberately destroys a sibling's prized possession after a conflict, not in the heat of a tantrum but later, with calculated intent. This dimension, more than the others, has been linked to the later development of conduct disorder and antisocial personality disorder, making it a particularly important area to assess during clinical evaluation.

Clinical Pearl

DSM-5 added severity specifiers for ODD: mild (symptoms confined to one setting), moderate (some symptoms in at least two settings), and severe (symptoms in three or more settings). Research suggests the angry/irritable mood dimension of ODD is a stronger predictor of later internalizing disorders (depression, anxiety), while the behavioral dimensions predict later conduct disorder and ASPD (Stringaris & Goodman, 2009). This dimensional finding has practical implications for the EPPP: when a question stem describes a child with ODD whose primary symptoms are chronic irritability and resentfulness, think about comorbid or future mood disorders; when the emphasis is on defiance, provocation, and vindictiveness, think about the developmental trajectory toward conduct disorder.

ODD prevalence is approximately 3.3%, with a male predominance in childhood that equalizes by adolescence — a gender ratio shift that likely reflects both differential socialization patterns and the increasing salience of relational aggression in adolescent girls. The disorder typically emerges in the preschool years and is usually evident before age 8, a time when children are first navigating structured expectations from adults outside the family. ODD often precedes the development of conduct disorder, and this sequential relationship is one of the best-established developmental pathways in child psychopathology. However, a crucial point to remember is that the majority of children with ODD do not progress to conduct disorder — many improve with appropriate intervention, and some outgrow the pattern as they develop better emotion-regulation skills and more adaptive coping strategies.

section_html:
Circadian Rhythm Sleep-Wake Disorders

These disorders involve a persistent or recurrent pattern of sleep disruption primarily due to alteration of the circadian system or misalignment between the endogenous circadian rhythm and the sleep-wake schedule required by an individual's environment.

Types

  • Delayed sleep-wake phase type: Habitual sleep-wake timing is delayed, usually by 2+ hours, relative to conventional times. Common in adolescents. The individual cannot fall asleep until very late (e.g., 2-6 AM) and has difficulty waking for school or work.
  • Advanced sleep-wake phase type: Habitual sleep-wake timing is advanced. More common in older adults. Individuals fall asleep and wake very early (e.g., sleep at 6-8 PM, wake at 2-5 AM).
  • Shift work type: Insomnia and/or excessive sleepiness due to a work schedule that overlaps the usual sleep period.
  • Jet lag type: Sleepiness and alertness occurring at inappropriate times relative to local time after travel across time zones.
  • Non-24-hour sleep-wake type: Pattern of sleep-wake cycles not synchronized to the 24-hour environment. Most common in blind individuals lacking light input to the suprachiasmatic nucleus.

Clinical Pearl

The suprachiasmatic nucleus (SCN) of the hypothalamus is the master circadian pacemaker. It is primarily entrained (synchronized) by light input via the retinohypothalamic tract. Melatonin, produced by the pineal gland under SCN control, promotes sleep onset and is used therapeutically for circadian rhythm disorders. Light therapy (bright light exposure) is the primary treatment for delayed sleep-wake phase disorder and seasonal affective disorder.
prev_last_paragraph: Distinguishing sleep terrors from nightmares: Sleep terrors occur during NREM Stage N3 (deep sleep), involve intense autonomic arousal, and the individual is typically amnestic for the episode. Nightmares occur during REM sleep, the individual fully awakens with recall of the dream content, and there is less autonomic arousal. Sleep terrors are most common in children ages 4-12 and typically resolve spontaneously.
rewritten_html:
Circadian Rhythm Sleep-Wake Disorders

Having explored how parasomnias like sleep terrors and nightmares emerge from disruptions within specific sleep stages, we now turn to a fundamentally different kind of sleep problem — one rooted not in what happens during sleep, but in when sleep happens. Consider a 16-year-old high school student who lies in bed wide awake until 3 AM every night, not because of anxiety or poor sleep hygiene, but because her internal biological clock is dramatically out of sync with the schedule her school demands. Or picture a night-shift nurse who struggles with crushing fatigue during her midnight-to-8 AM shifts, yet cannot fall asleep when she gets home in the morning because her body insists it is time to be awake. These individuals are experiencing the clinical consequences of a misaligned circadian rhythm.

Circadian rhythm sleep-wake disorders involve a persistent or recurrent pattern of sleep disruption that arises primarily from alteration of the body's circadian system or from a misalignment between the endogenous circadian rhythm and the sleep-wake schedule required by the individual's physical environment or social obligations. The key distinction from other sleep-wake disorders is that the sleep itself may be perfectly normal in architecture and quality — the problem is that it occurs at the wrong time. When individuals are allowed to sleep on their own preferred schedule, they typically sleep well; it is the collision between their internal clock and external demands that produces the distress and functional impairment warranting a clinical diagnosis.

Types

The DSM-5 identifies several subtypes of circadian rhythm sleep-wake disorder, each reflecting a different mechanism by which the internal clock and the external world fall out of alignment. Understanding these subtypes is clinically important because they differ in their typical populations, underlying causes, and treatment approaches.

  • Delayed sleep-wake phase type: Habitual sleep-wake timing is delayed, usually by 2+ hours, relative to conventional times. Common in adolescents. The individual cannot fall asleep until very late (e.g., 2-6 AM) and has difficulty waking for school or work. This is the adolescent who is mislabeled as "lazy" for sleeping through morning classes — her circadian clock is biologically shifted later, a phenomenon partly driven by pubertal hormonal changes. When allowed to sleep on her own schedule (e.g., during summer break), she sleeps normally and feels rested.
  • Advanced sleep-wake phase type: Habitual sleep-wake timing is advanced. More common in older adults. Individuals fall asleep and wake very early (e.g., sleep at 6-8 PM, wake at 2-5 AM). Picture a retired grandfather who falls asleep during the evening news at 7 PM and is wide awake, frustrated, at 3 AM with nothing to do — this is the mirror image of the delayed type, and it tends to become more prevalent with aging as the circadian system shifts earlier.
  • Shift work type: Insomnia and/or excessive sleepiness due to a work schedule that overlaps the usual sleep period. The night-shift nurse described above exemplifies this type. Her body's circadian system is promoting wakefulness during her work hours and sleep during her off hours — exactly the opposite of what her schedule demands. This type carries significant health risks, including increased rates of cardiovascular disease, metabolic disorders, and accidents.
  • Jet lag type: Sleepiness and alertness occurring at inappropriate times relative to local time after travel across time zones. A psychologist flying from New York to Tokyo may find herself wide awake at 2 AM local time and struggling to keep her eyes open during an afternoon conference — her circadian clock is still operating on Eastern Standard Time. Eastward travel (which requires advancing the clock) is generally harder to adapt to than westward travel.
  • Non-24-hour sleep-wake type: Pattern of sleep-wake cycles not synchronized to the 24-hour environment. Most common in blind individuals lacking light input to the suprachiasmatic nucleus. Because the endogenous circadian period is slightly longer than 24 hours (approximately 24.2 hours), individuals without photic entrainment gradually drift, falling asleep progressively later each day in a free-running pattern that cycles in and out of alignment with conventional schedules.

For the EPPP, remember that the delayed type is most strongly associated with adolescence, the advanced type with older adulthood, and the non-24-hour type with blindness. The shift work and jet lag types are situational — driven by external schedule demands rather than an intrinsic clock abnormality — but they can nonetheless produce clinically significant impairment requiring intervention.

Clinical Pearl

The suprachiasmatic nucleus (SCN) of the hypothalamus is the master circadian pacemaker — a tiny paired nucleus sitting just above the optic chiasm that orchestrates the body's roughly 24-hour biological rhythms. It is primarily entrained (synchronized) by light input via the retinohypothalamic tract, which is why light is the single most powerful tool for resetting circadian timing. Melatonin, produced by the pineal gland under SCN control, promotes sleep onset and is used therapeutically for circadian rhythm disorders. Its secretion is suppressed by light and increases in darkness, earning it the nickname "the hormone of darkness." Clinically, light therapy (bright light exposure in the morning) is the primary treatment for delayed sleep-wake phase disorder, and strategically timed melatonin administration can complement this approach. Notably, bright light therapy is also a first-line treatment for seasonal affective disorder — a connection that underscores the profound influence of circadian mechanisms on both sleep and mood.

section_html:
Gender Dysphoria

Gender dysphoria refers to the distress that may accompany the incongruence between one's experienced or expressed gender and one's assigned gender. DSM-5 renamed this from "gender identity disorder" to emphasize that gender nonconformity is not itself a disorder -- the clinical problem is the distress (dysphoria) that may accompany it.

Criteria in Children

Requires at least 6 of 8 criteria over at least 6 months, including a strong desire to be of the other gender or insistence that one is the other gender (or some alternative gender). Other criteria include strong preference for cross-gender roles in play, toys, and activities; strong preference for playmates of the other gender; strong rejection of typically gendered toys/activities; strong dislike of one's sexual anatomy; and strong desire for primary/secondary sex characteristics matching experienced gender.

Criteria in Adolescents and Adults

Requires at least 2 of 6 criteria over at least 6 months: marked incongruence between experienced/expressed gender and primary/secondary sex characteristics, strong desire to be rid of one's sex characteristics, strong desire for sex characteristics of the other gender, strong desire to be the other gender, strong desire to be treated as the other gender, and strong conviction that one has the typical feelings and reactions of the other gender.

Gottman's Research on Marital Interaction and Divorce Prediction

While Carter and McGoldrick's model addresses normative family transitions, John Gottman's longitudinal research on marital interaction provides critical insight into what predicts relationship dissolution at any stage. Through detailed observational coding of couples' conflict discussions, Gottman and Levenson identified four particularly destructive communication patterns, which Gottman termed the "Four Horsemen of the Apocalypse": criticism (attacking a partner's character rather than addressing a specific behavior), defensiveness (deflecting responsibility and counter-attacking), stonewalling (withdrawing from interaction and refusing to engage), and contempt.

Of these four toxic behaviors, contempt emerged as the most corrosive to relationship stability and the single strongest predictor of eventual divorce. Contempt differs from simple criticism in that it conveys hostility, disgust, and a fundamental disrespect for the partner as a person. It is expressed through sarcasm, mockery, eye-rolling, sneering, name-calling, and other behaviors that communicate superiority and disdain. Contempt signals a collapse of admiration and positive regard within the relationship, making constructive conflict resolution nearly impossible. Gottman's research demonstrated that he could predict divorce with remarkably high accuracy based on the ratio of positive to negative interactions during conflict, with contempt carrying the greatest predictive weight among negative behaviors.

Clinical Note

In couples therapy, the presence of contempt is a significant warning sign. Unlike criticism, which targets specific behaviors, contempt targets the partner's core identity and worth. Effective intervention often requires rebuilding a "culture of appreciation" within the relationship—helping partners recall and express fondness and admiration—before productive conflict management skills can take hold. When contempt is deeply entrenched and one or both partners are unwilling to shift this stance, the prognosis for the relationship is considerably poorer.

Clinical Pearl

The DSM-5 removal of "disorder" from the diagnostic name reflects the movement to depathologize gender diversity. The diagnosis exists primarily to enable access to medical treatment (hormone therapy, surgical interventions) and is distinct from sexual orientation. Research shows that gender dysphoria in childhood persists into adulthood in approximately 12-27% of cases, but persistence rates are much higher when dysphoria intensifies during adolescence (Steensma et al., 2013).

rewritten_html:
Gender Dysphoria

Having examined the etiology and treatment approaches for paraphilic disorders, we turn now to a diagnostic category that underwent one of the most significant reconceptualizations in the transition from DSM-IV to DSM-5. Consider a 14-year-old adolescent who has felt, for as long as they can remember, that their body does not match who they are inside. This incongruence isn't a matter of preference or curiosity — it is a source of profound, persistent distress that affects their daily functioning, social relationships, and emotional well-being. It is this distress, not the gender nonconformity itself, that defines the clinical condition we now call gender dysphoria.

Gender dysphoria refers to the distress that may accompany the incongruence between one's experienced or expressed gender and one's assigned gender. In a landmark shift, DSM-5 renamed this condition from "gender identity disorder" to emphasize a crucial distinction: gender nonconformity is not itself a mental disorder. Many individuals whose experienced gender differs from their assigned gender live full, healthy lives without clinically significant distress. The clinical problem, when it exists, is the dysphoria — the suffering, the anguish, the functional impairment that can accompany the felt mismatch between one's body and one's identity. This renaming was not merely semantic; it reflected a broader movement within psychiatry and psychology to depathologize gender diversity while still providing a diagnostic framework for individuals who need clinical support and access to gender-affirming medical care.

Criteria in Children

Diagnosing gender dysphoria in children requires careful attention to both the breadth and persistence of the child's experience. Imagine a six-year-old assigned male at birth who consistently and emphatically states, "I am a girl," who gravitates exclusively toward stereotypically feminine toys and activities, who prefers female playmates, and who expresses intense discomfort with their physical anatomy. The DSM-5 requires at least 6 of 8 criteria to be met over a period of at least 6 months. One criterion is considered essential: a strong desire to be of the other gender or insistence that one is the other gender (or some alternative gender different from the assigned gender). The remaining criteria capture a constellation of associated experiences, including a strong preference for cross-gender roles in make-believe play or fantasy; a strong preference for toys, games, and activities stereotypically associated with the other gender; a strong preference for playmates of the other gender; a strong rejection of toys, games, and activities typical of one's assigned gender; a strong dislike of one's sexual anatomy; and a strong desire for the primary or secondary sex characteristics that match one's experienced gender.

The high threshold of six out of eight criteria reflects the clinical reality that many children engage in some degree of gender-nonconforming behavior as a normal part of development. The DSM-5 criteria are designed to distinguish transient or partial gender exploration — which is common and developmentally typical — from the more pervasive, persistent, and distressing pattern that characterizes gender dysphoria as a clinical condition. Clinicians must also assess whether the child's experience is accompanied by clinically significant distress or impairment in social, school, or other important areas of functioning.

Criteria in Adolescents and Adults

The diagnostic criteria shift somewhat for adolescents and adults, reflecting the different developmental landscape in which gender dysphoria manifests after childhood. A young adult, for example, may describe an overwhelming sense that their secondary sex characteristics — breasts, facial hair, voice pitch — feel fundamentally wrong, alien to their sense of self. They may experience intense longing for the physical characteristics of a different gender and a deep conviction that their internal emotional life aligns with a gender other than the one they were assigned at birth. For this age group, the DSM-5 requires at least 2 of 6 criteria to be present for at least 6 months. These criteria include: a marked incongruence between one's experienced or expressed gender and one's primary and/or secondary sex characteristics; a strong desire to be rid of one's sex characteristics because of this incongruence; a strong desire for the sex characteristics of the other gender; a strong desire to be of the other gender (or some alternative gender); a strong desire to be treated as the other gender; and a strong conviction that one has the typical feelings and reactions of the other gender.

Notice that the threshold is lower for adolescents and adults (2 of 6) compared to children (6 of 8). This design reflects the recognition that by adolescence and adulthood, gender identity has consolidated considerably, and even two persistent markers of incongruence paired with clinically significant distress represent a meaningful clinical presentation. The condition must also be associated with clinically significant distress or impairment in social, occupational, or other important areas of functioning — a requirement that again underscores the DSM-5's emphasis on dysphoria rather than identity difference as the clinical target.

Gottman's Research on Marital Interaction and Divorce Prediction

While Carter and McGoldrick's model addresses normative family transitions, John Gottman's longitudinal research on marital interaction provides critical insight into what predicts relationship dissolution at any stage. Through detailed observational coding of couples' conflict discussions, Gottman and Levenson identified four particularly destructive communication patterns, which Gottman termed the "Four Horsemen of the Apocalypse": criticism (attacking a partner's character rather than addressing a specific behavior), defensiveness (deflecting responsibility and counter-attacking), stonewalling (withdrawing from interaction and refusing to engage), and contempt.

Of these four toxic behaviors, contempt emerged as the most corrosive to relationship stability and the single strongest predictor of eventual divorce. Contempt differs from simple criticism in that it conveys hostility, disgust, and a fundamental disrespect for the partner as a person. It is expressed through sarcasm, mockery, eye-rolling, sneering, name-calling, and other behaviors that communicate superiority and disdain. Contempt signals a collapse of admiration and positive regard within the relationship, making constructive conflict resolution nearly impossible. Gottman's research demonstrated that he could predict divorce with remarkably high accuracy based on the ratio of positive to negative interactions during conflict, with contempt carrying the greatest predictive weight among negative behaviors.

Clinical Note

In couples therapy, the presence of contempt is a significant warning sign. Unlike criticism, which targets specific behaviors, contempt targets the partner's core identity and worth. Effective intervention often requires rebuilding a "culture of appreciation" within the relationship—helping partners recall and express fondness and admiration—before productive conflict management skills can take hold. When contempt is deeply entrenched and one or both partners are unwilling to shift this stance, the prognosis for the relationship is considerably poorer.

Clinical Pearl

The DSM-5 removal of "disorder" from the diagnostic name reflects the movement to depathologize gender diversity. The diagnosis exists primarily to enable access to medical treatment (hormone therapy, surgical interventions) and is distinct from sexual orientation. Research shows that gender dysphoria in childhood persists into adulthood in approximately 12-27% of cases, but persistence rates are much higher when dysphoria intensifies during adolescence (Steensma et al., 2013). This finding has important clinical implications: clinicians working with prepubertal children should be cautious about making definitive predictions, while the intensification of dysphoria at puberty — when secondary sex characteristics begin to develop — is a strong indicator of persistence. Understanding these developmental trajectories is essential for guiding families and making informed decisions about the timing and appropriateness of gender-affirming interventions.

section_html:
Adjustment Disorders

Adjustment disorders involve the development of emotional or behavioral symptoms in response to an identifiable stressor occurring within 3 months of the onset of the stressor. Symptoms must be clinically significant (out of proportion to the stressor or causing significant impairment) and must resolve within 6 months of the termination of the stressor.

Subtypes

  • With depressed mood
  • With anxiety
  • With mixed anxiety and depressed mood
  • With disturbance of conduct
  • With mixed disturbance of emotions and conduct
  • Unspecified
