Consider a clinical example: you've conducted a custody evaluation, and one parent demands the raw data, stating they intend to post the other parent's responses on social media. Here, releasing the data could cause substantial harm — both to the other parent and potentially to the integrity of the assessment process. In such a scenario, you could ethically withhold the data despite having a signed release. But notice the careful language of the standard: this is a "may" provision, not a "shall." It gives you discretion, not a mandate. And critically, you must remain aware that applicable laws — such as HIPAA, which generally treats test data as part of the medical record — may override your ethical judgment and require release regardless. This intersection of ethics and law is a favorite EPPP testing point.

9.04(b) -- Absent Client Release

What happens when there is no signed client release? Perhaps the client refuses to authorize disclosure, or perhaps the request comes from a third party with no release on file. In the absence of a client release, psychologists provide test data only as required by law or court order. This is a firm boundary: without legal compulsion, you do not release test data to anyone the client hasn't authorized. A requesting attorney, an insurance company, or even another psychologist has no right to the data without either client consent or a legal mandate. This provision underscores the fundamental principle that test data, because they contain intimate details of a client's psychological functioning, deserve robust confidentiality protections.

For example, if a forensic psychologist receives a subpoena (not a court order) for test data and the client has not signed a release, the psychologist should not automatically comply. A subpoena is issued by an attorney, not a judge, and does not carry the same legal force as a court order. The appropriate response is typically to notify the client, seek legal guidance, and — if necessary — assert the privilege on the client's behalf until a judge rules on the matter. Understanding the difference between a subpoena and a court order in the context of releasing test data is essential both for ethical practice and for EPPP success.

Test Data vs. Test Materials

Test data (9.04) = the client's responses, scores, and behavioral observations -- generally released to the client upon request. Test materials (9.11) = the test itself (questions, stimuli, manuals, scoring keys) -- protected from release to maintain test security. A helpful mnemonic: test data are about the person; test materials are about the test. If a document would exist regardless of which client sat down — such as a test manual or a blank answer sheet — it is a test material. If it was created because this particular client participated — such as their scores, their specific answers, or your behavioral observations — it is test data. This distinction is frequently tested on the EPPP.

section_html:
Standard 9.10: Explaining Assessment Results

Regardless of whether the scoring and interpretation are done by psychologists, by employees or assistants, or by automated or other outside services, psychologists take reasonable steps to ensure that explanations of results are given to the individual or designated representative unless the nature of the relationship precludes provision of an explanation of results (such as in some organizational consulting, preemployment or security screenings, and forensic evaluations), and this fact has been clearly explained to the person being assessed in advance.

EPPP Tip

The default rule is that assessment results should be explained to the individual. Exceptions exist for organizational, forensic, and security contexts -- but only when the person was informed in advance that results would not be shared with them. The EPPP tests whether you understand both the rule and its exceptions.
prev_heading_text: Standard 9.09: Test Scoring and Interpretation Services
prev_last_paragraph: Psychologists who use computer-based test interpretation services must understand the limitations of such services. Automated interpretations are probabilistic statements based on group data and may not apply to a specific individual. The psychologist, not the computer program, is responsible for the final clinical interpretation.
rewritten_html:
Standard 9.10: Explaining Assessment Results

Imagine a client who has just completed a lengthy neuropsychological battery — three hours of testing that felt exhausting and, at times, anxiety-provoking. The testing is finished, the scores are computed, and now the client sits across from you and asks the most natural question in the world: "So, what did you find?" How you handle that moment — whether you provide a clear, compassionate explanation of what the results mean — is not merely good clinical practice. It is an ethical obligation codified in Standard 9.10 of the APA Ethics Code.

Having just explored the responsibilities psychologists carry when using scoring and interpretation services (Standard 9.09), we now turn to what happens after the numbers are generated: communicating those results to the people they belong to. No matter how sophisticated our instruments or how accurate our computer-generated interpretations, the assessment process remains incomplete until the person who was assessed understands what the findings mean for them.

Standard 9.10 establishes a clear default expectation: psychologists take reasonable steps to ensure that explanations of results are provided to the individual being assessed or to a designated representative. This obligation holds regardless of who actually scored and interpreted the test — whether the psychologist did it personally, delegated it to a trained employee or assistant, or used an automated or outside scoring service. The psychologist retains responsibility for ensuring that a meaningful explanation reaches the client.

Consider a school psychologist who administers a cognitive and achievement battery to a 9-year-old. The child's parents are the designated representatives, and Standard 9.10 requires the psychologist to take reasonable steps to explain the results to them in language they can understand — not simply mail home a printout of standard scores. Similarly, when a clinical psychologist administers a personality assessment to an adult therapy client, the psychologist should provide feedback that helps the client understand the findings and how they connect to treatment planning. This feedback session is often one of the most therapeutically powerful moments in the entire assessment process.

However, the standard recognizes that certain professional contexts create legitimate exceptions to this default rule. In some organizational consulting arrangements, preemployment or security screenings, and forensic evaluations, the nature of the professional relationship may preclude sharing results directly with the person assessed. A forensic psychologist conducting a competency-to-stand-trial evaluation for the court, for example, may not be in a position to provide a detailed explanation of findings to the defendant. A psychologist screening applicants for a law enforcement agency may report results only to the hiring authority. These are legitimate exceptions — but they come with a critical caveat: the person being assessed must be clearly informed in advance that they will not receive an explanation of results. This advance notification transforms what might otherwise feel like a baffling or unfair withholding of information into a transparent, ethically grounded boundary.

EPPP Tip

The default rule is that assessment results should be explained to the individual. Exceptions exist for organizational, forensic, and security contexts — but only when the person was informed in advance that results would not be shared with them. The EPPP tests whether you understand both the rule and its exceptions. When facing exam questions on this standard, look for answer choices that emphasize the two-part structure: (1) the general obligation to explain results, and (2) the requirement for prior notification when that obligation will not apply. A wrong answer on the exam often presents a scenario where the psychologist withholds results without having provided advance notice — that is the ethical violation the standard is designed to prevent.

section_html:
Standard 9.11: Maintaining Test Security

The term test materials refers to manuals, instruments, protocols, and test questions or stimuli. Psychologists make reasonable efforts to maintain the integrity and security of test materials and other assessment techniques consistent with law and contractual obligations, and in a manner that permits adherence to this Ethics Code.

Balancing Security and Client Rights

Test security concerns must be balanced against clients' rights to access their own data (9.04). The distinction between test data (which can be released to clients) and test materials (which should be protected) is critical. For example:

  • A client may receive their scores and responses (test data)
  • A client should not receive the test manual, scoring key, or stimulus materials (test materials)
  • When test data are intertwined with test materials (e.g., a response booklet that includes test questions), the psychologist must use professional judgment to balance client rights with test security
prev_last_paragraph: The default rule is that assessment results should be explained to the individual. Exceptions exist for organizational, forensic, and security contexts -- but only when the person was informed in advance that results would not be shared with them. The EPPP tests whether you understand both the rule and its exceptions.
rewritten_html:
Standard 9.11: Maintaining Test Security

Imagine a scenario: a client's attorney demands a complete copy of a neuropsychological test battery — not just the scores and responses, but the actual test booklets, stimulus cards, and scoring keys. If you hand everything over, the test is effectively compromised for future use — any future examinee who gains access to those materials could prepare responses in advance, rendering the instrument useless. But if you refuse entirely, you may appear to be withholding information the client has a right to see. This tension — between protecting the instruments that make valid assessment possible and honoring the rights of the people we assess — is exactly what Standard 9.11 addresses.

The term test materials refers to manuals, instruments, protocols, and test questions or stimuli — essentially, the proprietary components that make a test function as a standardized measurement tool. These materials often represent decades of research, careful norming, and significant financial investment by test publishers. Once compromised, a test may lose its validity entirely, which harms not just the publisher but every future client who might have benefited from an accurate assessment. Under Standard 9.11, psychologists are required to make reasonable efforts to maintain the integrity and security of test materials and other assessment techniques, doing so in a manner consistent with law, contractual obligations, and the broader Ethics Code.

Note the language carefully: the standard says "reasonable efforts," not absolute protection at all costs. This phrasing acknowledges that psychologists operate within legal systems that may, at times, compel disclosure. A court order, for instance, might override a psychologist's preference to keep materials secure. But even in such cases, the psychologist should advocate for protective measures — such as having materials reviewed only by a qualified professional rather than entered into open court records — to minimize unnecessary exposure.

Balancing Security and Client Rights

This is where the EPPP loves to test your understanding of a distinction introduced earlier in the Ethics Code (Standard 9.04): the difference between test data and test materials. These two categories may seem straightforward in theory, but in clinical practice they overlap in ways that demand careful professional judgment. Test security concerns must be balanced against clients' legitimate rights to access their own data, and getting this balance wrong — in either direction — can create serious ethical and legal problems.

Think of it this way: a client who completed an IQ assessment has a right to know their scores, to understand how they performed, and to obtain their responses if they request them. That information belongs in the domain of test data — it is about the client. But the test manual that explains how to administer and score the WAIS, the scoring algorithms, and the actual test questions themselves? Those are test materials — they belong to the instrument, not to the individual examinee. Releasing them would jeopardize the test's utility for everyone. Here is how the distinction plays out in practice:

  • A client may receive their scores and responses (test data)
  • A client should not receive the test manual, scoring key, or stimulus materials (test materials)
  • When test data are intertwined with test materials (e.g., a response booklet that includes test questions), the psychologist must use professional judgment to balance client rights with test security

That third bullet point is the one that generates the most exam questions — and the most real-world headaches. Consider a projective test response form where the client's answers are written directly on pages that also contain the test stimuli. You cannot release one without the other. In such cases, the psychologist might redact the stimulus portions, provide a summary of responses rather than the raw form, or release materials only to another qualified professional who can interpret them appropriately. The key principle the EPPP expects you to grasp is that neither test security nor client access is an absolute trump card; rather, psychologists must navigate the tension thoughtfully, document their reasoning, and aim for solutions that honor both values to the greatest extent possible.

section_html:
Standard 2.02: Providing Services in Emergencies

In emergencies, when psychologists are asked to provide services to individuals for whom other mental health services are not available, psychologists may provide such services to ensure that services are not denied. The services are discontinued as soon as the emergency has ended or appropriate services are available.

EPPP Tip

Standard 2.02 is the emergency exception to competence boundaries. On the EPPP, if a question describes a crisis situation (e.g., a natural disaster) where no other provider is available, the psychologist may provide services outside their typical area of competence. However, this is temporary -- they must stop once the emergency ends or a qualified provider is found.
prev_last_paragraph: When assuming forensic roles, psychologists must be knowledgeable about the judicial or administrative rules governing their participation.
rewritten_html:
Standard 2.02: Providing Services in Emergencies

Having established that psychologists must practice within clearly defined boundaries of competence, an important question naturally arises: What happens when a crisis erupts and no one else is available to help? Imagine a devastating hurricane strikes a coastal community. Evacuation shelters overflow with traumatized families, children separated from parents, and individuals experiencing acute psychotic episodes. The community's few mental health providers have evacuated or are themselves displaced. A psychologist who specializes in neuropsychological assessment — someone who has never conducted crisis intervention or disaster mental health work — arrives at a shelter as a volunteer. People desperately need psychological support right now. Should this psychologist turn them away because trauma intervention falls outside their typical scope of practice?

Standard 2.02 answers this question with a compassionate and practical provision. In emergencies, when individuals need psychological services and no other mental health professionals are available to provide them, psychologists may deliver services outside their usual areas of competence to ensure that people in crisis are not left without care. This standard recognizes a fundamental ethical reality: rigidly adhering to competence boundaries while someone suffers a preventable psychological crisis would itself constitute an ethical failure. The APA Ethics Code balances the imperative to practice competently with the imperative to prevent harm through inaction.

Critically, this emergency exception carries a built-in time limit. The psychologist must discontinue these services as soon as the emergency ends or as soon as appropriately trained providers become available — whichever comes first. The neuropsychologist volunteering at the hurricane shelter provides crisis counseling and psychological first aid for the duration of the acute disaster, but once trauma-specialized clinicians arrive or the emergency phase passes, that psychologist steps back and returns to their area of expertise. This provision is not a permanent expansion of one's competence — it is a temporary bridge that ensures no one falls through the cracks during a crisis.

Consider another scenario: a psychologist who works exclusively with adults in a private practice encounters a situation at a community health center during a regional emergency where the only patients seeking help are young children exhibiting acute stress reactions. Under ordinary circumstances, this psychologist would refer those children to a child specialist. But during the emergency, with no child psychologists available, Standard 2.02 permits — and arguably encourages — the psychologist to provide whatever supportive services they can. The ethical obligation to help in a crisis temporarily supersedes the usual requirement to stay within one's defined competence boundaries.

EPPP Tip

Standard 2.02 is the emergency exception to competence boundaries. On the EPPP, if a question describes a crisis situation (e.g., a natural disaster) where no other provider is available, the psychologist may provide services outside their typical area of competence. However, this is temporary — they must stop once the emergency ends or a qualified provider is found. Watch for answer choices that frame this as an absolute rule ("a psychologist must never practice outside their competence"); the emergency exception makes such absolutes incorrect. Also note that both conditions must be present: there must be a genuine emergency, and other appropriate services must be unavailable. A psychologist cannot invoke this standard simply because a situation feels urgent if qualified providers are accessible.

section_html:
Scope of Practice

Scope of practice refers to the legally defined range of activities that a licensed professional is authorized to perform. Scope of practice is established by state licensing laws and varies across jurisdictions.

Competence vs. Scope of Practice

These are related but distinct concepts:

Competence (Ethical)Scope of Practice (Legal)
Defined by the Ethics Code and professional standardsDefined by state statutes and licensing regulations
Based on individual training, education, and experienceBased on the profession's legally permitted activities
Self-assessed and regulated by professional normsExternally imposed by law and regulation
Can be narrower than scope of practiceSets the outer boundary of permitted practice
Example

A state's scope of practice for psychologists may include neuropsychological assessment. However, a psychologist trained only in clinical therapy has not established individual competence in neuropsychological assessment, even though it falls within the profession's legal scope of practice. The psychologist should not perform neuropsychological assessments without obtaining appropriate training.
prev_last_paragraph: EPPP questions about impaired psychologists test whether you know that the ethical response involves the psychologist taking responsibility for their own impairment. The first step is self-awareness; the second is taking appropriate corrective action (consultation, therapy, limiting practice). Colleagues who become aware of an impaired psychologist should attempt informal resolution (Standard 1.04) by speaking to the psychologist directly.
rewritten_html:
Scope of Practice

Having explored the ethical obligations surrounding competence — from maintaining boundaries of expertise to managing personal problems that could impair professional functioning — we now arrive at a concept that sits at the intersection of ethics and law. Consider this scenario: a clinical psychologist licensed in Oregon relocates to Texas. She has years of experience, strong training, and excellent clinical skills. But when she reviews Texas licensing regulations, she discovers that certain activities she routinely performed in Oregon are not included in the Texas scope of practice for psychologists. Despite being fully competent, she is not legally authorized to perform those activities in her new state. This distinction — between what you are trained to do and what the law says you may do — is one of the most tested concepts on the EPPP and one of the most consequential in real-world practice.

Scope of practice refers to the legally defined range of activities that a licensed professional is authorized to perform. Unlike competence, which is grounded in individual training and ethical standards, scope of practice is established by state licensing laws and varies across jurisdictions. A psychologist practicing in one state may have prescriptive authority, while a psychologist in a neighboring state does not — not because of differences in training, but because of differences in law. Understanding where scope of practice begins and ends is essential for ethical and legal practice, and for answering EPPP questions that probe the distinction between ethical obligations and legal boundaries.

Competence vs. Scope of Practice

These two concepts are closely related, and EPPP questions frequently test whether you can distinguish between them. Think of scope of practice as the outer legal fence around an entire profession's permitted activities, while competence is the smaller, individualized space within that fence where a particular psychologist is ethically qualified to work. A psychologist might be legally permitted to conduct forensic evaluations under state law, but if she has never received forensic training, she lacks the individual competence to do so ethically. Conversely, a psychologist might have extensive competence in an area — say, prescribing psychotropic medications after completing specialized training — but if her state's scope of practice laws do not authorize psychologists to prescribe, she cannot legally do so regardless of her expertise. The table below crystallizes these distinctions:

Competence (Ethical)Scope of Practice (Legal)
Defined by the Ethics Code and professional standardsDefined by state statutes and licensing regulations
Based on individual training, education, and experienceBased on the profession's legally permitted activities
Self-assessed and regulated by professional normsExternally imposed by law and regulation
Can be narrower than scope of practiceSets the outer boundary of permitted practice

Notice the asymmetry in the last row: a psychologist's individual competence can be — and often is — narrower than the profession's legal scope of practice. You are not expected to be competent in every activity your license theoretically permits. However, competence should never exceed scope of practice; no amount of training authorizes you to perform activities that your state's laws reserve for other professions. On the EPPP, the correct answer almost always recognizes that both conditions must be met: the activity must fall within the legal scope of practice, and the individual psychologist must possess the competence to perform it.

Example

A state's scope of practice for psychologists may include neuropsychological assessment. However, a psychologist trained only in clinical therapy has not established individual competence in neuropsychological assessment, even though it falls within the profession's legal scope of practice. The psychologist should not perform neuropsychological assessments without obtaining appropriate training. Now flip the scenario: imagine a psychologist with extensive neuropsychological training relocates to a jurisdiction where the scope of practice statute does not explicitly include neuropsychological assessment as a permitted activity for psychologists. Despite her deep competence, she would need to verify her legal authority before proceeding — because competence without legal authorization is not sufficient.

section_html:
Detailed Coverage of Each Standard

Each of the ten Ethical Standards is covered in detail in its own chapter. Standard 1 (Resolving Ethical Issues) is covered in the next chapter. Standards 2 through 8 each have dedicated chapters in Part A of this domain, while Standards 9 (Assessment) and 10 (Therapy) are also covered separately.
prev_last_paragraph: The ten Ethical Standards are the enforceable component of the Ethics Code. Each standard contains multiple subsections addressing specific behaviors and obligations.
rewritten_html:
Detailed Coverage of Each Standard

Now that you have a panoramic view of the ten Ethical Standards and their enforceable role in the Ethics Code, you may be wondering: how deeply should I understand each one? The answer — especially for the EPPP — is thoroughly. Each standard governs a distinct domain of professional conduct, from how you handle ethical dilemmas to how you conduct therapy, and each carries its own nuances, gray areas, and clinical implications that deserve careful exploration. Rather than compressing all of that complexity into a single chapter, this textbook dedicates an entire chapter to each standard so you can engage with the material at the depth the exam and your future practice demand.

The next chapter begins with Standard 1 (Resolving Ethical Issues), which fittingly addresses what psychologists should do when they encounter or suspect ethical violations — a natural starting point for any clinician building an ethical decision-making framework. From there, Standards 2 through 8 each receive dedicated chapters in Part A of this domain, walking you through competence, human relations, privacy and confidentiality, advertising, record keeping, education and training, and research. Standards 9 (Assessment) and 10 (Therapy) — the two standards you will encounter most frequently in day-to-day clinical work — also receive their own separate, in-depth coverage. Think of the chapters ahead as a guided tour through each standard, complete with clinical scenarios, common exam pitfalls, and the kind of concrete examples that transform abstract rules into intuitive professional habits.

section_html:
Pharmacokinetics (ADME)

Pharmacokinetics

Pharmacokinetics describes "what the body does to the drug" -- the processes of Absorption, Distribution, Metabolism, and Excretion (ADME) that determine a drug's concentration at its site of action over time.

Absorption

Absorption is the process by which a drug enters the bloodstream from its site of administration. For oral medications (the most common route for psychotropics), the drug must dissolve in the GI tract, cross the intestinal epithelium, and enter the portal circulation.

  • Oral bioavailability -- the fraction of an orally administered drug that reaches systemic circulation in unchanged form. This is always less than 100% for oral drugs due to incomplete absorption and first-pass metabolism.
  • First-pass metabolism -- after oral absorption, drugs pass through the liver via the portal vein before reaching systemic circulation. The liver may metabolize a significant portion of the drug on this "first pass," substantially reducing the amount of active drug that reaches the brain. Example: some drugs (e.g., buspirone) have very low oral bioavailability due to extensive first-pass metabolism.
  • Factors affecting absorption include: drug formulation, gastric pH, food in the stomach, GI motility, and drug-drug interactions at the gut level.

Distribution

Once absorbed, the drug is distributed throughout the body via the bloodstream. Several factors determine where the drug goes and how much reaches the brain:

  • Protein binding -- many drugs bind to plasma proteins (primarily albumin). Only the unbound (free) fraction is pharmacologically active, able to cross membranes, and available for metabolism. Drugs with high protein binding (e.g., >95%) may be displaced by other protein-bound drugs, leading to transient increases in the free fraction and potentially toxic effects.
  • Blood-brain barrier (BBB) -- a selective, semi-permeable barrier formed by tight junctions between brain capillary endothelial cells. Psychotropic medications must cross the BBB to exert their CNS effects. Lipophilic (fat-soluble), small, and uncharged molecules cross more readily. The BBB is the primary reason that many peripherally active drugs do not cause CNS side effects.
  • Volume of distribution (Vd) -- a theoretical measure of the total body space available to a drug. A large Vd indicates the drug distributes extensively into tissues (e.g., is highly lipophilic); a small Vd indicates it stays mostly in the plasma. Highly lipophilic psychotropics (e.g., diazepam) have large volumes of distribution and may accumulate in adipose tissue.

Metabolism (Biotransformation)

Drug metabolism, primarily occurring in the liver, converts drugs into more water-soluble compounds that can be excreted. Metabolism occurs in two phases:

  • Phase I reactions -- oxidation, reduction, and hydrolysis reactions that introduce or expose a functional group on the drug molecule. The most important Phase I enzymes are the cytochrome P450 (CYP450) family. Phase I reactions may produce active metabolites (e.g., fluoxetine is metabolized to the active metabolite norfluoxetine).
  • Phase II reactions -- conjugation reactions (glucuronidation, sulfation, acetylation) that attach a large polar group to the drug or its Phase I metabolite, making it highly water-soluble and readily excreted. Phase II metabolites are almost always pharmacologically inactive.
EPPP Tip

Some drugs (called prodrugs) are inactive when administered and must be metabolized to their active form. Others produce active metabolites that extend the drug's duration of action (e.g., fluoxetine's metabolite norfluoxetine has a half-life of 4-16 days). The distinction between Phase I and Phase II metabolism is commonly tested.

Excretion (Elimination)

Excretion is the removal of drugs and their metabolites from the body. The two primary routes are:

  • Renal excretion -- the kidneys filter water-soluble metabolites into the urine. This is the primary route for most drug metabolites. Impaired renal function can lead to drug accumulation and toxicity. Lithium, which is not metabolized but excreted entirely by the kidneys, is a critical example -- renal impairment, dehydration, or sodium depletion can cause dangerous lithium accumulation.
  • Hepatic (biliary) excretion -- some drugs are excreted into bile and eliminated in the feces. Some undergo enterohepatic recirculation, where the drug is reabsorbed from the intestines, effectively prolonging its duration of action.
prev_last_paragraph: Before studying individual medication classes, it is essential to understand the foundational principles that govern how drugs work in the body. This chapter covers pharmacokinetics (what the body does to the drug), pharmacodynamics (what the drug does to the body), and the major neurotransmitter systems targeted by psychotropic medications. These concepts underpin every medication chapter that follows and are frequently tested on the EPPP.
rewritten_html:
Pharmacokinetics (ADME)

Imagine a patient walks into your office reporting that her new SSRI "isn't working." She's been taking it for three days. Another patient, prescribed the same medication at the same dose, develops side effects that seem disproportionately intense. A third patient takes her pill with a large breakfast and notices different effects than when she takes it on an empty stomach. What accounts for these dramatically different experiences with the same drug? The answer lies in what happens to a medication from the moment it enters the body — a journey governed by four fundamental processes that every clinician must understand.

When we talk about psychotropic medications, we often focus on what a drug does to the brain — how it changes mood, reduces anxiety, or quiets hallucinations. But before any of that can happen, the body must first process the drug through a series of steps that determine how much of it actually reaches the brain, how long it stays there, and how it eventually leaves the body. These processes — collectively called pharmacokinetics — are the biological gatekeepers that stand between a pill on the tongue and a therapeutic effect in the mind.

Pharmacokinetics

Pharmacokinetics describes "what the body does to the drug" -- the processes of Absorption, Distribution, Metabolism, and Excretion (ADME) that determine a drug's concentration at its site of action over time. Understanding ADME explains why two patients on the same medication can have vastly different responses, why dosing schedules vary across drugs, and why certain medical conditions or drug combinations create dangerous interactions.

The ADME acronym provides a natural chronological framework: a drug must first be absorbed into the bloodstream, then distributed to its target site (for psychotropics, primarily the brain), then metabolized (chemically transformed, usually in the liver), and finally excreted from the body. Each step presents opportunities for variability — and each is a source of clinically important drug interactions, side effects, and dosing considerations that appear regularly on the EPPP.

Absorption

Consider why a clinician might choose to administer an antipsychotic via intramuscular injection during a psychiatric emergency rather than handing the patient a pill. The answer centers on absorption — the very first hurdle a drug must clear. For oral medications, which represent the most common route for psychotropics, the drug must dissolve in the gastrointestinal tract, cross the intestinal epithelium, and enter the portal circulation before it can travel to the brain. This journey introduces several bottlenecks that influence how much drug ultimately becomes available to do its work.

  • Oral bioavailability -- the fraction of an orally administered drug that reaches systemic circulation in unchanged form. This is always less than 100% for oral drugs due to incomplete absorption and first-pass metabolism. A drug with 20% oral bioavailability means that 80% of what the patient swallowed was lost before it ever reached the general bloodstream — a staggering amount of "wasted" medication that the body's own filtering systems removed.
  • First-pass metabolism -- after oral absorption, drugs pass through the liver via the portal vein before reaching systemic circulation. The liver may metabolize a significant portion of the drug on this "first pass," substantially reducing the amount of active drug that reaches the brain. This is why some medications work well when injected but poorly when swallowed: buspirone, for example, has very low oral bioavailability because the liver breaks down most of the drug before it ever reaches the systemic circulation. Intravenous and intramuscular routes bypass this first-pass effect entirely, which is why injectable medications can achieve faster onset and higher bioavailability.
  • Factors affecting absorption include: drug formulation (extended-release tablets dissolve more slowly than immediate-release), gastric pH, food in the stomach (some drugs are better absorbed with food, others are hindered by it), GI motility, and drug-drug interactions at the gut level. For instance, antacids can alter gastric pH enough to change how well certain psychotropics are absorbed.

Distribution

Once a drug has been absorbed into the bloodstream, it faces the next challenge: reaching its intended destination. For psychotropic medications, that destination is the brain — an organ the body guards behind one of its most formidable barriers. But even before the drug encounters that barrier, the bloodstream itself imposes constraints on how freely the drug can travel. Distribution describes the process by which a drug spreads from the bloodstream into the body's various tissues and compartments, and several key factors determine where the drug goes and how much reaches the brain:

  • Protein binding -- many drugs bind to plasma proteins (primarily albumin). Only the unbound (free) fraction is pharmacologically active, able to cross membranes, and available for metabolism. Think of albumin as a bus carrying drug molecules through the bloodstream: passengers on the bus (bound drug) can't get off to do their work until they're released. Drugs with high protein binding (e.g., >95%) may be displaced by other protein-bound drugs competing for the same binding sites, leading to transient increases in the free fraction and potentially toxic effects. This is why clinicians must be especially cautious when adding a highly protein-bound medication to a patient's existing regimen — the new drug may "bump" the existing drug off its albumin seats, temporarily flooding the system with active drug.
  • Blood-brain barrier (BBB) -- a selective, semi-permeable barrier formed by tight junctions between brain capillary endothelial cells. Psychotropic medications must cross the BBB to exert their CNS effects. Lipophilic (fat-soluble), small, and uncharged molecules cross more readily — which is why most effective psychotropics are designed to be lipophilic. The BBB is the primary reason that many peripherally active drugs do not cause CNS side effects; they simply cannot penetrate this biological checkpoint. The BBB also explains why certain infections of the brain are so difficult to treat: many antibiotics that work well elsewhere in the body cannot cross into the CNS in therapeutic concentrations.
  • Volume of distribution (Vd) -- a theoretical measure of the total body space available to a drug. A large Vd indicates the drug distributes extensively into tissues (e.g., is highly lipophilic); a small Vd indicates it stays mostly in the plasma. Highly lipophilic psychotropics such as diazepam have large volumes of distribution and may accumulate in adipose (fat) tissue. This accumulation has clinical consequences: in obese patients or elderly individuals with higher body fat percentages, highly lipophilic drugs can be stored in fat tissue and released slowly over time, prolonging their effects in sometimes unpredictable ways.

Metabolism (Biotransformation)

After a drug has been absorbed and distributed to its site of action, the body begins the process of breaking it down — transforming it from an active, lipophilic compound into something water-soluble enough to be expelled. Drug metabolism, primarily occurring in the liver, converts drugs into more water-soluble compounds that can be excreted. This biotransformation is not a single step but unfolds in two distinct phases, each with different clinical implications:

  • Phase I reactions -- oxidation, reduction, and hydrolysis reactions that introduce or expose a functional group on the drug molecule. The most important Phase I enzymes are the cytochrome P450 (CYP450) family — a group of liver enzymes that metabolize the majority of psychotropic medications. These enzymes are clinically crucial because they are subject to genetic variability (some patients are "fast metabolizers" and others "slow metabolizers"), and they can be inhibited or induced by other drugs, foods, and substances. Phase I reactions may produce active metabolites — breakdown products that themselves have pharmacological effects. For example, fluoxetine is metabolized to the active metabolite norfluoxetine, which continues working long after the parent drug would have worn off.
  • Phase II reactions -- conjugation reactions (glucuronidation, sulfation, acetylation) that attach a large polar group to the drug or its Phase I metabolite, making it highly water-soluble and readily excreted. Phase II metabolites are almost always pharmacologically inactive. Some drugs — notably lorazepam, oxazepam, and temazepam (remembered by the mnemonic "LOT") — bypass Phase I metabolism entirely and proceed directly to Phase II conjugation, making them safer choices for patients with compromised liver function or elderly patients whose Phase I enzymes may be less efficient.
EPPP Tip

Some drugs (called prodrugs) are inactive when administered and must be metabolized to their active form. Others produce active metabolites that extend the drug's duration of action (e.g., fluoxetine's metabolite norfluoxetine has a half-life of 4-16 days). The distinction between Phase I and Phase II metabolism is commonly tested. Remember: Phase I reactions (via CYP450 enzymes) can produce active metabolites and are vulnerable to drug interactions, while Phase II conjugation reactions generally inactivate compounds and are less affected by age and liver disease. Understanding this distinction helps explain why certain benzodiazepines are preferred in elderly or hepatically impaired patients.

Excretion (Elimination)

The final chapter in a drug's journey through the body is its removal — the process of excretion. No matter how effective a medication is, the body must eventually clear it and its metabolites. The rate and route of this clearance have profound clinical implications, particularly for drugs with narrow therapeutic windows where the difference between a therapeutic dose and a toxic one is small. The two primary routes of excretion are:

  • Renal excretion -- the kidneys filter water-soluble metabolites into the urine. This is the primary route for most drug metabolites. Impaired renal function can lead to drug accumulation and toxicity, which is why kidney function (often measured by creatinine clearance) must be monitored in patients on certain medications. Lithium is the most critical example for EPPP purposes: it is not metabolized at all but is excreted entirely by the kidneys. Because the kidneys handle lithium much the way they handle sodium, anything that alters sodium balance — renal impairment, dehydration, low-sodium diets, or medications like NSAIDs and thiazide diuretics — can cause dangerous lithium accumulation and toxicity. This is one of the most frequently tested pharmacokinetic principles on the exam.
  • Hepatic (biliary) excretion -- some drugs are excreted into bile and eliminated in the feces. Some undergo enterohepatic recirculation, where the drug excreted into the bile is reabsorbed from the intestines back into the bloodstream, effectively prolonging its duration of action. This recycling loop can be clinically significant — it means that the drug stays in the body longer than simple metabolism would predict, and anything that disrupts the reabsorption (such as certain antibiotics that alter gut flora) can change the drug's effective duration.

Together, these four ADME processes form the pharmacokinetic foundation for understanding every psychotropic medication you will encounter. In the next section, we turn to two pharmacokinetic concepts that follow directly from metabolism and excretion — half-life and steady state — which are essential for understanding dosing schedules, how long drugs remain active in the body, and how quickly a medication reaches its full therapeutic effect.

section_html:
Half-Life and Steady State

Half-Life (t1/2)

Half-life is the time required for the plasma concentration of a drug to decrease by 50%. It is the single most important pharmacokinetic parameter for understanding dosing frequency, time to steady state, and duration of drug effect after discontinuation.

Key Principles

  • Steady state is reached after approximately 5 half-lives of continuous dosing. At steady state, the amount of drug being administered equals the amount being eliminated, and plasma levels plateau.
  • Similarly, after discontinuation, it takes approximately 5 half-lives for a drug to be essentially eliminated from the body (~97% eliminated).
  • Half-life determines dosing frequency: drugs with short half-lives (e.g., venlafaxine, ~5 hours) often need twice-daily or extended-release dosing, while drugs with long half-lives (e.g., fluoxetine, ~2-6 days) may be given once daily.
  • Washout period -- the time needed for a drug to be cleared from the body before starting a new medication (to avoid interactions). This is directly related to half-life. Example: the 5-week washout required when switching from fluoxetine to an MAOI reflects fluoxetine's extremely long half-life (plus its active metabolite norfluoxetine).

Clinical Significance of Half-Life

DrugApproximate Half-LifeClinical Implication
Fluoxetine2-6 days (metabolite: 4-16 days)Longest SSRI half-life; lowest risk of discontinuation syndrome; 5-week washout before MAOI
Paroxetine~21 hoursShortest SSRI half-life; highest risk of discontinuation syndrome
Venlafaxine~5 hoursVery short; severe discontinuation if missed doses; requires extended-release formulation
Diazepam20-100 hours (active metabolite: up to 200 hours)Long-acting benzo; accumulates with repeated dosing, especially in elderly
Alprazolam~11 hoursShort-acting benzo; higher abuse potential; rebound anxiety between doses
Lithium~24 hoursNarrow therapeutic index; steady state in ~5 days; blood levels must be monitored

rewritten_html:
Half-Life and Steady State

Now that we've explored how drugs are absorbed, distributed, metabolized, and excreted — the ADME framework — a natural question arises: how long does a drug actually stay active in the body? The answer to this question shapes nearly every practical decision a prescriber makes, from how often to dose a medication to how long a patient must wait before safely switching to a new drug. It also explains one of the most clinically consequential phenomena you'll encounter: discontinuation syndrome. Understanding a drug's half-life gives you a powerful lens for predicting all of these outcomes.

Consider this scenario: A patient on paroxetine for generalized anxiety forgets to take her medication for two days while traveling. By the second evening, she experiences dizziness, electric shock-like sensations ("brain zaps"), irritability, and nausea. Meanwhile, a colleague who forgot his fluoxetine for the same two days notices nothing at all. What accounts for this dramatic difference? The answer lies entirely in the concept of half-life — and once you understand it, a wide range of clinical puzzles snap into focus.

Half-Life (t1/2)

Half-life is the time required for the plasma concentration of a drug to decrease by 50%. It is the single most important pharmacokinetic parameter for understanding dosing frequency, time to steady state, and duration of drug effect after discontinuation. A drug with a half-life of 24 hours, for example, will drop from 100% to 50% of its peak concentration in one day, to 25% the next day, and so on — each interval halving what remains.

Returning to our traveling patients, paroxetine has a half-life of roughly 21 hours — the shortest among the SSRIs — meaning that within about a day and a half of a missed dose, plasma levels have already plummeted to a fraction of their therapeutic concentration. Fluoxetine, by contrast, has a half-life of 2 to 6 days, and its active metabolite norfluoxetine lingers even longer. Two missed days barely registers in the body's drug concentration curve. This single pharmacokinetic property — half-life — explains why paroxetine carries the highest risk of discontinuation syndrome among the SSRIs and why fluoxetine carries the lowest.

Key Principles

Half-life governs several interconnected clinical principles that you should commit to memory. The most important of these is the concept of steady state — the point at which drug levels in the blood have stabilized because the rate of drug intake equals the rate of elimination. Think of it like filling a bathtub with a slow drain: at first, the water level rises quickly, but eventually, the inflow and outflow balance and the water level holds constant. Here are the key principles built on this foundation:

  • Steady state is reached after approximately 5 half-lives of continuous dosing. At steady state, the amount of drug being administered equals the amount being eliminated, and plasma levels plateau.
  • Similarly, after discontinuation, it takes approximately 5 half-lives for a drug to be essentially eliminated from the body (~97% eliminated).
  • Half-life determines dosing frequency: drugs with short half-lives (e.g., venlafaxine, ~5 hours) often need twice-daily or extended-release dosing, while drugs with long half-lives (e.g., fluoxetine, ~2-6 days) may be given once daily.
  • Washout period -- the time needed for a drug to be cleared from the body before starting a new medication (to avoid interactions). This is directly related to half-life. Example: the 5-week washout required when switching from fluoxetine to an MAOI reflects fluoxetine's extremely long half-life (plus its active metabolite norfluoxetine).

The "5 half-lives" rule is one of the highest-yield facts in psychopharmacology. To make it concrete: lithium has a half-life of approximately 24 hours. When a prescriber initiates lithium therapy, they know the drug will reach steady state in roughly 5 days (5 × 24 hours). This is precisely why lithium blood levels are typically drawn about one week after starting or adjusting a dose — checking before steady state would give a misleadingly low reading. Conversely, if a patient stops taking lithium, it takes approximately 5 days for the drug to be essentially cleared from the system.

The washout period concept deserves special attention because it has direct patient safety implications. When switching a patient from fluoxetine to a monoamine oxidase inhibitor (MAOI), the prescriber must account not only for fluoxetine's long half-life but also for its active metabolite norfluoxetine, which has a half-life of 4 to 16 days. Five half-lives of norfluoxetine at the upper range translates to roughly 80 days — but the standard clinical guideline rounds to a 5-week (35-day) washout, reflecting typical metabolizer profiles. Failing to observe this washout period risks serotonin syndrome, a potentially fatal condition. This is a favorite EPPP testing point.

Clinical Significance of Half-Life

The following table summarizes the half-lives of commonly tested psychotropic medications and their most important clinical implications. As you study it, notice how the half-life value predicts almost everything that matters clinically: discontinuation risk, abuse potential, accumulation in vulnerable populations, and monitoring requirements. Pay particular attention to the contrast between fluoxetine and paroxetine — both are SSRIs, yet their dramatically different half-lives produce very different clinical profiles.

DrugApproximate Half-LifeClinical Implication
Fluoxetine2-6 days (metabolite: 4-16 days)Longest SSRI half-life; lowest risk of discontinuation syndrome; 5-week washout before MAOI
Paroxetine~21 hoursShortest SSRI half-life; highest risk of discontinuation syndrome
Venlafaxine~5 hoursVery short; severe discontinuation if missed doses; requires extended-release formulation
Diazepam20-100 hours (active metabolite: up to 200 hours)Long-acting benzo; accumulates with repeated dosing, especially in elderly
Alprazolam~11 hoursShort-acting benzo; higher abuse potential; rebound anxiety between doses
Lithium~24 hoursNarrow therapeutic index; steady state in ~5 days; blood levels must be monitored

A few clinically important patterns emerge from this table. First, notice the benzodiazepine comparison: diazepam, with its extremely long half-life and long-acting active metabolite, accumulates significantly with repeated dosing — a particular hazard for elderly patients whose hepatic metabolism is slower, leading to excessive sedation and fall risk. Alprazolam, with its much shorter half-life, creates a different problem: plasma levels drop quickly between doses, producing rebound anxiety that can drive dose escalation and dependency. Second, note that venlafaxine's remarkably short half-life of approximately 5 hours makes it one of the most common culprits for discontinuation syndrome when patients miss even a single dose — which is why extended-release formulations were developed to smooth out the drug's concentration curve. Understanding these patterns through the lens of half-life transforms what might otherwise seem like arbitrary clinical facts into predictable, logical consequences of a single pharmacokinetic parameter.

section_html:
The CYP450 Enzyme System

Cytochrome P450 (CYP450)

The CYP450 system is a superfamily of liver enzymes responsible for the Phase I metabolism of approximately 75% of all clinically used drugs. Understanding CYP450 isoenzymes is essential for predicting drug-drug interactions -- one of the most commonly tested pharmacology topics on the EPPP.

Major CYP450 Isoenzymes

IsoenzymeMajor Substrates (metabolized by)Inhibitors (slow metabolism)Inducers (speed up metabolism)
CYP2D6 Many antidepressants (fluoxetine, paroxetine, venlafaxine), antipsychotics (haloperidol, risperidone), codeine, tamoxifen Fluoxetine, paroxetine, bupropion, duloxetine No clinically significant inducers known
CYP3A4 Benzodiazepines (alprazolam, midazolam), buspirone, carbamazepine, quetiapine, many other drugs (~50% of all medications) Fluvoxamine, ketoconazole, grapefruit juice, erythromycin Carbamazepine, phenytoin, St. John's Wort, rifampin
CYP1A2 Clozapine, olanzapine, duloxetine, theophylline, caffeine Fluvoxamine, ciprofloxacin Smoking (tobacco), charbroiled foods, omeprazole
CYP2C19 Citalopram, escitalopram, diazepam, some TCAs Fluoxetine, fluvoxamine, omeprazole Carbamazepine, St. John's Wort
EPPP Tip

When a CYP450 inhibitor is co-administered with a substrate of that enzyme, the substrate's metabolism is slowed, leading to increased plasma levels and potentially toxicity. When an inducer is added, the substrate is metabolized faster, leading to decreased plasma levels and potentially therapeutic failure. Example: adding fluoxetine (CYP2D6 inhibitor) to a patient on haloperidol (CYP2D6 substrate) will raise haloperidol levels, increasing the risk of EPS and other side effects.

Pharmacogenomics: Poor vs. Extensive Metabolizers

Genetic polymorphisms in CYP450 enzymes result in significant variability in how individuals metabolize drugs. This field is known as pharmacogenomics.

  • Poor metabolizers (PMs) -- have reduced or absent enzyme activity. Drugs metabolized by that enzyme accumulate to higher levels, increasing the risk of side effects and toxicity at standard doses. Example: CYP2D6 poor metabolizers may experience toxic effects from standard doses of codeine (though paradoxically, they may get less analgesic effect from codeine, since codeine requires CYP2D6 conversion to morphine).
  • Extensive metabolizers (EMs) -- have normal enzyme activity and respond predictably to standard doses.
  • Ultrarapid metabolizers (UMs) -- have excess enzyme activity due to gene duplication. They metabolize drugs too quickly, resulting in subtherapeutic levels at standard doses. Ultrarapid CYP2D6 metabolizers may convert codeine to morphine too rapidly, leading to opioid toxicity.
Example: Pharmacogenomic Testing

The FDA has recommended pharmacogenomic testing for certain drug-gene pairs. For example, CYP2D6 genotyping is recommended before prescribing codeine (risk of ultra-rapid metabolism causing morphine toxicity) and CYP2C19 testing can guide citalopram dosing (poor metabolizers require lower doses).

rewritten_html:
The CYP450 Enzyme System

Having explored half-life and steady state — the timing of how drugs accumulate and leave the body — we now turn to a question that is equally critical: what happens to a drug while it's inside the body? More specifically, what determines how quickly or slowly a drug is broken down? The answer lies primarily in the liver, where a remarkable family of enzymes processes the vast majority of psychiatric medications. Understanding this system is not merely an academic exercise. It is the key to predicting one of the most dangerous and commonly tested phenomena in clinical pharmacology: drug-drug interactions. When a patient on haloperidol is started on fluoxetine and suddenly develops severe extrapyramidal symptoms, or when a patient's clozapine levels plummet after they resume smoking, the explanation almost always traces back to the enzyme system we are about to examine.

Cytochrome P450 (CYP450)

The CYP450 system is a superfamily of liver enzymes responsible for the Phase I metabolism of approximately 75% of all clinically used drugs. These enzymes oxidize, reduce, or hydrolyze drug molecules — essentially transforming them into more water-soluble compounds that the body can excrete. Understanding CYP450 isoenzymes is essential for predicting drug-drug interactions — one of the most commonly tested pharmacology topics on the EPPP. Each isoenzyme is identified by a number-letter-number code (e.g., CYP2D6), where the number refers to the gene family, the letter to the subfamily, and the final number to the specific gene.

The clinical significance of the CYP450 system becomes clear when you realize that many psychotropic drugs are not only metabolized by specific CYP450 isoenzymes (making them "substrates") but also inhibit or induce those same enzymes — sometimes the very ones that metabolize other drugs the patient is taking. This creates a web of potential interactions that every prescriber, and every psychologist who collaborates with prescribers, must understand. The table below summarizes the four most clinically relevant CYP450 isoenzymes and the psychiatric medications most commonly associated with each.

Major CYP450 Isoenzymes

IsoenzymeMajor Substrates (metabolized by)Inhibitors (slow metabolism)Inducers (speed up metabolism)
CYP2D6 Many antidepressants (fluoxetine, paroxetine, venlafaxine), antipsychotics (haloperidol, risperidone), codeine, tamoxifen Fluoxetine, paroxetine, bupropion, duloxetine No clinically significant inducers known
CYP3A4 Benzodiazepines (alprazolam, midazolam), buspirone, carbamazepine, quetiapine, many other drugs (~50% of all medications) Fluvoxamine, ketoconazole, grapefruit juice, erythromycin Carbamazepine, phenytoin, St. John's Wort, rifampin
CYP1A2 Clozapine, olanzapine, duloxetine, theophylline, caffeine Fluvoxamine, ciprofloxacin Smoking (tobacco), charbroiled foods, omeprazole
CYP2C19 Citalopram, escitalopram, diazepam, some TCAs Fluoxetine, fluvoxamine, omeprazole Carbamazepine, St. John's Wort

A few patterns in this table are worth highlighting. Notice that CYP3A4 is by far the most "busy" isoenzyme, handling roughly half of all medications — which means interactions involving CYP3A4 are extremely common. Notice also that several SSRIs appear repeatedly as inhibitors across multiple enzymes: fluoxetine inhibits CYP2D6 and CYP2C19, while fluvoxamine inhibits CYP3A4, CYP1A2, and CYP2C19. This makes the SSRIs particularly important to track in polypharmacy scenarios. And notice the surprising entries — grapefruit juice as a CYP3A4 inhibitor, and tobacco smoking as a CYP1A2 inducer — because these represent non-drug exposures that can dramatically alter medication levels.

EPPP Tip

When a CYP450 inhibitor is co-administered with a substrate of that enzyme, the substrate's metabolism is slowed, leading to increased plasma levels and potentially toxicity. When an inducer is added, the substrate is metabolized faster, leading to decreased plasma levels and potentially therapeutic failure. Example: adding fluoxetine (CYP2D6 inhibitor) to a patient on haloperidol (CYP2D6 substrate) will raise haloperidol levels, increasing the risk of EPS and other side effects.

A simple mnemonic can help you keep the logic straight: Inhibitors Increase levels (both start with "I"), while inducers decrease levels (think of an inducer as "inducing" the enzyme to work harder and chew through the drug faster). For exam purposes, the most high-yield clinical scenario involves a patient stabilized on one medication who is then started on a second medication that inhibits the enzyme responsible for metabolizing the first. The predictable result — rising blood levels of the first drug — can produce toxicity that mimics overdose, new-onset side effects, or worsening of existing side effects. Conversely, when a patient on clozapine (a CYP1A2 substrate) resumes smoking after a hospitalization where smoking was prohibited, the tobacco smoke induces CYP1A2, clozapine levels drop, and the patient may relapse into psychosis — a scenario that appears frequently in clinical practice and on licensing exams.

Pharmacogenomics: Poor vs. Extensive Metabolizers

The CYP450 table above assumes that every patient's enzymes work at roughly the same efficiency — but this assumption is often wrong. Imagine two patients prescribed the same dose of codeine: one experiences no pain relief whatsoever, while the other is rushed to the emergency department with life-threatening respiratory depression. Both outcomes are explained not by dosing error or patient noncompliance, but by inherited genetic variations in a single enzyme. This is the domain of pharmacogenomics — the study of how genetic polymorphisms in drug-metabolizing enzymes (and other pharmacological targets) create clinically significant variability in drug response across individuals.

Genetic polymorphisms in CYP450 enzymes result in significant variability in how individuals metabolize drugs. Clinicians and researchers categorize patients into metabolizer phenotypes based on the functional status of their CYP450 genes:

  • Poor metabolizers (PMs) — have reduced or absent enzyme activity. Drugs metabolized by that enzyme accumulate to higher levels, increasing the risk of side effects and toxicity at standard doses. Example: CYP2D6 poor metabolizers may experience toxic effects from standard doses of codeine (though paradoxically, they may get less analgesic effect from codeine, since codeine requires CYP2D6 conversion to morphine).
  • Extensive metabolizers (EMs) — have normal enzyme activity and respond predictably to standard doses.
  • Ultrarapid metabolizers (UMs) — have excess enzyme activity due to gene duplication. They metabolize drugs too quickly, resulting in subtherapeutic levels at standard doses. Ultrarapid CYP2D6 metabolizers may convert codeine to morphine too rapidly, leading to opioid toxicity.

The codeine example is particularly instructive because it illustrates a crucial nuance: the clinical consequence of being a poor or ultrarapid metabolizer depends on whether the parent drug or the metabolite is the active compound. Codeine itself is a prodrug — it has little analgesic activity until CYP2D6 converts it to morphine. Poor metabolizers therefore get inadequate pain relief (too little morphine produced), while ultrarapid metabolizers generate dangerously high morphine levels (too much, too fast). In contrast, for a drug like haloperidol — which is itself the active compound — poor metabolizers would accumulate haloperidol to toxic levels, while ultrarapid metabolizers might not achieve therapeutic blood concentrations at standard doses. Always ask yourself: Is the drug itself active, or does it need enzymatic conversion to become active?

Example: Pharmacogenomic Testing

The FDA has recommended pharmacogenomic testing for certain drug-gene pairs. For example, CYP2D6 genotyping is recommended before prescribing codeine (risk of ultra-rapid metabolism causing morphine toxicity) and CYP2C19 testing can guide citalopram dosing (poor metabolizers require lower doses).

Pharmacogenomic testing is steadily moving from a research curiosity to a clinical standard of care, particularly in psychiatry where treatment response is often unpredictable and trial-and-error prescribing carries significant costs — both in patient suffering and in treatment delay. For the EPPP, the essential takeaway is straightforward: genetic variation in CYP450 enzymes means that the "standard dose" of a medication may be too much for some patients and too little for others, and understanding a patient's metabolizer status can transform prescribing from guesswork into precision medicine. As we turn next to pharmacodynamics — what drugs do to the body rather than what the body does to drugs — keep the CYP450 system in mind, because the plasma level of a drug (shaped by CYP450 metabolism) ultimately determines how strongly that drug acts on its pharmacodynamic targets.

section_html:
Pharmacodynamics

Pharmacodynamics

Pharmacodynamics describes "what the drug does to the body" -- how a drug produces its effects by interacting with molecular targets (typically receptors) in the body.

Drug-Receptor Interactions

Most psychotropic medications exert their effects by binding to specific receptors -- protein molecules on cell surfaces or within cells that normally respond to endogenous neurotransmitters or hormones. Key concepts include:

  • Agonist -- a drug that binds to a receptor and activates it, producing a biological response. It mimics the effect of the endogenous neurotransmitter. Example: benzodiazepines are agonists at the GABA-A receptor (they enhance GABA's effect at the receptor).
  • Antagonist -- a drug that binds to a receptor and blocks it, preventing activation by the endogenous neurotransmitter. It has affinity for the receptor but no intrinsic activity (efficacy). Example: haloperidol is a dopamine D2 receptor antagonist.
  • Partial agonist -- a drug that binds to and activates a receptor but produces only a submaximal response, even at full receptor occupancy. Partial agonists can act as functional agonists in low-neurotransmitter states and as functional antagonists in high-neurotransmitter states, providing a "stabilizing" effect. Example: aripiprazole is a partial agonist at the D2 receptor; buspirone is a partial agonist at 5-HT1A.
  • Inverse agonist -- a drug that binds to a receptor and produces an effect opposite to that of an agonist. This is distinct from an antagonist, which simply blocks receptor activation. Some researchers consider certain beta-carbolines to be inverse agonists at the benzodiazepine site on GABA-A receptors (they reduce GABA activity below baseline).

Affinity and Efficacy

  • Affinity -- how strongly a drug binds to its receptor. High affinity means the drug binds tightly and at low concentrations. Both agonists and antagonists have affinity.
  • Efficacy (intrinsic activity) -- the ability of a drug to activate the receptor once bound. Full agonists have high efficacy; partial agonists have intermediate efficacy; antagonists have zero efficacy.

Dose-Response Relationships

The relationship between drug dose and the magnitude of effect is described by the dose-response curve. Key parameters include:

  • ED50 -- the dose that produces a therapeutic effect in 50% of the population (or 50% of the maximal effect in a single individual).
  • LD50 -- the dose that is lethal to 50% of the population (determined in animal studies).
  • Therapeutic index (TI) -- the ratio of LD50 to ED50 (TI = LD50 / ED50). A higher therapeutic index means a wider margin of safety.

Potency vs. Efficacy

Potency vs. Efficacy

Potency refers to the amount of drug needed to produce a given effect (related to ED50) -- a more potent drug requires a lower dose. Efficacy refers to the maximum effect a drug can produce regardless of dose. A drug can be highly potent but have low maximum efficacy (and vice versa). For clinical purposes, efficacy is generally more important than potency -- a drug that requires a higher dose but achieves a better outcome is preferable to one that works at a lower dose but has a lower ceiling of effect.

Example: Potency vs. Efficacy in Antipsychotics

Haloperidol is a high-potency antipsychotic (effective at low doses, e.g., 2-10 mg), while chlorpromazine is a low-potency antipsychotic (requires higher doses, e.g., 200-800 mg). However, at their respective optimal doses, both achieve similar efficacy in treating psychotic symptoms. The key difference lies in their side effect profiles: high-potency agents cause more EPS; low-potency agents cause more sedation, orthostatic hypotension, and anticholinergic effects.
