EPPP Note: A diagnosis of intellectual disability requires: (1) significantly subaverage intellectual functioning (typically IQ ~70 or below), (2) concurrent deficits in adaptive functioning, and (3) onset during the developmental period (before age 18). An IQ score alone is never sufficient for the diagnosis.
prev_last_paragraph: The SB5's routing procedure directly addresses floor and ceiling concerns by tailoring item difficulty to each examinee's functional level. Because examinees begin subsequent subtests at a difficulty level matched to their performance on the routing subtests, very low-ability individuals receive easier item sets that can capture fine-grained differences among them, while very high-ability individuals encounter sufficiently challenging items. The SB5's extended IQ range of 40 to 160 further mitigates these effects compared to instruments with narrower score ranges. This makes the SB5 especially well-suited for evaluating individuals at extreme ends of the distribution, such as those being assessed for intellectual giftedness or intellectual disability.
rewritten_html:
IQ Classification System

Once you have administered a Wechsler scale or the SB5 and obtained a Full Scale IQ, the next clinical question is deceptively simple: what does this number actually mean? A parent sitting across the table from you doesn't think in standard deviations — they want to know whether their child's score is "normal," whether it signals a problem, or whether it reflects a gift that deserves enrichment. Clinicians, educators, and legal professionals all rely on a shared classification system to translate raw numbers into meaningful descriptive categories, and understanding this system is essential for accurate communication and responsible decision-making.

All three of the major intelligence batteries we have discussed — the WAIS-IV, WISC-V, and SB5 — share the same metric: a mean (M) of 100 and a standard deviation (SD) of 15. This common scaling is no accident; it allows direct comparison across instruments and across the lifespan. Because IQ scores are normally distributed, the familiar bell curve tells us exactly how many people fall within each standard deviation band. Roughly 68% of the population scores between 85 and 115 (within one SD of the mean), about 95% fall between 70 and 130 (within two SDs), and approximately 99.7% score between 55 and 145 (within three SDs). These statistical properties give rise to the classification system presented below, which you will encounter repeatedly on the EPPP and in clinical practice.

IQ RangeClassificationPercentile RangePrevalence
130+Very Superior / Extremely High98th+~2.2%
120-129Superior / Very High91st-97th~6.7%
110-119High Average75th-90th~16.1%
90-109Average25th-74th~50%
80-89Low Average9th-24th~16.1%
70-79Borderline2nd-8th~6.7%
69 and belowExtremely Low / Intellectual Disability rangeBelow 2nd~2.2%

Notice the symmetry in the table: the percentages at the tails mirror each other perfectly, which is exactly what you would expect from a normal distribution. The largest group — fully half the population — clusters in the Average range (IQ 90–109). Moving one standard deviation in either direction captures an additional 16.1% on each side (High Average and Low Average, respectively). At two standard deviations from the mean, we reach the boundaries that carry particular clinical weight: an IQ of 130 or above places an individual in the Very Superior range (98th percentile and above), while an IQ of 70 or below falls in the Extremely Low range (below the 2nd percentile).

These classification labels serve as a common clinical language, but experienced practitioners know they are not rigid diagnostic cutoffs. Consider a 10-year-old who earns a Full Scale IQ of 71 on the WISC-V. That score falls in the Borderline range — just one point above the traditional threshold for "significantly subaverage intellectual functioning." Does that single point mean the child does not have an intellectual disability? Not necessarily. IQ scores carry a band of measurement error (the standard error of measurement, or SEM), and clinicians must interpret them within confidence intervals rather than treating them as fixed values. This is precisely why classification systems are guides for clinical judgment, not substitutes for it.

It is also worth noting a subtle difference in labeling conventions across test publishers. The Wechsler scales historically used terms like "Very Superior" and "Borderline," while the SB5 adopted labels such as "Extremely High" and updated other descriptors. Despite these cosmetic differences, the underlying metric and the IQ ranges associated with each classification remain the same, and EPPP questions typically treat the labels as interchangeable. What matters most is that you understand the correspondence between IQ ranges, percentile ranks, and prevalence in the population — these relationships flow directly from the properties of the normal curve and appear across virtually every standardized cognitive measure.

EPPP Note: A diagnosis of intellectual disability requires: (1) significantly subaverage intellectual functioning (typically IQ ~70 or below), (2) concurrent deficits in adaptive functioning, and (3) onset during the developmental period (before age 18). An IQ score alone is never sufficient for the diagnosis.

The clinical note above deserves special emphasis because it captures one of the most commonly tested principles on the EPPP. Imagine a forensic psychologist evaluating a defendant for intellectual disability in a capital case — the stakes could not be higher. If the defendant's IQ is 68, that score alone does not establish the diagnosis. The clinician must also demonstrate that the individual exhibits significant limitations in adaptive functioning — the practical, everyday skills needed for independent living, such as communication, self-care, social participation, and community use. Furthermore, these deficits must have originated during the developmental period, generally defined as before age 18. This three-pronged requirement (subaverage IQ, adaptive deficits, and developmental onset) ensures that the diagnosis reflects a pervasive developmental condition rather than a momentary test performance or an acquired injury in adulthood. Remember: an IQ score opens the door to the diagnostic question, but adaptive behavior data and developmental history are what walk you through it.

section_html:
Factor Structure and CHC Theory

Modern intelligence tests are organized around the Cattell-Horn-Carroll (CHC) theory, which integrates Cattell and Horn's Gf-Gc theory with Carroll's three-stratum model:

  • Stratum III: General intelligence (g)
  • Stratum II: Broad abilities -- Gf (Fluid Reasoning), Gc (Crystallized Ability), Gv (Visual Processing), Gsm (Short-Term Memory), Gs (Processing Speed), Glr (Long-Term Retrieval), Ga (Auditory Processing), Gq (Quantitative Knowledge), and others
  • Stratum I: Narrow abilities (specific skills measured by individual subtests)

Gf vs. Gc

Research on cognitive training has revealed a notable relationship between working memory training and fluid intelligence. Studies, most notably by Jaeggi and colleagues (2008), demonstrated that when adults practiced intensive working memory tasks (such as the dual n-back paradigm) over multiple sessions, they showed measurable gains on fluid intelligence assessments — even when those Gf measures were structurally dissimilar to the training exercises. This finding was significant because it challenged the longstanding assumption that fluid reasoning capacity was essentially fixed and resistant to environmental intervention.

The theoretical explanation centers on the substantial cognitive overlap between working memory and fluid reasoning. Both abilities require maintaining and manipulating information in real time, inhibiting irrelevant stimuli, and managing attentional resources. By strengthening the executive control processes underlying working memory, training appears to produce transfer effects that generalize to novel problem-solving tasks characteristic of Gf measurement. The gains tended to be dose-dependent, with longer training periods producing larger improvements.

Clinical Note

While initial findings generated considerable enthusiasm, subsequent meta-analyses have produced mixed results regarding the durability and magnitude of far-transfer effects from working memory training to fluid intelligence. Clinicians should be cautious about overstating the benefits of commercial "brain training" programs. The evidence is strongest for structured, adaptive working memory interventions delivered over sustained periods, and even then, the extent to which gains persist after training cessation remains debated.

  • Fluid Intelligence (Gf): The ability to reason, solve novel problems, and identify patterns without relying on previously acquired knowledge. Largely biologically determined. Peaks in young adulthood and declines with age.
  • Crystallized Intelligence (Gc): Accumulated knowledge, vocabulary, and skills acquired through education and experience. Largely culturally and educationally influenced. Continues to grow throughout the lifespan (or at least remains stable into late life).
Aging Pattern: Gf declines with age (particularly after age 60-70), while Gc remains stable or increases through middle and later adulthood. This produces the "classic aging pattern" on the Wechsler scales: relatively preserved VCI with declining PSI and WMI scores. Processing speed (Gs) shows the earliest and most pronounced age-related decline.
prev_last_paragraph: Think of it this way: imagine you measured your height against a doorframe in 1997 and marked it at a certain point. If someone later replaced that doorframe with a taller one, your mark would appear lower — not because you shrank, but because the reference point changed. The Flynn Effect operates similarly. Clinicians must always check whether the test edition they are using — or interpreting results from — has current, appropriate norms, and they should be prepared to discuss the Flynn Effect whenever historical IQ scores are being used in high-stakes decisions.
rewritten_html:
Factor Structure and CHC Theory

Having explored the Flynn Effect — how rising population scores can shift the meaning of IQ numbers across generations — we now turn to a more fundamental question: What exactly are intelligence tests measuring? When a clinician administers the WAIS-IV or the SB5, the resulting scores are not random collections of numbers. They are organized around a theoretical architecture that specifies how cognitive abilities relate to one another, from the broadest general factor down to the narrowest task-specific skill. Understanding this architecture is essential for interpreting profiles, explaining discrepancies between index scores, and communicating results to clients and referral sources in a way that is both accurate and meaningful.

Consider a clinical scenario: A 34-year-old attorney is referred for neuropsychological evaluation after a mild traumatic brain injury. Her Full Scale IQ is 112 — solidly above average. But a closer look reveals a 25-point gap between her Verbal Comprehension Index and her Processing Speed Index. Is that discrepancy clinically meaningful, or just statistical noise? To answer that question, the clinician needs more than a table of scores — they need a theoretical framework that explains how different cognitive abilities are structured, how they develop, and how they can be independently affected by injury, aging, or neurological disease. That framework is the Cattell-Horn-Carroll (CHC) theory.

CHC theory represents the most widely accepted structural model of intelligence in contemporary psychometrics. It emerged from the integration of two influential traditions: the Gf-Gc theory developed by Raymond Cattell and John Horn, which distinguished fluid from crystallized abilities and eventually expanded to encompass multiple broad factors; and John Carroll's monumental three-stratum model, derived from his factor-analytic reanalysis of virtually every major dataset in the intelligence testing literature. When these two frameworks were synthesized, the result was an elegant hierarchical model organized across three levels, or strata:

  • Stratum III: General intelligence (g)
  • Stratum II: Broad abilities -- Gf (Fluid Reasoning), Gc (Crystallized Ability), Gv (Visual Processing), Gsm (Short-Term Memory), Gs (Processing Speed), Glr (Long-Term Retrieval), Ga (Auditory Processing), Gq (Quantitative Knowledge), and others
  • Stratum I: Narrow abilities (specific skills measured by individual subtests)

Think of CHC theory as a map of the cognitive terrain. At the top sits general intelligence — the broad factor that accounts for the positive correlations we observe across nearly all cognitive tasks. Below it sit approximately eight to ten broad ability domains, each representing a relatively independent dimension of cognitive functioning. And at the base are the narrow abilities — the specific skills tapped by individual subtests like Block Design, Digit Span, or Vocabulary. Modern editions of both the Wechsler scales and the Stanford-Binet were designed with CHC theory in mind, and their index scores correspond roughly to broad Stratum II abilities. This means that when you interpret a client's profile, you are implicitly navigating the CHC hierarchy — moving from the Full Scale IQ (an estimate of g) down through index scores (broad abilities) to individual subtests (narrow abilities).

Gf vs. Gc

Of all the broad abilities in the CHC model, the distinction between fluid and crystallized intelligence is arguably the most clinically consequential — and the most frequently tested on the EPPP. These two constructs capture a fundamental tension in how we think about cognitive ability: the difference between raw reasoning power and accumulated knowledge, between what your brain can do in the moment and what it has learned over a lifetime. Understanding this distinction helps clinicians interpret age-related cognitive changes, evaluate the fairness of testing for culturally diverse populations, and make sense of discrepant index scores in neuropsychological profiles.

Research on cognitive training has revealed a notable relationship between working memory training and fluid intelligence. Studies, most notably by Jaeggi and colleagues (2008), demonstrated that when adults practiced intensive working memory tasks (such as the dual n-back paradigm) over multiple sessions, they showed measurable gains on fluid intelligence assessments — even when those Gf measures were structurally dissimilar to the training exercises. This finding was significant because it challenged the longstanding assumption that fluid reasoning capacity was essentially fixed and resistant to environmental intervention.

The theoretical explanation centers on the substantial cognitive overlap between working memory and fluid reasoning. Both abilities require maintaining and manipulating information in real time, inhibiting irrelevant stimuli, and managing attentional resources. By strengthening the executive control processes underlying working memory, training appears to produce transfer effects that generalize to novel problem-solving tasks characteristic of Gf measurement. The gains tended to be dose-dependent, with longer training periods producing larger improvements.

Clinical Note

While initial findings generated considerable enthusiasm, subsequent meta-analyses have produced mixed results regarding the durability and magnitude of far-transfer effects from working memory training to fluid intelligence. Clinicians should be cautious about overstating the benefits of commercial "brain training" programs. The evidence is strongest for structured, adaptive working memory interventions delivered over sustained periods, and even then, the extent to which gains persist after training cessation remains debated. When clients or their families ask about brain training apps and cognitive enhancement products, a balanced response acknowledges the intriguing preliminary findings while emphasizing that real-world transfer and long-term durability remain open empirical questions.

  • Fluid Intelligence (Gf): The ability to reason, solve novel problems, and identify patterns without relying on previously acquired knowledge. Largely biologically determined. Peaks in young adulthood and declines with age.
  • Crystallized Intelligence (Gc): Accumulated knowledge, vocabulary, and skills acquired through education and experience. Largely culturally and educationally influenced. Continues to grow throughout the lifespan (or at least remains stable into late life).

A helpful way to remember the distinction: Imagine two people taking a crossword puzzle. Gc is what lets you fill in the answers you already know — vocabulary words, historical facts, general knowledge built up over years of reading and conversation. Gf is what lets you figure out the answer to a clue you've never encountered before by reasoning through the pattern of crossing letters and ruling out possibilities. One draws on the past; the other operates in the present. Both are critical to intelligent behavior, but they follow very different developmental trajectories and are affected by very different clinical conditions.

This divergence between Gf and Gc has profound implications for clinical assessment across the lifespan. A 72-year-old retired professor may dazzle you with a Vocabulary subtest score in the 95th percentile — her crystallized abilities, honed over decades of scholarship, remain intact or even continue to grow. But her Matrix Reasoning score may have slipped to the 50th percentile, reflecting the normal age-related decline in fluid reasoning. This pattern is not pathological; it is expected. However, if that same professor's crystallized abilities were also declining sharply, that would be a very different clinical picture — potentially signaling a neurodegenerative process rather than normal aging.

Aging Pattern: Gf declines with age (particularly after age 60-70), while Gc remains stable or increases through middle and later adulthood. This produces the "classic aging pattern" on the Wechsler scales: relatively preserved VCI with declining PSI and WMI scores. Processing speed (Gs) shows the earliest and most pronounced age-related decline. For the EPPP, remember that this classic aging pattern is considered normal — it becomes clinically significant only when the magnitude of decline exceeds what would be expected for a person's age and educational background, or when crystallized abilities themselves begin to erode.

heading_text: Overview of Disruptive, Impulse-Control, and Conduct Disorders
section_html:
Overview of Disruptive, Impulse-Control, and Conduct Disorders

This DSM-5 chapter groups disorders characterized by problems in the self-regulation of emotions and behaviors. These conditions manifest as behaviors that violate the rights of others (e.g., aggression, destruction of property) and/or bring the individual into significant conflict with societal norms or authority figures. These disorders are more common in males and typically have onset in childhood or adolescence.

Key Concept: Externalizing vs. Internalizing

Disruptive and conduct disorders are classified as externalizing disorders, meaning the core symptoms are directed outward toward the environment (aggression, defiance, rule violation). This contrasts with internalizing disorders (e.g., depression, anxiety), where distress is directed inward. However, significant comorbidity between externalizing and internalizing disorders is common.
rewritten_html:
Overview of Disruptive, Impulse-Control, and Conduct Disorders

Imagine a seven-year-old who throws chairs when frustrated, a teenager who deliberately sets fires in abandoned buildings, or a young adult who cannot resist shoplifting despite having money to pay. On the surface, these individuals look quite different — but they share a common thread that the DSM-5 recognizes: a persistent difficulty regulating emotions and behaviors in ways that bring them into serious conflict with other people, social norms, or authority figures. Understanding this shared thread is essential for clinicians, because these presentations are among the most frequent reasons children and adolescents are referred for psychological services.

The DSM-5 groups these conditions together in a single chapter — Disruptive, Impulse-Control, and Conduct Disorders — precisely because they all involve failures of self-regulation that manifest outwardly. The behaviors may take different forms: aggression toward people or animals, destruction of property, chronic defiance of rules, or impulsive acts that disregard consequences. What unites them is that the problem shows up in the environment rather than being suffered silently. Notably, these disorders are more common in males than females and typically emerge during childhood or adolescence, though some — such as intermittent explosive disorder and certain impulse-control conditions — may first present in adulthood.

For clinicians preparing to work with these populations, two critical principles stand out from the start. First, context matters enormously: a child growing up in a war zone or a dangerous neighborhood may display aggressive behavior that is adaptive rather than disordered. The DSM-5 cautions against pathologizing behavior that may be a reasonable response to a threatening environment. Second, these disorders rarely travel alone. Children diagnosed with Oppositional Defiant Disorder frequently meet criteria for ADHD; adolescents with Conduct Disorder often carry co-occurring depressive or substance use disorders. Recognizing these comorbid patterns is vital for treatment planning and prognosis.

Key Concept: Externalizing vs. Internalizing

One of the most useful frameworks in developmental psychopathology is the distinction between externalizing disorders and internalizing disorders. When a child's distress is directed outward toward the environment — through aggression, defiance, rule-breaking, or destruction — clinicians describe these as externalizing problems. The disruptive and conduct disorders are the prototypical externalizing conditions. By contrast, internalizing disorders such as depression and anxiety involve distress directed inward, manifesting as sadness, withdrawal, worry, or somatic complaints. In clinical practice, however, the boundary between these categories is far less tidy than it appears in textbooks. A child who punches a classmate (externalizing) may also be deeply anxious about a chaotic home life (internalizing). Research consistently shows significant comorbidity between externalizing and internalizing disorders, which means that a thorough assessment should always look beyond the presenting behavioral complaint to screen for emotional suffering that may be fueling — or accompanying — the disruptive behavior.

With this broader framework in mind, we turn next to the disorder that often represents the earliest point on the developmental spectrum of disruptive behavior: Oppositional Defiant Disorder. Understanding ODD — its symptom clusters, its developmental significance, and its relationship to more severe conduct problems — provides the foundation for everything that follows in this chapter.

section_html:
Social Anxiety Disorder

Social Anxiety Disorder (SAD) involves marked fear or anxiety about social situations in which the individual may be scrutinized by others. The individual fears acting in a way that will be negatively evaluated, leading to humiliation, embarrassment, or rejection.

Key Features

  • The social situations almost always provoke fear or anxiety
  • Situations are avoided or endured with intense fear or anxiety
  • The fear is out of proportion to the actual threat posed
  • Duration of at least 6 months
  • Specify if performance only (limited to speaking or performing in public)
Cognitive models (Clark & Wells, 1995) emphasize that individuals with SAD shift attention inward to monitor their own behavior and appearance, creating a distorted self-image that perpetuates anxiety in social situations.

SAD has a lifetime prevalence of approximately 12% in the United States and typically begins in the mid-teens, often following a history of social inhibition or shyness. The performance only specifier was new in DSM-5 and distinguishes individuals whose fears are restricted to public speaking or performance contexts.
prev_last_paragraph: Specific phobias are the most common anxiety disorder, with a lifetime prevalence of approximately 12.5%. They are often acquired through direct traumatic experience, observation, or informational transmission (Rachman, 1977).
rewritten_html:
Social Anxiety Disorder

Imagine a graduate student who has thoroughly prepared a case presentation for her practicum seminar. She knows the material cold — she could explain her conceptualization in her sleep. Yet as she walks toward the front of the room, her heart pounds, her face flushes, and her mind goes blank. She is certain that every person in the room can see her hands trembling, that they are judging her as incompetent. She stumbles through her presentation, then spends the rest of the day replaying every perceived misstep. This is not ordinary stage fright. This is Social Anxiety Disorder — and it is one of the most prevalent and impairing anxiety conditions clinicians encounter.

Having just explored how specific phobias involve intense fear tied to circumscribed objects or situations, we now turn to a disorder where the feared stimulus is fundamentally interpersonal: other people's judgment. Social Anxiety Disorder (SAD), previously known as social phobia, involves marked and persistent fear or anxiety about social situations in which the individual may be scrutinized by others. The core dread is not simply of the situation itself — it is of acting in a way that will be negatively evaluated, leading to humiliation, embarrassment, or rejection. Unlike the person with a specific phobia of heights who can simply avoid balconies, the person with SAD faces their feared stimulus every time they enter a classroom, attend a meeting, or make small talk at a gathering.

What makes SAD particularly insidious is its self-reinforcing quality. A person who fears negative evaluation begins monitoring themselves intensely during social interactions — scrutinizing their own words, facial expressions, and body language. This inward focus paradoxically makes them less attuned to actual social cues (like the friendly nods of listeners) and more convinced that they are performing badly. They leave the interaction believing their worst fears were confirmed, which strengthens avoidance the next time. This internal feedback loop is central to understanding why the disorder persists even when others perceive the individual as perfectly competent.

Key Features

The DSM-5 diagnostic criteria for Social Anxiety Disorder capture a pattern that goes well beyond ordinary shyness or nervousness. Consider the difference between a new employee who feels butterflies before her first team meeting versus someone who has called in sick three times this month specifically to avoid speaking up in those meetings. The diagnostic features reflect this level of intensity and impairment:

  • The social situations almost always provoke fear or anxiety
  • Situations are avoided or endured with intense fear or anxiety
  • The fear is out of proportion to the actual threat posed
  • Duration of at least 6 months
  • Specify if performance only (limited to speaking or performing in public)

The six-month duration requirement is particularly important for the EPPP. This criterion helps clinicians distinguish SAD from transient social anxiety that might arise during a stressful life transition — such as starting a new job or adjusting to college — and the chronic, entrenched pattern that characterizes the disorder. Additionally, clinicians must rule out that the fear and avoidance are not better explained by another condition, such as body dysmorphic disorder (where the person fears scrutiny of a perceived physical flaw) or autism spectrum disorder (where social difficulties stem from different underlying mechanisms).

Cognitive models (Clark & Wells, 1995) emphasize that individuals with SAD shift attention inward to monitor their own behavior and appearance, creating a distorted self-image that perpetuates anxiety in social situations.

The Clark and Wells (1995) cognitive model deserves particular attention because it has profoundly shaped evidence-based treatment for SAD. According to this model, when a person with SAD enters a feared social situation, they activate a set of negative beliefs about themselves ("I'm boring," "People will see how anxious I am"). These beliefs trigger a shift in attention — instead of focusing outward on the conversation or audience, the person turns their attention inward, constructing a mental image of how they believe they appear to others. This self-image is almost always distorted and catastrophic: they picture themselves visibly sweating, stammering, or looking foolish. Because they are relying on this internal "camera" rather than on actual social feedback, they leave the situation convinced that their worst fears came true. This model explains why people with SAD can receive compliments on a presentation yet remain certain it went terribly — they trusted their internal self-monitoring over external evidence.

Clinically, this has direct treatment implications. Cognitive-behavioral interventions for SAD often include behavioral experiments designed to shift attention outward, video feedback to correct distorted self-imagery, and systematic testing of catastrophic predictions. For example, a therapist might ask a client to deliberately focus on their conversational partner's responses during a social interaction and then compare what actually happened to what they predicted would happen.

SAD has a lifetime prevalence of approximately 12% in the United States, making it one of the most common mental disorders. It typically begins in the mid-teens, often following a history of social inhibition or behavioral inhibition temperament — that quiet, watchful child who clings to a parent at birthday parties and takes a long time to warm up to new people. Research consistently shows that behavioral inhibition in early childhood is one of the strongest temperamental risk factors for developing SAD later in life, though not all inhibited children go on to develop the disorder. Onset after age 25 is relatively uncommon; when social anxiety appears for the first time in adulthood, clinicians should carefully consider whether it might be secondary to another condition, such as depression or a medical illness.

The performance only specifier was introduced in DSM-5 and distinguishes individuals whose fears are restricted to public speaking or performance contexts from those with the more generalized form. This distinction matters both clinically and on the EPPP. A person with the performance only specifier may function well in one-on-one conversations, small group interactions, and even casual social gatherings — their anxiety is triggered specifically when they must perform or speak before an audience. In contrast, the generalized form of SAD involves fear across a broad range of social interactions, including casual conversations, eating in front of others, or even making eye contact. The performance only subtype tends to have a later onset, may be less associated with comorbid conditions, and sometimes responds well to beta-blockers (such as propranolol) taken before a performance — a pharmacological strategy that is less effective for generalized SAD, where SSRIs and comprehensive CBT are typically first-line treatments.

section_html:
Conduct Disorder (CD)

Conduct Disorder involves a repetitive and persistent pattern of behavior in which the basic rights of others or major age-appropriate societal norms are violated. The DSM-5 requires at least 3 of 15 criteria in the past 12 months, with at least 1 criterion present in the past 6 months, across four categories:

Symptom Categories

CategoryExamples
Aggression to people and animalsBullying, initiating fights, using weapons, physical cruelty to people or animals, forcing sexual activity
Destruction of propertyDeliberately setting fires, deliberately destroying property
Deceitfulness or theftBreaking into someone's house/car, lying to obtain goods, shoplifting
Serious violations of rulesStaying out late (before age 13), running away, truancy (before age 13)

Onset Specifiers

Childhood-Onset vs. Adolescent-Onset

Childhood-onset type: At least one criterion characteristic of CD prior to age 10. Associated with more persistent aggression, worse prognosis, and higher likelihood of developing ASPD in adulthood. Adolescent-onset type: No criteria present prior to age 10. Associated with less aggression, more influence of deviant peers, and a better prognosis. Unspecified onset: Criteria met but insufficient information to determine onset.

The Callous-Unemotional (CU) Specifier

The DSM-5 added the specifier "with limited prosocial emotions" (the callous-unemotional traits specifier). To qualify, the individual must display at least two of the following persistently over at least 12 months and in multiple settings:

  • Lack of remorse or guilt -- does not feel bad about misbehavior
  • Callous -- lack of empathy -- disregards others' feelings
  • Unconcerned about performance -- does not show concern about poor performance at school, work, or other activities
  • Shallow or deficient affect -- does not express emotions or appears insincere

EPPP Example

Children with CD and CU traits show distinct neurobiological features: reduced amygdala reactivity to fearful facial expressions, lower cortisol reactivity to stress, and diminished autonomic arousal (Frick et al., 2014). They tend to show proactive (instrumental) aggression rather than reactive aggression, and they respond poorly to punishment-based interventions but may respond to reward-based approaches.
prev_last_paragraph: ODD prevalence is approximately 3.3%, with a male predominance in childhood that equalizes by adolescence. It typically emerges in the preschool years and is usually evident before age 8. ODD often precedes the development of conduct disorder, but the majority of children with ODD do not progress to conduct disorder.
rewritten_html:
Conduct Disorder (CD)

While most children with Oppositional Defiant Disorder do not go on to develop more severe behavioral problems, some do — and when they do, the trajectory often leads to a diagnosis that carries significantly greater clinical and legal weight. Consider a 13-year-old who has moved far beyond arguing with teachers and defying household rules. He has been suspended for physically threatening classmates, was caught breaking into cars in his neighborhood, and recently set fire to a dumpster behind his school. His behavior is no longer simply oppositional — it has crossed into territory where the fundamental rights of others and basic societal norms are being violated in a persistent, escalating pattern.

Conduct Disorder involves exactly this kind of repetitive and persistent behavioral pattern — one in which the basic rights of others or major age-appropriate societal norms are violated. Unlike ODD, which is characterized by emotional dysregulation and defiance directed primarily toward authority figures, Conduct Disorder encompasses a broader and more serious range of behaviors including aggression, property destruction, deceit, and rule violations that can have profound consequences for victims and communities alike. The DSM-5 requires at least 3 of 15 criteria to have been present in the past 12 months, with at least 1 criterion present in the past 6 months, drawn from four distinct categories of conduct problems.

Symptom Categories

The DSM-5 organizes the 15 possible criteria for Conduct Disorder into four behavioral categories, each reflecting a different domain of antisocial behavior. Understanding these categories is essential not only for diagnostic accuracy but also for treatment planning, as the specific profile of behaviors often guides the intensity and type of intervention needed. Note that the behaviors range from interpersonal aggression to covert acts of deception and theft — a breadth that distinguishes CD from other disruptive behavior disorders.

CategoryExamples
Aggression to people and animalsBullying, initiating fights, using weapons, physical cruelty to people or animals, forcing sexual activity
Destruction of propertyDeliberately setting fires, deliberately destroying property
Deceitfulness or theftBreaking into someone's house/car, lying to obtain goods, shoplifting
Serious violations of rulesStaying out late (before age 13), running away, truancy (before age 13)

A clinically important detail for the EPPP: the threshold is three criteria from anywhere across these four categories, not one from each. A child who bullies, initiates physical fights, and has been cruel to animals meets criteria through a single category — aggression to people and animals — even if no property destruction, theft, or rule violations are present. Conversely, a pattern that spans all four categories may signal a more pervasive and entrenched behavioral disturbance.

Onset Specifiers

One of the most clinically significant distinctions in Conduct Disorder is not the specific behaviors displayed, but when those behaviors first appeared. Research consistently shows that the age of onset carries powerful prognostic implications — children who begin showing conduct problems early follow a fundamentally different developmental trajectory than those whose antisocial behavior first emerges in adolescence. The DSM-5 captures this distinction through onset specifiers that every clinician should understand.

Childhood-Onset vs. Adolescent-Onset

Childhood-onset type: At least one criterion characteristic of CD prior to age 10. This subtype is associated with more persistent and severe aggression, a worse overall prognosis, and a substantially higher likelihood of developing Antisocial Personality Disorder (ASPD) in adulthood. These children often show neurobiological risk factors including temperamental difficulties and cognitive deficits that predate their behavioral problems. Adolescent-onset type: No criteria present prior to age 10. This subtype is associated with less physical aggression, greater influence of deviant peer groups as a driving factor, and a considerably better prognosis — many of these adolescents desist from antisocial behavior as they transition into adulthood. Unspecified onset: Criteria for CD are met but there is insufficient information available to determine whether any criterion was present before age 10.

Think of it this way: childhood-onset CD often reflects a deeply rooted developmental vulnerability — a child who has been aggressive, deceitful, and rule-breaking from early elementary school is showing a pattern that is more trait-like and resistant to change. Adolescent-onset CD, by contrast, frequently reflects the powerful pull of social context — a teenager who falls in with an antisocial peer group and begins engaging in delinquent behavior she never exhibited before. This distinction has direct implications for treatment planning and for the conversations clinicians have with worried parents about what the future may hold.

The Callous-Unemotional (CU) Specifier

Perhaps the most important addition the DSM-5 made to the Conduct Disorder diagnosis was the recognition that not all children with CD are alike in their emotional processing. Some children who engage in serious conduct problems experience genuine remorse, react emotionally when confronted with the harm they have caused, and are distressed by their own behavior. Others, however, seem strikingly indifferent — they harm without guilt, manipulate without empathy, and appear unmoved by consequences. This latter group represents a clinically distinct subtype that carries a different neurobiological profile, different treatment needs, and a more concerning long-term trajectory.

The DSM-5 added the specifier "with limited prosocial emotions" (the callous-unemotional traits specifier) to capture this distinction. To qualify for this specifier, the individual must display at least two of the following characteristics persistently over at least 12 months and across multiple settings — not just at home or just at school, but in a pattern that is pervasive across the child's life:

  • Lack of remorse or guilt -- does not feel bad about misbehavior
  • Callous -- lack of empathy -- disregards others' feelings
  • Unconcerned about performance -- does not show concern about poor performance at school, work, or other activities
  • Shallow or deficient affect -- does not express emotions or appears insincere

The requirement that these traits be evident across multiple settings is critical for accurate diagnosis. A child who appears remorseless in the principal's office but breaks down crying at home when discussing the same incident is not displaying the pervasive emotional deficit that this specifier is designed to capture. Clinicians must gather information from multiple informants — parents, teachers, peers — to reliably assess whether callous-unemotional traits are truly present.

EPPP Example

Children with CD and CU traits show distinct neurobiological features: reduced amygdala reactivity to fearful facial expressions, lower cortisol reactivity to stress, and diminished autonomic arousal (Frick et al., 2014). They tend to show proactive (instrumental) aggression rather than reactive aggression, and they respond poorly to punishment-based interventions but may respond to reward-based approaches.

This neurobiological profile has direct treatment implications that are highly testable on the EPPP. Because children with CU traits show reduced fear reactivity and diminished sensitivity to punishment cues, traditional behavioral approaches that rely on consequences — time-outs, loss of privileges, suspension — tend to be ineffective. These children simply do not experience the aversive emotional response that makes punishment a learning signal. Instead, reward-based interventions that leverage their intact reward sensitivity show more promise. Clinically, this means that identifying CU traits early can fundamentally redirect the treatment approach a clinician selects, making the specifier far more than an academic distinction — it is a practical guide to intervention.

section_html:
Cluster C: Anxious or Fearful

Cluster C personality disorders are characterized by anxious and fearful behavior. They share features with anxiety disorders but are distinguished by their pervasiveness and ego-syntonic quality.

Avoidant Personality Disorder

A pervasive pattern of social inhibition, feelings of inadequacy, and hypersensitivity to negative evaluation. Features include avoidance of occupational activities involving interpersonal contact due to fear of criticism, unwillingness to get involved unless certain of being liked, restraint in intimate relationships due to shame, preoccupation with rejection in social situations, inhibited in new interpersonal situations, views self as inept/unappealing/inferior, and reluctance to take personal risks or engage in new activities.

Avoidant PD and social anxiety disorder share significant overlap. The key distinction is that avoidant PD involves a more pervasive pattern of avoidance and a more deeply ingrained sense of personal inadequacy that extends beyond specific social performance situations (Lampe & Malhi, 2018).

Dependent Personality Disorder

A pervasive and excessive need to be taken care of that leads to submissive and clinging behavior and fears of separation. Features include difficulty making everyday decisions without advice, needing others to assume responsibility for major life areas, difficulty expressing disagreement, difficulty initiating projects independently, going to excessive lengths to obtain nurturance, feeling uncomfortable or helpless when alone, urgently seeking another relationship when one ends, and unrealistic preoccupation with fears of being left to care for oneself.

Obsessive-Compulsive Personality Disorder (OCPD)

A pervasive pattern of preoccupation with orderliness, perfectionism, and mental and interpersonal control, at the expense of flexibility, openness, and efficiency. Features include preoccupation with details/rules/order, perfectionism interfering with task completion, excessive devotion to work, over-conscientiousness about morality, inability to discard worn-out objects, reluctance to delegate, miserly spending style, and rigidity/stubbornness.

OCPD vs. OCD

OCPD involves ego-syntonic traits -- the person's perfectionism and control feel consistent with who they are. OCD involves ego-dystonic obsessions and compulsions -- the person recognizes them as excessive and distressing. OCPD does not involve true obsessions or compulsions. Despite the name similarity, only about 23-32% of individuals with OCD also have OCPD. OCPD is the most prevalent personality disorder in the general population (approximately 3-8%).

prev_last_paragraph: Kohut's self psychology conceptualizes narcissistic pathology as resulting from empathic failures by early caregivers (selfobjects), leading to a fragmented self. Treatment involves providing empathic mirroring and idealizing transferences. Kernberg, in contrast, views narcissistic personality as a pathological grandiose self that defends against underlying aggression and envy, requiring confrontation of defenses in treatment.

rewritten_html:
Cluster C: Anxious or Fearful

Having explored the dramatic intensity of Cluster B — where emotion runs hot, boundaries blur, and interpersonal relationships often feel like high-stakes theater — we now turn to a fundamentally different emotional landscape. In Cluster C, the dominant theme shifts from externalized drama to internalized anxiety: a quiet, persistent dread that something will go wrong, that one is not good enough, or that one cannot survive without others. If Cluster B disorders are storms, Cluster C disorders are the fog that settles in and never fully lifts.

Cluster C personality disorders are characterized by anxious and fearful behavior that pervades nearly every domain of a person's life. While they share surface-level features with anxiety disorders such as social anxiety disorder, generalized anxiety disorder, and obsessive-compulsive disorder, the critical distinction lies in their pervasiveness and their ego-syntonic quality. A person with social anxiety disorder typically recognizes that their fear is excessive and wishes it would go away. A person with avoidant personality disorder, by contrast, may experience their withdrawal from others as simply "who I am" — a deeply embedded part of their identity rather than a symptom to be treated. This ego-syntonic nature makes Cluster C disorders particularly challenging in clinical work because clients often present for treatment of depression or situational distress rather than the personality pattern itself.

Avoidant Personality Disorder

Imagine a talented graphic designer who turns down a promotion to team lead — not because she lacks the skills, but because the role involves presenting ideas in meetings and receiving feedback from colleagues. She has declined every social invitation from coworkers for the past three years, eats lunch alone at her desk, and spends evenings replaying minor interactions, searching for evidence that someone judged her negatively. She desperately wants connection but is convinced that if people truly knew her, they would find her boring and inadequate. This is the painful paradox at the heart of avoidant personality disorder.

Avoidant personality disorder involves a pervasive pattern of social inhibition, feelings of inadequacy, and hypersensitivity to negative evaluation that begins by early adulthood and appears across multiple contexts. The diagnostic features paint a portrait of someone trapped between longing and fear: avoidance of occupational activities involving significant interpersonal contact due to fears of criticism or rejection, unwillingness to get involved with people unless certain of being liked, restraint within intimate relationships due to fear of being shamed or ridiculed, preoccupation with being criticized or rejected in social situations, inhibition in new interpersonal situations because of feelings of inadequacy, a view of oneself as socially inept, personally unappealing, or inferior to others, and a marked reluctance to take personal risks or engage in new activities because they may prove embarrassing.

Clinicians frequently encounter the diagnostic question of where avoidant personality disorder ends and social anxiety disorder begins — and the answer requires careful assessment. Both conditions involve fear of negative evaluation and avoidance of social situations, but avoidant personality disorder reaches deeper into the person's sense of self. The individual with avoidant PD does not simply fear performing poorly in a presentation; they carry a pervasive conviction of their own fundamental inadequacy that colors how they approach friendships, romantic relationships, career decisions, and even leisure activities. Their avoidance extends far beyond specific performance situations into a generalized withdrawal from life.

Avoidant PD and social anxiety disorder share significant overlap. The key distinction is that avoidant PD involves a more pervasive pattern of avoidance and a more deeply ingrained sense of personal inadequacy that extends beyond specific social performance situations (Lampe & Malhi, 2018).

Dependent Personality Disorder

Consider a 42-year-old man who has never lived alone. He moved from his parents' home directly into his first marriage, and when that marriage ended, he began a new relationship within weeks — not out of genuine romantic interest, but out of a paralyzing terror of being on his own. He asks his current partner to decide what he should wear, what he should order at restaurants, and whether he should accept a new job. When his partner travels for work, he calls his mother multiple times a day, unable to tolerate the feeling of having no one to guide him. He is not unintelligent or incapable; he simply cannot trust his own judgment and believes, at his core, that he is unable to function independently.

Dependent personality disorder revolves around a pervasive and excessive need to be taken care of that leads to submissive, clinging behavior and fears of separation. This need drives a constellation of recognizable features: difficulty making everyday decisions without an excessive amount of advice and reassurance from others, needing others to assume responsibility for most major areas of one's life, difficulty expressing disagreement with others due to fear of loss of support or approval, difficulty initiating projects or doing things independently because of a lack of self-confidence in judgment or abilities, going to excessive lengths — including volunteering to do unpleasant tasks — to obtain nurturance and support from others, feeling uncomfortable or helpless when alone because of exaggerated fears of being unable to care for oneself, urgently seeking another relationship as a source of care and support when a close relationship ends, and unrealistic preoccupation with fears of being left to take care of oneself.

In clinical practice, dependent personality disorder often becomes visible during transitions — a divorce, a partner's illness, the death of a parent — that strip away the person's primary source of guidance and support. Therapists should recognize that the submissive and self-effacing behaviors are not simply cultural deference or agreeableness; they reflect a deep-seated belief that survival itself depends on maintaining attachment to a caregiver figure. Treatment often involves gradually building the client's capacity for autonomous decision-making, starting with low-stakes choices and working upward, while carefully managing the therapeutic relationship so that the therapist does not inadvertently become a new dependency object.

Obsessive-Compulsive Personality Disorder (OCPD)

Picture an attorney who spends so many hours perfecting the formatting and footnotes of a legal brief that she misses the filing deadline entirely. Her desk drawers are organized with military precision, and she has fired three successive assistants because none could meet her standards for organizing client files. She works seventy-hour weeks — not because the firm demands it, but because she cannot tolerate the inefficiency of leisure. She keeps broken appliances in her garage because "they might be useful someday," yet she will not spend money on a vacation because it feels wasteful. When colleagues suggest she relax, she is genuinely puzzled; from her perspective, everyone else is simply careless.

Obsessive-compulsive personality disorder involves a pervasive pattern of preoccupation with orderliness, perfectionism, and mental and interpersonal control, at the expense of flexibility, openness, and efficiency. The diagnostic criteria capture someone who has organized their entire life around control yet paradoxically undermines their own effectiveness: preoccupation with details, rules, lists, order, organization, or schedules to the extent that the major point of the activity is lost; perfectionism that interferes with task completion; excessive devotion to work and productivity to the exclusion of leisure activities and friendships; over-conscientiousness, scrupulousness, and inflexibility about matters of morality, ethics, or values; inability to discard worn-out or worthless objects even when they have no sentimental value; reluctance to delegate tasks or work with others unless they submit to exactly the person's way of doing things; a miserly spending style toward both self and others, with money viewed as something to be hoarded for future catastrophes; and rigidity and stubbornness in interpersonal interactions.

One of the most important distinctions for the EPPP — and one of the most commonly tested — involves differentiating OCPD from its phonetic cousin, OCD. Despite sharing a name, these are fundamentally different conditions with different subjective experiences, and understanding the ego-syntonic versus ego-dystonic distinction is the key to telling them apart.

OCPD vs. OCD

OCPD involves ego-syntonic traits — the person's perfectionism and need for control feel consistent with who they are. They may acknowledge that others find them rigid, but they typically view their standards as appropriate and even virtuous. OCD, by contrast, involves ego-dystonic obsessions and compulsions — the person recognizes these experiences as excessive, irrational, and distressing. A person with OCD who washes their hands fifty times a day knows this is unreasonable and wishes they could stop; a person with OCPD who insists on a particular way of loading the dishwasher genuinely believes their method is the only correct one. OCPD does not involve true obsessions or compulsions in the clinical sense. Despite the name similarity, research finds that only about 23-32% of individuals with OCD also meet criteria for OCPD, underscoring that these are distinct conditions. Notably, OCPD is the most prevalent personality disorder in the general population, with estimates ranging from approximately 3-8%.

section_html:
Intermittent Explosive Disorder (IED)

Intermittent Explosive Disorder is characterized by recurrent behavioral outbursts representing a failure to control aggressive impulses. The outbursts are grossly out of proportion to the provocation and are not premeditated.

DSM-5 Criteria

  • Frequency: Verbal aggression (tantrums, tirades) or physical aggression toward property, animals, or others occurring twice weekly on average for 3 months (need not cause damage), OR three behavioral outbursts involving damage/destruction or physical assault within a 12-month period
  • The magnitude of aggression is grossly out of proportion to the provocation
  • Not premeditated or committed to achieve a tangible objective
  • Causes marked distress or impairment, or financial/legal consequences
  • Chronological age of at least 6 years (or equivalent developmental level)
  • Not better explained by another mental disorder, medical condition, or substance
Research suggests that IED involves dysregulation of serotonergic systems, particularly reduced serotonin activity in the prefrontal cortex, leading to impaired top-down regulation of aggression mediated by the amygdala (Coccaro et al., 2015).

rewritten_html:
Intermittent Explosive Disorder (IED)

Having explored Conduct Disorder — a pattern of persistent, rule-violating behavior that often begins in childhood — we now turn to a disorder that centers on a very different kind of aggression. Imagine a man in his thirties who is, by all accounts, generally reasonable and well-functioning. Yet several times a month, seemingly minor provocations — a slow driver, a misplaced remote control, a mildly dismissive comment from a coworker — ignite explosive rage that is wildly disproportionate to the trigger. He screams, throws objects, slams doors so hard the frame splinters. Minutes later, the storm passes, and he is flooded with remorse and confusion. He cannot explain what happened. Unlike the calculated, instrumental aggression seen in Conduct Disorder with callous-unemotional traits, these outbursts are impulsive, unplanned, and serve no strategic purpose. This is the clinical picture of Intermittent Explosive Disorder.

Intermittent Explosive Disorder is characterized by recurrent behavioral outbursts representing a failure to control aggressive impulses. The outbursts are grossly out of proportion to the provocation, are not premeditated, and are not committed to achieve a tangible objective — they are reactive eruptions, not instrumental acts. What distinguishes IED from ordinary anger is both the intensity and the frequency of these episodes, along with the distress and impairment they cause. Individuals with IED often describe their outbursts as "snapping" or feeling as though a switch has been flipped, followed by genuine regret once the episode subsides. Clinically, IED is important to recognize because it is more common than many clinicians expect — community prevalence estimates range from approximately 2.7% to 7.3% — and it carries significant consequences, including damaged relationships, job loss, legal problems, and physical injury to self or others.

DSM-5 Criteria

The DSM-5 criteria for IED are designed to capture two distinct patterns of aggressive outbursts, reflecting the clinical reality that some individuals display frequent lower-intensity episodes while others have rarer but more severe explosions. A clinician should be attentive to both patterns, as either can qualify for diagnosis. Importantly, the disorder requires a minimum chronological age of 6 years (or equivalent developmental level), which helps differentiate IED from the developmentally normative tantrums of early childhood. The full diagnostic picture includes the following criteria:

  • Frequency: Verbal aggression (tantrums, tirades) or physical aggression toward property, animals, or others occurring twice weekly on average for 3 months (need not cause damage), OR three behavioral outbursts involving damage/destruction or physical assault within a 12-month period
  • The magnitude of aggression is grossly out of proportion to the provocation
  • Not premeditated or committed to achieve a tangible objective
  • Causes marked distress or impairment, or financial/legal consequences
  • Chronological age of at least 6 years (or equivalent developmental level)
  • Not better explained by another mental disorder, medical condition, or substance

The differential diagnosis requirement is especially important for exam preparation. A clinician must rule out conditions where aggressive outbursts are better accounted for by another disorder. For example, aggression during a manic episode would be attributed to Bipolar Disorder, not IED. Similarly, the chronic irritability and anger outbursts seen in Disruptive Mood Dysregulation Disorder (DMDD) in children may superficially resemble IED, but DMDD is characterized by a persistently irritable or angry mood between outbursts — a feature not required in IED. Aggression in the context of Conduct Disorder or Antisocial Personality Disorder is typically more instrumental and goal-directed, whereas IED aggression is reactive and impulsive. Substance intoxication (particularly with alcohol or stimulants) and medical conditions affecting the central nervous system (such as traumatic brain injury or epilepsy) must also be excluded.

Consider a clinical vignette: A 28-year-old woman presents after her third road rage incident in six months, the most recent involving her slamming her car into a guardrail after another driver cut her off. Between episodes, she describes herself as "easygoing" and is genuinely distressed by her behavior. She has no history of conduct problems, substance use, mood episodes, or neurological conditions. Her outbursts are sudden, unplanned, and grossly disproportionate to the provocation. This presentation — episodic, impulsive, disproportionate aggression causing distress and impairment in an otherwise functioning adult — is a textbook case of IED.

Understanding the neurobiology of IED helps explain why these individuals seem unable to "just control themselves." The disorder appears to involve a breakdown in the brain's top-down regulatory system. Specifically, reduced serotonergic activity in the prefrontal cortex weakens the capacity to inhibit aggressive impulses generated by the amygdala. Think of it as a dimmer switch on impulse control: when prefrontal serotonin function is diminished, the amygdala's threat-response signals go unchecked, leading to explosive reactions to minor provocations. This neurobiological model has important treatment implications — selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs) have shown some efficacy in reducing aggressive outbursts in IED, and cognitive-behavioral interventions targeting anger management and impulse control are considered first-line psychosocial treatments.

Research suggests that IED involves dysregulation of serotonergic systems, particularly reduced serotonin activity in the prefrontal cortex, leading to impaired top-down regulation of aggression mediated by the amygdala (Coccaro et al., 2015).

section_html:
Bulimia Nervosa (BN)

Bulimia nervosa involves recurrent episodes of binge eating followed by inappropriate compensatory behaviors to prevent weight gain.

DSM-5 Criteria

  1. Recurrent episodes of binge eating (eating a definitively large amount of food in a discrete period with a sense of lack of control)
  2. Recurrent inappropriate compensatory behaviors to prevent weight gain (purging, fasting, excessive exercise)
  3. Both occur at least once per week for 3 months (reduced from twice per week in DSM-IV)
  4. Self-evaluation is unduly influenced by body shape and weight
  5. Does not occur exclusively during episodes of AN

EPPP Example

A key differential: AN binge-eating/purging type vs. BN. The distinguishing factor is body weight. If the individual is at a significantly low body weight and meets AN criteria, the diagnosis is AN binge-eating/purging type, even if binge-purge cycles are present. BN is diagnosed when the individual is at or above minimally normal weight. Note that BN no longer has purging/nonpurging subtypes in DSM-5.

Medical complications of BN include dental erosion (from stomach acid), parotid gland enlargement ("chipmunk cheeks"), Russell's sign (calluses on the knuckles from self-induced vomiting), esophageal tears (Mallory-Weiss syndrome), and metabolic alkalosis from purging.
prev_last_paragraph: AN has the highest mortality rate of any psychiatric disorder, approximately 5-10% per decade of illness. Deaths result from medical complications (cardiac arrhythmias, electrolyte imbalances) and suicide. Key medical findings include bradycardia, hypotension, lanugo hair, osteoporosis, and refeeding syndrome (dangerous electrolyte shifts upon nutritional restoration, particularly hypophosphatemia).
rewritten_html:
Bulimia Nervosa (BN)

Having examined anorexia nervosa — with its hallmark restriction and dangerously low body weight — we now turn to a disorder that shares many of the same preoccupations with weight and shape but follows a strikingly different behavioral pattern. Consider a college student who maintains a normal weight and appears healthy to friends and family. In private, however, she consumes enormous quantities of food in a single sitting — sometimes thousands of calories in under an hour — feeling utterly unable to stop. Afterward, overwhelmed by guilt and fear of weight gain, she forces herself to vomit before anyone notices. This cycle repeats several times a week, shrouded in secrecy and shame. This is the clinical picture of bulimia nervosa, a disorder defined by recurrent episodes of binge eating followed by inappropriate compensatory behaviors aimed at preventing weight gain.

What makes bulimia nervosa particularly insidious is its invisibility. Unlike anorexia nervosa, individuals with BN typically maintain a body weight that falls within or even above the normal range, which means the disorder can persist for years without detection by loved ones or even healthcare providers. The emotional toll, however, is enormous: individuals often describe feeling trapped in a cycle they cannot break, where binges provide momentary relief from negative emotions only to be replaced by intense self-loathing that fuels the compensatory behavior. Understanding this cycle — and the specific diagnostic criteria that distinguish BN from related disorders — is essential for accurate clinical assessment and effective intervention.

DSM-5 Criteria

The DSM-5 specifies five criteria that must be met for a diagnosis of bulimia nervosa. Clinicians should pay particular attention to the frequency and duration thresholds, which were revised from DSM-IV, as well as the critical weight-based distinction from anorexia nervosa.

  1. Recurrent episodes of binge eating (eating a definitively large amount of food in a discrete period with a sense of lack of control)
  2. Recurrent inappropriate compensatory behaviors to prevent weight gain (purging, fasting, excessive exercise)
  3. Both occur at least once per week for 3 months (reduced from twice per week in DSM-IV)
  4. Self-evaluation is unduly influenced by body shape and weight
  5. Does not occur exclusively during episodes of AN

The reduction in frequency threshold from twice per week (DSM-IV) to once per week (DSM-5) is a clinically meaningful change worth noting for the EPPP. This revision reflected research showing that individuals who binged and purged once weekly experienced levels of distress and impairment comparable to those meeting the older, stricter threshold. In practice, this means more individuals now qualify for a BN diagnosis rather than falling into an "other specified" category, which can improve access to evidence-based treatment.

EPPP Example

A key differential: AN binge-eating/purging type vs. BN. The distinguishing factor is body weight. If the individual is at a significantly low body weight and meets AN criteria, the diagnosis is AN binge-eating/purging type, even if binge-purge cycles are present. BN is diagnosed when the individual is at or above minimally normal weight. Note that BN no longer has purging/nonpurging subtypes in DSM-5. This is a frequently tested distinction — when an exam vignette describes someone who binges and purges, always check the stated body weight before choosing between AN binge-eating/purging type and BN. The behaviors may look identical; the weight is what determines the diagnosis.

Medical complications of BN are numerous and often serve as the first clinical clues that the disorder is present. These include dental erosion from repeated exposure to stomach acid — often noticed first by dentists — and parotid gland enlargement, sometimes called "chipmunk cheeks," which results from the chronic stimulation of salivary glands during purging episodes. Russell's sign, a classic physical finding, refers to calluses or scarring on the dorsum of the hand and knuckles caused by repeated contact with the teeth during self-induced vomiting. More serious complications include esophageal tears (Mallory-Weiss syndrome), which can lead to life-threatening bleeding, and metabolic alkalosis from the loss of hydrochloric acid through vomiting. Electrolyte disturbances — particularly hypokalemia — can lead to cardiac arrhythmias, making regular metabolic monitoring an essential component of care for individuals with BN.

Treatment for bulimia nervosa has a stronger evidence base than for many other eating disorders. Cognitive-behavioral therapy (CBT) is considered the gold-standard psychological treatment, targeting the distorted beliefs about weight and shape that maintain the binge-purge cycle. Among pharmacological interventions, fluoxetine (Prozac) is the only FDA-approved medication for BN and is typically prescribed at higher doses (60 mg) than those used for depression. For the EPPP, remember that BN tends to have a better prognosis than AN, though relapse rates remain significant, and comorbid conditions — particularly depression, anxiety disorders, and substance use disorders — are common and must be addressed in comprehensive treatment planning.

section_html:
Anorexia Nervosa (AN)

Anorexia nervosa is characterized by restriction of energy intake leading to a significantly low body weight, intense fear of gaining weight, and disturbance in the way body weight or shape is experienced.

DSM-5 Diagnostic Criteria

  1. Criterion A: Restriction of energy intake relative to requirements, leading to significantly low body weight in the context of age, sex, developmental trajectory, and physical health
  2. Criterion B: Intense fear of gaining weight or becoming fat, or persistent behavior that interferes with weight gain, even though at a significantly low weight
  3. Criterion C: Disturbance in the way body weight or shape is experienced, undue influence of body weight/shape on self-evaluation, or persistent lack of recognition of the seriousness of the current low body weight

Subtypes

  • Restricting type: Weight loss achieved primarily through dieting, fasting, and/or excessive exercise. No recurrent binge-eating or purging in the past 3 months.
  • Binge-eating/purging type: Recurrent episodes of binge eating or purging (self-induced vomiting, misuse of laxatives, diuretics, or enemas) during the past 3 months.

Clinical Pearl

DSM-5 made several important changes to AN criteria: (1) removed the specific BMI threshold and the word "refusal" to eat, replacing it with "restriction"; (2) removed the amenorrhea criterion, recognizing that AN occurs in males and post-menopausal women; (3) Criterion B no longer requires explicit acknowledgment of fear of weight gain -- persistent behavior interfering with weight gain suffices.

Medical Complications

AN has the highest mortality rate of any psychiatric disorder, approximately 5-10% per decade of illness. Deaths result from medical complications (cardiac arrhythmias, electrolyte imbalances) and suicide. Key medical findings include bradycardia, hypotension, lanugo hair, osteoporosis, and refeeding syndrome (dangerous electrolyte shifts upon nutritional restoration, particularly hypophosphatemia).
