prev_last_paragraph: Fairburn's (2003) transdiagnostic model proposes that eating disorders share a core psychopathology: the over-evaluation of eating, shape, and weight, and their control. This model is the basis for enhanced cognitive-behavioral therapy (CBT-E), which can be applied across eating disorder diagnoses.
rewritten_html:
Anorexia Nervosa (AN)

Having established that eating disorders share a core psychopathology — the over-evaluation of eating, shape, and weight — we now turn to the disorder where this disturbance reaches its most physically dangerous expression. Consider a 16-year-old cross-country runner whose coach praises her increasingly lean frame. She begins skipping meals, then cutting entire food groups, then exercising through injuries. Her parents notice her shrinking body, but she insists she feels "fine" and cannot see what everyone else sees. By the time she reaches the emergency department with a resting heart rate of 38 beats per minute, she weighs 85 pounds — and still believes her thighs are too large. This is the clinical reality of anorexia nervosa, a disorder characterized by restriction of energy intake leading to a significantly low body weight, intense fear of gaining weight, and a profound disturbance in the way body weight or shape is experienced.

What makes anorexia nervosa uniquely challenging — both clinically and conceptually — is that the individual's relentless pursuit of thinness often feels ego-syntonic. Patients frequently do not present for treatment voluntarily, and many actively resist intervention. The disorder entangles biology, cognition, and identity in ways that make it among the most difficult psychiatric conditions to treat, and as we will see, the most lethal.

DSM-5 Diagnostic Criteria

The DSM-5 organizes the diagnosis of anorexia nervosa around three core criteria, each capturing a different facet of the disorder — behavioral restriction, affective and motivational disturbance, and cognitive-perceptual disruption. Together, they paint a picture of someone who actively limits food intake, dreads weight gain, and experiences a fundamental distortion in how they perceive their own body.

  1. Criterion A: Restriction of energy intake relative to requirements, leading to significantly low body weight in the context of age, sex, developmental trajectory, and physical health
  2. Criterion B: Intense fear of gaining weight or becoming fat, or persistent behavior that interferes with weight gain, even though at a significantly low weight
  3. Criterion C: Disturbance in the way body weight or shape is experienced, undue influence of body weight/shape on self-evaluation, or persistent lack of recognition of the seriousness of the current low body weight

Notice how these criteria work together in clinical practice. A patient who meets Criterion A (dangerously low weight from restriction) but who recognizes the problem and wants to gain weight would not meet Criterion C. The DSM-5 requires the convergence of all three elements — the behavior, the fear or weight-interfering behavior, and the body image disturbance or denial — to distinguish anorexia nervosa from other conditions that cause weight loss, such as major depressive disorder, medical illness, or food insecurity.

Subtypes

Clinicians further classify anorexia nervosa into two subtypes based on the methods the individual uses to maintain their low weight. These subtypes carry different medical risk profiles and can shift over the course of the illness, so clinicians assign the subtype based on the patient's behavior over the preceding three months.

  • Restricting type: Weight loss achieved primarily through dieting, fasting, and/or excessive exercise. No recurrent binge-eating or purging in the past 3 months.
  • Binge-eating/purging type: Recurrent episodes of binge eating or purging (self-induced vomiting, misuse of laxatives, diuretics, or enemas) during the past 3 months.

The distinction matters because individuals with the binge-eating/purging subtype tend to have higher rates of impulsivity, substance use, and mood instability compared to those with the restricting subtype. They also face additional medical risks from purging behaviors, such as esophageal tears and severe dental erosion. Importantly, the binge-eating/purging type of anorexia nervosa differs from bulimia nervosa primarily by body weight — individuals with AN are at a significantly low weight, while those with bulimia nervosa typically maintain a normal or above-normal weight. This distinction will become clearer when we discuss bulimia nervosa in the next section.

Clinical Pearl

DSM-5 made several important changes to AN criteria: (1) removed the specific BMI threshold and the word "refusal" to eat, replacing it with "restriction"; (2) removed the amenorrhea criterion, recognizing that AN occurs in males and post-menopausal women; (3) Criterion B no longer requires explicit acknowledgment of fear of weight gain -- persistent behavior interfering with weight gain suffices.

These DSM-5 revisions deserve special attention for the EPPP. The shift from "refusal" to "restriction" was not merely semantic — "refusal" implied a willful, oppositional stance that stigmatized patients and poorly captured the complex motivational dynamics underlying food avoidance. Similarly, dropping the amenorrhea requirement broadened diagnostic access considerably. Under DSM-IV, a male patient who met every other criterion for anorexia nervosa could not technically receive the diagnosis, which clearly did not reflect clinical reality. Finally, the change to Criterion B acknowledges that many patients deny any fear of weight gain yet engage in persistent behaviors — such as excessive exercise, food rituals, or body checking — that actively prevent weight restoration. Clinicians can now diagnose AN based on observable behavior rather than relying solely on the patient's verbal report of subjective fear.

Medical Complications

Perhaps the single most critical fact to know about anorexia nervosa is this: AN carries the highest mortality rate of any psychiatric disorder, approximately 5-10% per decade of illness. To put this in perspective, a young woman diagnosed at age 18 faces a sobering probability of death by her late twenties simply from the medical ravages of sustained starvation or from suicide, which accounts for a significant proportion of AN-related deaths. The lethality of this disorder underscores why clinicians must take it seriously even when patients minimize their symptoms.

The medical complications of anorexia nervosa span virtually every organ system. Cardiac complications — including bradycardia (dangerously slow heart rate), hypotension, and fatal cardiac arrhythmias caused by electrolyte imbalances — represent the most common cause of medical death. The body's attempt to conserve heat in the face of lost subcutaneous fat produces lanugo hair, a fine downy growth over the body that patients often find distressing. Chronic nutritional deprivation leads to osteoporosis, which can cause fractures in young women who should be at the peak of bone density. Clinicians should also be prepared for the paradoxical danger of treatment itself: refeeding syndrome occurs when nutritional restoration triggers dangerous electrolyte shifts — particularly hypophosphatemia — as the body rapidly transitions from a catabolic to an anabolic state. This potentially fatal complication requires careful medical monitoring during the early stages of weight restoration, with slow caloric increases and frequent electrolyte monitoring.

For the EPPP, remember the key medical findings associated with AN: bradycardia, hypotension, lanugo hair, osteoporosis, electrolyte imbalances, and the risk of refeeding syndrome during treatment. Also remember that deaths result from both medical complications and suicide — a reminder that psychological assessment of suicidality remains essential even when the primary clinical focus is nutritional rehabilitation.

section_html:
Persistent Depressive Disorder (Dysthymia)

Persistent depressive disorder (PDD) consolidates what DSM-IV called dysthymic disorder and chronic major depressive disorder. It requires depressed mood for most of the day, for more days than not, for at least 2 years (1 year in children and adolescents), plus two or more of the following:

  • Poor appetite or overeating
  • Insomnia or hypersomnia
  • Low energy or fatigue
  • Low self-esteem
  • Poor concentration or difficulty making decisions
  • Feelings of hopelessness

EPPP Example

When a patient has PDD and also meets criteria for a major depressive episode, this is termed "double depression." The prognosis for double depression is worse than for MDD alone, with higher relapse rates and greater functional impairment (Klein et al., 2006).
prev_last_paragraph: The seasonal pattern specifier — commonly referred to as seasonal affective disorder (SAD) — has been associated with dysregulation of melatonin, a hormone produced by the pineal gland that helps regulate circadian rhythms and sleep-wake cycles. During shorter daylight periods in fall and winter, melatonin secretion increases and its normal diurnal rhythm may become disrupted, contributing to the onset of depressive symptoms such as hypersomnia, carbohydrate craving, and low energy. This photobiological mechanism provides the rationale for bright light therapy (phototherapy), which is considered a first-line treatment for winter-pattern SAD. Typically administered at 10,000 lux for 20–30 minutes each morning, light therapy suppresses excess melatonin production, shifts circadian phase, and has demonstrated efficacy comparable to antidepressant medication in mild-to-moderate seasonal depression.

rewritten_html:
Persistent Depressive Disorder (Dysthymia)

Having explored the episodic nature of major depressive disorder — with its distinct episodes, specifiers, and seasonal patterns — we now turn to a form of depression that is defined not by its intensity but by its sheer persistence. Imagine a client who, when asked how long they've felt depressed, pauses and says, "I honestly can't remember a time when I didn't feel this way." They don't describe the dramatic plunge into darkness that characterizes a major depressive episode; instead, they describe a low-grade, ever-present gray fog that has hung over their life for years. They still go to work, still manage their responsibilities — but with a chronic sense of heaviness, self-doubt, and joylessness that has become so familiar they wonder if it's simply their personality. This is the clinical portrait of Persistent depressive disorder (PDD).

PDD consolidates two previously separate diagnoses from DSM-IV — dysthymic disorder and chronic major depressive disorder — into a single diagnostic category. The core diagnostic requirement is depressed mood for most of the day, for more days than not, persisting for at least 2 years in adults (or 1 year in children and adolescents). During that two-year window, the person must never have been symptom-free for more than two consecutive months. In addition to the chronic depressed mood, the individual must exhibit two or more of the following symptoms:

  • Poor appetite or overeating
  • Insomnia or hypersomnia
  • Low energy or fatigue
  • Low self-esteem
  • Poor concentration or difficulty making decisions
  • Feelings of hopelessness

Notice that the symptom list for PDD is shorter and somewhat different from the nine-symptom criterion set for MDD. You won't find psychomotor changes, suicidal ideation, or anhedonia listed among the PDD criteria — though the individual may certainly experience these. The threshold for diagnosis is deliberately lower in terms of symptom count (two additional symptoms rather than four), reflecting the fact that PDD captures a chronic, lower-intensity form of depression. What it lacks in acute severity, it makes up for in duration and cumulative burden. Research consistently shows that PDD is associated with significant functional impairment, reduced quality of life, and substantial economic costs — in some studies rivaling or exceeding the impairment seen in episodic MDD, precisely because the suffering is so unrelenting.

A critical clinical consideration is that PDD can coexist with major depressive episodes. Because PDD is defined by chronicity rather than a specific severity level, individuals with PDD may periodically dip into episodes that meet full MDD criteria, layering acute severity onto an already chronic baseline. When this happens, the distinction between the disorders blurs — but DSM-5 handles this through specifiers rather than separate diagnoses. The clinician can note whether PDD occurs "with persistent major depressive episode," "with intermittent major depressive episodes, with current episode," or "with intermittent major depressive episodes, without current episode." Additional specifiers — such as anxious distress, atypical features, and early or late onset — can further characterize the presentation, helping clinicians tailor treatment planning to the individual's specific symptom profile.

From a treatment perspective, the chronicity of PDD poses unique challenges. Many clients with PDD have lived with their symptoms for so long that they have developed deeply ingrained cognitive patterns — pervasive schemas of inadequacy, helplessness, and pessimism — that are resistant to brief interventions. This is one reason why the Cognitive Behavioral Analysis System of Psychotherapy (CBASP), developed by James McCullough specifically for chronic depression, has shown particular promise for this population. Pharmacotherapy, especially with SSRIs or SNRIs, is also commonly used, and combination treatment (medication plus psychotherapy) tends to yield the best outcomes for chronic depression.

EPPP Example

When a patient has PDD and also meets criteria for a major depressive episode, this is termed "double depression." The concept of double depression is clinically important and frequently tested on the EPPP. Picture a client who has experienced a persistent low mood and low self-esteem for three years — meeting PDD criteria — and then develops a superimposed episode with markedly worsened sleep, appetite loss, suicidal ideation, and inability to function at work. This individual now carries both diagnoses simultaneously. The prognosis for double depression is worse than for MDD alone, with higher relapse rates, greater functional impairment, and a more treatment-resistant course (Klein et al., 2006). For exam purposes, remember that the key distinguishing feature is the chronic depressive baseline: the major depressive episode emerges against a backdrop of long-standing, lower-grade depressive symptoms, rather than arising from a period of normal mood.

As you prepare for the EPPP, keep the essential contrasts clear in your mind: MDD is defined by discrete episodes lasting at least two weeks with five or more symptoms; PDD is defined by chronic depressed mood lasting at least two years with two or more additional symptoms. MDD captures the acute peaks of depression; PDD captures the relentless undertow. And when both coexist — double depression — the clinical picture is more severe, more impairing, and more difficult to treat than either condition alone. With this understanding of the full spectrum of unipolar depressive disorders, we are now ready to explore what happens when depression alternates with its polar opposite — the elevated, expansive, or irritable mood states that define the bipolar disorders.

section_html:
Suicide Risk Assessment

Suicide is a critical topic for the EPPP. Key risk and protective factors include:

Clinical Note: No-Suicide Contracts

Historically, some clinicians have used no-suicide contracts (also called "contracts for safety") in which a client verbally or in writing agrees not to engage in self-harm. However, research consistently demonstrates that these agreements do not reduce the likelihood of suicidal behavior. A client in acute crisis may agree to such a contract to avoid hospitalization, to please the clinician, or out of social compliance — none of which reflect genuine safety. Furthermore, no-suicide contracts offer no legal protection to the therapist in the event of a client's suicide. Courts have not recognized these contracts as meeting the standard of care for suicide risk management. Current best practices instead emphasize the use of collaborative safety planning, which involves working with the client to identify warning signs, coping strategies, social supports, professionals to contact during crisis, and means restriction steps. The Stanley-Brown Safety Planning Intervention is a widely adopted evidence-based alternative that shifts the focus from a passive promise to an active, personalized set of strategies the client can use when suicidal urges arise. Clinicians should also conduct thorough, ongoing risk assessments and document clinical decision-making rather than relying on a signed agreement as a substitute for careful evaluation.

Clinical Note: No-Suicide Contracts

Historically, clinicians sometimes asked patients to sign a no-suicide contract (also called a "contract for safety"), in which the patient agrees not to engage in self-harm and to contact the clinician if suicidal urges arise. However, there is now broad professional consensus that these agreements lack empirical support as a suicide prevention strategy and may actually create a false sense of security for the clinician. No-suicide contracts have no legal standing, do not constitute adequate risk management, and may discourage deeper clinical exploration of suicidal ideation. Patients who are most at risk — those experiencing intense ambivalence, impulsivity, or psychotic symptoms — are precisely the individuals least able to honor such agreements.

Current best-practice guidelines recommend replacing no-suicide contracts with collaborative safety planning. A safety plan, developed jointly with the patient, identifies personal warning signs, internal coping strategies, social contacts and settings that provide distraction, individuals to contact for help, professionals and agencies to reach in crisis, and steps for restricting access to lethal means. The Stanley-Brown Safety Planning Intervention has demonstrated effectiveness in reducing subsequent suicidal behavior and increasing treatment engagement. Unlike a no-suicide contract, a safety plan is a clinical tool that empowers the patient with concrete, actionable steps rather than relying on a promise that may be impossible to keep during a crisis.

Risk Factors

  • Previous suicide attempt -- the single strongest predictor of completed suicide
  • Psychiatric diagnosis -- over 90% of completers had a diagnosable disorder, with depression and substance use being the most common
  • Hopelessness -- a stronger predictor of suicidal intent than depression severity (Beck et al., 1985)
  • Demographic factors: Males complete suicide at approximately 4 times the rate of females; females attempt suicide approximately 3 times as often as males
  • Access to lethal means, family history of suicide, recent losses, social isolation
  • Age: Highest rates in adults 45-64 and those 85+

Protective Factors

  • Social connectedness and reasons for living
  • Effective clinical care for mental and substance use disorders
  • Restricted access to lethal means
  • Cultural and religious beliefs that discourage suicide

Clinical Pearl

The Joiner interpersonal theory of suicide (2005) identifies three factors necessary for a lethal suicide attempt: thwarted belongingness (feeling disconnected), perceived burdensomeness (feeling like a burden to others), and acquired capability (reduced fear of death through habituation to pain and self-harm).
prev_last_paragraph: Cognitive-Behavioral Therapy (CBT) and Interpersonal Therapy (IPT) have the strongest evidence base for treating depression. CBT targets cognitive distortions and behavioral activation. IPT focuses on interpersonal disputes, role transitions, grief, and interpersonal deficits. Behavioral Activation (BA) -- increasing engagement in positively reinforcing activities -- has emerged as an effective standalone treatment, with efficacy comparable to full CBT in some studies (Dimidjian et al., 2006).
rewritten_html:
Suicide Risk Assessment

Having explored the major pharmacological and psychotherapeutic treatments for mood disorders, we now turn to what is arguably the most urgent clinical issue in all of mental health practice: the assessment of suicide risk. Every clinician will encounter suicidal clients — and how well you assess, document, and respond to that risk can literally mean the difference between life and death. For the EPPP, this topic is not only clinically essential but also heavily tested, spanning questions about risk factors, protective factors, evidence-based interventions, legal and ethical obligations, and the critical distinction between outdated practices and current best-practice guidelines.

Consider this scenario: A 52-year-old man presents to your outpatient practice following a recent divorce. He reports pervasive hopelessness, has been drinking heavily, and mentions — almost in passing — that he recently purchased a firearm "for protection." He denies active suicidal ideation when you ask directly. Should you feel reassured? The answer, of course, is no. Suicide risk assessment requires you to look beyond a client's self-report and integrate demographic data, psychiatric history, behavioral warning signs, and situational factors into a comprehensive clinical picture. Let's examine the key components you need to know.

Clinical Note: No-Suicide Contracts

Historically, some clinicians have used no-suicide contracts (also called "contracts for safety") in which a client verbally or in writing agrees not to engage in self-harm. However, research consistently demonstrates that these agreements do not reduce the likelihood of suicidal behavior. A client in acute crisis may agree to such a contract to avoid hospitalization, to please the clinician, or out of social compliance — none of which reflect genuine safety. Furthermore, no-suicide contracts offer no legal protection to the therapist in the event of a client's suicide. Courts have not recognized these contracts as meeting the standard of care for suicide risk management. Current best practices instead emphasize the use of collaborative safety planning, which involves working with the client to identify warning signs, coping strategies, social supports, professionals to contact during crisis, and means restriction steps. Clinicians should also conduct thorough, ongoing risk assessments and document clinical decision-making rather than relying on a signed agreement as a substitute for careful evaluation.

Clinical Note: No-Suicide Contracts

However, there is now broad professional consensus that these agreements lack empirical support as a suicide prevention strategy and may actually create a false sense of security for the clinician. No-suicide contracts have no legal standing, do not constitute adequate risk management, and may discourage deeper clinical exploration of suicidal ideation. Patients who are most at risk — those experiencing intense ambivalence, impulsivity, or psychotic symptoms — are precisely the individuals least able to honor such agreements.

Current best-practice guidelines recommend replacing no-suicide contracts with collaborative safety planning. A safety plan, developed jointly with the patient, identifies personal warning signs, internal coping strategies, social contacts and settings that provide distraction, individuals to contact for help, professionals and agencies to reach in crisis, and steps for restricting access to lethal means. Unlike a no-suicide contract, a safety plan is a clinical tool that empowers the patient with concrete, actionable steps rather than relying on a promise that may be impossible to keep during a crisis.

Risk Factors

Understanding suicide risk factors is essential for both clinical practice and the EPPP. No single risk factor is sufficient to predict suicide — rather, risk accumulates as multiple factors converge. Think of risk assessment as building a mosaic: each piece alone may seem incomplete, but together they reveal a clearer picture. The following risk factors are the most well-established in the research literature, and you should know them thoroughly for the exam.

  • Previous suicide attempt -- the single strongest predictor of completed suicide
  • Psychiatric diagnosis -- over 90% of completers had a diagnosable disorder, with depression and substance use being the most common
  • Hopelessness -- a stronger predictor of suicidal intent than depression severity (Beck et al., 1985)
  • Demographic factors: Males complete suicide at approximately 4 times the rate of females; females attempt suicide approximately 3 times as often as males
  • Access to lethal means, family history of suicide, recent losses, social isolation
  • Age: Highest rates in adults 45-64 and those 85+

The gender paradox in suicide — men die by suicide far more often, yet women attempt it far more frequently — is one of the most important distinctions to remember. This disparity is largely explained by method lethality: men are more likely to use firearms, while women more often use overdose or other methods that allow greater opportunity for intervention. This is also why means restriction (such as safely storing firearms or limiting access to medications) is one of the most effective suicide prevention strategies available, and why clinicians should always ask about access to lethal means during a risk assessment.

Notice that hopelessness, not depression severity per se, is the stronger predictor of suicidal intent. Aaron Beck and colleagues demonstrated this finding in landmark research, and it carries important clinical implications: a client whose depression is moderate but who feels utterly trapped and hopeless about the future may be at greater risk than someone with severe depressive symptoms who still holds some optimism. This is why assessment tools like the Beck Hopelessness Scale can provide clinically valuable information beyond standard depression measures.

Protective Factors

Effective suicide risk assessment doesn't stop at cataloging what makes a person vulnerable — it also requires identifying what keeps them alive. Protective factors are the counterweights to risk, and understanding them helps clinicians develop more nuanced, individualized safety plans. A person with multiple risk factors but strong reasons for living, robust social connections, and active engagement in treatment may be at meaningfully lower risk than their risk factor profile alone would suggest.

  • Social connectedness and reasons for living
  • Effective clinical care for mental and substance use disorders
  • Restricted access to lethal means
  • Cultural and religious beliefs that discourage suicide

Keep in mind that protective factors do not eliminate risk — they buffer against it. A clinician should never dismiss elevated risk simply because a client identifies reasons for living or reports religious beliefs against suicide. Instead, protective factors should be woven into the clinical formulation alongside risk factors to arrive at a balanced, well-documented assessment of overall suicide risk. On the EPPP, expect questions that require you to weigh both sides of this equation rather than relying on any single indicator in isolation.

Clinical Pearl

The Joiner interpersonal theory of suicide (2005) identifies three factors necessary for a lethal suicide attempt: thwarted belongingness (feeling disconnected), perceived burdensomeness (feeling like a burden to others), and acquired capability (reduced fear of death through habituation to pain and self-harm). What makes Joiner's model particularly powerful — and frequently tested on the EPPP — is its explanation of why most people who desire suicide never attempt it. According to the theory, suicidal desire arises from the intersection of thwarted belongingness and perceived burdensomeness, but desire alone is not sufficient. Only when a person has also developed acquired capability — through repeated exposure to painful or provocative experiences such as prior self-harm, combat exposure, childhood abuse, or even certain occupational risks — does the threshold for a lethal attempt get crossed. This three-factor model helps explain why previous suicide attempts are such a potent risk factor: each attempt may further habituate the individual to the fear and pain associated with self-injury, increasing acquired capability for future attempts.

heading_text: Alternative DSM-5 Model for Personality Disorders (AMPD)
section_html:
Alternative DSM-5 Model for Personality Disorders (AMPD)

Section III of the DSM-5 presents an alternative dimensional-categorical hybrid model for personality disorder diagnosis. This model proposes two core criteria:

Criterion A: Level of Personality Functioning

Assessed using the Level of Personality Functioning Scale (LPFS), which evaluates impairments across four elements:

  • Identity: Experience of oneself as unique; self-esteem stability; emotional range
  • Self-direction: Pursuit of goals; self-reflective functioning; internal standards
  • Empathy: Comprehension of others' experiences; tolerance of differing perspectives
  • Intimacy: Depth and duration of connection; desire and capacity for closeness

Criterion B: Pathological Personality Traits

Organized into five broad trait domains (with 25 trait facets):

  1. Negative Affectivity (vs. Emotional Stability)
  2. Detachment (vs. Extraversion)
  3. Antagonism (vs. Agreeableness)
  4. Disinhibition (vs. Conscientiousness)
  5. Psychoticism (vs. Lucidity)

The AMPD retains six specific personality disorders: antisocial, avoidant, borderline, narcissistic, obsessive-compulsive, and schizotypal. The remaining four (paranoid, schizoid, histrionic, dependent) can be described using Criterion A and B but are not retained as named types.
prev_last_paragraph: OCPD involves ego-syntonic traits -- the person's perfectionism and control feel consistent with who they are. OCD involves ego-dystonic obsessions and compulsions -- the person recognizes them as excessive and distressing. OCPD does not involve true obsessions or compulsions. Despite the name similarity, only about 23-32% of individuals with OCD also have OCPD. OCPD is the most prevalent personality disorder in the general population (approximately 3-8%).
rewritten_html:
Alternative DSM-5 Model for Personality Disorders (AMPD)

Having explored all ten personality disorders organized across three clusters, you may have noticed something unsettling: the categorical approach — you either have a disorder or you don't — often feels at odds with clinical reality. Patients rarely fit neatly into a single diagnostic box. Traits bleed across categories, comorbidity is the rule rather than the exception, and clinicians frequently disagree about where "personality style" ends and "personality disorder" begins. These frustrations are not new; they have fueled decades of debate about how personality pathology should be classified. In response, Section III of the DSM-5 presents a fundamentally different way of thinking about personality disorders — a dimensional-categorical hybrid model known as the Alternative DSM-5 Model for Personality Disorders, or AMPD.

Rather than asking simply "Does this person meet the threshold for Disorder X?", the AMPD asks two deeper questions: First, how impaired is this person's core sense of self and their capacity for relating to others? And second, which specific pathological personality traits characterize their difficulties? These two questions correspond to the model's two core criteria — Criterion A and Criterion B — which together provide a richer, more nuanced portrait of personality pathology than the traditional categorical approach alone.

Criterion A: Level of Personality Functioning

Think of a client who maintains a stable sense of who she is, sets meaningful goals, understands what her friends are feeling, and sustains close relationships even through conflict. Now think of another client who cannot describe himself without referencing other people's opinions, abandons goals impulsively, misreads the emotions of those around him, and cycles through intense but short-lived relationships. The difference between these two individuals is not simply that one "has" a personality disorder and the other does not — it is that they function at different levels of personality organization. Criterion A captures this dimension of impairment using a structured tool.

Assessed using the Level of Personality Functioning Scale (LPFS), Criterion A evaluates impairments across four elements that fall into two broad domains — self-functioning and interpersonal functioning. A moderate or greater level of impairment (rated on a 0-to-4 scale) is required for a personality disorder diagnosis under this model. The four elements are:

  • Identity: Experience of oneself as unique; self-esteem stability; emotional range
  • Self-direction: Pursuit of goals; self-reflective functioning; internal standards
  • Empathy: Comprehension of others' experiences; tolerance of differing perspectives
  • Intimacy: Depth and duration of connection; desire and capacity for closeness

Identity and self-direction together reflect self-functioning: Can this person maintain a coherent sense of who they are, and can they steer their own life in a purposeful direction? Empathy and intimacy together reflect interpersonal functioning: Can this person accurately understand others and build meaningful connections? Clinically, this framework is powerful because it moves beyond symptom checklists to examine the psychological infrastructure that underlies healthy personality — the very capacities that personality disorders disrupt most profoundly.

Criterion B: Pathological Personality Traits

While Criterion A tells you how impaired someone's personality functioning is, Criterion B tells you in what way that impairment is expressed. Two individuals may both show moderate impairment on the LPFS, yet look remarkably different in a clinical interview — one withdrawn and emotionally flat, the other volatile and antagonistic. Criterion B captures this variation through a dimensional trait system organized into five broad trait domains, each with specific facets underneath (25 facets total). Notably, each domain is conceptualized as the maladaptive pole of a spectrum that also has an adaptive opposite:

  1. Negative Affectivity (vs. Emotional Stability)
  2. Detachment (vs. Extraversion)
  3. Antagonism (vs. Agreeableness)
  4. Disinhibition (vs. Conscientiousness)
  5. Psychoticism (vs. Lucidity)

If these opposites remind you of the Big Five personality model (also called the Five-Factor Model), you are making exactly the right connection — the AMPD trait domains were designed to align with and extend that well-established research framework into the domain of pathology. For example, a patient high in Antagonism and Disinhibition but low in Negative Affectivity might present with the grandiose, exploitative, and impulsive profile characteristic of antisocial or narcissistic pathology. A patient high in Negative Affectivity and Detachment might present with the anxious withdrawal seen in avoidant pathology. This system allows clinicians to construct individualized trait profiles rather than forcing patients into a single diagnostic category.

The AMPD retains six specific personality disorders: antisocial, avoidant, borderline, narcissistic, obsessive-compulsive, and schizotypal. The remaining four (paranoid, schizoid, histrionic, dependent) can be described using Criterion A and B but are not retained as named types. This means that under the alternative model, a clinician can still diagnose these presentations — they simply do so by specifying the pattern of personality functioning impairment and pathological traits rather than applying a categorical label. For the EPPP, remember which six made the cut and which four did not — a frequently tested distinction that reflects the field's ongoing effort to balance clinical tradition with empirical evidence for dimensional approaches to personality pathology.

section_html:
Cluster A: Odd or Eccentric

Cluster A personality disorders are characterized by odd, eccentric thinking and behavior. There is a genetic association with schizophrenia spectrum disorders.

Paranoid Personality Disorder

A pervasive pattern of distrust and suspiciousness of others such that their motives are interpreted as malevolent. Features include suspecting exploitation or harm, doubting loyalty of friends, reluctance to confide, reading hidden meanings into benign remarks, bearing grudges, perceiving attacks on character, and recurring suspicions of partner infidelity.

Differential Diagnosis

Paranoid PD vs. delusional disorder (persecutory type): In paranoid PD, the suspicions are not of delusional intensity -- they are exaggerated interpretations but not fixed, false beliefs. Paranoid PD vs. paranoid schizophrenia: Paranoid PD lacks hallucinations, disorganized speech, and other psychotic features.

Schizoid Personality Disorder

A pervasive pattern of detachment from social relationships and a restricted range of emotional expression. Features include neither desiring nor enjoying close relationships, choosing solitary activities, little interest in sexual experiences, taking pleasure in few activities, lacking close friends, appearing indifferent to praise or criticism, and emotional coldness or flattened affect.

Schizotypal Personality Disorder

A pervasive pattern of social and interpersonal deficits marked by acute discomfort with close relationships, cognitive or perceptual distortions, and eccentricities of behavior. Features include ideas of reference, odd beliefs or magical thinking, unusual perceptual experiences, odd thinking and speech, suspiciousness, inappropriate or constricted affect, odd behavior or appearance, lack of close friends, and excessive social anxiety that does not diminish with familiarity.

Clinical Pearl

Schizotypal PD has the strongest genetic link to schizophrenia and is considered part of the schizophrenia spectrum. It involves quasi-psychotic symptoms (ideas of reference, magical thinking, perceptual distortions) that fall short of true psychosis. In the ICD-10, schizotypal disorder is classified as a psychotic disorder rather than a personality disorder.
