rewritten_html:
Extrapyramidal Symptoms (EPS)

Imagine a young man brought to the emergency department just hours after receiving his first injection of haloperidol. His neck is twisted painfully to one side, his eyes are locked in an upward gaze, and he is terrified. Or picture a middle-aged woman who has taken chlorpromazine faithfully for years and now cannot stop her tongue from darting in and out of her mouth — a movement she barely notices but that profoundly affects how others interact with her. These are not rare curiosities. They are among the most clinically significant and distressing adverse effects in all of psychopharmacology, and understanding them is essential for any practitioner who prescribes, monitors, or provides therapy to patients taking antipsychotic medications.

In the preceding section, we noted that high-potency typical antipsychotics such as haloperidol bind tightly to dopamine D2 receptors and carry a greater risk of movement-related side effects, while low-potency agents like chlorpromazine trade that risk for more sedation and anticholinergic burden. Now we turn to those movement-related side effects in detail — a family of disorders collectively known as extrapyramidal symptoms (EPS). These are movement disorders caused by dopamine D2 blockade in the nigrostriatal pathway, the brain circuit that fine-tunes voluntary movement. When antipsychotic drugs block too many D2 receptors in this pathway — particularly beyond the roughly 80% occupancy threshold — the delicate balance between dopamine and acetylcholine in the basal ganglia is disrupted, and motor control goes awry. They are most common with high-potency typical antipsychotics, though any agent with significant D2 antagonism can be the culprit.

What makes EPS especially important for clinical practice is that these symptoms unfold along a predictable timeline, from reactions that emerge within hours of the first dose to disorders that develop only after months or years of chronic treatment. Recognizing where a patient falls on that timeline is the key to accurate diagnosis and appropriate intervention. The table below summarizes the four major types of EPS, their characteristic timing, clinical presentation, and recommended treatments.

EPS TypeOnsetFeaturesTreatment
Acute dystoniaHours to daysSustained muscle contractions (torticollis, oculogyric crisis, opisthotonus); can be life-threatening if laryngeal muscles affectedAnticholinergics (benztropine/Cogentin, diphenhydramine/Benadryl)
AkathisiaDays to weeksSubjective restlessness; inability to sit still; often mistaken for agitationBeta-blockers (propranolol), benzodiazepines, dose reduction
Parkinsonism (pseudoparkinsonism)Weeks to monthsBradykinesia, rigidity, resting tremor, shuffling gait, mask-like faciesAnticholinergics (benztropine); amantadine; dose reduction
Tardive dyskinesiaMonths to yearsInvoluntary, repetitive movements (especially orofacial: lip smacking, tongue protrusion, chewing, grimacing); may be irreversibleDiscontinue or reduce offending agent if possible; valbenazine (Ingrezza) or deutetrabenazine (Austedo) -- VMAT2 inhibitors approved for TD

Let's walk through each of these in a bit more detail so the clinical picture comes alive. Acute dystonia is often the first EPS a patient encounters — and it can be genuinely frightening. A classic board-style vignette involves a young male patient (young men are at highest risk) who develops torticollis or oculogyric crisis within hours of starting a high-potency antipsychotic. The treatment is swift and gratifying: an intramuscular injection of benztropine or diphenhydramine typically resolves the crisis within minutes, restoring the dopamine-acetylcholine balance in the basal ganglia by blocking the acetylcholine side of the equation.

Akathisia, appearing within days to weeks, is more insidious. Patients describe an unbearable inner restlessness — a need to move, pace, or shift their weight — that can be so distressing it contributes to medication nonadherence or even suicidality. Crucially, akathisia is often mistaken for psychotic agitation, which can lead a clinician to increase the antipsychotic dose and inadvertently make the problem worse. This diagnostic trap is a favorite testing point on the EPPP. Unlike acute dystonia and parkinsonism, akathisia responds best not to anticholinergics but to beta-blockers like propranolol, benzodiazepines, or dose reduction of the offending agent.

Drug-induced parkinsonism (also called pseudoparkinsonism) develops over weeks to months and closely mimics idiopathic Parkinson's disease — bradykinesia, cogwheel rigidity, resting "pill-rolling" tremor, shuffling gait, and mask-like facies. The underlying mechanism is the same dopamine depletion in the nigrostriatal pathway. Anticholinergics such as benztropine or the dopamine-releasing agent amantadine are first-line treatments, along with dose reduction when clinically feasible.

Tardive dyskinesia (TD) is the most feared of all extrapyramidal symptoms because it typically appears only after months to years of antipsychotic use and may be irreversible even after the offending drug is stopped. The hallmark presentation involves involuntary, repetitive orofacial movements — lip smacking, tongue protrusion, lateral jaw movements, and grimacing — though the trunk and extremities can also be affected. The pathophysiology is thought to involve dopamine receptor supersensitivity that develops after prolonged blockade. In a paradox that the EPPP frequently tests, abruptly discontinuing the antipsychotic can temporarily unmask or worsen TD, because the supersensitive receptors are suddenly exposed to unblocked dopamine. Two VMAT2 (vesicular monoamine transporter 2) inhibitors — valbenazine (Ingrezza) and deutetrabenazine (Austedo) — are now FDA-approved specifically for the treatment of tardive dyskinesia, representing the first targeted pharmacotherapy for this condition.

EPPP Tip

Know the timeline: acute dystonia appears within hours to days, akathisia within days to weeks, parkinsonism within weeks to months, and tardive dyskinesia after months to years of use. TD is the most feared because it may be irreversible and paradoxically may worsen when the offending drug is discontinued. A helpful mnemonic for the order is "Days, Weeks, Months, Years" — the four EPS types march along this timeline in the same sequence they appear in the table. Also remember that akathisia is the one most commonly confused with worsening psychosis, and anticholinergics are not its first-line treatment — beta-blockers are.

section_html:
Metabolic Syndrome

Second-generation antipsychotics (especially clozapine and olanzapine) carry significant risk of metabolic syndrome, which includes:

  • Weight gain (often 10-30+ pounds)
  • Dyslipidemia (elevated triglycerides, decreased HDL)
  • Hyperglycemia / Type 2 diabetes
  • Hypertension

Metabolic monitoring (fasting glucose, lipid panel, weight, waist circumference, blood pressure) is recommended at baseline and at regular intervals for all patients on atypical antipsychotics.

Metabolic Risk by Medication (High to Low)

  1. Clozapine and Olanzapine (highest risk)
  2. Quetiapine and Risperidone (moderate risk)
  3. Aripiprazole, Ziprasidone, and Lurasidone (lowest risk)
prev_last_paragraph: While agranulocytosis is most closely associated with clozapine, it is important to recognize the broader category of neutropenia — a reduction in neutrophil count that compromises the body's ability to fight bacterial infections. Agranulocytosis represents the most severe end of this spectrum, defined by an absolute neutrophil count (ANC) below 500 cells/μL, which places the patient at critical risk for life-threatening infections. With clozapine, the incidence of agranulocytosis is approximately 1–2%, with the highest risk occurring during the first six months of treatment. Other second-generation antipsychotics (e.g., olanzapine, quetiapine) have been associated with neutropenia on rare occasions, though at rates far lower than clozapine. The mandatory blood monitoring program for clozapine — known as the Clozapine REMS (Risk Evaluation and Mitigation Strategy) — requires regular ANC checks: weekly for the first six months, biweekly for the next six months, and monthly thereafter if counts remain stable. Treatment must be immediately discontinued if ANC falls below specified thresholds. This monitoring requirement is a defining feature of clozapine management and a frequently tested concept.
rewritten_html:
Metabolic Syndrome

Having explored the hematological dangers of clozapine — particularly the life-threatening risk of agranulocytosis — we now turn to a different but equally consequential class of adverse effects that extends well beyond a single medication. Imagine a patient who begins olanzapine for treatment-resistant psychosis. Within six months, her psychotic symptoms have improved remarkably, but she has gained 25 pounds, her fasting blood glucose has climbed into the prediabetic range, and her triglyceride levels have doubled. Her psychiatrist now faces a painful clinical dilemma: the medication that rescued her mental health is simultaneously eroding her physical health. This scenario plays out routinely in clinical practice and illustrates why understanding metabolic syndrome is not a peripheral concern — it is central to responsible prescribing and long-term patient care.

Second-generation antipsychotics (especially clozapine and olanzapine) carry significant risk of metabolic syndrome, a cluster of interrelated metabolic disturbances that, when they co-occur, dramatically increase a patient's risk for cardiovascular disease, stroke, and premature death. The syndrome is not a single disease but rather a constellation of physiological changes that tend to travel together, each amplifying the danger of the others. Specifically, metabolic syndrome includes:

  • Weight gain (often 10-30+ pounds)
  • Dyslipidemia (elevated triglycerides, decreased HDL)
  • Hyperglycemia / Type 2 diabetes
  • Hypertension

The mechanisms behind these metabolic effects are complex and not fully understood, but they appear to involve the medications' actions on histamine H1 receptors and serotonin 5-HT2C receptors — both of which play roles in appetite regulation and energy metabolism. Clozapine and olanzapine have the strongest affinity for these receptors, which helps explain why they sit at the top of the metabolic risk hierarchy. The clinical significance cannot be overstated: individuals with serious mental illness already have a life expectancy 15 to 25 years shorter than the general population, and cardiovascular disease — fueled in part by antipsychotic-induced metabolic changes — is the leading cause of that mortality gap.

Because of these risks, metabolic monitoring (fasting glucose, lipid panel, weight, waist circumference, blood pressure) is recommended at baseline and at regular intervals for all patients on atypical antipsychotics. Guidelines from the American Diabetes Association and the American Psychiatric Association call for reassessing weight at every visit during the first several months, checking fasting glucose and lipids at 12 weeks, and then continuing surveillance at least annually thereafter. In practice, psychologists who work collaboratively with prescribers play an important role in ensuring that patients understand the importance of these monitoring protocols and in encouraging behavioral strategies — such as dietary modifications and physical activity programs — that can mitigate metabolic risk without requiring a medication change.

Metabolic Risk by Medication (High to Low)

Not all second-generation antipsychotics carry the same metabolic burden. Understanding the relative risk across medications is clinically essential because it directly informs treatment selection, especially for patients who already have risk factors such as obesity, family history of diabetes, or existing dyslipidemia. The hierarchy below is well established in the research literature and frequently tested on licensing examinations:

  1. Clozapine and Olanzapine (highest risk)
  2. Quetiapine and Risperidone (moderate risk)
  3. Aripiprazole, Ziprasidone, and Lurasidone (lowest risk)

A useful clinical mnemonic is to think of clozapine and olanzapine as the "metabolic heavyweights" — powerful in efficacy but equally potent in their metabolic toll. At the other end of the spectrum, aripiprazole, ziprasidone, and lurasidone are sometimes described as "metabolically friendly," though this label is relative rather than absolute; even these agents warrant baseline and ongoing monitoring. Ziprasidone, for example, carries its own unique concern — QTc prolongation — reminding clinicians that selecting a lower-metabolic-risk agent does not eliminate the need for vigilant safety monitoring. The clinical art lies in balancing symptom control against the full profile of side-effect risks for each individual patient, a calculation that shifts with every new piece of medical history.

section_html:
Overview

This chapter covers anxiolytics (medications used to treat anxiety disorders), including benzodiazepines and buspirone, as well as anti-dementia medications. These medication classes appear regularly on the EPPP because understanding their mechanisms, side effects, and clinical considerations is essential for psychologists collaborating with prescribers.
rewritten_html:
Overview

Imagine a client sitting across from you in your office, hands trembling, voice tight, describing panic attacks that have overtaken her daily life. Her psychiatrist has started her on a medication and wants your input on how the pharmacological intervention might interact with the cognitive-behavioral therapy you are providing. In that moment, your clinical effectiveness depends not just on your therapy skills but on your working knowledge of the medications your client is taking — how they work, what side effects to watch for, and how they might influence the therapeutic process itself.

This chapter focuses on anxiolytics — medications used to treat anxiety disorders — including benzodiazepines and buspirone, as well as anti-dementia medications that psychologists increasingly encounter when working with aging populations. These medication classes appear regularly on the EPPP, and for good reason: psychologists who collaborate with prescribers need a solid understanding of drug mechanisms, side effect profiles, and the clinical considerations that shape treatment decisions. Whether you are conducting a neuropsychological evaluation, providing psychotherapy, or consulting on a treatment team, knowing what these medications do — and what they cannot do — makes you a more effective clinician and a more informed advocate for your clients.

We will begin with the benzodiazepines, a class of medications that revolutionized the treatment of anxiety but that also carry significant risks, particularly around dependence and withdrawal. From there, we will move to buspirone and the anti-dementia drugs, building a practical pharmacological toolkit that connects directly to the kinds of clinical scenarios you will face both on the exam and in professional practice.

section_html:
Second-Generation (Atypical) Antipsychotics

Atypical antipsychotics block both dopamine D2 receptors and serotonin 5-HT2A receptors. This dual mechanism, known as serotonin-dopamine antagonism (SDA), is thought to reduce EPS risk and improve negative symptoms compared to typical antipsychotics.

Common Atypical Antipsychotics

Generic NameBrand NameNotable Features
ClozapineClozarilGold standard for treatment-resistant schizophrenia; lowest EPS risk; most effective for refractory positive and negative symptoms; also reduces suicidality in schizophrenia. SERIOUS RISK: agranulocytosis (1-2%) requiring mandatory blood monitoring (weekly for 6 months, then biweekly, then monthly)
RisperidoneRisperdalHigher EPS risk than other atypicals at higher doses (dose-dependent D2 blockade); significant prolactin elevation; available as long-acting injectable (Risperdal Consta)
OlanzapineZyprexaHighest risk of weight gain and metabolic syndrome; structurally similar to clozapine; effective but metabolic concerns limit use
QuetiapineSeroquelVery sedating at lower doses; used off-label for insomnia and anxiety; lower EPS risk; less prolactin elevation
ZiprasidoneGeodonWeight-neutral; lowest metabolic risk among atypicals; QT prolongation concern; should be taken with food for absorption
AripiprazoleAbilifyPartial dopamine agonist (D2 partial agonist); stabilizes dopamine activity; low EPS, low metabolic risk, low sedation; may cause akathisia
LurasidoneLatudaMust be taken with food (350+ calories); lower metabolic risk; approved for bipolar depression
EPPP Tip

Key facts to know: Clozapine = treatment-resistant schizophrenia + agranulocytosis risk + mandatory blood monitoring. Olanzapine = worst metabolic side effects. Aripiprazole = unique partial D2 agonist mechanism. Risperidone = highest prolactin elevation among atypicals.
prev_last_paragraph: Both involve hyperthermia and altered mental status, but NMS features lead-pipe rigidity and develops over days, while serotonin syndrome features hyperreflexia, clonus, and myoclonus and develops within hours. NMS is caused by dopamine blockade; serotonin syndrome by serotonin excess. This distinction is a classic exam question. A helpful way to remember: NMS is "slow and stiff" (developing over days with rigid muscles), while serotonin syndrome is "fast and twitchy" (developing within hours with jerky, hyperactive reflexes). Also consider the medication history — NMS follows antipsychotic use, while serotonin syndrome typically follows the initiation or dose increase of serotonergic drugs (SSRIs, SNRIs, MAOIs) or the combination of multiple serotonergic agents.
rewritten_html:
Second-Generation (Atypical) Antipsychotics

Having explored the serious adverse effects of first-generation antipsychotics — from the acute dystonic reactions that can frighten patients in their first days of treatment, to the potentially irreversible movements of tardive dyskinesia, to the life-threatening emergency of neuroleptic malignant syndrome — it becomes clear why the field was eager for alternatives. The development of second-generation antipsychotics represented a genuine paradigm shift in psychopharmacology, one driven by a deceptively simple question: What if an antipsychotic could block dopamine effectively enough to reduce psychosis while simultaneously buffering the brain against the movement disorders and motivational blunting that plagued older medications?

Atypical antipsychotics answered that question through a dual receptor strategy: they block both dopamine D2 receptors and serotonin 5-HT2A receptors. This dual mechanism, known as serotonin-dopamine antagonism (SDA), is thought to reduce EPS risk and improve negative symptoms compared to typical antipsychotics. Here's the logic: serotonin normally inhibits dopamine release in certain brain pathways. By blocking 5-HT2A receptors, atypicals essentially "release the brake" on dopamine in the nigrostriatal pathway (reducing movement side effects) and in the mesocortical pathway (potentially improving negative symptoms like flat affect and social withdrawal). Meanwhile, they still block enough D2 activity in the mesolimbic pathway to manage positive symptoms like hallucinations and delusions. Think of it as a more targeted approach — dampening dopamine where it's overactive while preserving or even enhancing dopamine function where it's needed.

Clinically, this matters enormously. Consider a 24-year-old graduate student experiencing his first episode of psychosis — auditory hallucinations and paranoid delusions that have disrupted his studies and relationships. His psychiatrist faces a choice: a first-generation antipsychotic that may effectively suppress his hallucinations but leave him cognitively dulled and at risk for debilitating movement disorders, or an atypical antipsychotic that may address his psychosis while better preserving his cognitive functioning and motivation. For a young person hoping to return to graduate school, that difference can shape the entire trajectory of recovery. This is why atypical antipsychotics have become first-line treatments for most patients with schizophrenia and other psychotic disorders — not because they are free of side effects (they certainly are not), but because their side effect profile is, for many patients, more manageable.

Common Atypical Antipsychotics

While all atypical antipsychotics share the general principle of serotonin-dopamine antagonism, they are far from interchangeable. Each has a distinct receptor binding profile that translates into a unique constellation of benefits, side effects, and clinical niches. The table below captures the most exam-relevant features of the major atypicals. Pay close attention to clozapine's special status, olanzapine's metabolic burden, aripiprazole's unique mechanism, and risperidone's tendency to elevate prolactin — these are the facts most commonly tested on the EPPP.

Generic NameBrand NameNotable Features
ClozapineClozarilGold standard for treatment-resistant schizophrenia; lowest EPS risk; most effective for refractory positive and negative symptoms; also reduces suicidality in schizophrenia. SERIOUS RISK: agranulocytosis (1-2%) requiring mandatory blood monitoring (weekly for 6 months, then biweekly, then monthly)
RisperidoneRisperdalHigher EPS risk than other atypicals at higher doses (dose-dependent D2 blockade); significant prolactin elevation; available as long-acting injectable (Risperdal Consta)
OlanzapineZyprexaHighest risk of weight gain and metabolic syndrome; structurally similar to clozapine; effective but metabolic concerns limit use
QuetiapineSeroquelVery sedating at lower doses; used off-label for insomnia and anxiety; lower EPS risk; less prolactin elevation
ZiprasidoneGeodonWeight-neutral; lowest metabolic risk among atypicals; QT prolongation concern; should be taken with food for absorption
AripiprazoleAbilifyPartial dopamine agonist (D2 partial agonist); stabilizes dopamine activity; low EPS, low metabolic risk, low sedation; may cause akathisia
LurasidoneLatudaMust be taken with food (350+ calories); lower metabolic risk; approved for bipolar depression

A few clinical stories bring these distinctions to life. Clozapine occupies a truly unique position: it is the only antipsychotic with robust evidence for treatment-resistant schizophrenia, typically defined as failure to respond adequately to at least two other antipsychotic trials. Imagine a patient who has been hospitalized repeatedly, tried haloperidol, risperidone, and olanzapine, and continues to hear commanding voices that make independent living impossible. Clozapine may be the medication that finally quiets those voices — and it is also the only antipsychotic proven to reduce suicidality in schizophrenia. But this remarkable efficacy comes with a serious catch: a 1-2% risk of agranulocytosis, a dangerous drop in white blood cells that can leave a patient fatally vulnerable to infection. This is why clozapine requires mandatory blood monitoring through a centralized registry — weekly complete blood counts for the first six months, biweekly for the next six months, and monthly thereafter. No blood draw, no medication. It's one of the most carefully regulated prescriptions in all of medicine.

Aripiprazole stands out for a completely different reason: its mechanism. Unlike every other antipsychotic — typical or atypical — aripiprazole is a partial dopamine agonist rather than a full antagonist. Think of a partial agonist as a "dopamine thermostat." In brain regions where dopamine is too high (the mesolimbic pathway in psychosis), it competes with dopamine at the receptor and reduces signaling — functioning more like a blocker. But in regions where dopamine is too low (the mesocortical pathway, contributing to negative symptoms), it provides just enough stimulation to partially restore function. This stabilizing quality means aripiprazole carries low risks for EPS, metabolic side effects, and sedation, making it an attractive first choice for many patients. Its most notable side effect is akathisia — that restless, driven-to-move feeling — which can be distressing enough to prompt discontinuation if not recognized and managed.

Risperidone behaves almost like a bridge between the typical and atypical worlds. At lower doses, it maintains a favorable atypical profile. But as the dose climbs, its D2 blockade intensifies, and it begins to look pharmacologically more like a conventional antipsychotic — with increased EPS risk and significant prolactin elevation. Elevated prolactin can cause galactorrhea (inappropriate breast milk production), menstrual irregularities, sexual dysfunction, and with chronic elevation, reduced bone density. For this reason, risperidone requires especially careful dose management, and clinicians should monitor for prolactin-related symptoms, particularly in younger patients and women of reproductive age.

Olanzapine is often described as one of the most effective atypicals for acute symptom control, but its reputation is shadowed by the most pronounced metabolic side effects in its class — substantial weight gain, dyslipidemia, and insulin resistance that can progress to type 2 diabetes. A patient started on olanzapine might gain 15 to 30 pounds within the first year, fundamentally altering their cardiovascular risk profile. This metabolic burden, discussed in detail in the next section on metabolic syndrome, means that olanzapine requires vigilant monitoring of weight, fasting glucose, and lipid panels — and often prompts a difficult clinical conversation about balancing psychiatric stability against long-term physical health.

EPPP Tip

Key facts to know: Clozapine = treatment-resistant schizophrenia + agranulocytosis risk + mandatory blood monitoring. Olanzapine = worst metabolic side effects. Aripiprazole = unique partial D2 agonist mechanism. Risperidone = highest prolactin elevation among atypicals.

A helpful mnemonic for the EPPP: think of the atypicals as having traded one set of problems for another. First-generation antipsychotics were "movement medications" — effective but plagued by EPS and tardive dyskinesia. Second-generation antipsychotics shifted the burden toward "metabolic medications" — generally easier on the motor system but introducing concerns about weight, diabetes, and cardiovascular risk. Neither generation is categorically superior; rather, the clinical art lies in matching the right medication to the right patient, weighing the specific risks that matter most for that individual's health, functioning, and quality of life.

section_html:
Buspirone (BuSpar)

Buspirone is a non-benzodiazepine anxiolytic used primarily for generalized anxiety disorder (GAD).

  • Mechanism: Partial agonist at serotonin 5-HT1A receptors; does not act on GABA receptors
  • Onset: Takes 2-4 weeks to reach full effect (similar to antidepressants), making it unsuitable for acute anxiety relief
  • Advantages: No sedation, no tolerance or dependence, no withdrawal syndrome, no cross-tolerance with alcohol/benzodiazepines, no abuse potential
  • Disadvantages: Slow onset; not effective for acute anxiety or panic; patients who have previously used benzodiazepines may perceive it as ineffective due to the absence of the immediate sedating effect
EPPP Tip

Buspirone is a favorite EPPP topic because it differs from benzodiazepines in every key way: slow onset, no sedation, no dependence, no withdrawal, no cross-tolerance with alcohol. If a question asks about an anxiolytic that is safe for patients with a history of substance abuse, buspirone is the answer.
prev_last_paragraph: Flumazenil is the specific benzodiazepine antagonist used to reverse benzodiazepine overdose. It competitively blocks the benzodiazepine binding site on the GABA-A receptor. Caution: it can precipitate seizures in patients with benzodiazepine dependence.
rewritten_html:
Buspirone (BuSpar)

Having just explored benzodiazepines — fast-acting, sedating, and carrying real risks of dependence and withdrawal — a natural clinical question arises: What do you prescribe for the patient who needs long-term anxiolytic treatment but has a history of alcohol dependence? Or the patient who cannot afford the cognitive dulling that benzodiazepines produce? This is exactly the clinical niche that Buspirone fills, and understanding how it differs from benzodiazepines in virtually every important dimension is essential for both the EPPP and real-world practice.

Imagine a 42-year-old accountant who presents with chronic, pervasive worry about finances, health, and family — classic generalized anxiety disorder (GAD). He also has a five-year history of alcohol use disorder and has been sober for eight months. His therapist has referred him for a medication evaluation. The prescriber immediately rules out benzodiazepines: they carry abuse potential, produce cross-tolerance with alcohol, and could jeopardize his recovery. Instead, the prescriber starts buspirone — a non-benzodiazepine anxiolytic that works through an entirely different mechanism and carries none of the dependency risks associated with the GABA-based medications discussed in the previous section.

  • Mechanism: Partial agonist at serotonin 5-HT1A receptors; does not act on GABA receptors
  • Onset: Takes 2-4 weeks to reach full effect (similar to antidepressants), making it unsuitable for acute anxiety relief
  • Advantages: No sedation, no tolerance or dependence, no withdrawal syndrome, no cross-tolerance with alcohol/benzodiazepines, no abuse potential
  • Disadvantages: Slow onset; not effective for acute anxiety or panic; patients who have previously used benzodiazepines may perceive it as ineffective due to the absence of the immediate sedating effect

The mechanism of buspirone is worth pausing on, because it explains nearly all of its clinical properties. Unlike benzodiazepines, which enhance GABA-A receptor function and produce immediate calming through widespread neural inhibition, buspirone works as a partial agonist at serotonin 5-HT1A receptors. This means it modulates serotonergic transmission in a gradual, modulatory fashion — much the way antidepressants do. The result is that therapeutic effects build over two to four weeks, and there is no immediate "hit" of sedation or euphoria. Because buspirone completely bypasses the GABA system, it produces no sedation, no motor impairment, no potentiation of alcohol effects, and no physiological dependence.

This last point — the absence of an immediate subjective effect — creates an interesting clinical challenge. Patients who have previously taken benzodiazepines often report that buspirone "doesn't work." They are accustomed to the rapid, tangible relief of a benzodiazepine and interpret the absence of that feeling as treatment failure. Clinicians must set expectations carefully at the outset: buspirone's benefits emerge gradually, and the absence of sedation is actually a feature, not a bug. This psychoeducation is part of responsible prescribing and can make the difference between treatment adherence and early dropout.

Consider another clinical scenario: a graduate student with GAD is terrified of becoming dependent on medication after watching a family member struggle with benzodiazepine withdrawal. Buspirone would be an ideal first-line choice — she can take it daily for months without developing tolerance, and if treatment is eventually discontinued, there is no withdrawal syndrome to manage. Contrast this with the careful taper required when discontinuing long-term benzodiazepine therapy, and the clinical appeal of buspirone for certain patient populations becomes immediately clear.

EPPP Tip

Buspirone is a favorite EPPP topic because it differs from benzodiazepines in every key way: slow onset, no sedation, no dependence, no withdrawal, no cross-tolerance with alcohol. If a question asks about an anxiolytic that is safe for patients with a history of substance abuse, buspirone is the answer. A helpful mnemonic: think of buspirone as the "anti-benzodiazepine" — for every characteristic feature of benzodiazepines (fast onset, sedation, dependence, withdrawal, cross-tolerance with alcohol, abuse potential), buspirone does the opposite. If an exam question describes a patient with anxiety and a substance use history, or asks which anxiolytic carries no risk of physiological dependence, buspirone should be your first thought.

section_html:
Benzodiazepines

Benzodiazepines are the most commonly prescribed anxiolytics. They enhance the effect of the inhibitory neurotransmitter GABA (gamma-aminobutyric acid) by binding to the GABA-A receptor complex and increasing the frequency of chloride channel opening, leading to neuronal inhibition.

Common Benzodiazepines

Generic NameBrand NameDurationNotable Features
DiazepamValiumLong-actingRapid onset; used for anxiety, seizures, muscle spasms, alcohol withdrawal; active metabolites prolong effects
LorazepamAtivanIntermediateNo active metabolites; safe in liver impairment; commonly used in acute agitation; IM administration well-absorbed
AlprazolamXanaxShort-actingMost commonly prescribed benzodiazepine; high abuse potential; significant rebound anxiety; commonly used for panic disorder
ClonazepamKlonopinLong-actingUsed for panic disorder, seizures, social anxiety; longer duration reduces interdose rebound
ChlordiazepoxideLibriumLong-actingHistorically used for alcohol withdrawal protocols; first benzodiazepine synthesized
TriazolamHalcionUltra-shortUsed as a hypnotic (sleep aid); risk of anterograde amnesia; very short half-life

Clinical Considerations

  • Rapid onset of action (minutes to hours), unlike antidepressants which take weeks
  • Tolerance and dependence develop with chronic use; benzodiazepines should generally be prescribed for short-term use
  • Withdrawal can be medically dangerous (seizures, delirium); must be tapered gradually, never stopped abruptly
  • Cross-tolerance exists with alcohol and barbiturates (all act on GABA receptors)
  • Benzodiazepines are respiratory depressants; combined with opioids or alcohol, the risk of fatal respiratory depression increases significantly
  • Older adults are at increased risk for falls, cognitive impairment, and paradoxical reactions (agitation, disinhibition)
Flumazenil (Romazicon)

Flumazenil is the specific benzodiazepine antagonist used to reverse benzodiazepine overdose. It competitively blocks the benzodiazepine binding site on the GABA-A receptor. Caution: it can precipitate seizures in patients with benzodiazepine dependence.
prev_last_paragraph: This chapter covers anxiolytics (medications used to treat anxiety disorders), including benzodiazepines and buspirone, as well as anti-dementia medications. These medication classes appear regularly on the EPPP because understanding their mechanisms, side effects, and clinical considerations is essential for psychologists collaborating with prescribers.
rewritten_html:
Benzodiazepines

Imagine a patient arriving at an emergency department in the grip of a severe panic attack — heart racing, chest tight, convinced she is dying. Within twenty minutes of receiving a medication, her breathing slows, her muscles relax, and the overwhelming terror begins to recede. The medication responsible for this rapid transformation is almost certainly a benzodiazepine. No other class of anxiolytic works this quickly, and that speed is both its greatest clinical asset and the source of its most serious risks.

Benzodiazepines are the most commonly prescribed anxiolytics, and understanding how they work begins with the brain's primary inhibitory neurotransmitter: GABA (gamma-aminobutyric acid). GABA acts as the nervous system's braking mechanism — when it binds to GABA-A receptors on neurons, it opens chloride channels that allow negatively charged chloride ions to flow into the cell, making the neuron less likely to fire. Benzodiazepines do not directly activate these receptors on their own. Instead, they bind to a specific site on the GABA-A receptor complex and enhance GABA's natural effect by increasing the frequency of chloride channel opening. Think of it this way: GABA is the driver pressing the brake pedal, and benzodiazepines make the brakes more responsive. The result is widespread neuronal inhibition — reduced anxiety, muscle relaxation, sedation, and anticonvulsant effects.

This mechanism is a high-yield distinction for the EPPP: benzodiazepines increase the frequency of chloride channel opening (they need GABA present to work), whereas barbiturates increase the duration of channel opening and can activate the receptor even without GABA — which is why barbiturate overdose is far more dangerous. Keeping this frequency-versus-duration distinction firmly in mind will help you navigate exam questions that compare these two drug classes.

Common Benzodiazepines

Benzodiazepines vary considerably in how quickly they take effect, how long they last, and what clinical situations they best serve. The table below summarizes the agents you are most likely to encounter on the EPPP. Pay special attention to duration of action and notable clinical features, as these details frequently appear in exam items — for example, knowing which benzodiazepine is safest in liver impairment, or which one carries the highest abuse potential.

Generic NameBrand NameDurationNotable Features
DiazepamValiumLong-actingRapid onset; used for anxiety, seizures, muscle spasms, alcohol withdrawal; active metabolites prolong effects
LorazepamAtivanIntermediateNo active metabolites; safe in liver impairment; commonly used in acute agitation; IM administration well-absorbed
AlprazolamXanaxShort-actingMost commonly prescribed benzodiazepine; high abuse potential; significant rebound anxiety; commonly used for panic disorder
ClonazepamKlonopinLong-actingUsed for panic disorder, seizures, social anxiety; longer duration reduces interdose rebound
ChlordiazepoxideLibriumLong-actingHistorically used for alcohol withdrawal protocols; first benzodiazepine synthesized
TriazolamHalcionUltra-shortUsed as a hypnotic (sleep aid); risk of anterograde amnesia; very short half-life

A few clinical pearls from this table deserve emphasis. Lorazepam's lack of active metabolites makes it the preferred choice when the liver cannot efficiently process drugs — as in elderly patients or those with hepatic disease. Alprazolam's short half-life means patients often experience rebound anxiety between doses, which can paradoxically drive dose escalation and increase dependence risk. And chlordiazepoxide holds a special place in psychopharmacology history: synthesized in 1955 by Leo Sternbach, it was the first benzodiazepine ever developed and launched the modern era of anxiolytic pharmacotherapy.

Clinical Considerations

The clinical profile of benzodiazepines is defined by a central tension: they are remarkably effective in the short term but carry substantial risks with prolonged use. As a psychologist consulting with prescribers or monitoring patients' treatment responses, you need to understand both sides of this equation. Consider a therapist working with a patient who has been taking alprazolam daily for two years. The patient reports that the medication "doesn't work like it used to" and has been taking extra pills on stressful days. This scenario illustrates several of the core clinical concerns outlined below.

  • Rapid onset of action (minutes to hours), unlike antidepressants which take weeks
  • Tolerance and dependence develop with chronic use; benzodiazepines should generally be prescribed for short-term use
  • Withdrawal can be medically dangerous (seizures, delirium); must be tapered gradually, never stopped abruptly
  • Cross-tolerance exists with alcohol and barbiturates (all act on GABA receptors)
  • Benzodiazepines are respiratory depressants; combined with opioids or alcohol, the risk of fatal respiratory depression increases significantly
  • Older adults are at increased risk for falls, cognitive impairment, and paradoxical reactions (agitation, disinhibition)

The concept of cross-tolerance is particularly important for clinical practice and the EPPP. Because benzodiazepines, alcohol, and barbiturates all enhance GABA activity, chronic use of any one of these substances produces tolerance to the others. This is why a patient with a history of heavy alcohol use may require higher-than-expected doses of a benzodiazepine for sedation — and it also explains why combining these substances is so dangerous. Their sedative and respiratory-depressant effects are additive, even synergistic, creating a potentially lethal combination.

Withdrawal from benzodiazepines deserves special emphasis because it is one of the few substance withdrawal syndromes that can be life-threatening. Abrupt discontinuation after chronic use can produce seizures, delirium, and in rare cases, death. For this reason, benzodiazepines must always be tapered gradually under medical supervision. The EPPP frequently tests the knowledge that both benzodiazepine and alcohol withdrawal can produce seizures — a fact that distinguishes these substances from opioids, whose withdrawal is extremely uncomfortable but rarely fatal.

For older adults, benzodiazepines pose unique hazards that psychologists should recognize. The Beers Criteria — a widely used guideline for medication safety in the elderly — lists benzodiazepines as potentially inappropriate medications for older adults due to increased sensitivity to sedation, heightened fall risk, and the possibility of paradoxical reactions in which the patient becomes more agitated or disinhibited rather than calmer. When you encounter an elderly patient who has become unexpectedly confused or combative after starting a new medication, consider whether a benzodiazepine might be the culprit.

Flumazenil (Romazicon)

Flumazenil is the specific benzodiazepine antagonist used to reverse benzodiazepine overdose. It works by competitively blocking the benzodiazepine binding site on the GABA-A receptor, effectively displacing the drug and restoring normal GABA function. While flumazenil can be lifesaving in acute overdose situations, it must be used with caution: in patients who have developed physical dependence on benzodiazepines, administering flumazenil can abruptly remove the drug's effect and precipitate dangerous withdrawal seizures. This is an important clinical detail that the EPPP may test — the reversal agent itself carries its own serious risks.

section_html:
Anti-Dementia Medications

Currently available medications for Alzheimer's disease provide symptomatic relief but do not halt or reverse the underlying neurodegenerative process.

Cholinesterase Inhibitors

These drugs inhibit the enzyme acetylcholinesterase, which breaks down acetylcholine, thereby increasing acetylcholine availability in the brain. They are used for mild to moderate Alzheimer's disease.

Generic NameBrand NameNotable Features
DonepezilAriceptMost commonly prescribed; once-daily dosing; approved for all stages of Alzheimer's; relatively well-tolerated
RivastigmineExelonAvailable as a transdermal patch (reduces GI side effects); also inhibits butyrylcholinesterase; approved for Parkinson's disease dementia
GalantamineRazadyneAlso modulates nicotinic acetylcholine receptors

Common side effects: Nausea, diarrhea, vomiting, decreased appetite, dizziness, bradycardia (all related to increased cholinergic activity).

Memantine (Namenda)

  • Mechanism: NMDA receptor antagonist; blocks excessive glutamate activity (thought to protect against excitotoxicity)
  • Uses: Moderate to severe Alzheimer's disease; often used in combination with a cholinesterase inhibitor
  • Side effects: Generally well-tolerated; dizziness, headache, constipation, confusion
EPPP Tip

Cholinesterase inhibitors (donepezil, rivastigmine, galantamine) work by increasing acetylcholine and are used for mild to moderate Alzheimer's. Memantine is an NMDA antagonist used for moderate to severe Alzheimer's. These drugs slow symptom progression but do NOT cure or reverse the disease.
prev_last_paragraph: Clinical NoteA musician experiencing hand tremor and rapid heartbeat before recitals may benefit from a single dose of propranolol taken 30–60 minutes before performing. However, a patient with pervasive worry, rumination, and emotional distress associated with GAD would not find adequate relief from a beta-blocker alone, because these drugs do not target the psychological dimensions of anxiety.
rewritten_html:
Anti-Dementia Medications

Imagine a 72-year-old retired professor who begins misplacing her keys, forgetting her grandchildren's names, and struggling to follow conversations she once led with ease. Her family, desperate for answers, asks whether medication can "fix" what's happening to her brain. This is one of the most heartbreaking conversations in clinical practice — because the honest answer is complicated. While we do have medications that can help, they work by managing symptoms and temporarily slowing cognitive decline, not by halting or reversing the disease itself. Understanding what these drugs can and cannot do is essential for any clinician working with aging populations, and it is a topic the EPPP expects you to know well.

Having just explored anxiolytics and sedatives — medications that modulate systems like GABA and serotonin to manage anxiety — we now shift to a very different clinical challenge: the progressive loss of cognitive function in Alzheimer's disease. The neurotransmitter systems involved here are different (primarily acetylcholine and glutamate), but the pharmacological logic is similar: identify what's going wrong at the neurochemical level and intervene to restore some degree of balance. Currently available medications for Alzheimer's disease provide symptomatic relief but do not halt or reverse the underlying neurodegenerative process. This distinction — palliative versus curative — is critical for setting realistic expectations with patients and families alike.

Cholinesterase Inhibitors

One of the earliest and most consistent findings in Alzheimer's disease research is the loss of cholinergic neurons — the brain cells that produce and release acetylcholine, a neurotransmitter critical for memory formation, attention, and learning. As these neurons degenerate, acetylcholine levels plummet, and cognitive function deteriorates. The pharmacological strategy behind cholinesterase inhibitors is elegant in its simplicity: if you can't produce enough acetylcholine, at least prevent the breakdown of what little remains. These drugs inhibit the enzyme acetylcholinesterase, which is responsible for breaking down acetylcholine in the synaptic cleft, thereby increasing acetylcholine availability in the brain. Think of it like plugging a leaky bucket — you're not adding more water, but you're keeping more of what you have. Cholinesterase inhibitors are the first-line treatment for mild to moderate Alzheimer's disease.

Generic NameBrand NameNotable Features
DonepezilAriceptMost commonly prescribed; once-daily dosing; approved for all stages of Alzheimer's; relatively well-tolerated
RivastigmineExelonAvailable as a transdermal patch (reduces GI side effects); also inhibits butyrylcholinesterase; approved for Parkinson's disease dementia
GalantamineRazadyneAlso modulates nicotinic acetylcholine receptors

For the EPPP, donepezil (Aricept) is the name you are most likely to encounter. It is the most widely prescribed cholinesterase inhibitor, largely because of its convenient once-daily dosing and its approval across all stages of Alzheimer's disease — mild, moderate, and severe. Rivastigmine is noteworthy for its transdermal patch formulation, which is particularly useful for patients who have difficulty swallowing pills or who experience significant gastrointestinal side effects. Galantamine adds a dual mechanism by also modulating nicotinic acetylcholine receptors, potentially enhancing cholinergic transmission through a second pathway.

Common side effects: Nausea, diarrhea, vomiting, decreased appetite, dizziness, bradycardia (all related to increased cholinergic activity). Because these drugs boost acetylcholine throughout the body — not just in the brain — the side effect profile reflects widespread cholinergic stimulation. Gastrointestinal symptoms are the most frequent reason patients discontinue treatment, which is why the transdermal patch formulation of rivastigmine can be a valuable clinical alternative.

Memantine (Namenda)

While cholinesterase inhibitors address the acetylcholine deficit in Alzheimer's disease, memantine targets a completely different neurotransmitter system: glutamate. In a healthy brain, glutamate is the primary excitatory neurotransmitter, essential for learning and memory. But in Alzheimer's disease, damaged neurons leak excessive glutamate, which overstimulates NMDA receptors on neighboring cells. This chronic overstimulation — called excitotoxicity — essentially floods neurons with calcium, leading to further cell damage and death. It's like leaving a faucet running until the sink overflows and damages the floor. Memantine works by partially blocking NMDA receptors, reducing this toxic flood without completely shutting down normal glutamate signaling.

  • Mechanism: NMDA receptor antagonist; blocks excessive glutamate activity (thought to protect against excitotoxicity)
  • Uses: Moderate to severe Alzheimer's disease; often used in combination with a cholinesterase inhibitor
  • Side effects: Generally well-tolerated; dizziness, headache, constipation, confusion

A key clinical point — and one the EPPP frequently tests — is that memantine occupies a different treatment niche than the cholinesterase inhibitors. While donepezil and its cousins are first-line for mild to moderate stages, memantine is reserved for moderate to severe Alzheimer's disease. In practice, clinicians often combine memantine with a cholinesterase inhibitor (most commonly donepezil) to target both the cholinergic and glutamatergic systems simultaneously, a strategy supported by evidence showing modest additional benefit over monotherapy.

EPPP Tip

Cholinesterase inhibitors (donepezil, rivastigmine, galantamine) work by increasing acetylcholine and are used for mild to moderate Alzheimer's. Memantine is an NMDA antagonist used for moderate to severe Alzheimer's. These drugs slow symptom progression but do NOT cure or reverse the disease.

section_html:
Standard 9.05: Test Construction

Psychologists who develop tests and other assessment techniques use appropriate psychometric procedures and current scientific or professional knowledge for test design, standardization, validation, reduction or elimination of bias, and recommendations for use.

This standard applies to psychologists who create new assessment instruments and requires that such instruments meet accepted standards for reliability, validity, and fairness.
prev_last_paragraph: Test data (9.04) = the client's responses, scores, and behavioral observations -- generally released to the client upon request. Test materials (9.11) = the test itself (questions, stimuli, manuals, scoring keys) -- protected from release to maintain test security. A helpful mnemonic: test data are about the person; test materials are about the test. If a document would exist regardless of which client sat down — such as a test manual or a blank answer sheet — it is a test material. If it was created because this particular client participated — such as their scores, their specific answers, or your behavioral observations — it is test data. This distinction is frequently tested on the EPPP.
rewritten_html:
Standard 9.05: Test Construction

Having explored the critical distinction between test data and test materials — and the responsibilities psychologists carry when releasing assessment information — we now turn to where every assessment instrument begins: its construction. Before a test can generate data worth protecting, before scores can be interpreted or released, someone must build the test itself. And Standard 9.05 establishes that this process is far from casual — it demands rigorous scientific discipline at every stage.

Consider a psychologist developing a new screening measure for postpartum depression tailored to a specific cultural community. She cannot simply compile a list of questions that seem relevant, administer them, and call the result a validated instrument. Instead, she must carefully evaluate whether her items capture the construct she intends to measure, whether the instrument produces consistent scores across administrations, whether it performs equitably across demographic groups, and whether adequate norms exist to guide interpretation. The stakes are enormous: a poorly constructed screening tool might miss mothers in genuine crisis or, conversely, pathologize normal cultural expressions of distress.

Standard 9.05 addresses exactly this responsibility: psychologists who develop tests and other assessment techniques use appropriate psychometric procedures and current scientific or professional knowledge for test design, standardization, validation, reduction or elimination of bias, and recommendations for use. In other words, the Ethics Code holds test developers to the same empirical rigor that the field demands in any scientific endeavor — because an assessment instrument is, at its core, a measurement tool, and measurement tools must be precise, fair, and well-calibrated.

This standard applies specifically to psychologists who create new assessment instruments, and it requires that such instruments meet accepted standards for reliability, validity, and fairness. Reliability means the instrument yields consistent, reproducible results; validity means it actually measures what it claims to measure; and fairness means the instrument does not systematically disadvantage particular groups due to cultural, linguistic, or demographic bias. A test that is reliable but biased — or valid for one population but untested in another — falls short of the standard's requirements.

For the EPPP, remember that Standard 9.05 is specifically about the construction side of assessment. It complements the standards that govern test use, interpretation, and data release by ensuring that the foundation — the instrument itself — is psychometrically sound. Think of it this way: Standards 9.02 through 9.04 govern how clinicians wield assessment tools responsibly, while 9.05 governs how developers forge those tools in the first place. A brilliant clinician cannot compensate for a fundamentally flawed instrument, which is why the Ethics Code addresses both sides of the equation.

section_html:
Standard 9.03: Informed Consent in Assessments

Psychologists obtain informed consent for assessments, evaluations, or diagnostic services, except when:

  1. Testing is mandated by law or governmental regulations
  2. Informed consent is implied because testing is conducted as a routine educational, institutional, or organizational activity (e.g., admission testing)
  3. The purpose of the testing is to evaluate decisional capacity

9.03(a) -- Explaining the Purpose

Informed consent includes an explanation of the nature and purpose of the assessment, fees, involvement of third parties, and limits of confidentiality in a language reasonably understandable to the person being assessed or their legal representative.

9.03(b) -- Individuals Lacking Capacity

For persons who lack the capacity to consent (e.g., due to cognitive impairment), psychologists provide appropriate explanation, seek the person's assent, consider preferences and best interests, and obtain consent from a legally authorized person.

9.03(c) -- Court-Ordered or Mandated Assessment

When services are court ordered or otherwise mandated, psychologists inform the individual of the nature of the anticipated services, including whether the services are court ordered or mandated and any limits of confidentiality, before proceeding.

EPPP Tip

Court-ordered assessments still require notification -- the psychologist must tell the individual about the nature of services and limits of confidentiality, even though the person cannot refuse the assessment. Informed consent is modified but not eliminated in mandated evaluations.
prev_last_paragraph: A psychologist administers an intelligence test normed on English-speaking Americans to a recent immigrant whose first language is Spanish. The psychologist must note the cultural and linguistic limitations of the assessment, consider using instruments validated for Spanish speakers, and avoid drawing definitive conclusions about intellectual ability based on the potentially biased results.
rewritten_html:
Standard 9.03: Informed Consent in Assessments

Imagine you're a psychologist about to begin a comprehensive neuropsychological evaluation with a new client. Before you open the first test booklet, there's a critical step that must occur — one that shapes the entire ethical foundation of the assessment process. The client needs to understand what's about to happen, why it's happening, who will see the results, and what the limits of privacy are. This is the essence of informed consent in assessments, and it's far more than a form to be signed. It represents the client's right to make a knowing, voluntary decision about participating in a process that could profoundly affect their life — from diagnostic labels to custody decisions to disability determinations.

Having just discussed the ethical use of assessments under Standard 9.02 — including the obligation to use instruments appropriate for the individual being tested — we now turn to what must happen before any assessment begins. Standard 9.03 establishes the requirement that psychologists obtain informed consent for assessments, evaluations, or diagnostic services. However, the Ethics Code recognizes that certain contexts make traditional informed consent impractical or unnecessary. Psychologists are not required to obtain informed consent in the following circumstances:

  1. Testing is mandated by law or governmental regulations
  2. Informed consent is implied because testing is conducted as a routine educational, institutional, or organizational activity (e.g., admission testing)
  3. The purpose of the testing is to evaluate decisional capacity

The third exception is particularly worth noting: if a psychologist has been asked to determine whether a person can make competent decisions — for example, an elderly patient whose family is concerned about dementia — requiring that person to provide truly informed consent before the evaluation would create a logical paradox. You'd be asking someone to demonstrate the very capacity you've been asked to assess. Similarly, when a court orders a forensic evaluation or when students routinely take placement tests at school, the traditional consent process is either legally superseded or contextually implied. Even so, as you'll see below, notification and explanation are never entirely waived.

9.03(a) -- Explaining the Purpose

When informed consent is required, it must be more than a vague assurance that "we'll be doing some testing today." Consider a parent bringing their child in for a psychoeducational evaluation. Ethical practice demands that the psychologist explain, in language the parent can readily understand, what types of tests will be administered, what they're designed to measure, how long the process will take, and what will happen with the results. Informed consent includes an explanation of the nature and purpose of the assessment, fees, involvement of third parties, and limits of confidentiality in a language reasonably understandable to the person being assessed or their legal representative. For instance, if the evaluation has been requested by the child's school district, the parent needs to know that a report will be shared with school personnel — this is the kind of third-party involvement that must be disclosed upfront. The key phrase here is "reasonably understandable": a psychologist working with a client who has limited education shouldn't rely on jargon-heavy consent forms but should instead use clear, plain language and check for genuine comprehension.

9.03(b) -- Individuals Lacking Capacity

Some of the most ethically delicate assessment situations arise when the person being evaluated cannot provide meaningful consent on their own — a young child, an adult with significant intellectual disability, or a patient with advanced Alzheimer's disease. In these cases, the psychologist's obligations don't simply vanish; they become layered. For persons who lack the capacity to consent (e.g., due to cognitive impairment), psychologists provide appropriate explanation at a level the person can understand, seek the person's assent even when formal consent isn't possible, consider the person's preferences and best interests, and obtain consent from a legally authorized person such as a guardian or parent. This standard reflects a deeply humanistic principle: even when someone cannot legally consent, their dignity and autonomy still matter. A psychologist evaluating a teenager with moderate intellectual disability should still explain, in simple terms, what the testing involves and why it's being done — and should pay attention to whether the teen seems willing or reluctant to participate. Obtaining a parent's signature on a consent form does not absolve the psychologist from engaging respectfully with the individual being assessed.

9.03(c) -- Court-Ordered or Mandated Assessment

Forensic and legal contexts create a unique tension in the consent process. When a judge orders a defendant to undergo a psychological evaluation, that individual cannot simply decline. Yet the absence of choice doesn't eliminate the psychologist's ethical responsibilities. When services are court ordered or otherwise mandated, psychologists inform the individual of the nature of the anticipated services, including whether the services are court ordered or mandated and any limits of confidentiality, before proceeding. Picture a forensic psychologist meeting with a parent involved in a custody dispute. Even though this parent must submit to the evaluation, the psychologist should clearly explain: "This evaluation was ordered by the court. I'll be assessing your parenting capacity and psychological functioning. My report will be submitted to the judge and will be available to both attorneys. I am not acting as your therapist, and what you tell me is not confidential in the way therapy would be." This kind of transparent notification protects the individual from the mistaken belief that they're in a therapeutic relationship and ensures they understand the evaluative — not supportive — nature of the interaction.

EPPP Tip

Court-ordered assessments still require notification -- the psychologist must tell the individual about the nature of services and limits of confidentiality, even though the person cannot refuse the assessment. Informed consent is modified but not eliminated in mandated evaluations. On the EPPP, watch for answer choices that suggest mandated evaluations require no communication with the examinee at all — that's incorrect. The obligation shifts from obtaining consent to providing clear, upfront notification. Think of it this way: the person loses the right to say no, but they never lose the right to know what's happening and why.

heading_text: Standard 2.04: Bases for Scientific and Professional Judgments
section_html:
Standard 2.04: Bases for Scientific and Professional Judgments

Psychologists' work must be based on established scientific and professional knowledge of the discipline. This means psychologists should rely on:

  • Peer-reviewed research and empirical evidence
  • Established theories grounded in scientific investigation
  • Professional guidelines and practice parameters
  • Clinical judgment informed by training and experience, not personal bias or speculation
Evidence-Based Practice

The APA Presidential Task Force (2006) defined evidence-based practice in psychology (EBPP) as the integration of the best available research with clinical expertise in the context of patient characteristics, culture, and preferences. EBPP is the operational expression of Standard 2.04.

next_heading_text: Standard 2.05: Delegation of Work to Others
rewritten_html:
Standard 2.04: Bases for Scientific and Professional Judgments

Imagine a psychologist who, after attending a weekend workshop on a novel therapeutic technique, begins applying it broadly across their caseload — despite the absence of controlled studies supporting its use and without consideration of how it fits the unique needs of each client. When a colleague questions the approach, the psychologist replies, "It just feels right to me." This scenario cuts to the heart of why Standard 2.04 exists: psychology's credibility as a profession depends on practitioners anchoring their work not in intuition or enthusiasm, but in the established scientific and professional knowledge base of the discipline.

Having explored in the previous section how psychologists maintain competence over time through ongoing education and self-assessment, we now turn to a closely related but distinct question: on what foundation should psychologists build their professional decisions in the first place? Standard 2.04 addresses this directly by requiring that every clinical judgment, assessment interpretation, treatment recommendation, and professional opinion be grounded in defensible, empirically informed reasoning. It is not enough to be competent in a general sense — one must also ensure that specific judgments flow from the right sources of knowledge.

In practice, this means psychologists should rely on multiple pillars of professional knowledge that reinforce and check one another:

  • Peer-reviewed research and empirical evidence
  • Established theories grounded in scientific investigation
  • Professional guidelines and practice parameters
  • Clinical judgment informed by training and experience, not personal bias or speculation

Consider how these pillars work together in a clinical context. A psychologist evaluating a child for ADHD would draw on peer-reviewed diagnostic criteria and validated rating scales (empirical evidence), use a developmental framework for understanding attention regulation (established theory), follow professional guidelines such as those published by the American Academy of Child and Adolescent Psychiatry (practice parameters), and integrate all of this with their own clinical observations and training — while remaining vigilant against confirmation bias or premature conclusions. Standard 2.04 does not require that every decision be dictated by a single study; rather, it demands that the overall reasoning process be scientifically grounded and professionally defensible.

This standard also serves as a safeguard against the misuse of professional authority. When a psychologist offers testimony in a custody hearing, writes a report for a disability determination, or recommends a particular treatment approach, the weight of that opinion derives from its scientific basis. Opinions rooted in personal ideology, unexamined assumptions, or outdated training undermine public trust and can cause real harm. Standard 2.04 thus functions as both an ethical mandate and a quality-control mechanism for the profession.

Evidence-Based Practice

The APA Presidential Task Force (2006) defined evidence-based practice in psychology (EBPP) as the integration of the best available research with clinical expertise in the context of patient characteristics, culture, and preferences. EBPP is the operational expression of Standard 2.04. Notice that this definition is intentionally three-legged: research evidence alone does not dictate practice, nor does clinical experience alone justify it. Instead, EBPP asks psychologists to weave together empirical findings, seasoned professional judgment, and a deep respect for the individual sitting across from them — their cultural background, values, and treatment goals. When exam questions reference Standard 2.04, they are often testing whether you understand that scientific grounding and individualized clinical reasoning are complementary, not competing, obligations.

As we move to Standard 2.05, we shift from the knowledge base underlying professional judgments to the practical question of how psychologists extend their work through others — and what responsibilities follow when tasks are delegated to supervisees, assistants, or other professionals.

section_html:
Standard 2.03: Maintaining Competence

Psychologists undertake ongoing efforts to develop and maintain their competence. This includes:

  • Staying current with scientific and professional developments in their areas of practice
  • Pursuing continuing education (CE) activities
  • Engaging in peer consultation and supervision
  • Reviewing current literature and research findings
  • Attending professional conferences and workshops

Continuing Education Requirements

Most state licensing boards require psychologists to complete a specified number of continuing education (CE) credits during each renewal period (typically 20-40 hours per biennium). Many states require specific CE topics such as ethics, cultural diversity, or evidence-based practice.

The Competence Constellation Model

Rodolfa et al. (2005) proposed a competence constellation model that distinguishes between foundational competencies and functional competencies:

Foundational CompetenciesFunctional Competencies
Reflective practice and self-assessmentAssessment, diagnosis, and case conceptualization
Scientific knowledge and methodsIntervention
Relationships (therapeutic alliance)Consultation
Ethical and legal standardsResearch and evaluation
Individual and cultural diversitySupervision and teaching
Interdisciplinary systemsManagement and administration
prev_last_paragraph: Standard 2.02 is the emergency exception to competence boundaries. On the EPPP, if a question describes a crisis situation (e.g., a natural disaster) where no other provider is available, the psychologist may provide services outside their typical area of competence. However, this is temporary — they must stop once the emergency ends or a qualified provider is found. Watch for answer choices that frame this as an absolute rule ("a psychologist must never practice outside their competence"); the emergency exception makes such absolutes incorrect. Also note that both conditions must be present: there must be a genuine emergency, and other appropriate services must be unavailable. A psychologist cannot invoke this standard simply because a situation feels urgent if qualified providers are accessible.
next_heading_text: Standard 2.04: Bases for Scientific and Professional Judgments
rewritten_html:
Standard 2.03: Maintaining Competence

Imagine a psychologist who earned their doctorate fifteen years ago. Their training was rigorous, their internship demanding, and they passed the EPPP on their first attempt. But since then, they haven't attended a single workshop, read a journal article, or sought peer consultation. They continue to use the same assessment instruments and therapeutic approaches they learned in graduate school — even as the evidence base has shifted dramatically beneath them. Are they still competent? The answer, according to the APA Ethics Code, is almost certainly no. Competence is not a credential you earn once and carry forever; it is a living commitment that demands ongoing cultivation throughout your career.

We've just seen how Standard 2.02 permits psychologists to temporarily step beyond their competence boundaries in genuine emergencies. Standard 2.03 addresses something more fundamental: the obligation to ensure that your existing competence doesn't erode over time. Where Standards 2.01 and 2.02 deal with the boundaries of competence — what you can and cannot practice — Standard 2.03 speaks to its depth and currency within the areas you already claim as your own.

Psychologists undertake ongoing efforts to develop and maintain their competence. This is not a vague aspiration but an active, career-long ethical obligation. In practice, maintaining competence includes:

  • Staying current with scientific and professional developments in their areas of practice
  • Pursuing continuing education (CE) activities
  • Engaging in peer consultation and supervision
  • Reviewing current literature and research findings
  • Attending professional conferences and workshops

Consider a clinical psychologist specializing in anxiety disorders. Over the past decade, the evidence base for treating specific phobias has evolved considerably — new research on inhibitory learning models has reshaped how many clinicians conceptualize and deliver exposure therapy. A psychologist who maintains competence would be aware of these developments, might attend a workshop on updated exposure protocols, and would integrate the best available evidence into their practice. One who does not risks providing outdated — and potentially less effective — care to their clients, even within their stated area of expertise.

Continuing Education Requirements

The ethical mandate of Standard 2.03 is reinforced by regulatory teeth. Most state licensing boards require psychologists to complete a specified number of continuing education (CE) credits during each renewal period (typically 20-40 hours per biennium). These requirements serve as a structural safeguard, ensuring that licensees engage in at least a minimum level of professional development. Many states go further by mandating specific CE topics such as ethics, cultural diversity, suicide prevention, or evidence-based practice — reflecting areas where outdated knowledge poses particular risk to the public.

It is worth noting, however, that CE requirements represent a floor, not a ceiling. Simply accumulating the minimum number of credits does not automatically mean a psychologist has fulfilled their ethical obligation under Standard 2.03. A neuropsychologist who completes all required CE hours in workshops on practice management, while neglecting to stay current with developments in neuroimaging or concussion assessment, may satisfy the licensing board's requirements but still fall short of the ethical standard. For the EPPP, remember that maintaining competence is first and foremost an ethical obligation — one that exists independently of, and often exceeds, state regulatory mandates.

The Competence Constellation Model

But what exactly does "competence" encompass? The concept is broader and more multidimensional than it might initially appear. A psychologist could be highly skilled in administering cognitive assessments but lack the reflective self-awareness to recognize when personal biases are affecting their clinical judgment. They might be an excellent therapist but a poor supervisor. Rodolfa et al. (2005) proposed a competence constellation model that captures this complexity by distinguishing between two categories: foundational competencies — the underlying knowledge, skills, and attitudes that support all professional functions — and functional competencies — the specific activities psychologists perform in their professional roles.

Think of foundational competencies as the soil from which all professional work grows, and functional competencies as the distinct plants that emerge from that soil. A psychologist's ability to conduct effective intervention (a functional competency) depends on their capacity for reflective self-assessment, their grasp of scientific methods, and their sensitivity to cultural diversity (all foundational competencies). This model is particularly useful for understanding why competence maintenance requires attention to both domains — a therapist who keeps up with the latest CBT protocols but neglects self-reflection about their own countertransference reactions has only partially maintained their competence.

Foundational CompetenciesFunctional Competencies
Reflective practice and self-assessmentAssessment, diagnosis, and case conceptualization
Scientific knowledge and methodsIntervention
Relationships (therapeutic alliance)Consultation
Ethical and legal standardsResearch and evaluation
Individual and cultural diversitySupervision and teaching
Interdisciplinary systemsManagement and administration

For the EPPP, the key takeaway from the competence constellation model is the distinction between these two tiers. If a question asks about self-assessment or cultural awareness, recognize these as foundational competencies — the bedrock that underlies all professional activity. If a question asks about assessment, therapy, consultation, or supervision, these are functional competencies — the specific professional roles psychologists perform. Understanding this framework helps you appreciate why Standard 2.03 demands such a broad commitment: maintaining competence means tending to both the roots and the branches of your professional practice.

heading_text: Standard 2.05: Delegation of Work to Others
section_html:
Standard 2.05: Delegation of Work to Others

Psychologists who delegate work to employees, supervisees, research or teaching assistants, or others:

  • Take reasonable steps to avoid delegating work to persons with a multiple relationship with those being served
  • Authorize only those responsibilities the person can be expected to perform competently based on their education, training, or experience
  • Ensure that such persons perform the services competently
Example

A psychologist delegates psychological testing administration to a psychometrist. Under 2.05, the psychologist must ensure the psychometrist is properly trained in administering the specific test, must supervise the work appropriately, and retains ultimate responsibility for the interpretation and clinical use of test results.
