EBPP is the operational expression of Standard 2.04.
rewritten_html:
Standard 2.05: Delegation of Work to Others

No psychologist works in complete isolation. Whether in a busy group practice, a university training clinic, or a research lab, the reality of professional life means that psychologists routinely rely on others — supervisees, psychometrists, research assistants, administrative staff — to carry out portions of their work. But here is the critical ethical question: when you hand off a task, you do not hand off responsibility. Standard 2.05 addresses exactly this tension, spelling out the obligations that follow whenever a psychologist delegates work to another person. If Standard 2.04 asks psychologists to ground their own judgments in science and professional knowledge, Standard 2.05 extends that commitment outward by ensuring that anyone acting on a psychologist's behalf also meets appropriate standards of competence and ethical conduct.

Consider a clinical psychologist who supervises a first-year practicum student in a community mental health center. The supervisor asks the student to conduct an intake interview with a new client. This seems routine enough — but what if the client presents with active suicidal ideation and a complex trauma history? The supervisor cannot simply assign the case and walk away. Standard 2.05 requires that the psychologist thoughtfully evaluate whether the student has the training and skill to handle the situation, provide adequate oversight, and step in when the demands of the case exceed the student's current competence. Delegation, in other words, is not abdication. It is a structured, ethically governed process.

Psychologists who delegate work to employees, supervisees, research or teaching assistants, or others must meet three interrelated obligations:

  • Take reasonable steps to avoid delegating work to persons with a multiple relationship with those being served — for instance, a psychologist should not ask a graduate assistant to score the neuropsychological battery of a client who happens to be the assistant's neighbor and close friend
  • Authorize only those responsibilities the person can be expected to perform competently based on their education, training, or experience — meaning you match the task to the delegate's actual skill level, not simply to what is convenient
  • Ensure that such persons perform the services competently — which requires ongoing supervision, review of work products, and a willingness to intervene when quality falls short

Notice how these three requirements work together as a coherent system. The first protects the integrity of the professional relationship by screening for conflicts of interest. The second sets appropriate boundaries on what is delegated in the first place. And the third imposes a continuing duty of quality assurance — the psychologist must monitor, not merely assign. Together, they reflect a core ethical principle: the delegating psychologist retains ultimate accountability for the services provided under their authority, regardless of who physically carries out the task.

Example

A psychologist delegates psychological testing administration to a psychometrist. Under 2.05, the psychologist must ensure the psychometrist is properly trained in administering the specific test, must supervise the work appropriately, and retains ultimate responsibility for the interpretation and clinical use of test results. If, for instance, the psychometrist deviates from standardized administration procedures — failing to time a subtest correctly or providing unauthorized prompts — the ethical responsibility falls squarely on the delegating psychologist. This is why careful initial training, clear written protocols, and periodic observation of the psychometrist's work are not just best practices but ethical imperatives under this standard.

For exam purposes, remember that Standard 2.05 is frequently tested in scenarios involving supervision and the use of unlicensed personnel. The key takeaway is straightforward but essential: delegation does not diminish the psychologist's responsibility. Whether the delegate is a seasoned psychometrist, a predoctoral intern, or an undergraduate research assistant, the psychologist must ensure that the work assigned falls within the person's competence, that multiple relationship concerns have been addressed, and that quality monitoring remains active throughout. When you encounter exam questions about who bears responsibility for errors made by a supervisee or assistant, the answer almost always points back to the supervising psychologist — because Standard 2.05 makes the ethical chain of accountability unmistakably clear.

section_html:
Standard 2.01: Boundaries of Competence

This subsection establishes the fundamental rule: psychologists provide services, teach, and conduct research only within the boundaries of their competence.

2.01(a) -- Education, Training, and Experience

Psychologists provide services in areas in which they have established competence through education, training, supervised experience, consultation, study, or professional experience. Competence is typically demonstrated through:

  • Graduate coursework in the specific area
  • Supervised clinical or research experience
  • Postdoctoral training or specialty fellowships
  • Continuing education in the specific domain
  • Peer consultation and supervision

2.01(b) -- New Areas of Practice

When psychologists wish to provide services in areas where recognized professional standards do not yet exist, they take reasonable steps to ensure the competence of their work and to protect clients, students, and others from harm. This provision acknowledges that psychology is an evolving field.

Example

A psychologist trained in cognitive-behavioral therapy wants to begin providing telepsychology services. Under 2.01(b), the psychologist should obtain training in telehealth best practices, learn the relevant technology, understand the legal requirements of interstate practice, and seek consultation from colleagues experienced in telepsychology before beginning.

2.01(c) -- Unfamiliar Populations

In areas where recognized training standards for serving specific populations do not yet exist, psychologists with closely related prior training or experience may provide such services, with appropriate study, training, supervision, and/or consultation. This is particularly relevant to working with diverse cultural, ethnic, or linguistic groups.

2.01(d) -- Forensic Activities

When psychologists are asked to provide services to individuals for whom appropriate mental health services are not available and for which psychologists have not obtained the requisite competence, they may provide services with the closest related competence -- but only until a qualified provider becomes available.

2.01(e) -- New Techniques

In emerging areas where generally recognized standards for preparatory training do not yet exist, psychologists take reasonable steps to ensure competence and protect clients from harm.

2.01(f) -- Familiarity with Relevant Factors

When assuming forensic roles, psychologists must be knowledgeable about the judicial or administrative rules governing their participation.
prev_last_paragraph: Professional competence refers to the ability to effectively and appropriately apply the knowledge, skills, and attitudes necessary to fulfill one's professional roles. It encompasses both intellectual understanding and practical skill, shaped by ongoing education and experience.
rewritten_html:
Standard 2.01: Boundaries of Competence

Imagine a psychologist who has spent her entire career specializing in adult anxiety disorders. One day, a desperate parent calls: their seven-year-old has been refusing to attend school, crying inconsolably each morning, and the family's pediatrician suspects separation anxiety disorder. The psychologist empathizes deeply and wants to help — but she has never treated a child. Should she take the case? This is precisely the kind of question that Standard 2.01 was designed to answer, and getting it right has profound implications for client welfare, professional integrity, and — not incidentally — the EPPP.

Having established in the preceding section that professional competence encompasses knowledge, skills, and attitudes shaped by ongoing education and experience, we now turn to the ethical boundaries that define where and how psychologists may practice. Standard 2.01 establishes the fundamental rule: psychologists provide services, teach, and conduct research only within the boundaries of their competence. This standard is not a single blanket prohibition — it is a nuanced, multi-part provision that addresses everything from foundational training requirements to the realities of emerging techniques, unfamiliar populations, and forensic contexts. Understanding each subsection is essential for ethical practice and for the licensing examination.

2.01(a) -- Education, Training, and Experience

At the heart of Standard 2.01 is a straightforward principle: psychologists provide services only in areas in which they have established competence through education, training, supervised experience, consultation, study, or professional experience. Returning to our opening scenario, the anxiety specialist would need to ask herself whether she has sufficient grounding in child development, pediatric assessment, and evidence-based interventions for children before accepting the referral. Simply being a licensed psychologist does not grant blanket authority to treat all populations or all conditions. Competence is typically demonstrated through:

  • Graduate coursework in the specific area
  • Supervised clinical or research experience
  • Postdoctoral training or specialty fellowships
  • Continuing education in the specific domain
  • Peer consultation and supervision

Think of competence as a credential that must be earned area by area, not a universal license to practice. A neuropsychologist with extensive training in traumatic brain injury assessment is not, by virtue of that expertise alone, competent to conduct child custody evaluations. Each new domain of practice requires its own foundation of preparation. On the EPPP, questions about this subsection often test whether a psychologist's existing training is sufficient for a novel request — or whether additional steps are needed before proceeding.

2.01(b) -- New Areas of Practice

Psychology does not stand still. New treatment modalities emerge, technology reshapes service delivery, and societal changes create demands that no graduate program could have anticipated a decade earlier. Subsection 2.01(b) addresses this reality directly: when psychologists wish to provide services in areas where recognized professional standards do not yet exist, they take reasonable steps to ensure the competence of their work and to protect clients, students, and others from harm. This provision acknowledges that psychology is an evolving field and that rigid adherence to only well-established practices would leave many clients without care — but it simultaneously insists that innovation must be pursued responsibly.

Example

A psychologist trained in cognitive-behavioral therapy wants to begin providing telepsychology services. Under 2.01(b), the psychologist should obtain training in telehealth best practices, learn the relevant technology, understand the legal requirements of interstate practice, and seek consultation from colleagues experienced in telepsychology before beginning.

Notice the key phrase: "reasonable steps." The Ethics Code does not demand perfection or the completion of an entirely new doctoral program before a psychologist enters an emerging area. Instead, it requires a thoughtful, documented effort to acquire the knowledge and skills needed to practice safely. This might involve attending workshops, reviewing the relevant literature, consulting with experienced colleagues, or arranging peer supervision. For EPPP purposes, remember that 2.01(b) applies when professional standards in the new area are not yet well established — distinguishing it from situations where standards exist but the individual psychologist simply hasn't met them.

2.01(c) -- Unfamiliar Populations

Consider a psychologist practicing in a rural community who begins receiving referrals from a recently resettled refugee population. She has strong general clinical skills but no formal training in working with this specific cultural group. Can she ethically see these clients? Subsection 2.01(c) provides guidance: in areas where recognized training standards for serving specific populations do not yet exist, psychologists with closely related prior training or experience may provide such services, with appropriate study, training, supervision, and/or consultation. This is particularly relevant to working with diverse cultural, ethnic, or linguistic groups, where the psychologist's existing therapeutic competence provides a foundation but culturally responsive practice demands additional learning.

The ethical mandate here is not to turn clients away simply because a perfect match of training and population does not exist — that approach could leave vulnerable communities entirely without care. Rather, the psychologist must actively seek out the knowledge she needs: reading the literature on the population's cultural context, consulting with cultural brokers or community leaders, pursuing relevant continuing education, and, when possible, arranging supervision with a colleague who has more experience with the population in question. This subsection reflects psychology's commitment to both competence and access to care.

2.01(d) -- Forensic Activities

Sometimes circumstances — rather than personal ambition — push a psychologist beyond their competence boundaries. Imagine a psychologist working as the sole mental health provider in a remote correctional facility. An inmate presents with symptoms suggesting a serious psychotic disorder, but the psychologist's training is primarily in substance use disorders, and no psychiatrist or psychologist with expertise in psychotic disorders is available for weeks. Subsection 2.01(d) addresses this predicament: when psychologists are asked to provide services to individuals for whom appropriate mental health services are not available and for which psychologists have not obtained the requisite competence, they may provide services with the closest related competence — but only until a qualified provider becomes available.

This is a stopgap provision, not a permanent license. The psychologist in this scenario would be ethically justified in providing basic stabilization and supportive care, but she must make active efforts to connect the client with a more qualified provider as soon as one can be located. For the EPPP, note the critical distinction between this subsection and the emergency provision in Standard 2.02 (which we will address next): 2.01(d) applies when services are unavailable for an extended period, not necessarily during an acute crisis. The emphasis is on providing the best available care while working toward an appropriate referral.

2.01(e) -- New Techniques

Closely related to 2.01(b), this subsection focuses specifically on emerging treatment techniques or assessment methods. In emerging areas where generally recognized standards for preparatory training do not yet exist, psychologists take reasonable steps to ensure competence and protect clients from harm. For example, when virtual reality exposure therapy was first introduced, no standardized training curriculum existed. A psychologist wishing to implement VR-based treatments would need to study the available evidence, consult with researchers developing the technology, practice the technique under supervision when possible, and carefully monitor client outcomes — all before integrating it into routine practice. The common thread across 2.01(b) and 2.01(e) is the obligation to act responsibly in the face of novelty, balancing innovation with client safety.

2.01(f) -- Familiarity with Relevant Factors

Forensic psychology sits at the intersection of clinical expertise and legal process, and this intersection creates unique competence demands. When assuming forensic roles, psychologists must be knowledgeable about the judicial or administrative rules governing their participation. This means understanding the rules of evidence, the standards for expert testimony (such as the Daubert or Frye standards, depending on jurisdiction), the specific legal questions at issue in the case, and the differences between therapeutic and forensic relationships. A psychologist who is an excellent clinician but unfamiliar with the adversarial nature of courtroom proceedings, the limits of confidentiality in forensic contexts, or the relevant legal standards of the jurisdiction risks providing testimony that is unhelpful, misleading, or ethically problematic. Before accepting a forensic role, a psychologist should ensure that her understanding of the legal landscape is as solid as her clinical knowledge.

Taken together, the subsections of Standard 2.01 create a flexible but demanding framework. They recognize that the world psychologists work in is dynamic — new populations, new technologies, new legal contexts — while insisting that the profession's first obligation is always to practice within the limits of what one can do competently and safely. As we turn next to Standard 2.02, we will see what happens when genuine emergencies override the usual boundaries.

heading_text: Overview of Standard 7: Education and Training
section_html:
Overview of Standard 7: Education and Training

Standard 7 (Education and Training) of the APA Ethics Code governs the ethical conduct of psychologists in academic and training settings. This standard addresses program design, accuracy in teaching, student disclosure requirements, mandatory therapy, performance evaluation, and prohibitions on sexual relationships with students and supervisees.

These provisions protect students and supervisees who are in inherently unequal power relationships with their educators and training supervisors.
rewritten_html:
Overview of Standard 7: Education and Training

Imagine a first-year doctoral student who receives harsh, unexplained feedback on a clinical practicum evaluation — feedback that seems to reflect her supervisor's personal frustration rather than any objective assessment of her skills. She wants to challenge it, but she also knows this supervisor will be grading her for the next two semesters and writing her internship recommendation letters. Where does she turn? What protections exist for her? Now consider the reverse: a training director who must address a student's emerging impairment that could endanger future clients, yet wants to handle the situation fairly and without overstepping ethical boundaries. These are the kinds of dilemmas that make Standard 7 (Education and Training) of the APA Ethics Code not merely an administrative guideline but a vital safeguard for everyone involved in the formation of new psychologists.

Standard 7 governs the ethical conduct of psychologists who design academic programs, teach courses, supervise trainees, and evaluate student performance. Its provisions span a wide range of concerns — from the accuracy and currency of what is taught in the classroom, to the boundaries around requiring personal therapy or self-disclosure from students, to the critical prohibition against sexual relationships between educators and those they train. Each of these provisions reflects a single, unifying principle: the training relationship is characterized by an inherent and significant power differential, and that imbalance demands explicit ethical guardrails to prevent exploitation, favoritism, and harm.

If you have already studied Standard 3 (Multiple Relationships) and Standard 10 (Therapy), you will notice familiar themes here — boundary management, informed consent, and the responsible use of authority. Standard 7 applies those broad principles specifically to the academic and supervisory context, where the stakes are uniquely high: students depend on faculty for grades, recommendations, and ultimately the professional gatekeeping decisions that determine who enters the field. A supervisor's ethical lapse in this context can derail a career, compromise a student's wellbeing, or — if impaired trainees are not properly identified — put future clients at risk.

As you work through the subsections that follow, pay attention to how each provision balances two sometimes competing obligations: protecting the welfare and autonomy of students and supervisees, while also upholding the profession's responsibility to ensure that only competent, ethical practitioners advance through the training pipeline. Understanding this tension is essential not only for the EPPP but for the everyday ethical reasoning you will use throughout your career as a psychologist.

section_html:
Standard 2.06: Personal Problems and Conflicts

This subsection addresses situations where a psychologist's personal problems may interfere with professional functioning.

2.06(a) -- Awareness of Personal Problems

Psychologists refrain from initiating an activity when they know or should know that there is a substantial likelihood that their personal problems will prevent them from performing their work-related activities in a competent manner.

2.06(b) -- Taking Appropriate Action

When psychologists become aware of personal problems that may interfere with their performing work-related duties adequately, they take appropriate measures such as:

  • Obtaining professional consultation or assistance
  • Determining whether they should limit, suspend, or terminate work-related duties
  • Seeking personal therapy
  • Taking a leave of absence if necessary
EPPP Tip

EPPP questions about impaired psychologists test whether you know that the ethical response involves the psychologist taking responsibility for their own impairment. The first step is self-awareness; the second is taking appropriate corrective action (consultation, therapy, limiting practice). Colleagues who become aware of an impaired psychologist should attempt informal resolution (Standard 1.04) by speaking to the psychologist directly.

prev_last_paragraph: A psychologist delegates psychological testing administration to a psychometrist. Under 2.05, the psychologist must ensure the psychometrist is properly trained in administering the specific test, must supervise the work appropriately, and retains ultimate responsibility for the interpretation and clinical use of test results.
rewritten_html:
Standard 2.06: Personal Problems and Conflicts

Imagine a psychologist going through a bitter divorce. She finds herself distracted during therapy sessions, losing focus on what clients are saying, and at times feeling so emotionally overwhelmed that she struggles to maintain appropriate boundaries. One evening, she realizes she gave a client advice that reflected her own marital frustrations rather than the client's therapeutic needs. This scenario — a psychologist whose personal difficulties spill over into professional work — is precisely what Standard 2.06 was designed to address, and it represents one of the most commonly tested ethics topics on the EPPP.

Having just explored Standard 2.05 and the psychologist's responsibility when delegating work to others, we now turn inward — to the psychologist's responsibility to monitor their own functioning. While the previous standards focus on ensuring others are competent, Standard 2.06 asks a more personal and sometimes uncomfortable question: Am I currently competent to do this work? Psychologists are human beings, subject to the same stressors, grief, illness, substance use difficulties, and emotional turmoil that bring clients into treatment. The Ethics Code recognizes this reality and provides clear guidance on what psychologists must do when personal problems threaten their professional effectiveness.

2.06(a) -- Awareness of Personal Problems

The first component of this standard establishes a preventive obligation: psychologists must not begin professional activities when they know — or reasonably should know — that their personal problems create a substantial likelihood of impaired performance. Notice the language here is forward-looking and proactive. It does not merely say "stop when you notice harm." It says don't start if impairment is foreseeable. For example, a psychologist recently diagnosed with a serious substance use disorder should not take on a caseload of new clients struggling with addiction when the psychologist's own condition is untreated and likely to compromise clinical judgment. Similarly, a psychologist experiencing acute grief after the sudden death of a child would need to carefully evaluate whether beginning bereavement counseling with new clients is something they can do competently at that moment.

This standard also includes the important "should know" qualifier, which means that willful blindness is not an excuse. A psychologist who is drinking heavily every night and arriving at work hungover cannot later claim, "I didn't realize it was affecting my work." The standard holds psychologists to the level of awareness that a reasonable professional would have about how their personal difficulties might impair their competence.

2.06(b) -- Taking Appropriate Action

When psychologists become aware — whether gradually or suddenly — that personal problems are beginning to interfere with their ability to perform work-related duties adequately, the Ethics Code requires them to take concrete, appropriate steps. Insight alone is not enough; action must follow awareness. The standard identifies several potential responses, and in practice the right course of action depends on the severity and nature of the impairment:

  • Obtaining professional consultation or assistance
  • Determining whether they should limit, suspend, or terminate work-related duties
  • Seeking personal therapy
  • Taking a leave of absence if necessary

Consider a clinical psychologist who begins experiencing significant anxiety after being the victim of a violent crime. She notices that conducting trauma-focused therapy sessions triggers her own distress, and her case notes are becoming less thorough. The ethically appropriate response is not to simply "push through." Instead, she might first consult with a trusted colleague, then enter her own therapy, and simultaneously decide to refer her trauma-focused clients to another provider while she recovers — continuing to see only those clients whose treatment does not exacerbate her symptoms. If her symptoms worsen, a temporary leave of absence may become necessary. The key principle is that the psychologist bears primary responsibility for recognizing and addressing their own impairment — not their clients, not their employer, and not a licensing board.

EPPP Tip

EPPP questions about impaired psychologists test whether you know that the ethical response involves the psychologist taking responsibility for their own impairment. The first step is self-awareness; the second is taking appropriate corrective action (consultation, therapy, limiting practice). Colleagues who become aware of an impaired psychologist should attempt informal resolution (Standard 1.04) by speaking to the psychologist directly. On exam questions, be wary of answer choices that jump immediately to filing an ethics complaint — the Ethics Code favors informal resolution as a first step when feasible. Also remember that Standard 2.06 places the burden of self-monitoring squarely on the impaired psychologist; waiting for someone else to notice the problem does not satisfy the standard's requirements.

rewritten_html:
Ethical Standards Overview (Standards 1-10)

Now that we've explored the aspirational General Principles — the moral compass of the profession — it's time to turn to the part of the Ethics Code that has real teeth. Imagine a psychologist who maintains a sexual relationship with a current therapy client, or a researcher who fabricates data. These aren't just violations of lofty ideals; they are breaches of specific, enforceable rules that can result in formal sanctions, loss of licensure, or expulsion from the APA. The ten Ethical Standards are where the Ethics Code shifts from aspiration to obligation, spelling out precisely what psychologists must and must not do in their professional conduct.

Unlike the General Principles (which cannot be the basis for an ethics complaint), the Ethical Standards are the enforceable component of the Ethics Code. Each standard contains multiple subsections addressing specific behaviors and obligations across the full range of professional activities — from how you obtain informed consent, to when you may break confidentiality, to how authorship credit should be assigned on a publication. On the EPPP, you will encounter scenarios that require you to identify which specific standard applies, so familiarity with the scope of each one is essential. Think of the ten standards as ten rooms in a house: each room covers a distinct domain of practice, and knowing which room you're in helps you quickly locate the relevant rule.

The table below provides a high-level map of all ten standards. As you review it, notice how the standards are organized roughly by context — beginning with how to handle ethical dilemmas themselves (Standard 1), moving through the foundations of competent and respectful practice (Standards 2–4), and then addressing specific professional activities such as advertising, record keeping, teaching, research, assessment, and therapy (Standards 5–10). Each of these standards will receive detailed coverage in the sections that follow, but this overview will serve as your orienting framework — the table of contents for the enforceable ethical obligations that govern every facet of psychological practice.

StandardTitleKey Topics
1Resolving Ethical IssuesConflicts with law/organizations, informal resolution, reporting violations, cooperating with ethics committees, improper complaints, discrimination against complainants
2CompetenceBoundaries of competence, providing services in emergencies, maintaining competence, bases for scientific judgments, delegation, personal problems
3Human RelationsUnfair discrimination, sexual harassment, multiple relationships, conflicts of interest, third-party requests, exploitative relationships, informed consent
4Privacy and ConfidentialityMaintaining confidentiality, discussing limits, recording, minimizing intrusions, disclosures, consultations, use of confidential information
5Advertising and Other Public StatementsAvoidance of false statements, statements by others, descriptions of workshops, media presentations, testimonials, in-person solicitation
6Record Keeping and FeesDocumentation, maintenance/dissemination/disposal of records, withholding records for nonpayment, fees and financial arrangements, bartering, referral fees, accuracy in reports to payors
7Education and TrainingDesign of programs, descriptions of programs, accuracy in teaching, student disclosure requirements, mandatory individual/group therapy, assessing student performance, sexual relationships with students
8Research and PublicationIRB approval, informed consent, deception, debriefing, inducements, animal research, reporting results, plagiarism, publication credit, sharing data, reviewers
9AssessmentBases for assessments, use of assessments, informed consent, release of test data, test construction, interpreting results, assessment by unqualified persons, obsolete tests, test scoring, explaining results, maintaining test security

A useful EPPP study strategy is to associate each standard number with a keyword: 1 = Resolution, 2 = Competence, 3 = Relationships, 4 = Confidentiality, 5 = Public Statements, 6 = Records and Fees, 7 = Training, 8 = Research, 9 = Assessment, 10 = Therapy. When a test question describes a clinical or professional scenario, mentally scan this list to identify which domain is implicated — then recall the specific obligations within that standard. In the sections ahead, we will walk through each standard in detail, examining the subsections that are most frequently tested and the clinical situations that bring them to life.

section_html:
Structure of the Ethics Code

The APA Ethics Code consists of four major components:

  1. Preamble -- States the purpose and scope of the Ethics Code. It establishes that psychologists commit to increasing knowledge, improving conditions, and helping the public develop informed judgments about behavior.
  2. General Principles (A through E) -- Aspirational goals that guide psychologists toward the highest ideals. They are not enforceable but provide a framework for ethical reasoning.
  3. Ethical Standards (1 through 10) -- Enforceable rules that set mandatory obligations. Violations can result in sanctions, license revocation, or expulsion from APA.
  4. Introduction and Applicability -- Clarifies how the Code applies, its relationship to law, and issues of jurisdiction.

The Preamble

The Preamble describes the mission of psychology and the purpose of the Ethics Code. It acknowledges that psychologists occupy roles as researchers, educators, diagnosticians, therapists, supervisors, consultants, administrators, social interventionists, and expert witnesses. The Preamble stresses that the Code applies to these roles only in the context of scientific, educational, or professional activities.

General Principles (Aspirational)

The five General Principles guide psychologists toward ethical ideals. For the EPPP, memorize each principle and know that they are aspirational, not enforceable.

PrincipleCore FocusKey Idea
A: Beneficence and NonmaleficenceDo good; do no harmPsychologists strive to benefit those with whom they work and guard against factors that might lead to misuse of influence. They manage personal, financial, social, organizational, or political factors that could lead to harm.
B: Fidelity and ResponsibilityTrust, professional responsibilityPsychologists establish relationships of trust, are aware of their responsibilities to society and the communities they serve, and consult with colleagues to prevent unethical conduct. They donate a portion of professional time for little or no compensation (pro bono).
C: IntegrityHonesty, truthfulnessPsychologists seek to promote accuracy, honesty, and truthfulness. They do not steal, cheat, or engage in fraud, subterfuge, or intentional misrepresentation of fact. They keep promises and avoid unwise or unclear commitments.
D: JusticeFairness, equal accessPsychologists recognize that fairness and justice entitle all persons to access the contributions of psychology and to equal quality in processes, procedures, and services. They exercise reasonable judgment and take precautions to ensure bias does not lead to unjust practices.
E: Respect for People's Rights and DignityAutonomy, privacy, diversityPsychologists respect the dignity and worth of all people and the rights of individuals to privacy, confidentiality, and self-determination. They are aware of cultural, individual, and role differences including those based on age, gender, race, ethnicity, national origin, religion, sexual orientation, disability, language, and socioeconomic status.
EPPP Tip

A common EPPP question format presents a scenario and asks which General Principle applies. Remember: Principle B (Fidelity and Responsibility) is the one that mentions pro bono work and concern for colleagues' ethical behavior. Principle D (Justice) specifically addresses fairness and bias.

rewritten_html:
Structure of the Ethics Code

Now that we've distinguished between aspirational principles and enforceable standards, let's zoom out and look at how the entire Ethics Code is organized — because understanding the architecture of the Code helps you navigate it efficiently, both in practice and on the EPPP. Think of the Code as a building: the Preamble lays the foundation and explains why the building exists, the General Principles describe the aspirational vision for what the building should look like at its best, the Ethical Standards provide the load-bearing walls that must not be compromised, and the Introduction and Applicability section tells you who must follow the building codes and under what circumstances. Each component serves a distinct purpose, and exam questions frequently test whether you know which part does what.

The APA Ethics Code consists of four major components, each playing a specific role in guiding professional conduct:

  1. Preamble -- States the purpose and scope of the Ethics Code. It establishes that psychologists commit to increasing knowledge, improving conditions, and helping the public develop informed judgments about behavior.
  2. General Principles (A through E) -- Aspirational goals that guide psychologists toward the highest ideals. They are not enforceable but provide a framework for ethical reasoning.
  3. Ethical Standards (1 through 10) -- Enforceable rules that set mandatory obligations. Violations can result in sanctions, license revocation, or expulsion from APA.
  4. Introduction and Applicability -- Clarifies how the Code applies, its relationship to law, and issues of jurisdiction.

Notice the critical distinction embedded in this structure: the General Principles set the ceiling — the highest ideals a psychologist should strive for — while the Ethical Standards set the floor — the minimum behaviors that are required. A psychologist who violates an Ethical Standard can face formal disciplinary action, but a psychologist who falls short of a General Principle cannot be sanctioned on that basis alone. This distinction is one of the most frequently tested concepts on the EPPP, so it is worth anchoring firmly in your understanding before moving forward.

The Preamble

Imagine you are opening a professional guidebook for the first time. Before you encounter any rules or aspirational goals, you want to understand the purpose behind the document — who it's for, what it's trying to accomplish, and why it matters. That is exactly the function of the Preamble. It describes the mission of psychology and the purpose of the Ethics Code, setting the stage for everything that follows. The Preamble acknowledges that psychologists occupy an extraordinarily wide range of roles — as researchers, educators, diagnosticians, therapists, supervisors, consultants, administrators, social interventionists, and expert witnesses — and that the ethical obligations captured in the Code apply to all of these roles.

An important nuance is that the Preamble stresses that the Code applies to these roles only in the context of scientific, educational, or professional activities. This means that the APA Ethics Code does not govern every aspect of a psychologist's personal life, but rather the professional activities that define their work. For example, a psychologist's behavior at a family reunion is generally outside the scope of the Code, but their behavior at a professional conference or in a therapy session is squarely within it. Understanding this boundary of applicability can help you reason through tricky exam scenarios where the line between personal and professional behavior is blurred.

General Principles (Aspirational)

Picture a newly licensed psychologist sitting down to decide whether to accept a complex forensic case that falls at the edge of her competence. She knows what the enforceable standards require, but she also wants to go beyond the minimum — she wants to embody the best of what the profession stands for. The five General Principles are the compass she turns to. They guide psychologists toward ethical ideals — the kind of practice that not only avoids harm but actively promotes human welfare, trust, honesty, fairness, and dignity. For the EPPP, memorize each principle and know that they are aspirational, not enforceable. No psychologist can be sanctioned solely for failing to meet a General Principle, but these principles provide the moral reasoning framework that often informs interpretation of the enforceable standards.

Each of the five principles captures a distinct dimension of ethical excellence. A helpful mnemonic is B-FI-JR — Beneficence, Fidelity, Integrity, Justice, Respect — though the official ordering uses the letters A through E. Let's look at each one in detail, along with the core ideas the EPPP expects you to recognize:

PrincipleCore FocusKey Idea
A: Beneficence and NonmaleficenceDo good; do no harmPsychologists strive to benefit those with whom they work and guard against factors that might lead to misuse of influence. They manage personal, financial, social, organizational, or political factors that could lead to harm.
B: Fidelity and ResponsibilityTrust, professional responsibilityPsychologists establish relationships of trust, are aware of their responsibilities to society and the communities they serve, and consult with colleagues to prevent unethical conduct. They donate a portion of professional time for little or no compensation (pro bono).
C: IntegrityHonesty, truthfulnessPsychologists seek to promote accuracy, honesty, and truthfulness. They do not steal, cheat, or engage in fraud, subterfuge, or intentional misrepresentation of fact. They keep promises and avoid unwise or unclear commitments.
D: JusticeFairness, equal accessPsychologists recognize that fairness and justice entitle all persons to access the contributions of psychology and to equal quality in processes, procedures, and services. They exercise reasonable judgment and take precautions to ensure bias does not lead to unjust practices.
E: Respect for People's Rights and DignityAutonomy, privacy, diversityPsychologists respect the dignity and worth of all people and the rights of individuals to privacy, confidentiality, and self-determination. They are aware of cultural, individual, and role differences including those based on age, gender, race, ethnicity, national origin, religion, sexual orientation, disability, language, and socioeconomic status.

To bring these principles to life, consider a clinical scenario: a psychologist working in a rural community discovers that her only colleague in town has been practicing while impaired due to substance use. Principle A (Beneficence and Nonmaleficence) compels her to consider the potential harm to clients. Principle B (Fidelity and Responsibility) reminds her of her obligation to address unethical conduct among colleagues — not to look the other way. Principle C (Integrity) requires her to be honest in any reporting or consultation she undertakes. Principle D (Justice) asks her to consider whether vulnerable populations in the community are being disproportionately affected. And Principle E (Respect for People's Rights and Dignity) requires her to handle the situation in a way that respects the dignity of both the impaired colleague and the affected clients. In this single scenario, all five principles are at play — which illustrates why understanding them as an interconnected framework, rather than isolated definitions, is so valuable.

EPPP Tip

A common EPPP question format presents a scenario and asks which General Principle applies. Remember: Principle B (Fidelity and Responsibility) is the one that mentions pro bono work and concern for colleagues' ethical behavior. Principle D (Justice) specifically addresses fairness and bias. When two principles seem to apply, focus on which principle most directly addresses the specific ethical concern described in the question stem — the EPPP rewards precision in matching principles to scenarios.

section_html:
Standard 3.02: Sexual Harassment

Psychologists do not engage in sexual harassment, which consists of sexual solicitation, physical advances, or verbal or nonverbal conduct that is sexual in nature and that either:

  • Is unwelcome, offensive, or creates a hostile workplace or educational environment, and the psychologist knows or is told this, or
  • Is sufficiently severe or intense to be abusive to a reasonable person in the context

Sexual harassment can occur between any parties in a professional relationship: psychologist-client, supervisor-supervisee, professor-student, or between colleagues.
prev_last_paragraph: Note the word "unfair" in this standard. Not all differential treatment constitutes discrimination. For example, using age-appropriate assessment instruments or adapting therapy techniques for clients with disabilities is appropriate differential treatment, not unfair discrimination.
rewritten_html:
Standard 3.02: Sexual Harassment

Having established that psychologists must not engage in unfair discrimination based on personal characteristics, the Ethics Code turns to a specific and particularly harmful form of misconduct: sexual harassment. This standard exists because the power dynamics inherent in psychological practice — between therapist and client, supervisor and supervisee, professor and student — create contexts where sexual misconduct can cause profound harm. A supervisee who receives sexually suggestive comments from a training director may feel unable to object for fear of career repercussions. A graduate student subjected to unwanted physical contact from a professor may endure it silently rather than risk academic standing. The Ethics Code addresses these realities directly and unequivocally.

Psychologists do not engage in sexual harassment, which consists of sexual solicitation, physical advances, or verbal or nonverbal conduct that is sexual in nature and that either:

  • Is unwelcome, offensive, or creates a hostile workplace or educational environment, and the psychologist knows or is told this, or
  • Is sufficiently severe or intense to be abusive to a reasonable person in the context

Notice the important structure of this standard: it provides two independent pathways by which conduct qualifies as sexual harassment. Under the first prong, the psychologist has been informed — or otherwise knows — that the behavior is unwelcome. Imagine a clinical supervisor who repeatedly makes flirtatious remarks to a supervisee; when the supervisee finally says "that makes me uncomfortable," any continuation of such behavior clearly meets this criterion. Under the second prong, the conduct is so severe or intense that no explicit objection is necessary — a reasonable person standard applies. For example, a psychologist who makes graphic sexual comments during a professional meeting would violate this standard regardless of whether anyone explicitly objects, because the behavior is abusive to any reasonable person in that context.

Sexual harassment can occur between any parties in a professional relationship: psychologist-client, supervisor-supervisee, professor-student, or between colleagues. For exam preparation, it is essential to remember that this standard is not limited to situations involving direct clinical contact. A psychologist who sends sexually suggestive emails to a colleague or who makes persistent sexual jokes in a departmental meeting is equally subject to this prohibition. The common thread is that the psychologist's professional role carries ethical obligations that extend across all professional contexts, not just the therapy room.

When studying this standard, also note how it differs from the later standards addressing sexual intimacies with clients (Standards 10.05–10.08). Standard 3.02 broadly prohibits sexual harassment in all professional relationships, while the later standards specifically address romantic and sexual relationships with current and former therapy clients. Both are critical, but this standard casts the wider net — applying to every professional context in which a psychologist operates.

section_html:
Standard 3.01: Unfair Discrimination

Psychologists do not engage in unfair discrimination based on age, gender, gender identity, race, ethnicity, culture, national origin, religion, sexual orientation, disability, socioeconomic status, or any basis proscribed by law. This applies to all professional activities.

EPPP Tip

Note the word "unfair" in this standard. Not all differential treatment constitutes discrimination. For example, using age-appropriate assessment instruments or adapting therapy techniques for clients with disabilities is appropriate differential treatment, not unfair discrimination.
prev_last_paragraph: The standard applies across all professional roles -- therapy, assessment, research, teaching, supervision, and consultation -- and emphasizes that the power differential inherent in psychologists' roles creates special obligations to protect those with whom they work.
rewritten_html:
Standard 3.01: Unfair Discrimination

Having established that Standard 3 governs how psychologists navigate their professional relationships — and that the inherent power differential in these roles creates special obligations — we turn now to the very first provision in this standard: the prohibition against unfair discrimination. This standard comes first for good reason. Before we can discuss the nuances of multiple relationships, informed consent, or collaborative practice, we must establish a foundational principle: every person who encounters a psychologist in a professional context deserves to be treated equitably, regardless of who they are.

Consider a clinical scenario: A psychologist working in a community mental health center receives a referral for a new client — a 68-year-old transgender woman who recently immigrated from Guatemala and uses a wheelchair. Before the psychologist has even met this client, multiple dimensions of identity are already present in the room. Standard 3.01 makes clear that none of these characteristics — not her age, gender identity, national origin, disability status, nor any other protected characteristic — may serve as a basis for unfair discrimination in the services she receives. She is entitled to the same quality of care, the same professional respect, and the same access to psychological services as any other client who walks through that door.

Psychologists do not engage in unfair discrimination based on age, gender, gender identity, race, ethnicity, culture, national origin, religion, sexual orientation, disability, socioeconomic status, or any basis proscribed by law. This prohibition is sweeping in its scope — it applies to all professional activities, whether the psychologist is conducting therapy, performing assessments, teaching a graduate course, supervising a trainee, designing a research study, or consulting with an organization. The standard recognizes that discrimination can surface in subtle ways across all of these contexts: in who gets accepted into a training program, in how quickly a clinician returns phone calls, in whose research contributions are acknowledged, and in whose pain is taken seriously.

What makes this standard particularly important for practice — and particularly testable on the EPPP — is the careful inclusion of the word "unfair." This single word carries enormous weight because it acknowledges a crucial clinical reality: not all differential treatment is discriminatory. In fact, ethical practice often requires psychologists to treat people differently based on their individual characteristics and needs. A neuropsychologist who selects an age-normed cognitive battery for an elderly client is engaging in appropriate differential treatment. A therapist who modifies session structure — perhaps incorporating more frequent breaks or providing materials in larger print — for a client with a physical disability is practicing responsively, not discriminatorily. A school psychologist who conducts a bilingual evaluation for a child whose primary language is Spanish is honoring best practices, not showing favoritism. The ethical line is crossed not when treatment differs, but when that difference is rooted in bias, prejudice, or stereotyping rather than in the genuine needs of the individual.

EPPP Tip

Note the word "unfair" in this standard. Not all differential treatment constitutes discrimination. For example, using age-appropriate assessment instruments or adapting therapy techniques for clients with disabilities is appropriate differential treatment, not unfair discrimination. On the exam, watch for answer choices that conflate responsive, individualized practice with discriminatory behavior — the Ethics Code explicitly carves out space for clinically appropriate differentiation. The key question is always whether the differential treatment serves the client's welfare or reflects the psychologist's bias.

It is also worth noting that Standard 3.01 uses the phrase "or any basis proscribed by law," which means the list of protected categories is not exhaustive. As laws evolve at the federal, state, and local levels — for instance, expanding protections based on veteran status, genetic information, or other characteristics — psychologists are expected to remain current and ensure their practices do not violate those evolving legal standards. This provision ties the Ethics Code to the broader legal landscape, reminding psychologists that ethical obligations and legal requirements often work hand in hand, and that the floor of acceptable conduct may shift upward over time.

With this foundational principle in place — that psychologists must treat all individuals equitably across every professional context — we can now examine how Standard 3 addresses specific forms of conduct that violate this principle, beginning with the prohibition against sexual harassment.

section_html:
Applicability and Enforcement

Several important points about the scope and enforcement of the Ethics Code frequently appear on the EPPP:

  • The Ethics Code applies to APA members and to psychologists licensed under state laws that adopt the Code, covering professional, scientific, and educational activities.
  • The Code does not apply to psychologists' purely private conduct that is not connected to their professional roles.
  • Lack of awareness or misunderstanding of an Ethical Standard is not a defense to a charge of unethical conduct.
  • The Ethics Code is not intended to be a basis of civil liability; whether a psychologist has violated the Ethics Code does not itself determine legal liability.
  • The modifiers "reasonably," "appropriate," and "potentially" in the Standards allow for professional judgment but require that the psychologist's actions be justifiable given the circumstances.
  • When the Ethics Code establishes a higher standard than the law, psychologists must meet the ethical standard. When the law establishes a higher standard, psychologists must comply with the law.
Example

A state law requires psychologists to report suspected child abuse. Even if a psychologist feels that reporting might damage the therapeutic relationship, the legal mandate overrides the ethical preference for maintaining confidentiality. Conversely, if the Ethics Code requires informed consent in a situation where local law is silent, the psychologist should still obtain informed consent.
prev_last_paragraph: Some ethicists (e.g., Meara, Schmidt, & Day, 1996) argue that ethical codes focused solely on rules are insufficient. A virtue ethics approach asks not just "what should I do?" but "what kind of person should I be?" The virtues of prudence, integrity, respectfulness, and benevolence complement the enforceable standards of the Ethics Code.
rewritten_html:
Applicability and Enforcement

Having explored how psychologists navigate ethical dilemmas through structured decision-making models and virtue-based reflection, a practical question naturally follows: To whom does the Ethics Code actually apply, and what happens when its standards collide with the law? These are not abstract concerns — they surface regularly on the EPPP and in real-world professional life. Consider a psychologist who maintains a private social media account where they post controversial personal opinions. Does the Ethics Code govern that behavior? Or imagine a clinician practicing in a state whose mandatory reporting laws seem to conflict with ethical confidentiality standards. Which authority prevails? The answers hinge on understanding the scope and enforcement principles embedded in the Code itself, and mastering these nuances is essential for both the licensing exam and competent professional practice.

Several important points about the scope and enforcement of the Ethics Code frequently appear on the EPPP, and each one carries implications that extend far beyond test preparation into the daily realities of psychological practice:

  • The Ethics Code applies to APA members and to psychologists licensed under state laws that adopt the Code, covering professional, scientific, and educational activities.
  • The Code does not apply to psychologists' purely private conduct that is not connected to their professional roles.
  • Lack of awareness or misunderstanding of an Ethical Standard is not a defense to a charge of unethical conduct.
  • The Ethics Code is not intended to be a basis of civil liability; whether a psychologist has violated the Ethics Code does not itself determine legal liability.
  • The modifiers "reasonably," "appropriate," and "potentially" in the Standards allow for professional judgment but require that the psychologist's actions be justifiable given the circumstances.
  • When the Ethics Code establishes a higher standard than the law, psychologists must meet the ethical standard. When the law establishes a higher standard, psychologists must comply with the law.

Let's unpack several of these points, because EPPP questions often test subtle distinctions within them. The scope of the Code is deliberately broad — it covers not just therapy but also research, teaching, supervision, forensic work, consulting, and organizational roles. However, the boundary is drawn at professional activity. A psychologist's weekend hobby of competitive chess or their personal religious practices fall outside the Code's reach, unless those activities become intertwined with their professional role in a way that could cause harm to those they serve.

The "ignorance is no excuse" principle deserves special emphasis. A newly licensed psychologist who has never read Standard 3.05 on multiple relationships cannot cite unfamiliarity as a defense if an ethics complaint is filed. This principle places an affirmative obligation on every psychologist to know the Code thoroughly — a responsibility that begins in graduate training and continues throughout one's career. For EPPP purposes, remember that this applies equally to seasoned practitioners and recent graduates.

The distinction between ethical violations and legal liability is another frequently tested concept. An ethics board might find that a psychologist violated a standard, but that finding does not automatically mean the psychologist is liable in a civil lawsuit. Conversely, a court might find legal liability even when no ethical violation occurred. These are parallel but independent systems of accountability, and the EPPP expects you to understand that they operate on different tracks.

The use of qualifying language — words like "reasonably", "appropriate," and "potentially" — is intentional and clinically significant. These modifiers acknowledge that psychology is practiced in complex, often ambiguous situations where rigid rules cannot anticipate every scenario. However, this flexibility is not a blank check. A psychologist invoking professional judgment must be prepared to demonstrate that their decisions were thoughtful, informed by the available evidence, and defensible to a reasonable peer. Think of it as guided discretion rather than unchecked autonomy.

Perhaps the most practically consequential rule involves the interplay between ethical standards and legal requirements. The governing principle follows a "higher standard" rule: whichever authority — law or ethics — sets the more protective or stringent standard is the one the psychologist must follow. This creates a dynamic hierarchy that shifts depending on the specific situation, the jurisdiction, and the ethical standard at issue. When a genuine conflict exists that cannot be resolved by following the higher standard, psychologists are expected to make known their commitment to the Ethics Code and take reasonable steps to resolve the conflict in a manner consistent with the General Principles.

Example

A state law requires psychologists to report suspected child abuse. Even if a psychologist feels that reporting might damage the therapeutic relationship, the legal mandate overrides the ethical preference for maintaining confidentiality. Conversely, if the Ethics Code requires informed consent in a situation where local law is silent, the psychologist should still obtain informed consent. In both cases, the "higher standard" principle is at work — whichever authority provides greater protection to the public is the one the psychologist must honor. A useful test-taking heuristic: when an EPPP question presents a conflict between ethics and law, first determine which standard is more protective, and then select the answer that follows that higher standard.

section_html:
Standard 3.07: Third-Party Requests for Services

When psychologists agree to provide services at the request of a third party, they clarify at the outset:

  • The nature of the relationship with each party
  • The role of the psychologist (e.g., therapist vs. evaluator)
  • The probable uses of the services provided or information obtained
  • Limits of confidentiality

This standard commonly applies in forensic, organizational, custody evaluation, and insurance-related contexts.
prev_last_paragraph: A psychologist is hired by a company to conduct fitness-for-duty evaluations. The psychologist also owns stock in a competitor company. If the evaluation results could affect the stock value of the competitor, a conflict of interest exists. The psychologist should disclose the conflict or decline the engagement.
rewritten_html:
Standard 3.07: Third-Party Requests for Services

Imagine this scenario: A parent calls your office to schedule a therapy appointment — not for themselves, but for their 17-year-old child who is reluctant to attend. Or consider a corporate human resources director who contacts you to provide anger management counseling for an employee following a workplace incident. In both cases, the person sitting across from you in session is not the person who initiated — and may be paying for — the service. This triangular arrangement raises a crucial question: Who is the client? The answer is rarely as simple as it seems, and getting it wrong can lead to serious ethical violations, damaged trust, and even legal liability. Standard 3.07 addresses precisely this kind of complexity, building on the conflict-of-interest concerns we just examined by focusing on situations where someone other than the direct recipient is requesting or funding psychological services.

When psychologists agree to provide services at the request of a third party, they clarify at the outset:

  • The nature of the relationship with each party
  • The role of the psychologist (e.g., therapist vs. evaluator)
  • The probable uses of the services provided or information obtained
  • Limits of confidentiality

These four clarification requirements are not mere formalities — they form the ethical scaffolding that protects everyone involved. Consider why each matters. A psychologist conducting a child custody evaluation at the request of a family court must make clear to both parents that the psychologist's role is that of an evaluator, not a therapist. The information gathered will be used to inform the court's custody decision, and statements made during the evaluation are not protected by the same confidentiality that would apply in a therapeutic relationship. Without these explicit clarifications, a parent might mistakenly treat the evaluation interview like a therapy session, sharing deeply personal material under the assumption that it will remain private — only to find those disclosures detailed in a court report.

This standard commonly applies in forensic, organizational, custody evaluation, and insurance-related contexts. In forensic settings, an attorney may retain a psychologist to evaluate a defendant's competency to stand trial. In organizational consulting, a company may hire a psychologist to assess leadership potential among executives. In insurance contexts, a managed care company may authorize a set number of sessions and expect progress reports. In each of these situations, the psychologist must proactively clarify the arrangement before services begin. The key principle is transparency at the outset — not after misunderstandings have already taken root. When a psychologist waits until midway through an evaluation to explain that findings will be shared with the referring attorney, the ethical damage is already done, because the examinee's informed consent was never truly informed.

A useful clinical rule of thumb: whenever someone other than the person receiving services is paying for, requesting, or directing those services, Standard 3.07 is activated. The psychologist should document these clarifications in writing, ideally through an informed consent document that all relevant parties review and sign. This protects the psychologist, the individual receiving services, and the third party by ensuring that expectations are aligned from the very first interaction. On the EPPP, questions involving third-party requests frequently test whether candidates can identify which clarifications are required and when they must occur — the answer is always at the outset, before services begin.

section_html:
Sexual Relationships: Standards 3.05 and 10.05-10.08

Sexual intimacies with clients and other protected parties receive special attention in the Ethics Code:

SituationStandardRule
Sexual intimacies with current therapy clients10.05Always prohibited
Sexual intimacies with relatives/significant others of current clients10.06Always prohibited
Therapy with former sexual partners10.07Always prohibited -- psychologists do not accept as therapy clients persons with whom they have engaged in sexual intimacies
Sexual intimacies with former therapy clients10.08Prohibited for at least two years after termination, and even after two years only in the most unusual circumstances with the burden on the psychologist to demonstrate no exploitation
Sexual relationships with current students/supervisees7.07Always prohibited
EPPP Tip

The two-year rule (10.08) is one of the most tested facts in the Ethics domain. Remember: the two-year clock starts at termination, not at the start of therapy. Even after two years, the burden falls on the psychologist to prove the relationship is not exploitative. Most ethics scholars advise that sexual relationships with former clients should always be avoided.
prev_last_paragraph: A psychologist in solo private practice creates a professional will designating a trusted colleague — a licensed clinical psychologist in the same community — as her professional executor. The document specifies that, in the event of the psychologist's sudden incapacity, the executor will secure all client files, contact active clients to arrange referrals, and ensure that records are maintained in compliance with state retention requirements. The psychologist provides the executor with a sealed envelope containing the location of electronic and paper records, passwords for the electronic health record system, and a current list of active clients.
rewritten_html:
Sexual Relationships: Standards 3.05 and 10.05-10.08

Few ethical violations carry as much potential for harm — or as much clarity in the Ethics Code — as sexual relationships between psychologists and the people they serve. Consider a scenario: a therapist has been working with a client through a painful divorce for eight months. Over time, the client begins expressing romantic interest, telling the therapist, "You understand me better than anyone ever has." The therapist, recently single, finds the feelings mutual. What happens next is not a gray area — it is one of the most unambiguous prohibitions in all of professional psychology. The power differential inherent in the therapeutic relationship means that any sexual contact constitutes a fundamental betrayal of the trust clients place in their psychologists, regardless of who initiates the contact or how genuine the feelings may seem.

Having examined exploitative relationships broadly in the preceding section, we now turn to the specific standards that address sexual intimacies — a domain where the APA Ethics Code draws its sharpest and most carefully delineated lines. These standards span multiple sections of the Code, reflecting the reality that sexual boundary violations can occur not only in therapy but also in supervisory relationships, teaching contexts, and interactions with clients' family members. Understanding exactly which relationships are always prohibited, which carry time-limited restrictions, and where the burden of proof falls is essential both for ethical practice and for success on the EPPP.

Sexual intimacies with clients and other protected parties receive special attention in the Ethics Code, with each standard addressing a distinct relational configuration:

SituationStandardRule
Sexual intimacies with current therapy clients10.05Always prohibited
Sexual intimacies with relatives/significant others of current clients10.06Always prohibited
Therapy with former sexual partners10.07Always prohibited -- psychologists do not accept as therapy clients persons with whom they have engaged in sexual intimacies
Sexual intimacies with former therapy clients10.08Prohibited for at least two years after termination, and even after two years only in the most unusual circumstances with the burden on the psychologist to demonstrate no exploitation
Sexual relationships with current students/supervisees7.07Always prohibited

Notice the pattern across these standards: four of the five situations involve absolute, unconditional prohibitions. There is no exception for mutual consent, no carve-out for cases where the client initiates, and no consideration of how brief or intensive the professional relationship may have been. Standard 10.06 is particularly worth examining — it extends the prohibition beyond the client to include the client's relatives and significant others, recognizing that sexual involvement with a client's family member can be just as damaging to the therapeutic relationship and to the client's well-being as direct sexual contact with the client.

Standard 10.07 operates in the reverse direction and is sometimes overlooked: a psychologist must never accept someone as a therapy client if the two have previously been sexually intimate. The reasoning is straightforward — a prior sexual relationship would fatally compromise the objectivity and professional boundary structure that effective therapy requires. Imagine a psychologist who begins providing couples therapy and discovers that one partner is a former romantic interest. The ethical course is clear: the psychologist cannot serve as the therapist, regardless of how distant the prior relationship may be.

The one standard that permits any flexibility at all is 10.08, governing sexual intimacies with former therapy clients. Even here, the Code imposes a mandatory two-year waiting period after termination, and the language makes clear that this waiting period is a floor, not a ceiling. After two years, such a relationship is permissible only "in the most unusual circumstances," and the burden of proof falls squarely on the psychologist to demonstrate that no exploitation has occurred. Factors the psychologist must consider include the length and nature of the therapy, the client's current mental status, the likelihood that the client's feelings are rooted in transference, and the circumstances of termination — including whether termination was undertaken specifically to pursue the relationship, which would itself be ethically problematic.

EPPP Tip

The two-year rule (10.08) is one of the most tested facts in the Ethics domain. Remember: the two-year clock starts at termination, not at the start of therapy. Even after two years, the burden falls on the psychologist to prove the relationship is not exploitative. Most ethics scholars advise that sexual relationships with former clients should always be avoided. On the exam, if a question describes a psychologist entering a sexual relationship with a former client 18 months after termination — regardless of any other mitigating details — the answer is that this constitutes an ethics violation. The two-year minimum is absolute and admits no exceptions.

section_html:
Informed Consent in Therapy (Standard 10.01)

Psychologists inform clients as early as possible in the therapeutic relationship about:

  • The nature and anticipated course of therapy
  • Fees, billing practices, and insurance involvement
  • The limits of confidentiality
  • The extent and limits of the therapist's involvement of third parties
  • The client's right to refuse or withdraw from treatment
  • Potential risks and benefits of treatment
  • Available alternatives to the proposed treatment

When the client is legally incapable of giving informed consent (e.g., a minor or an individual adjudicated incompetent), the psychologist provides an appropriate explanation, seeks the individual's assent, considers preferences and best interests, and obtains appropriate permission from a legally authorized person.
