Most ethics scholars advise that sexual relationships with former clients should always be avoided.
rewritten_html:
Informed Consent in Therapy (Standard 10.01)

Having explored the complex boundaries surrounding sexual relationships in professional practice, we turn now to a foundational obligation that shapes the very first moments of any therapeutic relationship: informed consent. Consider this scenario — a new client arrives for an initial session, anxious and uncertain about what therapy will involve. She has never seen a psychologist before and assumes that everything she says will be kept in absolute confidence, that she can stop at any time without consequence, and that she won't be charged for missed appointments. If the psychologist simply launches into assessment or intervention without addressing any of these assumptions, the entire therapeutic relationship rests on a shaky ethical foundation. Standard 10.01 exists precisely to prevent this situation, ensuring that clients enter treatment as informed participants rather than passive recipients of care.

The principle underlying informed consent in therapy is deceptively simple: clients deserve to know what they are agreeing to before they agree to it. But in practice, this obligation requires psychologists to cover a surprisingly broad range of topics — and to do so as early as feasible in the therapeutic relationship. Think of informed consent not as a single form to be signed, but as an ongoing conversation that begins at the first contact and may need to be revisited as circumstances change throughout treatment.

Psychologists inform clients as early as possible in the therapeutic relationship about the following key elements:

  • The nature and anticipated course of therapy
  • Fees, billing practices, and insurance involvement
  • The limits of confidentiality
  • The extent and limits of the therapist's involvement of third parties
  • The client's right to refuse or withdraw from treatment
  • Potential risks and benefits of treatment
  • Available alternatives to the proposed treatment

Each of these elements serves a distinct protective function. Discussing the nature and anticipated course of therapy helps clients form realistic expectations — a client beginning exposure therapy for PTSD, for example, needs to understand that treatment may temporarily increase distress before it brings relief. Clarifying fees and billing practices prevents misunderstandings that can erode the therapeutic alliance; imagine a client who discovers only after several sessions that her insurance does not cover the psychologist's services, leaving her with an unexpected bill of several hundred dollars. Explaining the limits of confidentiality is perhaps the most clinically consequential element — clients must understand before they disclose sensitive information that certain revelations, such as imminent danger to self or others, or suspected child abuse, may compel the psychologist to break confidentiality. Without this foreknowledge, a breach of confidentiality — even a legally mandated one — can feel like a profound betrayal.

Equally important is informing clients about their right to refuse or withdraw from treatment at any time. This element reinforces the voluntary nature of the therapeutic relationship and helps protect against the power differential inherent in the psychologist-client dynamic. Clients should also be told about potential risks and benefits, which requires the psychologist to exercise honest clinical judgment rather than overselling the promise of therapy. Finally, discussing available alternatives — such as group therapy, medication, or different therapeutic modalities — respects the client's autonomy to choose among viable options.

When the client is legally incapable of giving informed consent — for instance, a seven-year-old child referred for behavioral problems, or an adult who has been adjudicated incompetent due to severe cognitive impairment — the psychologist's obligations do not simply disappear. Instead, Standard 10.01 requires a layered approach: the psychologist provides an age-appropriate or capacity-appropriate explanation of what will occur, actively seeks the individual's assent (their agreement to participate, even if it does not carry legal force), considers the person's preferences and best interests, and obtains appropriate permission from a legally authorized person such as a parent, guardian, or court-appointed representative. This approach honors the dignity of individuals who cannot legally consent while still ensuring that someone with legal authority has formally agreed to treatment. For EPPP purposes, remember that assent from the client and consent from the legal guardian are both required — one does not substitute for the other.

section_html:
Therapeutic Index

The therapeutic index (TI) is a critical concept for understanding medication safety. It quantifies the margin between a drug's effective dose and its toxic or lethal dose.

Narrow Therapeutic Index Drugs

Drugs with a narrow TI have a small margin between the therapeutic and toxic dose. These drugs require careful dosing, blood level monitoring, and vigilance for drug interactions.

DrugTherapeutic RangeMonitoring Notes
Lithium0.6-1.2 mEq/LToxicity at >1.5 mEq/L; affected by sodium intake, hydration, renal function, and NSAIDs; requires regular blood level monitoring and renal/thyroid function tests
Carbamazepine4-12 mcg/mLAutoinduction of its own metabolism (levels decrease over first few weeks); requires CBC monitoring due to rare aplastic anemia; potent CYP3A4 inducer
Valproate50-125 mcg/mLHepatotoxicity risk; teratogenic (neural tube defects); monitor liver function and platelet counts
Clozapine350-600 ng/mL (suggested)Risk of agranulocytosis requires mandatory ANC monitoring; also monitor for metabolic syndrome, myocarditis, seizures

Wide Therapeutic Index Drugs

Drugs with a wide TI have a large margin of safety. Routine blood level monitoring is generally not necessary.

  • SSRIs -- wide therapeutic index; difficult to cause lethal overdose with SSRIs alone. This is a major advantage over TCAs and MAOIs, particularly in patients with suicidal ideation.
  • Most benzodiazepines (when taken alone) -- wide TI, but significantly narrowed when combined with other CNS depressants (alcohol, opioids).
EPPP Tip

The EPPP frequently tests the clinical monitoring requirements for narrow therapeutic index drugs, especially lithium. Know the therapeutic range, signs of toxicity, and factors that alter lithium levels (dehydration, NSAIDs, diuretics, sodium restriction). Lithium toxicity presents as coarse tremor, ataxia, slurred speech, confusion, and can progress to seizures, coma, and death.
prev_last_paragraph: Haloperidol is a high-potency antipsychotic (effective at low doses, e.g., 2-10 mg), while chlorpromazine is a low-potency antipsychotic (requires higher doses, e.g., 200-800 mg). However, at their respective optimal doses, both achieve similar efficacy in treating psychotic symptoms. The key difference lies in their side effect profiles: high-potency agents cause more EPS; low-potency agents cause more sedation, orthostatic hypotension, and anticholinergic effects. This means that when a clinician chooses between these medications, the decision is not about which one "works better" for psychosis — they are comparably efficacious — but rather about which side effect profile is more acceptable for the individual patient.
rewritten_html:
Therapeutic Index

Having explored how drugs produce their effects — through receptor binding, dose-response relationships, and potency — we now turn to a concept that bridges pharmacodynamics and patient safety: how close is the dose that helps a patient to the dose that could harm or even kill them? Consider this scenario: a psychiatrist prescribes lithium for a patient with bipolar I disorder. The medication works beautifully at a blood level of 1.0 mEq/L, stabilizing the patient's mood for the first time in years. But if that same patient becomes dehydrated during a summer heat wave, or starts taking ibuprofen for a sore knee, their lithium level could climb to 1.8 mEq/L — suddenly entering dangerous territory with tremors, confusion, and the risk of seizures. The difference between healing and harm was razor-thin. This is exactly the kind of clinical reality that the therapeutic index helps us understand and anticipate.

The therapeutic index (TI) is a quantitative measure of a drug's safety margin — the ratio between the dose (or blood level) that produces toxic effects and the dose that produces therapeutic effects. A drug with a high therapeutic index has a wide cushion between what helps and what harms, while a drug with a low (narrow) therapeutic index demands precision, vigilance, and regular monitoring. For psychologists, understanding the therapeutic index is essential not only for EPPP preparation but for real-world consultation — it shapes which medications require blood draws, which drug combinations become dangerous, and why certain prescribing decisions carry more inherent risk than others.

Narrow Therapeutic Index Drugs

Some of the most important medications in psychiatry are also among the most dangerous to prescribe carelessly. Drugs with a narrow therapeutic index have a small margin between the blood concentration that produces benefit and the concentration that produces toxicity. Think of it like driving on a mountain road with no guardrails — there's very little room for error before you go over the edge. These medications require meticulous dosing, regular blood level monitoring, and constant vigilance for drug interactions or physiological changes that could shift the balance from therapeutic to toxic.

For psychologists, understanding which medications carry narrow therapeutic indices is clinically essential. When a patient on lithium reports increased thirst, tremor, or gastrointestinal distress, recognizing these as potential early signs of toxicity — rather than dismissing them as benign complaints — could be lifesaving. Similarly, knowing that a patient's new NSAID prescription or crash diet could elevate their lithium level transforms the psychologist from a passive observer into an active safety partner in the treatment team. The table below summarizes the key narrow-TI medications you'll encounter in psychiatric practice and on the EPPP.

DrugTherapeutic RangeMonitoring Notes
Lithium0.6-1.2 mEq/LToxicity at >1.5 mEq/L; affected by sodium intake, hydration, renal function, and NSAIDs; requires regular blood level monitoring and renal/thyroid function tests
Carbamazepine4-12 mcg/mLAutoinduction of its own metabolism (levels decrease over first few weeks); requires CBC monitoring due to rare aplastic anemia; potent CYP3A4 inducer
Valproate50-125 mcg/mLHepatotoxicity risk; teratogenic (neural tube defects); monitor liver function and platelet counts
Clozapine350-600 ng/mL (suggested)Risk of agranulocytosis requires mandatory ANC monitoring; also monitor for metabolic syndrome, myocarditis, seizures

Notice a pattern in the table: every narrow-TI drug comes with a specific monitoring protocol. Lithium demands regular serum level checks along with renal and thyroid function tests, because lithium is cleared by the kidneys and can suppress thyroid function over time. Carbamazepine presents a unique pharmacokinetic challenge called autoinduction — it accelerates its own metabolism over the first several weeks, meaning blood levels can drop even though the patient's dose hasn't changed, requiring dose adjustments and repeated monitoring. Valproate requires liver function and platelet monitoring because of hepatotoxicity and thrombocytopenia risk, and it is a potent teratogen — a critical consideration for women of childbearing age. Clozapine, the gold-standard treatment for refractory schizophrenia, carries the rare but potentially fatal risk of agranulocytosis, which is why patients must be enrolled in a mandatory monitoring program (the REMS program in the United States) with regular absolute neutrophil count (ANC) blood draws.

Wide Therapeutic Index Drugs

In contrast, some medications offer a generous safety margin — you would have to take many times the therapeutic dose before approaching truly dangerous territory. These wide-TI drugs represent a significant clinical advantage, particularly when treating patients who may be at risk for intentional or accidental overdose. Routine blood level monitoring is generally unnecessary for these medications, which reduces both the burden on patients and the cost of treatment.

  • SSRIs -- wide therapeutic index; difficult to cause lethal overdose with SSRIs alone. This is a major advantage over TCAs and MAOIs, particularly in patients with suicidal ideation.
  • Most benzodiazepines (when taken alone) -- wide TI, but significantly narrowed when combined with other CNS depressants (alcohol, opioids).

The clinical significance of this distinction cannot be overstated. Consider a depressed patient who expresses passive suicidal ideation. A prescriber choosing between a tricyclic antidepressant (TCA) like amitriptyline and an SSRI like sertraline faces a critical safety calculation: a two-week supply of a TCA can be lethal in overdose, while even a large overdose of an SSRI alone rarely causes death. This is one of the primary reasons SSRIs became first-line treatments for depression — not because they are necessarily more effective than older antidepressants, but because they are dramatically safer. Likewise, the wide-TI characterization of benzodiazepines comes with an enormous asterisk: when combined with other CNS depressants such as alcohol or opioids, benzodiazepines become far more dangerous, as the respiratory depression effects compound synergistically. This interaction has driven much of the current clinical concern about co-prescribing benzodiazepines and opioids, a topic we'll revisit in the next section on drug-drug interactions.

EPPP Tip

The EPPP frequently tests the clinical monitoring requirements for narrow therapeutic index drugs, especially lithium. Know the therapeutic range, signs of toxicity, and factors that alter lithium levels (dehydration, NSAIDs, diuretics, sodium restriction). Lithium toxicity presents as coarse tremor, ataxia, slurred speech, confusion, and can progress to seizures, coma, and death.

section_html:
Drug-Drug Interactions

Drug-drug interactions are a major clinical concern and a frequently tested EPPP topic. Interactions can be classified into two broad categories:

Pharmacokinetic Interactions

These interactions alter the ADME of one drug by another, changing the drug's plasma concentration:

  • CYP450 inhibition -- one drug inhibits the metabolism of another, causing the second drug to accumulate (increased levels, greater risk of toxicity). Example: fluvoxamine (CYP1A2 inhibitor) dramatically increases clozapine levels (CYP1A2 substrate), potentially causing toxicity.
  • CYP450 induction -- one drug induces (increases the expression of) CYP450 enzymes, causing a second drug to be metabolized faster (decreased levels, reduced efficacy). Example: carbamazepine (CYP3A4 inducer) reduces the effectiveness of oral contraceptives (CYP3A4 substrate).
  • Protein binding displacement -- one highly protein-bound drug displaces another from plasma proteins, transiently increasing the free fraction of the displaced drug.
  • Altered renal excretion -- drugs that affect renal function or urinary pH can alter the excretion rate of other drugs. Example: thiazide diuretics reduce lithium clearance, increasing lithium levels and toxicity risk.

Pharmacodynamic Interactions

These interactions occur when drugs act on the same or related receptor systems, altering the overall pharmacological effect without changing drug concentrations:

  • Additive effects -- the combined effect equals the sum of each drug's individual effect (1 + 1 = 2). Example: combining two CNS depressants (e.g., a benzodiazepine and alcohol) produces additive sedation.
  • Synergistic effects -- the combined effect is greater than the sum of individual effects (1 + 1 = 3). Example: combining an SSRI with an MAOI can produce synergistic serotonergic effects, potentially causing life-threatening serotonin syndrome.
  • Antagonistic effects -- one drug reduces or blocks the effect of another (1 + 1 = 0.5). Example: a dopamine agonist used for Parkinson's disease may counteract the dopamine-blocking effects of an antipsychotic.
EPPP Tip

Key drug-drug interactions to know: (1) SSRI + MAOI = serotonin syndrome (requires 2-week washout, 5 weeks for fluoxetine); (2) lithium + NSAIDs or diuretics = lithium toxicity; (3) carbamazepine + oral contraceptives = contraceptive failure; (4) fluvoxamine + clozapine = clozapine toxicity; (5) benzodiazepines + alcohol/opioids = respiratory depression. Psychologists must understand these interactions even though they typically do not prescribe, because they assess patient presentation and coordinate with prescribers.

Know the therapeutic range, signs of toxicity, and factors that alter lithium levels (dehydration, NSAIDs, diuretics, sodium restriction). Lithium toxicity presents as coarse tremor, ataxia, slurred speech, confusion, and can progress to seizures, coma, and death.
rewritten_html:
Drug-Drug Interactions

In the previous section, we examined the therapeutic index — the narrow window between a drug's effective dose and its toxic dose. But here's a critical clinical reality: that window can shift dramatically when a patient is taking more than one medication. A drug that sits safely within its therapeutic range in isolation can suddenly become dangerous — or ineffective — when another substance enters the picture. This is the domain of drug-drug interactions, and in a world where polypharmacy is the norm rather than the exception, understanding these interactions is essential for patient safety.

Consider a patient with treatment-resistant schizophrenia who is stable on clozapine. Her psychiatrist adds fluvoxamine to address co-occurring OCD symptoms. Within days, she becomes increasingly sedated, her white blood cell count drops, and she develops a dangling gait. What happened? Fluvoxamine powerfully inhibited the liver enzyme responsible for metabolizing clozapine, causing clozapine to accumulate to toxic levels. No one changed her clozapine dose — yet her body was suddenly exposed to far more of the drug than intended. Scenarios like these illustrate why drug-drug interactions are among the most frequently tested pharmacological topics on the EPPP, and why psychologists — even those who do not prescribe — must be able to recognize when a patient's symptoms may stem from a medication interaction rather than a worsening of their psychiatric condition.

Drug-drug interactions can be classified into two broad categories: those that change how much drug is available in the body (pharmacokinetic interactions) and those that change what the drug does once it gets there (pharmacodynamic interactions). Let's explore each in turn.

Pharmacokinetic Interactions

Recall from our earlier discussion that pharmacokinetics describes the journey a drug takes through the body — absorption, distribution, metabolism, and excretion (ADME). Pharmacokinetic interactions occur when one drug alters any phase of that journey for another drug, effectively changing its plasma concentration. The patient may be taking the same dose, but the amount of active drug circulating in the bloodstream is now higher or lower than expected. These interactions are particularly insidious because they can mimic toxicity or treatment failure without any change in the prescribed regimen.

  • CYP450 inhibition -- one drug inhibits the metabolism of another, causing the second drug to accumulate (increased levels, greater risk of toxicity). The clozapine scenario described above is a classic example: fluvoxamine (a potent CYP1A2 inhibitor) dramatically increases clozapine levels (a CYP1A2 substrate), potentially causing dangerous toxicity. Think of inhibition as one drug clogging the metabolic drain — the second drug has nowhere to go and builds up.
  • CYP450 induction -- one drug induces (increases the expression of) CYP450 enzymes, causing a second drug to be metabolized faster (decreased levels, reduced efficacy). Example: carbamazepine (a CYP3A4 inducer) ramps up the enzymatic machinery that breaks down oral contraceptives (CYP3A4 substrates), reducing their effectiveness and potentially leading to unintended pregnancy. If inhibition clogs the drain, induction opens it wider — the second drug washes out before it can do its job.
  • Protein binding displacement -- many drugs travel through the bloodstream bound to plasma proteins like albumin, and only the unbound (free) fraction is pharmacologically active. When one highly protein-bound drug displaces another from these binding sites, the free fraction of the displaced drug transiently spikes. Though the body typically compensates quickly through increased metabolism and excretion, this temporary surge can be clinically significant for narrow therapeutic index drugs like warfarin.
  • Altered renal excretion -- drugs that affect kidney function or urinary pH can change how quickly other drugs are cleared from the body. This is the mechanism behind one of the most high-yield interactions for the EPPP: thiazide diuretics reduce lithium clearance because the kidneys handle lithium and sodium similarly — when sodium reabsorption increases (as with thiazides), lithium reabsorption increases in parallel, causing lithium levels to rise and increasing the risk of the toxicity signs we discussed in the previous section.

Pharmacodynamic Interactions

While pharmacokinetic interactions change how much drug reaches its target, pharmacodynamic interactions change what happens when two drugs act on the same or related receptor systems simultaneously. The drug concentrations themselves remain unchanged — it is the biological effect that is amplified, diminished, or qualitatively altered. These interactions are often more predictable if you understand each drug's mechanism of action, which is precisely why the EPPP expects you to connect pharmacological mechanisms to clinical outcomes.

  • Additive effects -- the combined effect equals the sum of each drug's individual effect (1 + 1 = 2). Imagine a patient who takes a prescribed benzodiazepine for anxiety and then drinks several glasses of wine. Both substances enhance GABAergic inhibition through slightly different mechanisms, and the resulting sedation is the straightforward sum of both contributions — sometimes enough to dangerously suppress consciousness and respiration.
  • Synergistic effects -- the combined effect is greater than the sum of individual effects (1 + 1 = 3). The most dangerous example in psychopharmacology is the combination of an SSRI with an MAOI. Each drug increases serotonin through a different mechanism — SSRIs block reuptake while MAOIs prevent breakdown — but together they flood the synapse with serotonin far beyond what either drug alone could produce. The result can be life-threatening serotonin syndrome, characterized by hyperthermia, muscle rigidity, autonomic instability, and altered mental status.
  • Antagonistic effects -- one drug reduces or blocks the effect of another (1 + 1 = 0.5). Consider a patient with both Parkinson's disease and psychosis. The dopamine agonist prescribed for Parkinson's directly opposes the dopamine-blocking antipsychotic — each drug undermines the other. This clinical dilemma is a real-world illustration of antagonistic pharmacodynamic interactions, and it explains why atypical antipsychotics with more selective receptor profiles (like quetiapine or clozapine) are often preferred in this population.
EPPP Tip

Key drug-drug interactions to know: (1) SSRI + MAOI = serotonin syndrome (requires 2-week washout, 5 weeks for fluoxetine due to its long half-life active metabolite); (2) lithium + NSAIDs or diuretics = lithium toxicity; (3) carbamazepine + oral contraceptives = contraceptive failure; (4) fluvoxamine + clozapine = clozapine toxicity; (5) benzodiazepines + alcohol/opioids = respiratory depression. Psychologists must understand these interactions even though they typically do not prescribe, because they assess patient presentation and coordinate with prescribers. On the exam, if a patient's symptoms suddenly worsen or new symptoms emerge after a medication is added, always consider a drug-drug interaction as the explanation before assuming the psychiatric condition itself has changed.

section_html:
Standard 4.01: Maintaining Confidentiality

Psychologists have a primary obligation to take reasonable precautions to protect confidential information obtained through or stored in any medium. This includes:

  • Information obtained in clinical practice, research, teaching, and consultation
  • Data stored electronically, on paper, or in any other format
  • Information shared orally in sessions, consultations, or supervisory contexts

The duty extends beyond active professional relationships. Psychologists must protect confidential information even after the professional relationship has ended and after the client has died (in most jurisdictions).
prev_heading_text: Overview of Standard 4: Privacy and Confidentiality
prev_last_paragraph: Privacy is the right of individuals to control access to information about themselves. Confidentiality is the ethical obligation of the psychologist not to disclose information obtained in a professional relationship. Privilege (or testimonial privilege) is a legal right that protects clients from having their confidential communications disclosed in legal proceedings without their consent. Privilege belongs to the client, not the psychologist.
next_heading_text: Standard 4.02: Discussing the Limits of Confidentiality
rewritten_html:
Standard 4.01: Maintaining Confidentiality

Consider the following scenario: A psychologist finishes a long day of therapy sessions and stops at a coffee shop, where she runs into a colleague. Over lattes, they begin chatting about a particularly challenging case — a well-known local business owner struggling with substance use. The psychologist doesn't mention the client by name, but she shares enough details that the colleague, who also works in the community, quickly figures out who the client is. No form was signed, no legal subpoena was issued — yet a fundamental ethical boundary has just been crossed. This everyday moment illustrates why Standard 4.01 exists and why it demands more than good intentions. It demands reasonable precautions, active vigilance, and a deeply internalized commitment to safeguarding the information clients entrust to us.

In the preceding section, we distinguished among three foundational concepts: privacy as an individual's right to control personal information, confidentiality as the psychologist's ethical duty not to disclose that information, and privilege as the legal protection against compelled disclosure in court. Standard 4.01 takes the concept of confidentiality and operationalizes it — spelling out exactly what psychologists must do to honor this obligation across every context in which they work. It is, in many respects, the backbone of the entire Standard 4 framework.

Psychologists have a primary obligation to take reasonable precautions to protect confidential information obtained through or stored in any medium. The phrase "reasonable precautions" is deliberately broad, because the threats to confidentiality shift with context, technology, and setting. What counts as reasonable in a solo private practice looks quite different from what is reasonable in a multidisciplinary hospital unit or a university-based research lab. Regardless of setting, the obligation encompasses the following domains:

  • Information obtained in clinical practice, research, teaching, and consultation
  • Data stored electronically, on paper, or in any other format
  • Information shared orally in sessions, consultations, or supervisory contexts

Notice how expansive this list is. A graduate student's therapy role-play recording used in a practicum class, a dataset of anonymized survey responses stored on a cloud server, a voicemail left by a distressed client on a psychologist's office phone — all of these fall under the protective umbrella of Standard 4.01. The standard does not limit its scope to what happens behind a closed therapy door; it follows confidential information wherever it travels and however it is stored.

The duty extends beyond active professional relationships. Psychologists must protect confidential information even after the professional relationship has ended and after the client has died (in most jurisdictions). This is a point that catches many trainees off guard. Imagine a psychologist who retires and donates old filing cabinets to a thrift store without first shredding their contents, or a researcher who leaves a university position and abandons a hard drive containing participant data in a shared office. In both cases, the professional relationship is long over — but the ethical obligation to protect that information is very much alive. Even the death of a client does not automatically extinguish confidentiality; in most jurisdictions, the duty persists, and disclosure typically requires consent from a legally authorized representative of the deceased client's estate.

For the EPPP, remember that Standard 4.01 sets the broadest possible stage: it applies to all information, in all formats, across all professional roles, and it endures beyond the termination of the relationship and, in most cases, beyond the client's death. The sections that follow — beginning with Standard 4.02 on discussing the limits of confidentiality — build on this foundation by addressing the specific circumstances under which this bedrock obligation may be qualified or overridden.

section_html:
Confidentiality in Group Therapy

In group therapy, the psychologist cannot guarantee that other group members will maintain confidentiality. The ethical obligation is to:

  • Discuss the importance of confidentiality with all group members at the outset
  • Establish group rules regarding confidentiality
  • Inform members that the psychologist cannot guarantee that other group members will not disclose information
  • Address breaches of confidentiality if they occur within the group
prev_last_paragraph: Working with minors presents unique confidentiality challenges because the legal right to consent (and access information) typically belongs to the parent or legal guardian, while the therapeutic relationship depends on the minor's trust.
rewritten_html:
Confidentiality in Group Therapy

We have just explored the delicate balance of confidentiality when working with minors — a context in which the therapist must navigate between parental rights and the therapeutic alliance with a young client. Group therapy introduces a different but equally challenging confidentiality dilemma: the therapist is no longer the only other person in the room who hears what the client shares. Imagine a substance abuse recovery group in which one member, in a moment of vulnerability, discloses a relapse. The therapist is bound by ethical and legal obligations to protect that information — but the eight other group members sitting in that circle are not. Any one of them could mention it to a mutual acquaintance, post about it on social media, or inadvertently reference it in a conversation. This fundamental reality — that the psychologist cannot control the behavior of other group participants — makes confidentiality in group therapy one of the most frequently tested ethical concepts on the EPPP.

Unlike individual therapy, where the therapist holds near-complete control over disclosure, group therapy inherently involves multiple parties who are not bound by the same professional ethical codes or legal statutes that govern the psychologist. A therapist who conducts couples therapy, family therapy, or any group modality faces the uncomfortable truth that confidentiality protections weaken the moment more non-professionals are present. The ethical obligation, therefore, shifts from guaranteeing confidentiality to managing expectations and minimizing risk. The psychologist's responsibility is not to promise what cannot be delivered but to take every reasonable step to create a culture of discretion within the group.

Specifically, the psychologist's ethical obligations regarding confidentiality in group settings include the following key actions:

  • Discuss the importance of confidentiality with all group members at the outset
  • Establish group rules regarding confidentiality
  • Inform members that the psychologist cannot guarantee that other group members will not disclose information
  • Address breaches of confidentiality if they occur within the group

Consider how this plays out in practice. A psychologist leading an anxiety management group at a university counseling center begins the first session by explaining that everything shared within the group should remain within the group — and then adds, clearly and without hedging, that while the therapist is ethically and legally bound to protect their disclosures, other group members are not held to the same standard. This honest framing serves a dual purpose: it respects participants' autonomy by allowing them to make informed decisions about what they share, and it protects the therapist from liability should a breach occur. Group members might then collaboratively develop a confidentiality agreement — a shared commitment that, while not legally enforceable, sets a clear behavioral norm.

What happens when a breach does occur? Suppose a member of a grief support group learns that another member mentioned her late husband's cause of death to a coworker. The psychologist has an obligation to address this breach within the group — not punitively, but therapeutically. This might involve revisiting the group's confidentiality norms, processing the feelings of betrayal and vulnerability the breach has caused, and reinforcing the expectation that disclosures stay within the room. In some cases, a breach may be so damaging that it disrupts the therapeutic environment entirely, requiring the psychologist to make clinical judgments about the group's continued viability or composition.

The critical takeaway for the EPPP is this: the psychologist's duty is to inform, educate, and establish norms around confidentiality in group settings — but the psychologist cannot guarantee the behavior of non-professionals. This distinction between the therapist's obligation (which is robust) and the therapist's power (which is limited) is a nuance that exam questions frequently probe. Understanding this distinction will help you navigate not only test items but also the real-world complexities of running effective and ethically sound group treatments.

section_html:
Overview of Professional Issues

This chapter covers the legal, regulatory, and professional practice issues that define the practice of psychology. Topics include malpractice liability, supervision models, licensure and credentialing, prescriptive authority, telepsychology, and forensic psychology. These areas are tested on the EPPP because they define the boundaries and responsibilities of professional practice.
rewritten_html:
Overview of Professional Issues

Imagine you are a newly licensed psychologist who receives a frantic voicemail from a former client's attorney — a malpractice liability claim has been filed against you. Your heart races. You wonder: Did I document that risk assessment thoroughly enough? Was my informed consent process adequate? Did I consult with a colleague when the case became complicated? In that moment, every professional practice guideline you ever studied suddenly matters in the most personal way possible. The legal, regulatory, and ethical frameworks that govern psychology are not abstract rules — they are the very structures that protect both clients and practitioners when things go wrong.

This chapter explores the professional practice issues that define the boundaries, responsibilities, and evolving landscape of psychological practice. From the moment you sit for your licensure exam to the day you supervise your own trainees, these topics will shape virtually every clinical decision you make. We will examine how malpractice law creates accountability, how supervision models ensure competent training, how licensure and credentialing systems safeguard the public, and how emerging areas like prescriptive authority and telepsychology are reshaping what it means to be a psychologist in the twenty-first century. Forensic psychology — where clinical expertise meets the courtroom — rounds out the chapter with its own unique demands on professional judgment.

These topics appear on the EPPP not merely because they are important to know, but because they reflect the day-to-day reality of professional practice. A psychologist who understands dual relationships only in the abstract may not recognize one unfolding in their own caseload. A clinician unfamiliar with the legal standard for malpractice may fail to take the very steps that would have prevented a lawsuit. Throughout this chapter, we will ground each concept in realistic clinical scenarios so that these principles become part of your professional instinct — not just material to memorize, but wisdom to practice by. Let us begin where the stakes are highest: understanding when professional conduct crosses the line into liability.

section_html:
Mandated Reporting

Psychologists are mandated reporters in all 50 states for suspected child abuse and neglect. Key points:

  • Reporting is based on reasonable suspicion, not certainty. Psychologists do not need to conduct an investigation before reporting.
  • Most states extend mandated reporting to elder abuse and abuse of dependent adults.
  • Failure to report when mandated can result in criminal penalties, civil liability, and ethics violations.
  • Good-faith reports are typically protected by immunity statutes that shield reporters from liability even if the report proves unfounded.
  • Mandated reporting obligations override both confidentiality and privilege.
prev_last_paragraph: In group therapy, the psychologist cannot guarantee that other group members will maintain confidentiality. The ethical obligation is to:
rewritten_html:
Mandated Reporting

Having explored the unique confidentiality challenges in group therapy — where the therapist cannot guarantee that fellow members will protect each other's disclosures — we now turn to a situation where the psychologist is not merely permitted but legally compelled to break confidentiality. Imagine this scenario: during an individual session, a parent casually mentions disciplining their six-year-old by holding the child's hand over a hot stove burner. The child, the parent explains, "needs to learn consequences." Your stomach drops. You know this conversation has just triggered a legal obligation that supersedes everything else in the therapeutic relationship — your duty as a mandated reporters to file a report with child protective services.

In all 50 U.S. states, psychologists are legally designated as mandated reporters for suspected child abuse and neglect. This is not a discretionary ethical guideline — it is a legal requirement backed by statute. The threshold for reporting is critically important and often misunderstood by early-career clinicians: reporting is based on reasonable suspicion, not certainty. You do not need to verify the abuse, gather corroborating evidence, or conduct any kind of independent investigation before making a report. In fact, attempting to investigate on your own can delay the report and may itself constitute a violation. If the information you have would lead a reasonable person to suspect that abuse or neglect has occurred, your obligation is triggered immediately.

Most states extend these mandated reporting requirements beyond children to include elder abuse and abuse of dependent adults — individuals who, because of age, disability, or other vulnerabilities, may be unable to protect themselves. A psychologist treating an elderly patient who arrives with unexplained bruises and expresses fear of a caregiver faces the same legal imperative as one who suspects a child is being harmed. The specific definitions and procedures vary by jurisdiction, which is why familiarity with your state's reporting statutes is not optional — it is a core professional competency.

The consequences of failing to report when mandated are severe and multifaceted. A psychologist who does not file a required report may face criminal penalties (including fines and, in some jurisdictions, misdemeanor charges), civil liability if the victim suffers additional harm that a timely report might have prevented, and formal ethics complaints that can jeopardize licensure. Consider the weight of that combination: a single failure to act can simultaneously expose you to prosecution, a lawsuit, and the loss of your professional standing.

To encourage compliance and protect those who report in good faith, most states have enacted immunity statutes that shield mandated reporters from civil or criminal liability even if the report ultimately proves unfounded. This legal protection exists precisely because the system depends on reporters acting on suspicion rather than certainty — and the cost of a false report is deemed far less harmful than the cost of an unreported case of abuse. As long as the report is made in good faith and based on reasonable suspicion, the reporter is protected.

Perhaps the most important principle for exam preparation — and for clinical practice — is this: mandated reporting obligations override both confidentiality and privilege. No therapeutic relationship, no matter how clinically sensitive or legally protected, can shield a psychologist from the duty to report suspected abuse. When a client discloses information that triggers a mandated report, the psychologist must act, even if doing so disrupts the therapeutic alliance. This is one of the clearest examples in professional psychology of a situation where the law draws a bright line that the clinician cannot negotiate around, and it underscores why informed consent at the outset of treatment should always include a clear explanation of the limits of confidentiality — including mandated reporting obligations.

section_html:
Standard 4.05: Disclosures

Psychologists may disclose confidential information with the appropriate consent of the client or as mandated or permitted by law for valid purposes including:

  • Providing professional services to the client
  • Obtaining professional consultations
  • Protecting the client, psychologist, or others from harm
  • Obtaining payment for services

When a client has died, questions often arise about who may authorize the release of confidential records. Under most legal frameworks, the authority to consent to disclosure of a deceased person's protected information transfers to the personal representative of the decedent. This individual is typically the executor named in the person's will, the administrator of the estate appointed by a court, or another legally designated representative. Psychologists should verify the legal standing of any individual requesting access to a deceased client's records before releasing information. A family member who is not serving in a formal legal capacity (e.g., an adult child who is not the executor) does not automatically have the right to obtain confidential records, even if the request seems reasonable or well-intentioned. HIPAA similarly recognizes the personal representative of a deceased individual as the party authorized to exercise the decedent's rights with respect to protected health information.

Clinical Note

When a client dies, a spouse or family member may contact you requesting therapy records. Before disclosing any information, request documentation establishing that the person is the legally authorized representative of the estate (e.g., letters testamentary, court appointment as administrator). Absent such documentation, the psychologist should decline the request and direct the individual to obtain proper legal authorization.

Standard 4.06: Consultations

When consulting with colleagues, psychologists do not disclose confidential information that could reasonably lead to the identification of a client unless they have obtained prior consent or the disclosure cannot be avoided. They share only information necessary for the consultation purpose.

rewritten_html:
Standard 4.05: Disclosures

Imagine you are treating a client who has recently expressed suicidal ideation. In the same week, an insurance company calls requesting session notes for reimbursement, a colleague asks you to consult on a similar case, and your client's estranged parent phones demanding to know what their adult child has been discussing in therapy. Each of these situations involves a potential disclosure of confidential information — and each demands a different response. Standard 4.05 provides the ethical framework for navigating exactly these moments, spelling out when disclosure is permissible and under what conditions.

The APA Ethics Code recognizes that confidentiality, while foundational, is not absolute. Psychologists may disclose confidential information when they have obtained the appropriate consent of the client or when disclosure is mandated or permitted by law. Crucially, any such disclosure must serve a valid purpose. Standard 4.05 identifies four recognized categories of permissible disclosure:

  • Providing professional services to the client
  • Obtaining professional consultations
  • Protecting the client, psychologist, or others from harm
  • Obtaining payment for services

Notice the logic behind these categories: each one reflects a situation in which withholding information would actually undermine the client's welfare, the safety of others, or the functioning of the professional relationship itself. A psychologist who refuses to share any diagnostic information with an insurance company, for example, may inadvertently prevent the client from receiving the coverage they need. Likewise, a psychologist who never consults with colleagues out of rigid adherence to confidentiality may miss clinical insights that would improve treatment. The key ethical skill is discerning which disclosures are justified and limiting what is shared to the minimum necessary for the purpose at hand.

One of the most sensitive disclosure questions arises when a client passes away. A grieving spouse calls your office, tearfully asking to read their partner's therapy notes — perhaps hoping to understand struggles the client never shared openly. The request feels deeply human and reasonable. But ethically and legally, the question is not whether the request is sympathetic; it is whether the person making it has the legal authority to access the deceased client's protected information.

Under most legal frameworks, the authority to consent to disclosure of a deceased person's confidential records transfers to the personal representative of the decedent. This individual is typically the executor named in the person's will, the administrator of the estate appointed by a court, or another legally designated representative. Psychologists should verify the legal standing of any individual requesting access to a deceased client's records before releasing information. A family member who is not serving in a formal legal capacity — for example, an adult child who was emotionally close to the client but was not named as executor — does not automatically have the right to obtain confidential records, even if the request seems reasonable or well-intentioned. HIPAA similarly recognizes the personal representative of a deceased individual as the party authorized to exercise the decedent's rights with respect to protected health information. This means that death does not dissolve confidentiality; it simply transfers the authority to authorize disclosure to a legally defined party.

Clinical Note

When a client dies, a spouse or family member may contact you requesting therapy records. Before disclosing any information, request documentation establishing that the person is the legally authorized representative of the estate (e.g., letters testamentary, court appointment as administrator). Absent such documentation, the psychologist should decline the request and direct the individual to obtain proper legal authorization. Responding with empathy while maintaining this boundary is essential — you can acknowledge the person's grief and explain the legal requirements without being dismissive or cold.

Standard 4.06: Consultations

Having just explored the conditions under which psychologists may disclose confidential information, it is important to focus on one of the most common everyday disclosure scenarios: consultation with colleagues. Consultation is a cornerstone of competent practice — it helps psychologists refine diagnostic impressions, navigate ethical dilemmas, and improve treatment planning. But every consultation carries a confidentiality risk, because sharing clinical details with a colleague inherently moves private information beyond the therapy room.

Standard 4.06 addresses this tension directly. When consulting with colleagues, psychologists do not disclose confidential information that could reasonably lead to the identification of a client unless they have obtained prior consent or the disclosure cannot be avoided. Even when some disclosure is necessary, they share only information essential to the consultation purpose — nothing more. Consider a psychologist who wants a colleague's perspective on a complex trauma case. Rather than saying, "My client Maria, the local school principal, described the following incident," the psychologist should strip identifying details: "I'm working with a middle-aged professional in a leadership role who presented with the following symptoms." This practice of de-identification honors the spirit of Standard 4.06 and protects the client while still allowing the consulting psychologist to benefit from peer expertise.

heading_text: The Tarasoff Duty: Duty to Warn and Protect
section_html:
The Tarasoff Duty: Duty to Warn and Protect

The landmark case Tarasoff v. Regents of the University of California established the legal foundation for the duty to protect third parties from client violence.

Tarasoff I (1974) -- Duty to Warn

The California Supreme Court initially ruled that therapists have a duty to warn identifiable potential victims when a client communicates a credible threat of violence.

Tarasoff II (1976) -- Duty to Protect

On rehearing, the court expanded the ruling to establish a broader duty to protect, which may be discharged through various means, not solely by warning the potential victim. Protective actions include:

  • Warning the intended victim directly
  • Notifying law enforcement
  • Hospitalizing the client (voluntary or involuntary)
  • Increasing the frequency of therapy sessions
  • Modifying the treatment plan to reduce risk
  • Other reasonable steps to protect the identified victim
Elements Required for Tarasoff Duty

Most jurisdictions require: (1) a special relationship exists between the therapist and the dangerous individual (i.e., a treatment relationship); (2) the client makes a credible, serious threat of physical violence; and (3) the threat is directed toward an identifiable potential victim.

Variations Across Jurisdictions

Not all states have adopted the Tarasoff ruling. Some states have enacted statutes that impose a duty to warn or protect, while others have rejected it entirely. On the EPPP, the general principle tested is awareness that such a duty exists and knowing the basic elements required to trigger it.

Example

A client tells their therapist, "I'm going to kill my ex-wife when she picks up the kids on Friday." This statement involves a serious threat, an identifiable victim, and an apparent timeline. The therapist has a duty to take protective action, which may include warning the ex-wife, contacting police, and potentially seeking involuntary hospitalization for the client.

prev_last_paragraph: A common EPPP trap: A subpoena alone does NOT require disclosure of confidential records. The psychologist should consult an attorney, notify the client, and may assert privilege on the client's behalf. Only a court order (signed by a judge) compels disclosure. Know this distinction well.

rewritten_html:
The Tarasoff Duty: Duty to Warn and Protect

We've just explored the limits of confidentiality — including the critical distinction between a subpoena and a court order. But there is perhaps no more dramatic exception to confidentiality than the one that arises when a client threatens to harm another person. Imagine this scenario: During a therapy session, a university student calmly describes his plan to kill a woman who has rejected him romantically. He names her. He describes when and how he intends to do it. The therapist, bound by confidentiality, alerts campus police but does not contact the intended victim or her family. Weeks later, the student carries out his plan, and the woman is murdered. This is not a hypothetical — it is essentially what happened in one of the most consequential legal cases in the history of mental health practice.

The landmark case Tarasoff v. Regents of the University of California established the legal foundation for the duty to protect third parties from client violence. It forever changed the way clinicians think about the boundary between therapeutic confidentiality and public safety — and it remains one of the most heavily tested topics on the EPPP. The case unfolded in two stages, each with distinct implications for clinical practice.

Tarasoff I (1974) -- Duty to Warn

In the initial ruling, the family of Tatiana Tarasoff sued the University of California after a therapist at the university's counseling center failed to warn Tatiana that his client, Prosenjit Poddar, had expressed intent to kill her. The California Supreme Court initially ruled that therapists have a duty to warn identifiable potential victims when a client communicates a credible threat of violence. The court's now-famous language captured the principle starkly: the protective privilege of confidentiality ends where the public peril begins. Under this first ruling, the obligation was specific and narrow — the therapist needed to directly warn the person at risk.

Tarasoff II (1976) -- Duty to Protect

Two years later, the same case returned to the California Supreme Court for rehearing, and the justices recognized that a rigid "warn only" standard was both impractical and clinically limiting. On rehearing, the court expanded the ruling to establish a broader duty to protect, which may be discharged through various means, not solely by warning the potential victim. This was a pivotal shift: rather than prescribing a single action, the court acknowledged that clinicians are in the best position to determine which protective steps are appropriate given the circumstances. Protective actions include:

  • Warning the intended victim directly
  • Notifying law enforcement
  • Hospitalizing the client (voluntary or involuntary)
  • Increasing the frequency of therapy sessions
  • Modifying the treatment plan to reduce risk
  • Other reasonable steps to protect the identified victim

Notice the clinical flexibility built into this list. A therapist treating a client who makes a vague but concerning statement might first intensify sessions and adjust the treatment plan, while a therapist confronted with a specific, imminent threat might need to simultaneously call law enforcement and contact the intended victim. The standard is one of reasonableness — what would a prudent mental health professional do under similar circumstances? For the EPPP, remember that Tarasoff II's "duty to protect" is the broader, more current standard, and it superseded the narrower "duty to warn" from Tarasoff I.

Elements Required for Tarasoff Duty

Most jurisdictions require: (1) a special relationship exists between the therapist and the dangerous individual (i.e., a treatment relationship); (2) the client makes a credible, serious threat of physical violence; and (3) the threat is directed toward an identifiable potential victim.

These three elements serve as a practical threshold for clinicians. Without a treatment relationship, there is no special duty. Without a credible threat — as opposed to vague frustration or passing anger — the duty is not triggered. And without an identifiable victim, the clinician has no one specific to protect. Consider a client who says, "Sometimes I just want to hurt everyone." While this warrants clinical attention and thorough risk assessment, it likely does not meet the Tarasoff threshold because there is no identifiable intended victim. Contrast this with a client who says, "I have a gun, and I'm going to shoot my neighbor David when he gets home tonight." Here, all three elements converge: special relationship, credible threat, and identifiable victim.

Variations Across Jurisdictions

One of the most important — and most frequently tested — nuances of the Tarasoff duty is that it does not apply uniformly across the United States. Not all states have adopted the Tarasoff ruling. Some states have enacted statutes that impose a duty to warn or protect, while others have rejected it entirely. Texas, for instance, has historically not recognized a Tarasoff-type duty, while states like California and many others have codified it in statute. Some jurisdictions frame the duty as mandatory (the clinician must take protective action), while others frame it as permissive (the clinician may breach confidentiality to protect a potential victim without fear of liability, but is not required to do so). On the EPPP, the general principle tested is awareness that such a duty exists and knowing the basic elements required to trigger it.

For exam purposes, unless a question specifies a particular state's law, apply the general Tarasoff II framework: when a therapist has a special relationship with a client who makes a credible, serious threat against an identifiable victim, the therapist has a duty to take reasonable steps to protect that person. Also keep in mind that the Tarasoff duty represents a legally mandated exception to confidentiality — it is not something the psychologist chooses to do as a matter of personal judgment, but something the law requires in jurisdictions that have adopted the standard.

Example

A client tells their therapist, "I'm going to kill my ex-wife when she picks up the kids on Friday." This statement involves a serious threat, an identifiable victim, and an apparent timeline. The therapist has a duty to take protective action, which may include warning the ex-wife, contacting police, and potentially seeking involuntary hospitalization for the client.

Before we move on to HIPAA and federal privacy protections, remember this key takeaway: the Tarasoff duty is among the most critical exceptions to confidentiality you will encounter — both on the EPPP and in clinical practice. When in doubt, think through the three elements (special relationship, credible threat, identifiable victim), consider the full range of protective actions available to you, and document your reasoning thoroughly. A clinician who conducts a careful risk assessment and takes reasonable protective steps is far better positioned — ethically, legally, and clinically — than one who either ignores a threat or reflexively breaches confidentiality without adequate justification.

heading_text: Overview of Standard 6: Record Keeping and Fees
section_html:
Overview of Standard 6: Record Keeping and Fees

Standard 6 (Record Keeping and Fees) of the APA Ethics Code covers documentation practices, fee arrangements, bartering, and billing accuracy. These provisions protect both clients and the integrity of the profession by ensuring transparent financial dealings and proper record management.

Standard 6 is tested on the EPPP because fee-related ethical violations can directly exploit clients and damage the therapeutic relationship.
rewritten_html:
Overview of Standard 6: Record Keeping and Fees

Imagine a psychologist who sees a client for two years of intensive therapy, carefully documenting session notes, treatment plans, and progress summaries. When the client later requests records for a new provider, the psychologist realizes that months of documentation are missing, fee agreements were never formalized in writing, and several insurance claims contain diagnostic codes that don't match the actual treatment provided. What began as simple administrative oversight has now created a cascade of ethical, legal, and clinical problems — problems that could harm the client, expose the psychologist to board complaints, and undermine public trust in the profession. Scenarios like this are exactly why the APA devoted an entire standard to the seemingly mundane but critically important topics of record keeping and fees.

Standard 6 (Record Keeping and Fees) of the APA Ethics Code addresses the full landscape of documentation practices, fee arrangements, bartering, and billing accuracy. At first glance, these may seem like administrative details far removed from the therapeutic encounter itself. But consider how deeply financial and documentation practices are woven into the fabric of the professional relationship. A client who doesn't understand the fee structure may feel blindsided by an unexpected bill — and that sense of betrayal can rupture therapeutic trust in an instant. A psychologist who fails to maintain adequate records may be unable to ensure continuity of care, defend clinical decisions in a legal proceeding, or provide the documentation a client needs for disability benefits or custody evaluations. These provisions exist to protect both clients and the integrity of the profession by ensuring transparent financial dealings and proper record management throughout every phase of service delivery.

It is worth noting that fee-related ethical violations are not merely technicalities — they can directly exploit clients and cause real harm to the therapeutic relationship. Consider the inherent power differential in therapy: clients are often vulnerable, may be experiencing financial stress alongside psychological distress, and may feel unable to question or challenge a clinician's billing practices. Standard 6 establishes guardrails that require psychologists to be forthright about costs, honest in their billing, and conscientious in their documentation. These principles apply whether a psychologist is working in private practice, a hospital system, a forensic setting, or a community mental health clinic.

Standard 6 is tested on the EPPP because the board recognizes that ethical competence extends beyond the therapy room and into the business practices that frame psychological services. Examinees should expect questions that test their understanding of when and how to establish fee arrangements, the conditions under which bartering may be ethically permissible, the requirements for maintaining and disposing of records, and the obligations surrounding accurate billing and reporting. As we move through the specific subsections of Standard 6, keep in mind the overarching principle: transparency and honesty in record keeping and financial dealings are not ancillary to good clinical practice — they are fundamental to it.

heading_text: Overview of Standard 8: Research and Publication
section_html:
Overview of Standard 8: Research and Publication

Standard 8 (Research and Publication) of the APA Ethics Code covers ethical requirements for conducting research, including IRB approval, informed consent, use of deception, debriefing, animal research, and publication practices. This standard ensures the protection of research participants and the integrity of scientific knowledge.

Research ethics is heavily tested on the EPPP, with frequent questions about the Belmont Report, deception in research, debriefing requirements, and authorship credit.
rewritten_html:
Overview of Standard 8: Research and Publication

Imagine a graduate student who has just completed a groundbreaking study on the efficacy of a novel intervention for treatment-resistant depression. The results are promising, the data are compelling — but during the write-up, her faculty advisor insists on first authorship despite having contributed only the lab space. Meanwhile, a colleague in the next office is designing a study that involves deceiving participants about the true purpose of the experiment, and he's unsure whether his protocol truly justifies the deception. Down the hall, another researcher realizes she forgot to obtain proper institutional approval before collecting pilot data and wonders whether those data can ever be published. Each of these scenarios touches on a different facet of the same ethical standard — one that governs how psychological science is conducted, reported, and shared with the world.

Standard 8 (Research and Publication) of the APA Ethics Code is the most comprehensive standard in the code, addressing the full lifecycle of scientific inquiry — from the initial design of a study through the treatment of participants to the final publication of findings. It establishes ethical requirements for obtaining Institutional Review Board (IRB) approval, securing meaningful informed consent from research participants, navigating the use of deception, providing thorough debriefing, conducting humane animal research, and upholding integrity in publication and authorship practices. At its core, this standard serves two fundamental purposes: protecting the welfare and dignity of research participants, and preserving the integrity of the scientific knowledge base upon which the entire profession depends.

Why does this matter so profoundly for clinical psychologists — many of whom see themselves primarily as practitioners rather than researchers? Because the science-practitioner model that defines our profession means that every clinician relies on research to guide treatment decisions, and many clinicians contribute to the evidence base through their own scholarly work. When research ethics are compromised — whether through coerced participation, fabricated data, or misattributed authorship — the ripple effects extend far beyond the laboratory. Patients receive treatments based on flawed evidence. Public trust in psychological science erodes. And vulnerable populations, who have historically borne the greatest burden of unethical research practices, face renewed risk of exploitation.

Research ethics is heavily tested on the EPPP, with frequent questions about the Belmont Report and its three core principles (respect for persons, beneficence, and justice), the conditions under which deception in research may be ethically justified, the specific requirements for debriefing participants after a study, and the rules governing authorship credit and publication practices. Understanding these topics requires more than rote memorization — it demands an appreciation for why these protections exist and how they apply in the complex, sometimes ambiguous situations that real researchers face every day. The sections that follow will walk through each of these areas in detail, grounding the ethical principles in clinical and research scenarios that bring them to life.

section_html:
Licensure and Certification

Understanding the distinction between licensure, certification, and credentialing is important for both professional practice and the EPPP.

Key Definitions

TermDefinition
LicensureA state-granted legal authorization to practice psychology. Licensure is mandatory for independent practice and is governed by each state's psychology licensing board. It is a form of statutory law.
CertificationA voluntary credential awarded by a professional organization (not the state) indicating that a psychologist has met specific standards of training and competence in a specialty area. Example: Board certification by ABPP.
CredentialingA general term encompassing both licensure and certification, as well as institutional privileges (e.g., hospital credentialing).
ABPPThe American Board of Professional Psychology offers board certification in specialty areas (clinical, counseling, neuropsychology, forensic, etc.). ABPP certification is voluntary and indicates advanced competence.

Typical Licensure Requirements

  • Doctoral degree in psychology from an accredited program (APA or CPA accredited, or equivalent)
  • Supervised professional experience (typically 1-2 years postdoctoral)
  • Passing score on the EPPP (Examination for Professional Practice in Psychology)
  • Additional state-specific requirements (e.g., jurisprudence exam, oral examination, state-specific written exam)
  • Continuing education for license renewal
EPPP Tip

Licensure is mandatory and state-regulated; certification (e.g., ABPP) is voluntary and organization-based. Licensure laws define the scope of practice; certification indicates specialty competence within that scope. State licensing boards have the authority to discipline licensees, including suspending or revoking licenses.
prev_last_paragraph: A pre-doctoral intern provides therapy to a suicidal client but does not conduct a formal risk assessment or develop a safety plan. The supervisor does not review the case or ask about high-risk clients. If the client attempts suicide, the supervisor could be held liable under both vicarious liability (for the intern's negligence) and direct liability (for inadequate supervision).
rewritten_html:
Licensure and Certification

Imagine you've completed your doctoral degree, finished your internship, accumulated thousands of supervised hours — and a prospective client calls asking for help. Can you see them independently? The answer depends entirely on whether your state has granted you a license to practice. Without it, even the most well-trained psychologist cannot legally offer independent services. As the preceding section on supervision illustrated, the relationship between supervisors and trainees is governed by layers of legal accountability. But what transforms a trainee into an independent practitioner in the first place? That transformation is a legal one, and it hinges on the concepts of licensure, certification, and credentialing — distinctions that carry real consequences for professional practice and that appear frequently on the EPPP.

These terms are sometimes used interchangeably in casual conversation, but they refer to fundamentally different processes with different legal implications. One is a legal requirement enforced by the state; another is a voluntary professional achievement. Confusing them can lead to misunderstandings about what a psychologist is authorized to do — and who has the power to discipline or restrict that authorization. Let's unpack each one carefully.

Key Definitions

TermDefinition
LicensureA state-granted legal authorization to practice psychology. Licensure is mandatory for independent practice and is governed by each state's psychology licensing board. It is a form of statutory law.
CertificationA voluntary credential awarded by a professional organization (not the state) indicating that a psychologist has met specific standards of training and competence in a specialty area. Example: Board certification by ABPP.
CredentialingA general term encompassing both licensure and certification, as well as institutional privileges (e.g., hospital credentialing).
ABPPThe American Board of Professional Psychology offers board certification in specialty areas (clinical, counseling, neuropsychology, forensic, etc.). ABPP certification is voluntary and indicates advanced competence.

Think of it this way: licensure is the gate that allows you into independent practice — no license, no practice. Certification, by contrast, is the badge that signals you've gone above and beyond within a particular specialty. A clinical psychologist might be fully licensed by the state of California and also hold ABPP board certification in clinical neuropsychology. The license gives them the legal right to practice; the ABPP certification tells peers, employers, and the public that they've demonstrated advanced competence in that specialty area. Credentialing is the broadest umbrella term — it covers licensure, certification, and even the institutional review process a hospital might conduct before granting a psychologist admitting privileges.

Typical Licensure Requirements

Although specific requirements vary from state to state, the pathway to licensure follows a broadly consistent trajectory across the United States. Each step is designed to ensure that independently practicing psychologists have the academic foundation, supervised clinical experience, and demonstrated competence necessary to protect the public. The typical requirements include the following:

  • Doctoral degree in psychology from an accredited program (APA or CPA accredited, or equivalent)
  • Supervised professional experience (typically 1-2 years postdoctoral)
  • Passing score on the EPPP (Examination for Professional Practice in Psychology)
  • Additional state-specific requirements (e.g., jurisprudence exam, oral examination, state-specific written exam)
  • Continuing education for license renewal

Notice that licensure is not a one-time achievement — it requires ongoing maintenance through continuing education, ensuring that practitioners stay current with evolving research, ethical standards, and clinical methods. A psychologist who earns a license in one state and later moves to another cannot simply begin practicing in the new jurisdiction; they must meet that state's specific requirements, which may include additional examinations or supervised hours. This state-by-state variation is an important point to remember: because licensure is governed by statutory law at the state level, there is no single national psychology license.

Consider a practical scenario: Dr. Martinez completes her doctorate at an APA-accredited program, finishes two years of postdoctoral supervision, passes the EPPP, and obtains her license in Texas. Five years later, she relocates to New York. Despite her years of experience and her Texas license, she must apply for licensure in New York and satisfy that state's specific requirements — which may include a jurisprudence exam covering New York's mental health laws — before she can see clients independently. This is a direct consequence of licensure being a state-level legal authorization rather than a national credential.

EPPP Tip

Licensure is mandatory and state-regulated; certification (e.g., ABPP) is voluntary and organization-based. Licensure laws define the scope of practice; certification indicates specialty competence within that scope. State licensing boards have the authority to discipline licensees, including suspending or revoking licenses. On exam questions, pay close attention to who has the authority to act: a professional organization like APA can sanction a member or revoke membership, but only a state licensing board can revoke a psychologist's legal right to practice. This distinction between organizational ethics enforcement and state regulatory power is a frequently tested concept.

section_html:
Prescriptive Authority

The question of whether psychologists should have the legal authority to prescribe psychotropic medications has been a major professional issue.

  • Currently, psychologists in a small number of jurisdictions have obtained prescriptive authority (e.g., New Mexico, Louisiana, Illinois, Iowa, Idaho, Colorado, and the U.S. military and Indian Health Service)
  • Prescriptive authority typically requires additional postdoctoral training in psychopharmacology (a master's-level program in clinical psychopharmacology)
  • The APA has adopted a policy supporting the pursuit of prescriptive authority for appropriately trained psychologists
  • Opposition comes primarily from organized medicine (AMA) and some within psychology who argue it changes the profession's identity
  • The Department of Defense's Psychopharmacology Demonstration Project (PDP) demonstrated that appropriately trained psychologists could safely and effectively prescribe medications
prev_last_paragraph: As you'll see in the next section on prescriptive authority, the boundaries of scope of practice are not static — they evolve as the profession advances, as new competencies develop, and as legislatures respond to changing healthcare needs. Understanding scope of practice as a living, jurisdiction-specific framework is essential for ethical and legally sound professional conduct.
rewritten_html:
Prescriptive Authority

As we discussed in the preceding section, scope of practice is not a fixed boundary — it shifts as professions evolve, as competencies expand, and as legislatures respond to real-world healthcare demands. Perhaps no issue illustrates this dynamic quality more dramatically than the ongoing movement to grant psychologists the legal authority to prescribe psychotropic medications. This is one of the most consequential and contested professional developments in modern psychology, and it shows up regularly on the EPPP because it sits at the intersection of ethics, law, training standards, and public health policy.

Consider a clinical psychologist working in a rural community mental health center. The nearest psychiatrist is 90 miles away with a six-month waitlist. The psychologist's patient — a 34-year-old veteran with worsening major depressive disorder — desperately needs a medication adjustment, but access barriers make timely psychiatric consultation nearly impossible. Scenarios like this one have driven the push for prescriptive authority, the legal right for specially trained psychologists to prescribe psychotropic medications. Advocates argue that expanding prescriptive privileges addresses critical gaps in mental healthcare access, particularly in underserved rural and military populations where psychiatrists are scarce.

The road to prescriptive authority began with a landmark initiative: the Department of Defense's Psychopharmacology Demonstration Project (PDP), conducted from 1991 to 1997. In this project, a small cohort of military psychologists received intensive training in psychopharmacology and were subsequently authorized to prescribe medications within military settings. The results were striking — independent evaluations concluded that these psychologists prescribed safely and effectively, with outcomes comparable to those of physician prescribers. The PDP provided the empirical foundation that proponents needed, demonstrating that the question was not whether psychologists could prescribe competently, but whether the profession and legal system would allow it.

Building on the PDP's success, several jurisdictions have since enacted legislation granting psychologists prescriptive authority.
